manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Diffusion of Food Coloring in Hot and Cold WaterI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Diffusion Speed of Food Coloring in Hot vs Cold WaterSubject: Natural Science - PhysicsExperiment Objective: To observe and compare the diffusion speed of food coloring in hot and cold water, and understand the effect of temperature on molecular motion.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo 500mL transparent beakers, hot water at 80℃, cold water at 10℃, red food coloring, dropper, thermometer (optional), stopwatch or camera for recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean 500mL beakers on a stable table. Pour 500mL of hot water (80℃) into one beaker and 500mL of cold water (10℃) into the other.2. Labeling: Clearly mark the beakers as hot water and cold water.3. Core Operation: Using a dropper, add one drop of red food coloring into the center of each beaker at the same time.4. Observation: Do not stir. Observe and record the diffusion process of the food coloring in both beakers until the color becomes evenly distributed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The water in both beakers is colorless and transparent.2. During Diffusion: In the hot water, the red coloring spreads rapidly, forming visible swirling patterns. In the cold water, the coloring spreads slowly and remains concentrated for a longer time.3. Final State: The hot water becomes uniformly red much faster than the cold water.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleDiffusion occurs due to the random motion of water molecules. At higher temperatures, molecules move faster, increasing the diffusion rate. Therefore, food coloring diffuses more quickly in hot water than in cold water.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Temperature affects diffusion speed by changing molecular motion. Minimum assumptions: water is liquid, food coloring is soluble, and higher temperature increases molecular kinetic energy.Phased Storyline: (1) Two beakers with hot and cold water are presented side by side; (2) red food coloring is added simultaneously to both; (3) coloring spreads rapidly in hot water and slowly in cold water; (4) hot water reaches uniform color first. Visibility requirements: clear view of both beakers in the same frame, stable perspective, and visible color gradients to verify diffusion differences.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Low-Friction Cart Collision (Elastic vs Inelastic)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Low-Friction Cart Collision on a Track (Elastic vs Inelastic)2. Subject: Physics – Mechanics3. Experiment Objective: To compare elastic and inelastic collisions by observing the motion of two carts on a low-friction track, and to understand momentum conservation and energy transformation through visual evidence.II. Experimental EquipmentLow-friction straight track; two identical carts; spring bumpers (mounted on both carts for elastic trial); putty pads or clay (mounted on both carts for inelastic trial); end stops or release mechanisms; camera or smartphone with tripod; marked starting positions on the track.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the track on a level surface. Fix the camera on a tripod facing the side of the track and lock focus. Mark identical starting positions at both ends.Trial A – Elastic Collision: Mount springs on the facing ends of both carts. Place each cart at the marked starting positions. Release both carts simultaneously so they roll toward each other. Record the motion.Trial B – Inelastic Collision: Replace springs with putty pads so the carts can stick together. Reset carts to the same marked starting positions. Release simultaneously and record.Completion: Stop recording, remove carts, and clean attachments.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaElastic Collision: Carts approach, springs compress briefly at contact, then carts rebound and separate, moving away from each other.Inelastic Collision: Carts approach, contact via putty pads, stick together, and move as a single combined cart with reduced speed.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIn both trials, total momentum of the two-cart system is approximately conserved due to low external friction. In the elastic collision, kinetic energy is largely conserved, leading to rebound. In the inelastic collision, kinetic energy is partly converted into internal energy (deformation), causing the carts to stick together and move with a common velocity.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: comparison of elastic and inelastic collisions using low-friction carts, assuming negligible external forces and identical cart masses. Minimum assumptions include straight, level track, low friction, simultaneous release, and fixed camera perspective.Expected phased storyline: (1) Two carts start from opposite ends at identical marked positions; (2) carts glide smoothly toward each other; (3a) spring trial: brief compression at contact followed by clear rebound and separation; (3b) putty trial: contact followed by sticking; (4) post-collision motion shows either separation (elastic) or joint motion (inelastic). Camera remains fixed side-on to ensure visibility of approach, contact, and outcome.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Angular Momentum Conservation on a Swivel ChairI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstration of Angular Momentum Conservation Using a Swivel Chair2. Subject: Physics – Mechanics3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the law of conservation of angular momentum by comparing the rotational speed of a person on a freely rotating swivel chair when holding dumbbells with arms pulled in versus extended outward.II. Experimental EquipmentFreely rotating swivel chair (low friction), two identical dumbbells, stopwatch or timer (optional), fixed camera on tripod for time-lapse recording, flat laboratory floor.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the swivel chair on a flat floor, ensure it can rotate freely. Set the camera on a tripod with fixed focus, facing the chair.2. Initial State: The person sits upright on the chair, holding one dumbbell in each hand with arms extended horizontally. Feet are lifted slightly off the floor.3. Start Rotation: An assistant gently spins the chair. After release, no external force is applied.4. Core Operation: While rotating, the person slowly pulls both arms inward toward the chest, keeping dumbbells close to the body.5. Second Operation: After several rotations, the person slowly extends both arms outward again to the original position.6. End: Allow the chair to rotate until it naturally slows down. Stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. With arms extended, the rotation speed is relatively slow.2. When arms are pulled inward, the rotation speed noticeably increases.3. When arms are extended outward again, the rotation speed decreases.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhen no external torque acts on the system, the total angular momentum remains constant. Pulling the arms inward reduces the moment of inertia, so the angular velocity increases. Extending the arms outward increases the moment of inertia, so the angular velocity decreases. This demonstrates the law of conservation of angular momentum (L = Iω = constant).VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the chair rotates freely; keep feet off the floor; move arms smoothly to avoid wobbling; maintain fixed camera focus throughout the recording.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Conservation of angular momentum in a closed rotational system. Minimum assumptions: negligible external torque, freely rotating chair, constant mass distribution except for arm movement.Phased storyline: (1) Initial rotation with arms extended and slower angular speed; (2) causal transition where arms move inward leading to visibly faster rotation; (3) reverse transition where arms extend outward causing rotation to slow. Visibility requirements: full view of chair, arms, and dumbbells; stable camera and consistent framing to verify speed changes over time.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Sharp Metal Needle vs Smooth Metal Sphere Producing Sparks from a Van de GraaffI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Sharp Needle and Smooth Sphere Discharge Comparison Using a Van de Graaff GeneratorSubject: Physics – ElectrostaticsObjective: To compare electric discharge behavior of a sharp conductor and a smooth conductor by observing sparks and corona when facing a running Van de Graaff generator.II. EquipmentVan de Graaff generator (running), sharp metal needle (grounded), smooth metal sphere (grounded), insulating stand, grounding wires, ruler or marked track, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the Van de Graaff generator on an insulating table and start it. Wear safety goggles.2. Setup: Fix a grounded sharp metal needle on the left side facing the generator dome; fix a grounded smooth metal sphere on the right side at the same height. Ensure both are clearly grounded.3. Initial Position: Set both targets at a safe distance (no discharge).4. Core Operation: Slowly move both targets closer to the dome simultaneously. Hold briefly, then move them farther away. Repeat this approach–separation cycle several times.5. Shutdown: Move targets away, turn off the generator, then disconnect grounding wires.IV. Observation of Phenomena1. As distance decreases, the sharp needle shows faint glow or small, frequent discharges (corona), often without loud sparks.2. The smooth sphere shows fewer but brighter, louder sparks when sufficiently close.3. When moved farther away, discharges weaken or stop for both targets.V. Experimental Principle SummaryElectric field strength is greater at sharp points, causing air ionization and corona discharge that leaks charge continuously, preventing large spark buildup. Smooth spheres distribute charge evenly, allowing charge accumulation and sudden breakdown of air, producing bright sparks. Distance controls electric field strength and discharge occurrence.VI. PrecautionsDo not touch metal parts during operation; ensure proper grounding; keep face and hands at a safe distance.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Electrostatic discharge dependence on conductor shape under high voltage, assuming a running Van de Graaff, grounded targets, and air breakdown. Minimum assumptions: left target is a sharp needle, right target is a smooth sphere, both grounded, distance to dome changes.Phased storyline: (1) Generator running with both targets far—no sparks; (2) targets approach—needle shows continuous faint corona while sphere remains mostly quiet; (3) closer approach—sphere emits bright intermittent sparks while needle still lacks large sparks; (4) targets withdraw—discharges cease. Visibility requirements: clear left–right framing, visible distance change, sparks/glow clearly observable near target tips.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Egg Dropped onto Rigid Surface vs Pillow2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics (Mechanics)3. Experiment Objective: To compare the effects of impact force on a raw egg when dropped onto different surfaces, and to understand how stopping time affects force during a collision.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical raw eggs; rigid tabletop; thick pillow; measuring tape or ruler; camera or smartphone with fixed focus; stable stand or tripod; optional split-screen or post-editing software.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the rigid tabletop and thick pillow side by side. Ensure both landing surfaces are level. Set up the camera directly in front, fixing focus and framing both landing areas.2. Height Setting: Measure and mark the same drop height above both surfaces.3. Core Operation: Hold one raw egg above the tabletop (left side) and the other above the pillow (right side). Release both eggs simultaneously from the same height.4. Recording: Capture the entire process using fixed-focus or time-lapse recording without moving the camera.5. Completion: After impact, stop recording and inspect both eggs.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both eggs are intact before being dropped.2. Impact Observation: The egg striking the rigid tabletop stops abruptly and cracks or breaks; the egg striking the pillow slows down over a longer time and remains intact or only slightly cracked.3. Final State: Clear difference in shell damage between the two eggs.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleWhen an object falls, gravity gives it speed. Upon impact, the change in momentum is similar for both eggs, but the stopping time differs. The rigid surface causes a very short stopping time, resulting in a large force that breaks the egg. The pillow increases the stopping time, reducing the average force and protecting the egg. This demonstrates the relationship F = Δp / Δt.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse raw eggs of similar size; ensure simultaneous release; keep camera stable; clean broken egg promptly to avoid slipping hazards.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Impact force depends on stopping time for the same momentum change. Minimum assumptions: identical eggs, same height, gravity-dominated motion, different surface compliance. Phased storyline: (1) Split-screen setup with rigid table left and pillow right; (2) simultaneous release from equal height; (3) synchronized fall under gravity; (4) collision—sudden stop and break on table vs cushioned stop on pillow; (5) final contrast in egg states. Visibility constraints: fixed camera focus, clear view of egg deformation and shell state after impact, no camera movement during drop.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Stream of Water Bending Toward a Charged BalloonI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Stream of Water Bending Toward a Charged Balloon or RodSubject: Physics – ElectrostaticsExperiment Objective: To observe the interaction between a charged object and a neutral water stream, and to understand electrostatic attraction caused by polarization.II. Experimental MaterialsFaucet with running water, sink, balloon (or plastic rod), dry fabric or wool cloth.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Turn on the faucet and adjust it to form a thin, steady, continuous stream of water flowing vertically into the sink.2. Charging the Object: Rub the balloon or plastic rod firmly with a dry fabric for several seconds to give it an electric charge.3. Core Operation: Slowly bring the charged balloon or rod close to the side of the water stream without touching the water.4. Holding Observation: Hold the charged object near the stream for a brief moment and observe the change in the water stream.5. Withdrawal: Gradually move the charged object away from the water stream and continue observing.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The water stream flows straight downward.During Approach: As the charged balloon or rod approaches, the water stream bends toward the charged object.During Holding: While the charged object is held nearby, the water remains bent toward it.After Removal: When the charged object is moved away, the water stream gradually returns to its original vertical path.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleRubbing the balloon or rod transfers electric charge to it. When the charged object is brought near the neutral water stream, the electric field causes charges within the water molecules to rearrange (polarization). The side of the water stream closer to the charged object experiences a stronger attraction, causing the stream to bend toward the charged object. When the charged object is removed, the electric influence disappears and the water stream returns to its original direction.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Electrostatic attraction between a charged object and a neutral water stream via polarization. Minimum assumptions: a visibly charged balloon/rod, a thin continuous water stream, and close side approach without contact. Phased storyline: (1) establish a steady vertical water stream; (2) rub balloon/rod to charge it; (3) approach from the side causing visible bending toward the object; (4) briefly hold to maintain bending; (5) withdraw the object and show the stream straightening. Visibility constraints: the bending direction and recovery must be clearly observable in a single continuous view, with the charged object and water stream simultaneously in frame.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Moving a Bar Magnet In and Out of a Coil Connected to a GalvanometerI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Moving a Bar Magnet In and Out of a Coil Connected to a Galvanometer2. Subject: Physics – Electromagnetism3. Experiment Objective: To observe electromagnetic induction by moving a bar magnet in and out of a copper wire coil and to understand the relationship between magnetic flux change and induced current through galvanometer deflection.II. Experimental EquipmentBar magnet (clearly marked N and S poles), copper wire coil (multiple turns), analog galvanometer (center-zero type), connecting wires, stand or holder (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the coil on a stable surface and connect its two ends to the terminals of the analog galvanometer. Ensure the needle rests at zero.2. Initial Observation: Keep the bar magnet stationary outside the coil and observe the galvanometer needle.3. Core Operation – Insertion: Hold the bar magnet and slowly push one pole into the center of the coil. Observe the galvanometer needle deflection.4. Core Operation – Withdrawal: Pull the bar magnet out of the coil along the same axis and observe the needle deflection again.5. Repeat: Change the speed of motion or reverse the magnet poles and repeat the insertion and withdrawal to compare effects.6. End: Stop moving the magnet and confirm that the galvanometer needle returns to zero.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. When the magnet is stationary outside or inside the coil, the galvanometer needle remains at zero.2. When the magnet is pushed into the coil, the needle deflects to one side.3. When the magnet is pulled out of the coil, the needle deflects to the opposite side.4. Faster motion of the magnet produces a larger needle deflection.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates electromagnetic induction. When the bar magnet moves relative to the coil, the magnetic flux through the coil changes, inducing an electric current. The direction of the induced current depends on whether the magnetic flux is increasing or decreasing, which is shown by opposite deflections of the galvanometer needle. When there is no change in magnetic flux, no current is induced.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Electromagnetic induction, requiring the assumption that changing magnetic flux in a closed circuit induces an electric current detectable by a galvanometer.Mechanistic Assumptions: A visible bar magnet with fixed poles, a stationary copper coil forming a closed circuit, and an analog galvanometer whose needle deflects proportionally to induced current.Phased Storyline: (1) Initial static state: magnet outside coil, needle at zero; (2) Action phase: magnet pushed into coil, causing flux increase and needle deflection; (3) Transition: magnet pulled out, flux decreases and needle deflects oppositely; (4) End state: magnet stops, needle returns to zero. Visibility requires a clear view of the magnet motion and galvanometer needle throughout.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Newton’s Cradle Demonstrating Conservation of Momentum and EnergyI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Newton’s Cradle Demonstrating Conservation of Momentum and Energy2. Subject: Physics – Mechanics3. Experiment Objective: To observe momentum transfer and approximate energy conservation in elastic collisions using a tabletop Newton’s cradle, and to understand how mechanical energy is transferred through identical masses.II. Experimental EquipmentTabletop Newton’s cradle with five identical metal balls suspended by equal-length strings on a rigid frame; stable tabletop or desk; ruler or visual reference (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the Newton’s cradle on a stable, horizontal tabletop. Ensure all five metal balls are aligned in a straight line and just touching at rest.2. Initial State Check: Confirm that all balls are identical in size and mass, strings are untwisted, and the balls are motionless.3. Core Operation: Gently pull the leftmost ball horizontally away from the other four balls to a small height without twisting the string.4. Release: Release the leftmost ball without pushing, allowing it to swing freely and strike the row of balls.5. Repetition: Allow the system to oscillate naturally for several cycles without interference.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial Impact: The released leftmost ball strikes the stationary row of balls.2. Immediate Result: The leftmost ball comes nearly to rest, while the rightmost ball swings outward with approximately the same height as the released ball.3. Repeated Motion: The rightmost ball swings back, strikes the row, and causes the leftmost ball to swing out.4. Energy Loss: After multiple cycles, the height of the swinging balls gradually decreases until the system comes to rest.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Conservation of Momentum: During the short collision, external forces are negligible, so the total momentum of the system is conserved. Momentum is transmitted through the stationary balls.2. Approximate Conservation of Mechanical Energy: Because the collisions are nearly elastic, most kinetic energy is transferred from one ball to another, resulting in similar swing heights.3. Energy Dissipation: Over time, sound, heat, and air resistance cause gradual loss of mechanical energy, leading to reduced oscillation amplitude.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Newton’s cradle demonstrates conservation of momentum and approximate conservation of mechanical energy in nearly elastic collisions among identical masses. Minimum assumptions include identical balls, aligned suspension, negligible external forces during collision, and elastic contact.Expected Phenomena Storyline: (1) Static alignment of five identical metal balls on a tabletop cradle. (2) Leftmost ball is pulled back and released. (3) Impact transfers momentum through the middle balls. (4) Rightmost ball swings out to a similar height. (5) Alternating oscillations continue for multiple cycles with gradually decreasing height. The camera should maintain a clear frontal or slightly angled view so collisions, swing height, and sequence are visibly verifiable.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Sealed Syringe with Air Expanding When Warmed and Contracting When CooledI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Air Expansion and Contraction in a Sealed Syringe2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics3. Experiment Objective: To observe that air expands when heated and contracts when cooled by monitoring the volume change of a sealed syringe placed in hot and ice water.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo transparent beakers; hot water (about 500 mL, 80℃); ice water (about 500 mL, 0℃, with ice present); one 20 mL syringe with the nozzle tightly sealed; thermometer (optional for confirmation); towel or gloves for handling hot beaker.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two beakers side by side on the table. Pour 500 mL of 80℃ hot water into the left beaker and 500 mL of 0℃ ice water into the right beaker. Ensure the syringe is sealed and the plunger can move freely.2. Heating Operation: Slowly place the sealed syringe vertically into the hot water beaker, keeping the syringe fully immersed but not touching the bottom. Observe the position of the syringe plunger.3. Cooling Operation: After observation, remove the syringe and immediately place the same sealed syringe into the ice water beaker. Again observe the position of the syringe plunger.4. Completion: Remove the syringe, wipe off water, and place all equipment back neatly.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before immersion, the syringe plunger stays at its initial scale position.2. In Hot Water: After being placed in 80℃ hot water, the syringe plunger gradually moves outward, indicating an increase in the volume of air inside.3. In Ice Water: When transferred to 0℃ ice water, the syringe plunger gradually moves inward, indicating a decrease in the volume of air inside.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesAir is a gas whose volume changes with temperature. When the sealed syringe is heated in hot water, the air molecules move faster and occupy more space, causing the plunger to move outward (thermal expansion). When the syringe is cooled in ice water, air molecules move more slowly and occupy less space, causing the plunger to move inward (thermal contraction). This demonstrates the principle that gases expand when warmed and contract when cooled.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the syringe is well sealed; air leakage will affect results.2. Handle hot water carefully to avoid burns.3. Observe the plunger position from the side to reduce reading errors.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Gas thermal expansion and contraction under temperature change, assuming a sealed container with movable boundary (syringe plunger) and constant external pressure from water.Minimum mechanistic assumptions: The syringe contains air only, is airtight, and the plunger can slide smoothly; temperature change of surrounding water transfers heat to the air.Phased storyline for video evaluation:Phase 1 (Setup): Two beakers appear side by side, clearly distinguished as hot (left) and ice (right), with a sealed 20 mL syringe visible.Phase 2 (Heating): Syringe is placed into hot water; after a brief moment, the plunger visibly moves outward.Phase 3 (Cooling): The same syringe is moved into ice water; the plunger then visibly moves inward.Key causal transitions: Immersion in hot water leads to air expansion → plunger moves out; immersion in ice water leads to air contraction → plunger moves in.Visibility constraints: Camera should clearly show plunger scale and its direction of movement; left–right positioning of beakers must remain consistent for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Motion of a Simple Pendulum (Rigid String)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Motion of a Simple Pendulum under Gravity2. Subject: Physics – Mechanics (Natural Science)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the periodic motion of a simple pendulum bob constrained by a rigid string, and to relate the observed motion to gravitational restoring force and pendulum principles using time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentMetal pendulum bob (spherical, solid), rigid and inextensible string, ceiling-mounted fixed pivot or support frame, stable support stand (if ceiling is unavailable), camera or smartphone with tripod, time-lapse or fixed-focus recording function, marker or tape for reference position.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Securely fix one end of the rigid string to the ceiling pivot. Attach the metal pendulum bob to the other end, ensuring the string is taut and the bob hangs freely without touching surrounding objects. Place a visible reference marker directly below the equilibrium position.2. Camera Setup: Mount the camera on a tripod facing the plane of motion. Fix the focus and exposure to avoid refocusing during motion. Ensure the entire swing path of the bob is within the frame.3. Initial Displacement: Using a hand, gently pull the pendulum bob sideways to a small angle (less than about 15° from the vertical) without twisting the string.4. Release: Release the bob smoothly without pushing, allowing it to move freely under gravity.5. Recording: Start time-lapse or continuous recording immediately after release, capturing several oscillations.6. Completion: Stop recording after clear repeated oscillations are captured. Allow the pendulum to come to rest naturally.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The pendulum bob is displaced from its equilibrium position and momentarily at rest.2. Motion after Release: The bob swings downward, accelerates toward the lowest point, then decelerates as it rises to the opposite side.3. Repeated Motion: The bob continues to swing back and forth along the same arc with gradually decreasing amplitude due to air resistance and friction.4. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Rotating a Wire Loop Between Magnet Poles (Changing Magnetic Flux)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Rotating a Wire Loop Between Magnet Poles (Changing Magnetic Flux)2. Subject: Physics - Electromagnetism3. Experiment Objective: To observe electromagnetic induction by rotating a rectangular wire loop steadily between the north and south poles of a fixed horseshoe magnet, and to understand the relationship between changing magnetic flux and induced current through the deflection of an analog galvanometer.II. Experimental EquipmentRectangular wire loop (mounted on a rotating axle or handle), fixed horseshoe magnet (clearly marked N and S poles), connecting wires, analog galvanometer (center-zero type preferred), support stand or base, stable light source, camera mounted on tripod with fixed focus (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the horseshoe magnet firmly on the table or stand, ensuring the north and south poles face each other with a clear gap between them. Mount the rectangular wire loop so that it can rotate smoothly in the gap between the two poles. Connect the two ends of the wire loop to the terminals of the analog galvanometer using connecting wires. Set up the camera on a tripod, adjust framing to include the loop, magnet poles, and galvanometer, and fix the focus.2. Initial Observation: Ensure the wire loop is stationary at first. Observe and record that the galvanometer pointer rests at the zero position, indicating no current in the circuit.3. Core Operation: Rotate the rectangular wire loop steadily and uniformly around its axis, so that it continuously cuts through the magnetic field lines between the north and south poles of the magnet. Maintain a constant rotation speed during observation.4. Observation During Rotation: While the loop rotates, observe the galvanometer pointer. Continue rotating for several cycles to clearly show repeated deflections.5. Completion: Gradually stop the rotation of the wire loop. Observe the galvanometer pointer returning to the zero position. Turn off the camera and dismantle the setup if required.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: When the wire loop is stationary between the magnet poles, the galvanometer pointer remains at zero, showing no induced current.2. During Rotation: As the wire loop rotates steadily, the galvanometer pointer deflects alternately to the left and right, indicating that an induced current is generated and that its direction changes periodically.3. After Stopping: When the rotation stops, the galvanometer pointer returns to zero, indicating that the induced current disappears when there is no change in magnetic flux.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the principle of electromagnetic induction. When the rectangular wire loop rotates in the magnetic field between the north and south poles of the horseshoe magnet, the magnetic flux through the loop changes continuously. According to Faraday’s law of electromagnetic induction, a changing magnetic flux induces an electromotive force in the conductor, resulting in an induced current in the closed circuit. The alternating deflection of the galvanometer pointer shows that both the magnitude and direction of the induced current depend on the rate and direction of change of magnetic flux. When the loop stops rotating, the magnetic flux remains constant, so no induced current is produced.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the magnet is fixed securely to prevent movement during rotation.2. Rotate the wire loop smoothly and at a steady speed to obtain clear and regular galvanometer deflections.3. Avoid loose wire connections, which may cause unstable or weak galvanometer readings.4. Keep the camera focus fixed throughout the experiment to ensure consistent time-lapse recording.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: electromagnetic induction caused by changing magnetic flux. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: a fixed horseshoe magnet provides a stable magnetic field; a rectangular wire loop rotates steadily within the field; the loop is part of a closed circuit connected to an analog galvanometer; changing flux induces current.Expected phased storyline: Phase 1 (Setup and Rest): stationary wire loop between clearly marked N and S poles, galvanometer at zero. Phase 2 (Rotation): loop rotates steadily; magnetic flux through the loop changes; galvanometer needle alternately deflects left and right in sync with rotation. Phase 3 (Stop): rotation ceases; flux becomes constant; galvanometer returns to zero. Visibility constraints: camera framing must include magnet poles, rotating loop, and galvanometer needle simultaneously, with fixed focus to verify continuous causal relationships.

manual: Instructions for the Physics Experiment: Rapid Air Expansion in a Sealed Bottle Producing a Condensation CloudI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Rapid Air Expansion in a Sealed Bottle Producing a Condensation Cloud2. Subject: Physics - Thermodynamics3. Experiment Objective: To observe the cooling effect of rapid air expansion and understand how adiabatic expansion leads to condensation of water vapor into a visible cloud.II. Experimental EquipmentClear plastic bottle (1–2 L, dry inside), rubber stopper with airtight fit, hand air pump, quick-release valve (or ball valve), safety goggles.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Ensure the bottle is clean and dry inside. Insert the stopper firmly into the bottle mouth to create an airtight seal. Connect the hand pump and quick-release valve to the stopper. Put on safety goggles.Pressurization: Use the hand pump to steadily pump air into the sealed bottle. Pump until noticeable resistance is felt, indicating increased internal pressure.Core Operation: Hold the bottle steady and point it away from the face. Suddenly open the quick-release valve to allow the compressed air inside the bottle to expand rapidly.Conclusion: After the pressure is released, close the valve, disconnect the apparatus, and return the equipment to its original state.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The bottle appears clear, with transparent air inside and no visible cloud.2. During Pressurization: No visible change inside the bottle; pressure builds silently.3. At Valve Release: A brief hissing sound is heard. A white, mist-like condensation cloud suddenly appears inside the bottle and may partially escape, then quickly dissipates.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates rapid (adiabatic) expansion of compressed air. When the valve is suddenly opened, the high-pressure air expands quickly, doing work on the surroundings. Because the expansion is very fast, there is little heat exchange with the environment, so the air temperature drops. The cooling causes water vapor in the air to condense into tiny droplets, forming a visible condensation cloud.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the bottle is rated for pressure and free of cracks. Do not over-pressurize. Always point the bottle away from people when releasing the valve. Wear eye protection throughout the experiment.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Faraday Cage Shielding with Metal Mesh and ElectroscopeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Faraday Cage Shielding Demonstration Using Metal Mesh and Gold-Leaf Electroscope2. Subject: Physics – Electrostatics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the electrostatic shielding effect of a Faraday cage, showing that external electric charges do not affect the electric state inside a closed conducting enclosure.II. Experimental EquipmentMetal mesh Faraday cage (cylindrical or box-shaped, electrically continuous), insulating stand, gold-leaf electroscope, charged plastic rod (charged by friction), insulating handle, camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the metal mesh Faraday cage on an insulating stand. Ensure the cage is electrically isolated from the ground. Place the gold-leaf electroscope centrally inside the cage, with its leaves initially collapsed.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera position and focus to clearly include the cage and the electroscope inside. Do not adjust focus during the experiment.3. Approach without Contact: Charge the plastic rod by rubbing it with dry cloth. Slowly bring the charged rod close to the outside of the metal mesh without touching it. Observe the electroscope leaves.4. External Contact: Touch the charged rod to the outside surface of the metal mesh cage, then withdraw it. Observe the electroscope leaves.5. Internal Contact (Control Step): Carefully insert the charged rod through an opening and briefly touch the electroscope terminal inside the cage, then withdraw it. Observe the electroscope leaves.6. End: Remove the rod and allow the system to return to its initial state.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Electroscope leaves are closed and stationary.2. Rod Approaches Cage Exterior: No noticeable deflection of the electroscope leaves.3. Rod Touches Cage Exterior: Electroscope leaves remain closed; no sustained deflection observed.4. Rod Touches Electroscope Inside Cage: Electroscope leaves diverge明显ly, indicating charging.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA Faraday cage is a closed conducting enclosure. When an external charged object approaches or contacts the cage, charges redistribute on the outer surface of the conductor. The electric field inside the conducting enclosure remains zero, so objects inside are shielded from external electrostatic influence. Only when charge is directly introduced inside the cage does the electroscope respond.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the cage is conductive and electrically continuous; keep the cage insulated from ground; avoid touching the cage with bare hands during observation; maintain fixed camera focus throughout recording.

Visibility constraints: camera must clearly show the electroscope leaves inside the mesh and maintain fixed focus to verify lack or presence of deflection across phases.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Inertia Phenomenon Demonstration (Egg Falling into Cup)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Inertia Phenomenon Demonstration (Egg Falling into Cup)2. Subject: Physics – Natural Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the inertia of objects by observing that an egg tends to maintain its state of rest when an external support is quickly removed.II. Experimental EquipmentGlass cup (one, with a flat mouth), hard cardboard (slightly larger than the cup mouth), raw egg (one), flat table surface.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the glass cup upright on a stable table. Ensure the table surface is level.2. Setup: Place the hard cardboard flat on the mouth of the glass so that it fully covers the opening. Gently place the egg at the center of the cardboard, keeping it balanced and still.3. Core Operation: Hold the cardboard at one side and quickly pull it out horizontally in one smooth motion, without lifting upward.4. Completion: Observe the motion of the egg immediately after the cardboard is removed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The egg is stationary on the cardboard above the glass.2. During Operation: When the cardboard is pulled out quickly, it moves away horizontally while the egg shows almost no horizontal movement.3. Final Result: The egg falls vertically downward and drops into the glass cup.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates inertia, a fundamental property of matter. According to Newton’s First Law, an object at rest tends to remain at rest unless acted upon by an external force. When the cardboard is pulled out quickly, the friction between the cardboard and the egg is very small and acts for a very short time, so it cannot significantly change the egg’s state of rest. Under the action of gravity, the egg then falls straight down into the glass.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Verification of Free Fall Motion Being Independent of MassI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Verification of Free Fall Motion Being Independent of Mass2. Subject: Physics – Mechanics (Natural Science)3. Experiment Objective: To verify that in free fall, objects with different masses fall with the same acceleration, and that free fall motion is independent of mass when air resistance is minimized.II. Experimental EquipmentWooden ball (100 g), iron ball (500 g), identical in shape and volume; release device or hand-held release frame ensuring simultaneous release; elevated platform or stand (2–3 m height); flat landing surface; camera or mobile phone with time-lapse or slow-motion function; measuring tape.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Measure and confirm that both balls have the same shape and volume but different masses. Set up a stable elevated platform and ensure the landing area is flat and safe.2. Positioning: Place both balls side by side at the same height using a release device or both hands, ensuring their bottoms are level.3. Recording Setup: Position the camera to capture both the moment of release and the landing area. Activate time-lapse or slow-motion recording.4. Core Operation: Release both balls simultaneously without applying extra force.5. Observation and Recording: Observe and record the falling process and the moment when both balls land.6. Repeat (Optional): Repeat the experiment several times to reduce accidental error.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. At release, both balls begin to fall at the same time from the same height.2. During the fall, both balls move downward with increasing speed.3. At landing, the wooden ball and iron ball reach the ground almost simultaneously.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIn free fall near the Earth’s surface, the acceleration due to gravity is constant (g ≈ 9.8 m/s²) and independent of an object’s mass. When air resistance is negligible, objects of different masses but similar shapes fall with the same acceleration, so they land at the same time if released simultaneously from the same height.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Electroscope Leaves Spreading with Increased ChargeI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Electroscope Leaves Spread Wider When More Charge Is AddedSubject: Physics - ElectricityObjective: To observe that the divergence angle of electroscope leaves increases with added electric charge and decreases after discharge, understanding charge transfer and electrostatic repulsion.II. EquipmentTabletop electroscope with two thin metal leaves enclosed in a glass jar; charged rod (plastic or glass); dry cloth for charging the rod; human hand for discharge; camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the electroscope on a stable tabletop. Ensure the metal leaves are initially closed and the camera focus is fixed on the leaves.2. Charging the Rod: Rub the rod with a dry cloth to give it electric charge.3. Core Operation (Charging): Gently touch the charged rod to the metal terminal on top of the electroscope, then remove it. Repeat this touching action several times, allowing charge to accumulate.4. Discharging: Briefly touch the top terminal with a hand to discharge the electroscope.5. Recording: Keep the camera fixed and record the entire process in time-lapse to capture gradual changes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The two metal leaves hang close together with little or no separation.2. During Repeated Charging: Each time the charged rod touches the terminal, the leaves spread farther apart; the divergence angle increases progressively.3. After Discharge: When the hand touches the terminal, the leaves quickly move closer together or collapse back to the initial state.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleWhen a charged rod touches the electroscope terminal, electric charge is transferred to the electroscope. Both metal leaves receive the same type of charge and repel each other due to electrostatic repulsion, causing them to spread apart. Repeated charging adds more charge, increasing the repulsive force and widening the leaf separation. Touching the terminal with a hand allows charge to flow to the ground, reducing the charge on the leaves and causing them to collapse.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Increased electric charge on an electroscope leads to stronger electrostatic repulsion between identically charged metal leaves, observable as greater leaf divergence, and grounding removes charge. Minimum assumptions: a conductive electroscope with two leaves, a charged rod capable of charge transfer, and grounding via a human hand.Phased storyline: (1) Initial neutral electroscope with closed leaves; (2) charged rod contacts terminal causing leaves to spread; (3) repeated contacts cause progressively wider spreading; (4) hand briefly touches terminal, grounding the electroscope and causing rapid leaf collapse. Visibility constraints: camera remains fixed, leaves clearly visible through glass, divergence angle changes must be observable in time-lapse.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Bar Magnet Moving Through a Coil Connected to a Bi-Color LEDI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Bar Magnet Moving Through a Coil Connected to a Bi-Color LED2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics (Electromagnetic Induction)3. Experiment Objective: To observe electromagnetic induction by moving a cylindrical bar magnet through a wire coil connected to a bi-color LED, and to understand how the direction and speed of motion affect induced current.II. Experimental EquipmentCylindrical bar magnet (1), insulated wire coil with multiple turns (1), bi-color LED (red/green, 1), connecting wires, coil stand or holder, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the coil on a stable stand and connect its two ends to the bi-color LED using wires. Ensure the LED is clearly visible.2. Initial State Check: Hold the bar magnet away from the coil; confirm that the LED is off.3. Slow Pass: Slowly insert the cylindrical bar magnet through the center of the coil from one side and pull it out from the other side. Observe the LED.4. Fast Pass: Quickly move the magnet through the coil in the same direction and observe the LED again.5. Reverse Direction: Move the magnet back through the coil in the opposite direction (one slow or fast pass is sufficient) and observe the LED color.6. Pause Inside: Hold the magnet stationary inside the coil for a brief moment, then remove it.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. When the magnet is not moving, the LED remains off.2. During the slow pass, the LED lights dimly with one color.3. During the fast pass, the LED lights more brightly than during the slow pass.4. When the magnet moves in the opposite direction, the LED lights with the opposite color.5. When the magnet is held still inside the coil, the LED turns off.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates electromagnetic induction. When the bar magnet moves relative to the coil, the magnetic flux through the coil changes, inducing an electric current. The induced current lights the LED. Faster motion causes a greater rate of change of magnetic flux, producing a larger induced current and a brighter LED. Reversing the direction of motion reverses the direction of the induced current, causing the bi-color LED to change color. When the magnet is stationary, the magnetic flux is constant, so no current is induced and the LED remains off.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Electromagnetic induction caused by changing magnetic flux in a coil. Minimum assumptions: a fixed coil connected to a bi-color LED, a cylindrical bar magnet that can move smoothly through the coil, and LED behavior that reflects current direction and magnitude.Phased storyline: (1) Static baseline – magnet away or held still in the coil, LED off. (2) Slow motion phase – magnet slowly passes through coil, LED lights dimly with one color. (3) Fast motion phase – magnet quickly passes through coil, LED lights more brightly. (4) Direction change – magnet moves back through coil, LED color reverses. (5) Pause verification – magnet held still again, LED off. Camera should maintain a clear view of the coil and LED to verify brightness and color changes.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Siphon Phenomenon DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Siphon Phenomenon Demonstration2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics (Fluid Mechanics)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the siphon phenomenon by observing the spontaneous flow of liquid from a higher container to a lower container through a tube filled with liquid, and to understand the role of gravity and pressure difference in fluid motion.II. Experimental Equipment1. Beaker A (1): transparent beaker, placed at a higher position, containing red-colored water.2. Beaker B (1): transparent beaker, placed at a lower position, initially empty.3. Rubber tube (1): flexible transparent tube, length sufficient to connect the two beakers.4. Support or stand (optional): to ensure a clear height difference between the two beakers.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place beaker A on a stable platform so that it is clearly higher than beaker B. Pour red water into beaker A until it is about half full. Ensure beaker B is empty and placed at a lower position.2. Tube Filling: Completely fill the rubber tube with water in advance, ensuring no air bubbles remain inside the tube.3. Tube Insertion: Insert one end of the water-filled rubber tube into beaker A, making sure the end is fully submerged in the red water. Insert the other end into beaker B, keeping this end lower than the liquid level in beaker A.4. Observation Setup: Keep both ends of the tube submerged during insertion to prevent air from entering the tube.5. Start of Experiment: Release the tube and observe the liquid flow without adding any external force.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Beaker A contains red water; beaker B is empty; the rubber tube is fully filled with water and contains no air.2. During the Experiment: Red water begins to flow automatically from beaker A through the rubber tube into beaker B.3. Resulting State: The liquid level in beaker A gradually decreases, while the liquid level in beaker B gradually increases. The flow continues until the liquid levels in the two beakers become equal or the inlet end in beaker A is exposed to air.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe siphon phenomenon occurs due to the combined effect of gravity and pressure difference. When the tube is completely filled with liquid and both ends are submerged, gravity causes the liquid in the longer descending section of the tube to fall, creating a lower pressure at the top of the tube. Atmospheric pressure acting on the liquid surface in the higher beaker pushes the liquid into the tube, maintaining continuous flow. As long as the outlet is lower than the liquid surface in the source beaker and no air enters the tube, the siphon effect continues.VI. Experimental Precautions1. The rubber tube must be completely filled with water; any air bubbles will interrupt the siphon.2. The outlet end of the tube must be lower than the liquid surface in beaker A.3. Ensure stable placement of beakers to avoid accidental height changes during the experiment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: The siphon phenomenon, defined as liquid flowing from a higher container to a lower container through a fully liquid-filled tube under gravity and atmospheric pressure, without external pumping. Minimum assumptions: two open containers, a clear height difference, a continuous liquid column in the tube, and gravity acting downward.Expected phased storyline: Phase 1 (Setup) – Two transparent beakers are visible, beaker A higher with red water, beaker B lower and empty; a rubber tube is shown fully filled with water. Phase 2 (Connection) – Both ends of the tube are inserted into the respective beakers, with no air entering the tube. Phase 3 (Flow) – Red water visibly begins to move through the tube from beaker A to beaker B. Phase 4 (Result) – The liquid level in A decreases while the level in B increases. Visibility constraints: the height difference, tube continuity, and direction of liquid motion must be clearly visible in the frame to verify causal correctness.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Observation of Neon Sign Tube Light Through a Glass PrismI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Observation of Neon Sign Tube Emission Spectrum Using a Glass PrismSubject: Physics – Optics and Atomic PhysicsExperiment Objective: To observe the characteristic red-orange light emitted by a neon sign tube when powered, and to view the dispersion of this light through a glass prism, thereby understanding gas discharge luminescence and light dispersion.II. Experimental EquipmentNeon sign tube (sealed neon gas discharge tube), regulated power supply suitable for neon tubes, connecting wires with insulation, glass prism, prism holder or stand, darkened background or dim room, safety gloves (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the neon sign tube securely on an insulating support. Position the glass prism on a stable holder in front of the tube. Dim the ambient light to enhance visibility.2. Connection: Ensure the power supply is switched off. Connect the electrodes of the neon sign tube to the power supply using insulated wires.3. Powering the Tube: Switch on the power supply gradually to energize the neon sign tube.4. Observation Through Prism: Align the glass prism so that the emitted light from the glowing tube passes through it. Observe the emergent light on the other side of the prism.5. Shutdown: Turn off the power supply after observation and disconnect the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before powering, the neon tube is unlit and transparent.2. After Powering: The tube emits a bright, uniform red-orange glow along its length.3. Prism Observation: When viewed through the glass prism, the emitted light is refracted and dispersed, showing separation into colored components dominated by red-orange hues.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhen an electric current passes through low-pressure neon gas, neon atoms are excited by electron collisions. As excited atoms return to lower energy states, they emit light with characteristic wavelengths, producing a red-orange glow. A glass prism disperses light due to wavelength-dependent refraction, allowing observation of the spectral characteristics of the neon emission.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use only appropriate power supplies designed for neon tubes.2. Avoid touching exposed electrodes during operation.3. Ensure the prism and tube are securely placed to prevent tipping or breakage.

manual: Instructions for the Physics Experiment: Two People on Wheeled Stools Pushing Off Each OtherI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Two People on Wheeled Stools Pushing Off Each Other2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics (Mechanics)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that when only internal forces act within a system, the total momentum of the system remains conserved, and the center of mass of the system remains at rest or moves uniformly. Through observation of two people pushing off each other on wheeled stools, students understand Newton’s third law and the conservation of momentum.II. Experimental Equipment1. Two identical wheeled stools (with low friction wheels).2. Smooth, level floor (to minimize external horizontal forces such as friction).3. Two experimenters of similar mass (or record masses if different).4. Camera or mobile phone mounted on a tripod, with fixed focus and fixed position, capable of time-lapse or continuous recording.5. Marker or tape on the floor to indicate the initial position (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   (1) Place the two identical wheeled stools on a smooth, horizontal floor facing each other.   (2) Adjust the camera so that both stools and the surrounding motion area are fully visible; fix the focus and keep the camera stationary.   (3) Ensure both experimenters sit upright on the stools with feet lifted off the floor to avoid external forces.2. Initial State Setup:   (1) The two experimenters sit still on the stools, facing each other.   (2) Both experimenters extend their arms and place their hands together, gently touching.   (3) Confirm that the system is initially at rest.3. Core Operation:   (1) On a clear signal, both experimenters push against each other using their hands.   (2) The push should be brief and applied only through hand contact, without touching the floor or other objects.4. Observation and Recording:   (1) After pushing off, both stools roll away from each other.   (2) Continue recording until the stools move steadily apart.5. Experiment Completion:   (1) Stop the recording.   (2) Ensure the area is safe before standing up and ending the experiment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both people and stools are stationary, hands touching, and the system is at rest.2. During the Push: At the moment of hand contact force, both people exert forces on each other simultaneously.3. After the Push: The two stools roll apart in opposite directions. If the two people have similar mass, they move away at similar speeds; if their masses differ, the lighter person moves away faster.4. Overall Observation: The midpoint between the two people (center of mass of the system) remains approximately in the same position.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Newton’s Third Law: When person A pushes person B, person B simultaneously pushes person A with an equal magnitude and opposite direction force.2. Conservation of Momentum: Since the system is initially at rest and external horizontal forces are negligible, the total momentum of the two-person system remains zero. Therefore, the momenta of the two people after pushing off are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.3. Center of Mass Principle: With no net external force acting on the system, the center of mass of the two-person system remains at rest, even though the two individuals move apart.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the floor is smooth and level to reduce friction.2. Do not let feet touch the ground during the push to avoid introducing external forces.3. Push gently to ensure safety and prevent falling.4. Keep the camera fixed to ensure accurate observation of motion.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: conservation of momentum and Newton’s third law in an isolated system with only internal forces. Minimum assumptions: smooth floor, negligible external horizontal forces, identical wheeled stools, initial rest state, and simultaneous mutual push through hand contact. Expected phased storyline: (1) Initial still frame with two people facing each other on stools, hands touching; (2) brief action phase where both apply force simultaneously; (3) separation phase where stools roll apart in opposite directions; (4) final phase showing continued motion apart with the midpoint remaining approximately fixed. Camera must remain fixed and wide enough to verify opposite directions, relative speeds, and center-of-mass behavior.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Discharge of a Negatively Charged Gold-Leaf Electroscope by Ultraviolet LightI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Zinc Plate on a Negatively Charged Gold-Leaf Electroscope Illuminated by Visible and Ultraviolet Light2. Subject: Physics – Modern Physics (Photoelectric Effect)3. Experiment Objective: To observe that ultraviolet light can cause a negatively charged gold-leaf electroscope with a zinc plate to discharge, while visible light cannot, and to understand the basic principle of the photoelectric effect.II. Experimental EquipmentGold-leaf electroscope (with metal cap), clean zinc plate, charging rod (e.g., ebonite rod and fur), visible light lamp, ultraviolet lamp, lamp stand to ensure equal distance, camera with fixed focus for time-lapse photography, darkened room (recommended for clarity).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the gold-leaf electroscope on a stable table. Fix the zinc plate firmly on the metal cap of the electroscope. Set the camera directly facing the gold leaves and fix the focus and position.2. Charging: Use the charging rod to give the electroscope a negative charge. Observe that the gold leaves diverge and remain open, indicating successful charging.3. Visible Light Illumination: Place the visible light lamp at a fixed distance from the zinc plate. Turn on the lamp and illuminate the zinc plate for a short time while recording. Do not change the lamp distance or camera focus.4. Observation under Visible Light: Observe and record the state of the gold leaves.5. Ultraviolet Light Illumination: Replace the visible lamp with the ultraviolet lamp at the same distance. Turn on the UV lamp and illuminate the zinc plate while continuing the recording.6. Observation under Ultraviolet Light: Observe and record the change in the gold leaves until a clear phenomenon appears.7. End of Experiment: Turn off the lamp, stop recording, and discharge the electroscope safely.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: After negative charging, the gold leaves are clearly separated and remain stable.2. Under Visible Light: When illuminated by visible light, the gold leaves show little or no change and remain separated.3. Under Ultraviolet Light: When illuminated by ultraviolet light, the gold leaves gradually come closer together and eventually collapse, indicating discharge of the electroscope.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the photoelectric effect. Ultraviolet light has sufficiently high frequency to cause electrons to be emitted from the zinc plate. When electrons are emitted, the negatively charged electroscope loses charge, causing the gold leaves to collapse. Experiment Objective: To observe electrostatic attraction caused by a statically charged object and understand polarization of neutral objects through visual phenomena.II. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Sealed Bottle with Balloon Heated in Hot Water BathI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Expansion and Contraction of Air in a Sealed Bottle2. Subject: Natural Science - Physics3. Experiment Objective: To observe the expansion of air when heated and contraction when cooled by using a clear glass bottle sealed with a stretched balloon, and to understand the effect of temperature on gas volume.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass bottle (dry, intact), latex balloon (elastic, unstretched initially), hot water (about 70–80°C), cooler water (room temperature or cold), two heat-resistant containers, towel or gloves (for safety), camera or smartphone with fixed focus.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the glass bottle is completely dry. Stretch the balloon slightly and tightly fit it over the mouth of the bottle to form a sealed system.2. Initial Observation: Place the bottle at room temperature and observe the balloon; it should be flat or slightly sagging.3. Heating Stage: Carefully place the sealed bottle into a container of hot water, ensuring the water level is below the balloon. Keep the setup still and fix the camera focus for time-lapse recording.4. Observation During Heating: Maintain the bottle in hot water for a short time and observe the balloon gradually expanding.5. Experimental EquipmentLong straight copper wire (sufficient length to stand vertically), clear plastic or glass sheet with a central hole, iron filings, DC power supply (with switch), connecting wires, insulating base or tabletop support, camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse recording).III. Experiment Title: Comparison of Sliding Motion of a Rubber Eraser and a Metal Block on Identical Ramps2. Subject: Physics - Mechanics (Friction)3. Experiment Objective: To observe how different materials slide on the same inclined plane and understand the effect of friction on motion.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical adjustable ramps, rubber eraser (cuboid, matte surface), metal block (cuboid, smooth surface), flat table, angle-adjusting support.III. Experimental Procedure1. Place two identical ramps side-by-side on a flat table, ensuring the same length and surface.2. Place the rubber eraser on the left ramp and the metal block on the right ramp at the same starting position near the top.3. Summary of Experimental PrincipleWhen an object is on an inclined plane, it begins to slide only when the component of gravity along the slope exceeds the maximum static friction. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Rotating Two Linear Polarizing Filters in Front of a Light SourceI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Brightness Change Caused by Rotating Two Linear Polarizing Filters2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics (Optics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand how the relative angle between two linear polarizing filters affects the intensity of transmitted light, verify Malus’ Law qualitatively, and demonstrate polarization effects using a fixed camera for time-lapse recording.II. Experimental Equipment1. Bright white light source (LED panel or lamp with diffuser, stable brightness)2. Two linear polarizing filters of similar size3. Camera or smartphone with manual focus capability4. Tripod or stable camera mount5. Filter holder or hands for manual rotation6. Dark or neutral background (optional, for contrast)III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup Preparation: Place the bright white light source facing the camera. Fix the camera on a tripod directly in front of the light source. Set the camera to manual focus and lock focus and exposure to prevent automatic adjustment during recording.2. Filter Arrangement: Hold or mount the first linear polarizing filter directly in front of the light source. Keep this filter fixed throughout the experiment.3. Second Filter Placement: Place the second linear polarizing filter directly in front of the first filter, ensuring the two filters are parallel and aligned along the same optical axis.4. Core Operation: Start recording or time-lapse capture. Slowly rotate the second (front) polarizing filter by hand through 360 degrees, repeating the rotation multiple times at a steady speed.5. Observation and Completion: Continue rotating until several cycles of brightness change are clearly recorded. Stop recording and remove the filters.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: When the transmission axes of the two filters are aligned, the light appears bright in the camera frame.2. During Rotation: As the second filter is rotated, the brightness of the transmitted light gradually decreases.3. Minimum Brightness: When the two polarizers are approximately perpendicular (90 degrees), the light becomes very dim or nearly dark.4. Repetition: As rotation continues, brightness increases again, repeating a periodic bright–dark–bright pattern with each 180-degree rotation.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Light from the source is initially unpolarized. After passing through the first linear polarizing filter, it becomes linearly polarized.2. The second polarizing filter only transmits the component of light aligned with its transmission axis.3. According to Malus’ Law, the transmitted light intensity depends on the square of the cosine of the angle between the polarization directions of the two filters.4. When the axes are parallel, maximum light is transmitted; when perpendicular, minimum light is transmitted, producing the observed periodic brightness change.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the camera focus and exposure are fixed to avoid artificial brightness changes.2. Rotate the filter smoothly to maintain clear temporal continuity in the video.3. Keep the filters clean and flat to avoid scattering or uneven brightness.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Linear polarization and intensity modulation using two linear polarizing filters. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: unpolarized white light becomes linearly polarized after the first filter; the second filter transmits only the component aligned with its axis; camera focus and exposure remain fixed.Phased storyline: (1) Initial setup shows a bright, uniform white light with two stacked polarizers in front of the camera. (2) With axes aligned, the scene appears bright. (3) As the front polarizer rotates, brightness decreases smoothly. (4) Near 90-degree relative angle, the scene becomes darkest. (5) Continued rotation restores brightness, repeating periodically. Visibility constraints: filters must be clearly visible, rotation must be continuous, and the camera viewpoint must remain fixed to verify causal relationships.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Circular Drum Membrane Vibrating in One Normal Mode PatternI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Normal Mode Vibration of a Circular Drum Membrane2. Subject: Physics – Waves and Vibrations3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the normal mode vibration pattern of a circular membrane by visualizing nodal lines using fine sand when the membrane is driven at a fixed frequency.II. Experimental EquipmentCircular drum membrane (taut and uniformly tensioned), mechanical shaker with frequency controller, signal generator and power amplifier (if required), fine dry sand, camera with tripod (capable of time-lapse or fixed-focus recording), stand and clamps, power supply.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fix the circular drum membrane horizontally on a rigid frame. Ensure the membrane is evenly tensioned and free of wrinkles. Place the setup on a stable table.2. Sand Application: Evenly sprinkle a thin layer of fine sand over the surface of the membrane, avoiding piles or uneven distribution.3. Driving Setup: Attach the mechanical shaker to the membrane at a suitable coupling point (usually near the rim or center, depending on design). Set the shaker to a predetermined fixed frequency corresponding to a known normal mode.4. Camera Setup: Place the camera directly above the membrane. Fix the focus, exposure, and viewpoint. Do not adjust the camera during the experiment.5. Core Operation: Turn on the mechanical shaker and allow the membrane to vibrate continuously at the fixed frequency.6. Observation and Recording: Observe the motion of the sand as the membrane vibrates. Record the process using time-lapse or continuous video until a stable sand pattern appears.7. Completion: Turn off the shaker after a clear pattern is formed. Save the recorded footage for analysis and clean the membrane.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The sand is uniformly distributed on the stationary membrane.2. During Vibration: As the membrane vibrates, sand grains bounce and migrate away from regions of large amplitude.3. Final Pattern: Sand accumulates along stationary nodal lines, forming a clear geometric pattern characteristic of a single normal mode of the circular membrane.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleA circular membrane supports discrete normal modes of vibration, each with a specific frequency and nodal pattern. When the membrane is driven at a fixed frequency matching one normal mode, standing waves are established. Points on nodal lines remain stationary, while antinodes oscillate with maximum amplitude. Fine sand is expelled from vibrating antinodes and settles on nodal lines, making the normal mode pattern visible.VI. Experimental Precautions1. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Rolling Ball Chooses a Curved Groove over a Longer Straight ChannelI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Rolling Ball Chooses a Curved Groove over a Longer Straight ChannelSubject: Natural Science - PhysicsObjective: To demonstrate that, when released from the same height, a steel ball rolling along a longer curved path that dips and rises can reach the finish earlier than a ball rolling along a shorter straight path, illustrating the role of gravitational acceleration and path shape.II. EquipmentTwo identical steel balls; straight groove; curved groove with a steep initial dip and a rise to the same finish height; adjustable support stand; release gate or hand release; ruler or height marker; camera with tripod (fixed focus, time-lapse mode).III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Mount the straight groove and the curved groove so their starting points are at exactly the same height and their ending points are at the same height. Ensure both grooves are smooth and firmly fixed.2. Camera: Place the camera on a tripod facing both grooves; fix focus and enable time-lapse or continuous recording. Do not move the camera during the experiment.3. Placement: Put one steel ball at the start of each groove, aligned at the same horizontal level.4. Release: Release both balls simultaneously without pushing, ensuring they start only under gravity.5. Recording: Allow both balls to roll until they reach the finish; keep recording until both have arrived.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial state: Both balls are stationary at the same height.During motion: The ball on the curved groove accelerates rapidly along the steep dip and gains speed earlier; the ball on the straight groove accelerates more slowly.Result: Although the curved groove is longer, the ball on it reaches the finish first; the straight-groove ball arrives later.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe experiment demonstrates that travel time depends not only on path length but on how gravitational potential energy is converted into kinetic energy. The curved groove provides a steeper initial descent, giving the ball a higher speed earlier. Maintaining this higher speed over most of the path allows it to reach the finish sooner, illustrating the brachistochrone principle in an intuitive form.VI. PrecautionsEnsure identical balls and equal start heights; release simultaneously; keep grooves smooth and camera fixed.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Oscillation in Multiple Identical Mass–Spring Systems with Different Initial DisplacementsSubject: Physics – Mechanics (Simple Harmonic Motion)Objective: To demonstrate that for identical mass–spring systems, the oscillation period is independent of initial displacement, by observing three vertical systems released simultaneously from different initial positions.II. Experimental EquipmentThree identical springs; three identical masses; rigid support frame; clamps/hooks; ruler or scale; colored markers or colored tape (three distinct colors); camera or smartphone with fixed focus; tripod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Mount three identical springs vertically on the same support so they hang side by side. Attach identical masses to the springs.2. Marking: Mark each mass with a distinct color (e.g., red, blue, green) for identification.3. Initial Displacement: Pull each mass downward to a different vertical displacement from equilibrium (small, medium, large), keeping motion purely vertical.4. Camera Preparation: Place the camera on a tripod in front of the systems. Fix focus, angle, and framing; do not move the camera during recording. Enable time-lapse or accelerated recording if available.5. Simultaneous Release: Release all three masses at the same time without pushing them.6. Observation: Record the motion for several oscillation cycles.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Three colored masses are held at different vertical positions.2. After Release: All masses begin vertical oscillatory motion.3. Key Phenomenon: Although amplitudes and phases differ, the three masses complete oscillations with the same period.4. Over Time: The relative timing of peaks and troughs remains consistent, demonstrating identical oscillation periods.V. Experimental Principle SummaryFor a vertical mass–spring system undergoing simple harmonic motion, the period T = 2π√(m/k), which depends only on the mass m and spring constant k. Since all three systems have identical m and k, their periods are the same, regardless of different initial displacements (amplitudes). Gravity shifts the equilibrium position but does not change the oscillation period.VI. PrecautionsEnsure springs and masses are identical; release simultaneously without extra force; keep motion vertical; maintain fixed camera position for accurate comparison.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Identical mass–spring systems in simple harmonic motion have the same oscillation period independent of initial displacement.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Linear (Hookean) springs, identical masses and spring constants, small to moderate oscillations, vertical motion under gravity, fixed camera perspective.Expected Phenomena Storyline: (1) Three colored masses are shown at different initial vertical displacements. (2) All are released simultaneously. (3) Each mass oscillates up and down vertically. (4) Despite different amplitudes and phases, their oscillations share the same period, visible through synchronized timing of repeated cycles. Visibility Constraints: Side-by-side layout, distinct colors, fixed camera focus, and sufficient duration to observe multiple cycles.
