manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Visible Spectrum Color Mixing (Green + Blue)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visible Spectrum Color Mixing Experiment (Green + Blue)2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics (Optics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the additive color mixing effect of green and blue light by overlapping green and blue laser beams on a white screen, and to understand the basic principle of additive color mixing in the visible spectrum.II. Experimental EquipmentGreen laser light source (low-power, continuous output), blue laser light source (low-power, continuous output), optical mounts or adjustable holders, white screen or white paper, optical bench or flat tabletop, power supply or batteries for lasers, laser safety goggles (recommended).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the white screen vertically at one end of the optical bench or tabletop. Secure the green and blue laser light sources on adjustable holders so that both can project light toward the screen.2. Individual Beam Adjustment: Turn on the green laser only and adjust its position and angle so that a clear green spot appears on the white screen. Turn off the green laser. Then turn on the blue laser and similarly adjust it to form a clear blue spot on the screen.3. Optical Path Overlap: Turn on both the green and blue lasers simultaneously. Carefully adjust the angles and positions of the two lasers so that the green and blue spots gradually move closer together and finally overlap on the white screen.4. Observation: Observe the color of the overlapping region on the white screen and compare it with the colors of the individual green and blue light spots.5. Completion: Turn off both laser sources after observation. Restore the equipment to its original state.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: When only one laser is on, a single-colored light spot (green or blue) appears on the white screen.2. During Overlap: As the green and blue light spots overlap, the overlapping area changes color.3. Final Phenomenon: The overlapping region appears cyan (blue-green), which is different from pure green or pure blue, while the non-overlapping regions remain green and blue respectively.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates the principle of additive color mixing of light. In the visible spectrum, green light and blue light are primary colors of additive mixing. When green and blue light overlap on a white screen, their light intensities add together and stimulate the human eye’s cone cells simultaneously, producing the perception of cyan. This shows that different colors of light can combine to form new colors through additive mixing, which is the fundamental principle behind color displays and lighting technologies.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not look directly into the laser beams to avoid eye injury.2. Ensure the lasers are securely fixed to prevent accidental movement.3. Use low-power lasers suitable for classroom demonstrations.4. Perform the experiment in a moderately dim environment for clearer observation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: additive color mixing of visible light using green and blue lasers. Minimum assumptions: green and blue are primary additive colors; a white screen reflects combined light without altering color; overlapping beams add light intensities.Phased storyline: Phase 1 – show separate green and blue laser spots on a white screen. Phase 2 – adjust optical paths so the two spots move closer together. Phase 3 – beams overlap, forming a distinct cyan region while original colors remain visible outside the overlap. Visibility constraints: camera must clearly capture the white screen head-on, distinguish green, blue, and cyan regions, and show the causal transition from separation to overlap within a short, continuous sequence.

Basic InformationExperiment Title: Dry Ice Sublimation on a TabletopSubject: Natural Science - PhysicsObjective: Observe and understand the sublimation of dry ice (solid CO2) directly into gas at room conditions through time-lapse observation.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Light Dispersion (Prism Light Splitting)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Light Dispersion by a Prism2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics (Optics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe that when sunlight passes through a prism, white light is dispersed into a band of seven colors, and to identify the distribution and order of these colors.II. Experimental EquipmentTriangular glass prism, sunlight (direct sunlight near a window or outdoors), white screen or white paper, prism holder or stable flat surface, darkened room or shaded environment (recommended).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the white screen on a table or wall. Choose a location where a narrow beam of sunlight can enter the room.2. Prism Placement: Put the prism on a stable surface near the sunlight beam. Adjust the prism so that sunlight enters one face of the prism at an angle.3. Core Operation: Slowly rotate or adjust the prism until the emerging light is projected onto the white screen.4. Observation: Observe the light on the screen carefully and note the appearance of a colored light band.5. Completion: Fix the prism position once the clearest spectrum is obtained, then record the observed colors and their order.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Sunlight appears as white light before entering the prism.2. During the Experiment: After passing through the prism, the white light spreads out into a continuous band of colors on the screen.3. Final Observation: The color band shows seven colors in order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. Red is least deviated, and violet is most deviated.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhite light is composed of light with different wavelengths. When white light enters a prism, different wavelengths are refracted by different amounts due to their different speeds in glass. This causes the light to separate into a spectrum of seven colors, a phenomenon known as dispersion.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not look directly at the sun to avoid eye damage.2. Ensure the prism is stable to prevent it from falling and breaking.3. Perform the experiment in a slightly darkened environment to make the spectrum clearer.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Light dispersion caused by wavelength-dependent refraction in a prism. Minimum assumptions: white light contains multiple wavelengths; a glass prism refracts light; different wavelengths bend by different angles. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) sunlight appears as white light; (2) white light enters the prism; (3) refraction occurs at the prism surfaces; (4) light separates into a visible spectrum projected onto a screen; (5) a stable seven-color band appears in the order red to violet. Visibility constraints: the prism, incoming light path, and projected spectrum must be clearly visible in the same spatial frame, with a stable camera angle allowing verification of color order and dispersion.

Experiment Objective: To observe the refraction of light at the boundary between air and water by visually identifying the apparent bending of a chopstick, and to understand the basic law of light refraction.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Brachistochrone Curve DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Motion Time on a Straight Track and a Cycloidal TrackSubject: Physics – Classical MechanicsObjective: To demonstrate that, under gravity and negligible friction, a ball traveling along a cycloidal (brachistochrone) track reaches the same endpoint in less time than a ball on a straight track due to greater initial acceleration.II. Experimental EquipmentCycloidal track (inverted cycloid shape), straight track, two identical steel balls, adjustable stand or frame, release mechanism or manual release marker, stopwatch (optional), ruler or alignment guide.III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Fix the straight track and the cycloidal track on the same frame so that they share the same starting point and the same ending point in height and horizontal position.2. Preparation: Place one identical ball at the starting point of each track. Ensure both balls are at rest and aligned at the same height.3. Release: Release both balls simultaneously without pushing them, ensuring they start only under the influence of gravity.4. Observation: Observe the motion of both balls as they roll along their respective tracks toward the ending point.5. Completion: Note which ball reaches the ending point first. Repeat the experiment if necessary to confirm the result.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both balls start from rest at the same height.2. During Motion: The ball on the cycloidal track descends steeply at first, gaining speed rapidly, while the ball on the straight track accelerates more slowly.3. Final State: The ball on the cycloidal track reaches the ending point first, even though the straight track is shorter in length.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe cycloidal curve is the brachistochrone, the path of shortest descent time under gravity without friction. Its near-vertical initial segment provides greater initial acceleration, allowing the ball to gain high speed early. Although the straight path is shorter, its smaller initial acceleration results in a longer total travel time. Therefore, the cycloidal path yields the fastest average speed and shortest descent time.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Relationship between Earthquake Frequency and Building Height AmplitudeI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Effect of Vibration Frequency on Oscillation Amplitude of Different HeightsSubject: Physics – Mechanics and VibrationObjective: To simulate the relationship between earthquake frequency and building height response, and understand resonance by observing amplitude changes with frequency.II. Experimental EquipmentSmall horizontal vibration table with adjustable frequency; rigid base fixed on the table; three identical plastic balls; three slender, flexible metal rods of different effective heights; power controller for vibration table.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fix the base firmly on the vibration table. Ensure the table can vibrate horizontally.2. Assembly: Mount three identical plastic balls vertically on the base using slender, flexible metal rods. The rods should have different heights while other conditions remain the same.3. Initial State: Set the vibration table to the lowest frequency and turn on the power. Observe that all balls swing with very small amplitudes.4. Core Operation: Gradually and continuously increase the vibration frequency at a steady rate.5. Observation: At each frequency range, observe and compare the swing amplitude of the three balls, noting when a ball shows a明显 increase in amplitude.6. Termination: After passing through the resonance ranges, turn off the vibration table and allow all balls to come to rest.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. At low frequency, all balls oscillate slightly with small amplitudes.2. As frequency increases, one ball first shows a明显增大的 swing amplitude, while the others remain relatively small.3. With further increase in frequency, the first ball’s amplitude decreases, and another ball reaches its maximum amplitude.4. Each ball has a different frequency at which its swing amplitude is maximal.V. Experimental Principle SummaryEach ball–rod system has its own natural frequency determined mainly by its effective height. When the driving frequency of the vibration table approaches a system’s natural frequency, resonance occurs, leading to a large oscillation amplitude. Taller systems have lower natural frequencies, while shorter systems have higher natural frequencies. This experiment models how buildings of different heights respond differently to earthquake frequencies, explaining why certain buildings are more strongly affected by specific earthquakes.VI. PrecautionsEnsure the base is firmly fixed; increase frequency slowly to clearly observe resonance; keep hands away from moving parts during operation.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Isochronous Curve Sliding ExperimentI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Sliding Motion on an Isochronous Curve2. Subject: Physics – Mechanics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the isochronous property of a pendulum track, showing that objects released from different positions on the same isochronous curve reach the same endpoint in the same amount of time.II. Experimental EquipmentIsochronous (cycloid-shaped) track or pendulum track (1 set); identical small balls (3–5, same size and mass); fixed support frame; marked finish line at the lowest point of the track; release mechanism or hand release; camera or recording device.III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Secure the isochronous track on the support frame so it is stable. Mark the lowest point of the track as the finish line. Position the camera to clearly capture the entire track, the balls, and the finish line.2. Placement of Balls: Place several identical balls at different starting positions along the same side of the isochronous curve, ensuring they are at different heights but on the same track.3. Synchronized Release: Without pushing or applying extra force, release all balls simultaneously. This can be done by lifting a common barrier or releasing them by hand at the same moment.4. Observation: Allow the balls to slide freely along the track under gravity. Record the motion and carefully observe the order and timing at which the balls reach the finish line.5. Completion: Stop recording after all balls reach the finish line. Reset the apparatus if repeated trials are needed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Balls are stationary at different heights on the same isochronous curve.2. During Motion: After release, all balls begin sliding simultaneously, following the curved track with increasing speed near the bottom.3. Final Observation: Despite different starting positions, the balls reach the finish line at the same time or nearly the same time.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAn isochronous curve (such as a cycloid) has the property that the time taken for an object to slide to the lowest point under gravity is independent of its starting position. This occurs because the curve’s shape balances path length and acceleration due to gravity, ensuring equal descent times. This experiment visually verifies the isochronous property of the curve.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure balls are identical to avoid mass or size effects; release without pushing; keep the track clean and smooth; ensure the camera view clearly shows the synchronized release and finish line.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Wood Block Floating While Adding StonesI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Floating Wooden Block with Rising Water LevelSubject: Natural Science – PhysicsObjective: To demonstrate that when additional objects are added to water, the water level rises while the immersed volume of a freely floating object remains unchanged, verifying the principle of buoyancy.II. Experimental EquipmentClear transparent cup, clean water, small wooden block (able to float), several small stones, flat table surface.III. Experimental Procedure1. Place the clear cup on a stable table and fill it with water to about two-thirds full.2. Gently place the wooden block into the water and allow it to float freely without touching the cup walls or bottom.3. Observe the initial water level and the immersed portion of the wooden block.4. Add small stones into the cup one by one, letting each stone sink to the bottom before adding the next.5. Ensure the wooden block remains floating freely throughout the process.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initially, the wooden block floats on the water with a fixed portion submerged.2. As stones are added, the water surface rises gradually.3. Despite the rising water level, the immersed volume of the wooden block remains essentially unchanged.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAccording to Archimedes’ principle, a floating object displaces a volume of water equal to its weight. When stones are added, they displace additional water, causing the overall water level to rise. However, the weight of the wooden block does not change, so the buoyant force required to support it remains the same, and thus its immersed volume stays constant.

Minimum assumptions: the wooden block floats freely, stones sink, and water is incompressible.Phased Storyline: (1) Establish baseline—clear cup with water and a floating wooden block; (2) Action—stones added sequentially, each sinking to the bottom; (3) Transition—water level rises gradually after each stone; (4) Outcome—block continues floating with unchanged immersed volume. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Relationship Between Shadow Size and Distance from Light SourceI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Shadow Size Changes with Distance from Light Source2. Subject: Natural Science - Physics (Optics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand how the size and position of a shadow change when the distance between an object and a light source changes, verifying that a closer object produces a larger shadow.II. Experimental EquipmentWooden pole (straight, about 1.5–2 m tall), single streetlamp (or fixed point light source), flat open ground (dimly lit square), measuring tape or ground markers (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Choose a dimly lit square at night. Ensure only one streetlamp acts as the main light source. Place the wooden pole upright on flat ground.2. Initial Position: Set the pole at a farther distance from the streetlamp. Ensure the pole is vertical and stable.3. Observation at Distance: Observe and note the length and position of the pole’s shadow on the ground.4. Core Operation: Gradually move the pole closer to the streetlamp in several steps, keeping it upright and aligned.5. Continuous Observation: At each new position, observe changes in the shadow’s length and how its end shifts on the ground.6. Completion: Stop when the pole is close to the streetlamp and make a final observation of the shadow.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. When the pole is far from the light source, the shadow is relatively short and closer to the pole’s base.2. As the pole is moved closer to the streetlamp, the shadow gradually becomes longer and extends farther across the ground.3. The direction of the shadow remains generally opposite to the light source, while its end moves outward as length increases.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesLight travels in straight lines. The shadow is formed because the pole blocks part of the light. When the pole is closer to the light source, the light rays spread out more after being blocked, causing the shadow to become larger and longer. When the pole is farther away, the light rays are more parallel at the pole’s position, producing a smaller shadow. This demonstrates that shadow size is directly related to the distance between the object and the light source.

Experiment Objective: To verify that, under identical conditions, a bulb connected with a copper wire is brighter than when connected with an iron wire, and to understand the effect of material resistance on electric current.II. Experimental EquipmentBattery (1), small bulb with holder (1), switch (1), copper wire (fixed length, 1 piece), iron wire (same length as copper wire, 1 piece), connecting wires, insulating base.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the battery, switch, and bulb on the base. Ensure the copper and iron wires are straightened and confirmed to be the same length.Circuit Setup with Copper Wire: Connect the battery, switch, bulb, and copper wire in series according to the correct circuit order. Close the switch.Observation 1: Observe and record the brightness of the bulb when the copper wire is used.Circuit Replacement with Iron Wire: Open the switch, carefully remove the copper wire, and replace it with the iron wire of the same length, keeping all other components unchanged. Close the switch again.Observation 2: Observe and record the brightness of the bulb when the iron wire is used.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. When the copper wire is connected, the bulb lights up brightly.2. When the iron wire replaces the copper wire, the bulb still lights up but is noticeably dimmer.3. The brightness difference is obvious under identical conditions.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesDifferent metal wires have different electrical resistances. Copper has a lower resistance than iron. Under the same voltage and wire length, a copper wire allows a larger current to pass through the circuit, making the bulb brighter. An iron wire has higher resistance, resulting in smaller current and a dimmer bulb.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the copper and iron wires are of the same length.2. Do not change the battery or bulb during comparison.3. Always open the switch before changing wires to ensure safety.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Different conductive materials with the same length affect current and bulb brightness due to different electrical resistance. Minimum assumptions: a simple series circuit works correctly, the battery voltage is constant, and the bulb brightness reflects current strength.Expected phenomenon storyline: Phase 1 – A complete circuit with a copper wire is connected and the switch is closed, causing the bulb to glow brightly. Phase 2 – The circuit is opened, the copper wire is replaced by an iron wire of identical length, and the switch is closed again. Phase 3 – The bulb lights up but with clearly reduced brightness. Visibility requirements: clear view of wiring order, explicit wire replacement, and side-by-side or sequential brightness comparison under unchanged conditions.

manual: Experiment Title: Observation of Image Characteristics in a Plane MirrorSubject: Physics – Optics (Natural Science)Experiment Objective: To verify that a plane mirror forms an image that is upright, the same size as the object, and laterally inverted by observing the simultaneous motion of a raised hand and its reflection.Experimental Equipment: One vertical plane mirror (clean and flat); one participant; well-lit indoor space.Experimental Procedure:1. Place the plane mirror vertically against a wall.2. The participant stands upright directly in front of the mirror at a normal viewing distance, facing it.3. Keep the body still and eyes focused on the mirror image.4. Slowly raise the left hand from the side up to shoulder height.5. Observe the movement of the hand and the corresponding movement of the image in the mirror.Observation of Experimental Phenomena:- The image in the mirror remains upright.- When the left hand is raised, the image appears to raise its right hand.- The height, shape, and speed of the image’s hand match those of the real hand.- The motion of the object and image occurs simultaneously.Summary of Experimental Principle:A plane mirror forms a virtual image that is upright, the same size as the object, and laterally inverted. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Blowing Air to Move a CartI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Blowing Air to Move a CartSubject: Physics - Natural ScienceExperiment Objective: To verify that air flow can exert a force on an object, causing a cart to move in the direction of the air flow, and that stronger air flow produces faster motion.II. Experimental EquipmentSmall wheeled cart (lightweight), horizontal table or desk (smooth surface), straw (straight, clean), optional tape to mark starting position.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the horizontal table in a stable position. Put the small wheeled cart on the table and ensure it is at rest. Optionally mark the starting position of the cart.2. Positioning: Hold the straw behind the cart, aligned with the direction in which the cart can roll freely. Keep the straw a short distance from the back of the cart without touching it.3. Gentle Blowing: Blow gently through the straw toward the back of the cart for a short time. Observe the cart’s movement.4. Strong Blowing: Return the cart to its original resting position. Blow more strongly through the straw toward the cart and observe the movement again.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The cart is stationary on the horizontal table.2. Gentle Blowing: When air is gently blown, the cart moves forward slowly in the direction of the air flow.3. Strong Blowing: When air is blown more strongly, the cart moves forward faster, showing a clear increase in speed compared with gentle blowing.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAir has mass and can exert a force when it flows. Blowing air through the straw creates moving air that pushes on the cart. This force causes the cart to move in the direction of the air flow. When the blowing is stronger, the air flow is stronger, producing a larger force on the cart, so the cart accelerates more and moves faster.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the table surface is smooth and level. Do not let the straw touch the cart during blowing. Blow steadily to make the comparison between gentle and strong air flow clear.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Air flow can exert force on objects, and greater air flow strength produces greater motion effects. Minimum assumptions: a lightweight wheeled cart on a horizontal, low-friction surface; visible human blowing action through a straw; airflow direction aligned with cart motion.Phased Storyline: (1) Static setup phase: camera shows a horizontal table with a small cart at rest and a straw positioned behind it. (2) Gentle-action phase: gentle blowing produces slow, short forward motion of the cart. (3) Strong-action phase: stronger blowing produces noticeably faster and longer forward motion. Visibility requirements: cart wheels and table surface must remain in frame; relative speed difference between the two phases must be visually obvious; camera perspective should remain stable to allow direct comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Reflection of Light at Normal Incidence on a Plane MirrorI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Reflection of Light at Normal Incidence on a Plane Mirror2. Subject: Physics – Optics3. Experiment Objective: To verify that when light is incident normally on a plane mirror, the reflected light travels back along the same straight line in the opposite direction, demonstrating the law of reflection.II. Experimental EquipmentPlane mirror (medium size), flashlight (with a focused beam), table, wall or screen opposite the flashlight, darkened room (slightly dim), optional tape or stand to fix mirror position.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the plane mirror vertically on a table, ensuring the mirror surface is perpendicular to the tabletop. Darken the room slightly so light paths are visible.2. Alignment: Hold the flashlight so that its beam is directed straight toward the center of the mirror surface, as close to perpendicular (normal incidence) as possible.3. Core Operation: Turn on the flashlight and keep it steady, maintaining the vertical alignment toward the mirror.4. Observation: Observe the path of the incident beam and the reflected beam, and look for a bright spot formed on the wall along the same straight line as the incident beam.5. Completion: Turn off the flashlight and restore normal room lighting.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The incident light beam travels in a straight line toward the mirror.2. After striking the mirror at normal incidence, the reflected light travels back along the same line in the opposite direction.3. A clear and bright light spot appears on the wall, aligned with the incident beam path.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleA plane mirror reflects light according to the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. When light strikes the mirror at normal incidence (angle of incidence = 0°), the reflected light retraces the same path in the opposite direction. This experiment visually confirms the rectilinear propagation of light and the reflection law.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Reflection of light at normal incidence on a plane mirror. Minimum assumptions: light travels in straight lines in a uniform medium; a plane mirror reflects light according to the law of reflection; normal incidence means the incident ray is perpendicular to the mirror surface.Expected phased storyline: (1) Setup phase – a plane mirror stands vertically on a table in a dim room, with a flashlight positioned facing it. (2) Action phase – the flashlight is turned on and aimed perpendicular to the mirror, producing a straight incident beam. (3) Causal transition – upon hitting the mirror, the light reflects according to the law of reflection. (4) Result phase – the reflected beam travels back along the same line in the opposite direction, forming a clear, aligned spot on the wall. Visibility constraints: the room must be dim enough to see the beam paths, and the camera angle should show both the mirror surface and the aligned incident/reflected beams clearly.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Vibration of a Tuning Fork Causes Water SplashesI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Vibration of a Tuning Fork Causes Water Splashes2. Subject: Natural Science - Physics3. Experiment Objective: To verify that a vibrating object can transfer energy to a medium and cause visible effects, by observing water splashes produced when a vibrating tuning fork touches the water surface.II. Experimental EquipmentMetal tuning fork (1), small hammer or rubber mallet (1), shallow container or dish, clean still water.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Pour a small amount of clean water into the shallow container and place it on a stable surface. Ensure the water surface is calm and still.2. Holding the Equipment: Hold the metal tuning fork firmly by its handle with one hand, and hold the small hammer with the other hand.3. Striking the Tuning Fork: Use the hammer to strike one prong of the tuning fork once with moderate force to make it vibrate.4. Core Operation: Immediately after striking, bring the vibrating tuning fork so that its prongs lightly touch the surface of the still water.5. Observation: Keep the tuning fork in light contact with the water for a short moment while carefully observing the water surface.6. Completion: Remove the tuning fork from the water and allow the vibration to stop.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The water surface is smooth and still before contact.2. During Contact: When the vibrating tuning fork touches the water, dense and fine small splashes appear instantly on the water surface.3. End State: The splashes continue briefly and gradually disappear as the tuning fork vibration weakens and stops.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleA tuning fork vibrates after being struck, moving its prongs back and forth rapidly. When the vibrating prongs touch the water surface, they transfer mechanical energy to the water, disturbing it and causing small splashes. As the vibration decreases, the energy transfer weakens and the splashes stop. This demonstrates that vibration is a form of motion that can transfer energy to surrounding media.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Mechanical vibration transfers energy to a medium and produces observable effects. Minimum assumptions: a metal tuning fork can vibrate after being struck, water responds visibly to rapid contact, and hand actions are continuous and realistic.Phased storyline: (1) Still setup with calm water and visible tools; (2) single clear strike causing visible vibration; (3) immediate light contact between vibrating prongs and water; (4) instant appearance of dense fine splashes; (5) splashes fade as vibration decays. Visibility constraints: close framing on tuning fork prongs and water surface, continuous shot without cuts, clear view of hand movements and causal transitions.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Charged Particle Paths in a Magnetic Field (Detector Model)2. Subject: Natural Science – Astrophysics & Astronomy3. Experiment Objective: To observe how charged particle trajectories change in a uniform magnetic field by comparing straight-line motion with curved paths when the field is switched on and reversed, and to understand the Lorentz force principle used in particle detectors.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent cylindrical detector chamber; charged particle source (emitting electrons or similar charged particles); uniform magnetic field generator (solenoid or equivalent) with reversible current; power supply and switch; track-visualization medium (gas with ionization glow or simulated visible tracks); observation window or camera.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the cylindrical detector is transparent and sealed. Place the charged particle source at the center or base of the chamber. Set the magnetic field to OFF.2. Baseline Observation (Field OFF): Activate the particle source. Observe and record the particle paths inside the chamber.3. Magnetic Field ON: Switch on the uniform magnetic field in a fixed direction. Keep the particle source emitting and observe the change in particle trajectories.4. Magnetic Field Reversal: Reverse the direction of the magnetic field while maintaining the same field strength. Observe the new trajectories.5. Completion: Switch off the particle source and magnetic field. End observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. With magnetic field OFF: Charged particles travel in approximately straight-line paths from the source.2. With magnetic field ON: Particle paths curve smoothly into circular or helical arcs within the detector.3. With magnetic field REVERSED: The curvature direction of the particle paths reverses, forming arcs bending the opposite way.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCharged particles moving in a magnetic field experience the Lorentz force, which acts perpendicular to both the particle velocity and the magnetic field. Without a magnetic field, particles move straight. When a uniform magnetic field is applied, the perpendicular force causes circular or helical motion. Reversing the magnetic field reverses the force direction, leading to opposite curvature. This principle underlies trajectory reconstruction in particle detectors.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the magnetic field is uniform; keep field strength constant when reversing direction; maintain clear visibility of tracks; follow electrical safety procedures.

Experimental EquipmentInfrared array camera with display or computer interface; tripod or fixed mount; dark room or light-proof enclosure; cool background surface (wall or board at room temperature or lower); warm object (heated metal block, warm water bottle, or hand); power supply; time-lapse or continuous recording function.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Darken the room completely and eliminate visible light sources. Mount the infrared array camera on a tripod facing a uniform cool background. Set the camera to time-lapse or continuous recording mode.Core Operation: Hold the warm object outside the field of view. Slowly move it horizontally across the camera field of view at a constant speed. When the object reaches the center of the frame, pause for 1 to 2 seconds, then continue moving until it exits the frame.Recording and Ending: Stop the recording after the object fully leaves the field of view. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Covered Mass Beneath a Stretched Fabric Bending Paths of Rolling MarblesSubject: Natural Science – Astrophysics & AstronomyExperiment Objective: To simulate how mass curves space and alters motion paths by observing how a hidden central mass deforms a stretched elastic fabric and bends the rolling paths of glass marbles; to record the process using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentCircular rigid frame (diameter 40–60 cm), elastic fabric (e.g., spandex or lycra), heavy spherical mass (metal ball or weight), opaque cover cloth, glass marbles (5–10, identical size), camera or smartphone with tripod, stable table or stand.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Secure the elastic fabric tightly over the circular frame so it is flat and evenly stretched. Place the frame horizontally on a stable support. Position the heavy mass directly under the center of the fabric so it is hidden from view, then cover the underside with opaque cloth.Camera Setup: Mount the camera above the frame, centered vertically. Fix focus and exposure; enable time-lapse or continuous recording without refocusing.Core Operation: Gently place one glass marble at the outer edge of the fabric and release it without pushing. Repeat with additional marbles from different edge positions, allowing each to roll freely.Recording: Keep the camera fixed while marbles roll across the fabric, curve inward, and spiral or fall toward the center depression.Completion: Stop recording after all marbles have completed their motion. Remove marbles and safely dismantle the setup.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The fabric appears flat from above; the central mass is not visible. Marbles at the edge are stationary.During Motion: As marbles roll, their paths curve toward the center instead of moving in straight lines. Marbles released at higher speeds may spiral around the center before descending.Final State: Marbles settle near the central depression formed by the hidden mass.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe hidden mass stretches the elastic fabric downward, creating a curved surface. Rolling marbles follow the curved geometry, resulting in bent trajectories toward the mass. This serves as a two-dimensional analogy for gravity in astrophysics, where mass curves spacetime and influences the motion of objects.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the fabric is evenly stretched to avoid asymmetric paths. Release marbles gently without external force. Keep the camera fixed throughout recording. Prevent marbles from falling off the frame.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Using a fabric-and-marble analogy to demonstrate how mass curves space and alters motion paths. Minimum assumptions: an elastic surface under tension, a hidden central mass causing deformation, and marbles moving only under gravity along the surface. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) flat-looking fabric with no visible mass; (2) marbles released from the edge begin moving; (3) fabric deformation causes inward-curving marble paths; (4) marbles spiral or converge near the center. Visibility constraints: overhead fixed camera, clear view of marble trajectories, stable lighting, and no camera refocus to allow time-lapse verification of curved paths and causal sequence.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Gas Discharge Tube Glowing When High Voltage Is AppliedI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Gas Discharge Tube Glowing Under High Voltage2. Subject: Natural Science – Astrophysics & Astronomy3. Experiment Objective: To observe the luminous phenomenon produced by a gas discharge tube under high voltage, understand gas ionization and emission of light, and relate the phenomenon to astrophysical emission spectra.II. Experimental EquipmentSealed glass gas discharge tube (filled with low-pressure gas such as neon or argon), high-voltage power supply with adjustable voltage control, insulated connecting wires, tube holder or stand, dark laboratory environment, safety gloves and insulating mat.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Place the gas discharge tube securely on the holder in a darkened laboratory. Ensure the power supply voltage control is set to off (zero). Check that all connections are insulated and secure.Equipment Connection: Connect both ends of the sealed glass gas discharge tube to the output terminals of the high-voltage power supply using insulated wires.Core Operation: With one hand clearly visible, slowly turn the voltage control knob from off toward on, gradually increasing the applied voltage.Observation: Continuously observe the tube as the voltage increases, focusing on changes inside the tube.Conclusion and Shutdown: After observing the glow, slowly turn the voltage control back to off, then disconnect the power supply after the glow fully disappears.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The gas discharge tube is dark and transparent with no visible light emission.2. During Voltage Increase: As the voltage reaches a threshold, the gas inside the tube begins to glow. The glow appears along the length of the tube and becomes brighter as voltage increases.3. Stable State: A steady, uniform colored glow is observed inside the tube while voltage is maintained.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhen a high voltage is applied across a low-pressure gas in a sealed tube, free electrons are accelerated by the electric field and collide with gas atoms. These collisions excite the atoms to higher energy states. When the atoms return to lower energy states, they emit light at characteristic wavelengths, producing a visible glow. This principle is fundamental to understanding emission spectra observed in astrophysics, such as those from nebulae and interstellar gas clouds.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the laboratory is dark to enhance visibility of the glow. Do not touch the tube or exposed connectors during operation. Always increase and decrease voltage slowly to avoid electrical hazards.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Gas discharge and light emission caused by ionization of low-pressure gas under high voltage. Minimum assumptions: a dark lab, a sealed glass gas discharge tube, a functional high-voltage power supply, and a human hand operating the voltage control.Phased Storyline: (1) Initial dark scene with inactive tube and power supply off; (2) hand turns the voltage control from off toward on; (3) at sufficient voltage, gas inside the tube ionizes and begins to glow; (4) glow stabilizes and becomes brighter as voltage increases. Visibility constraints: the lab must be dark enough to clearly see the glow, the tube interior must be visible, and the hand–control interaction must be clearly shown to verify causality.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Balloon Rupture Dispersing Colored Powder to Model Supernova EjectaI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Balloon Rupture Dispersing Colored Powder to Model Supernova Ejecta2. Subject: Natural Science – Astrophysics & Astronomy3. Experiment Objective: To model the radial expansion of supernova ejecta by observing the rapid outward dispersal of colored powder after a balloon rupture; to practice controlled experimental setup and fixed-focus time-lapse observation.II. Experimental EquipmentThin latex balloon, colored powder (chalk powder or cornstarch with pigment), string or thread, support frame or hook, pin or needle, camera or smartphone with tripod, protective goggles, mask, and newspaper or tray for cleanup.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Wear goggles and mask. Cover the floor with newspaper. Fill a thin latex balloon with a small amount of colored powder and tie it securely.Suspension Setup: Use string to suspend the balloon freely in mid-air from a support so it does not touch other objects.Camera Setup: Place the camera on a tripod facing the balloon. Fix focus and exposure. Set time-lapse or high-frame-rate recording.Core Operation: Start recording. Gently approach with a pin and puncture the balloon at one point.Completion: Allow the powder to fully disperse and settle. Stop recording and clean the area.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The balloon is intact, spherical, and stationary with colored powder confined inside.Rupture Moment: Upon puncture, the balloon rapidly tears.After Rupture: Colored powder disperses outward in all directions, forming a roughly radial cloud before slowing and falling under gravity.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment models supernova ejecta expansion. When the balloon ruptures, internal pressure confinement is suddenly removed, allowing the powder to move outward rapidly. This radial dispersal qualitatively represents how stellar material is expelled into space during a supernova explosion, though without gravity-free conditions or true explosive energy.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse minimal powder to avoid inhalation hazards. Maintain distance during rupture. Ensure camera focus is fixed before puncturing. Clean thoroughly after the experiment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Radial expansion of supernova ejecta modeled by sudden release of confined material. Minimum assumptions: a suspended container, internal material under slight pressure, instantaneous rupture, fixed camera viewpoint.Phased storyline: (1) Stable suspended balloon with visible colored powder; (2) pin-induced rupture event; (3) immediate radial dispersal of powder forming an expanding cloud; (4) dispersion slows and settles under gravity. Visibility constraints: clear side view, fixed focus, unobstructed background to verify radial motion and causal sequence.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Curved Deflection of Steel Balls by a MagnetI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Curved Deflection of Steel Balls Passing a Heavy Magnet2. Subject: Natural Science – Astrophysics & Astronomy (analogy to gravitational deflection)3. Experiment Objective: To observe how a central attractive force alters the trajectory of moving objects, and to compare the deflection of two identical steel balls launched at different speeds past a fixed heavy magnet on a smooth surface using time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentSmooth horizontal table or air-hockey style surface; heavy permanent magnet (disk or block type); two identical steel balls; launch guide or ruler for consistent direction; tape or marker for fixing magnet position; camera or smartphone with tripod; time-lapse or fixed-focus recording mode.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the smooth table in a stable, well-lit environment. Fix the heavy magnet firmly at the exact center of the table using tape so it cannot move.2. Camera Setup: Mount the camera directly above the table, ensure the entire table is in frame, and lock focus and exposure. Set to time-lapse or continuous recording.3. Launch Setup: Choose one edge of the table as the launch edge. Align a ruler or guide so both steel balls can be launched along the same initial straight-line path that passes near, but not directly toward, the magnet.4. Slow Ball Launch: Gently roll the first steel ball along the guide with a relatively low speed so that it passes the magnet at a close distance. Allow it to complete its motion and come to rest.5. Fast Ball Launch: Using the same guide and starting point, launch the second steel ball with a noticeably higher speed so it passes the magnet along the same initial path.6. Recording: Ensure both launches are clearly recorded under identical camera conditions. Stop recording after both balls have completed their trajectories.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both steel balls initially move in straight lines on the smooth surface when far from the magnet.2. Near the Magnet: As each ball passes near the heavy magnet, its path bends toward the magnet due to magnetic attraction.3. Speed Comparison: The slower ball shows a larger curvature (greater deflection), while the faster ball shows a smaller curvature and passes the magnet with less deviation.4. Final Paths: After passing the magnet, each ball continues along a new straight-line direction different from its original path.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe experiment demonstrates how an attractive central force changes the trajectory of a moving object. The magnetic force between the steel ball and the magnet acts perpendicular to the ball’s initial motion, causing curved deflection. A slower ball spends more time under the influence of the magnetic force, resulting in greater deflection, while a faster ball experiences less deflection. This setup provides a tabletop analogy to astrophysical phenomena such as gravitational deflection of objects moving past massive bodies.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the table is level and smooth to minimize friction effects.2. Fix the magnet securely so it does not slide toward the ball.3. Use identical steel balls to ensure fair comparison.4. Keep camera focus fixed to avoid visual inconsistencies in time-lapse footage.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: attractive central force causing curved trajectories, analogous to gravitational deflection. Minimum assumptions: smooth low-friction surface, fixed central magnet, identical steel balls, same initial direction with different speeds. Expected phased storyline: (1) static setup with central magnet and clear launch edge; (2) first, slower ball moves straight then curves strongly toward magnet; (3) second, faster ball follows same initial line but curves less; (4) both exit along new straight paths. Verification requires overhead fixed-focus view so curvature and relative deflection are clearly visible and comparable.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Horizontal Launch vs Vertical Drop of a BallSubject: Natural Science – Astrophysics & Astronomy (Classical Mechanics)Objective: To demonstrate that horizontal motion does not affect vertical falling time by comparing a horizontally launched ball with a vertically dropped ball from the same height.II. EquipmentTable with a sharp edge (uniform height), two identical solid balls (same size, mass, and color), ruler or meter stick (optional), flat floor area, camera or observer at the side (optional for recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the table on a flat floor. Ensure sufficient space in front of the table edge. Verify the two balls are identical.2. Positioning: Hold one ball at the table edge, ready to be pushed horizontally. Hold the second ball at the same height directly above the floor beside the table edge.3. Simultaneous Release: At the same moment, gently push the first ball horizontally off the table (no upward or downward force) while releasing the second ball straight down.4. Observation: Watch both balls from release until they strike the floor.5. Completion: Note the timing and positions where both balls hit the floor.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both balls start at the same vertical height; one has horizontal velocity, the other has none.2. During Motion: The launched ball follows a curved (parabolic) path; the dropped ball falls straight down.3. Final State: Both balls hit the floor at nearly the same time, though at different horizontal positions.V. Experimental Principle SummaryThe experiment demonstrates the independence of horizontal and vertical motion. Both balls have the same initial vertical velocity (zero) and experience the same gravitational acceleration downward. Therefore, their vertical motions are identical, causing them to reach the floor simultaneously. The horizontal velocity only affects horizontal displacement, not falling time.VI. PrecautionsEnsure simultaneous release; avoid adding vertical force during the horizontal launch; keep observers clear of the landing area.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Independence of horizontal and vertical motion under uniform gravity. Minimum assumptions: constant gravitational acceleration, negligible air resistance, identical balls, same initial height, simultaneous release.Phased Storyline: (1) Setup—two identical balls aligned at the same table height; (2) Action—one ball pushed horizontally as the other is released vertically at the same instant; (3) Motion—horizontal ball shows forward motion plus downward fall, vertical ball falls straight down; (4) Outcome—both contact the floor at nearly the same time. Visibility constraints: side view showing table edge, trajectories, and floor contact clearly to verify simultaneity and differing paths.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Liquid in a Clear Rotating Container Forming a Curved SurfaceI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Curved Liquid Surface in a Rotating Container2. Subject: Natural Science – Astrophysics & Astronomy (Classical Mechanics Analogy)3. Experiment Objective: To observe how rotation affects a liquid surface, understand the effect of rotation and effective centrifugal force on fluids, and relate the phenomenon to rotating reference frames in astronomy.II. Experimental EquipmentClear cylindrical container (transparent plastic or glass), clean water, motorized turntable with adjustable speed, stable base, camera or smartphone with tripod, optional ruler or scale for height reference.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the motorized turntable on a stable, level surface. Fix the clear cylindrical container at the center of the turntable. Pour water into the container to about half its height. Set the camera on a tripod facing the container and fix the focus.2. Initial Observation: Ensure the turntable is not rotating. Observe that the water surface is flat and horizontal.3. Core Operation: Start the turntable at a low speed. Gradually increase the rotation speed in a smooth and continuous manner.4. Time-Lapse Recording: Keep the camera focus and position fixed while recording or taking time-lapse images during the speed increase.5. Completion: After clear surface curvature is observed, stop increasing speed and allow the rotation to stabilize. Turn off the turntable after observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. At rest, the water surface is flat.2. As rotation begins, the water near the walls slowly climbs upward.3. With higher rotation speed, the surface becomes clearly curved, lower in the center and higher at the edges, forming a smooth concave shape.4. At constant speed, the curved surface remains stable.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhen the container rotates, the water experiences an outward effective centrifugal force in the rotating frame. This force increases with distance from the rotation axis, causing water to move outward and upward along the container walls. Gravity pulls downward, and the balance between gravity and the centrifugal effect produces a curved liquid surface shaped like a paraboloid. This experiment models rotating systems in astrophysics, such as accretion disks and rotating planets.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the container is firmly fixed to prevent slipping. Do not overfill the container. Increase rotation speed gradually to avoid splashing. Keep electrical components away from water.

(3) Stabilization phase – at higher constant speed, a clear, smooth curved surface forms, lowest at the center and highest at the edges. Visibility constraints: the container must be transparent, the camera angle must clearly show the water surface profile, and focus must remain fixed to verify gradual, causal surface deformation.

Handheld infrared camera (with color temperature display enabled)2. Room-temperature tabletop (wood or plastic surface)3. Warm ceramic mug (filled with hot water, surface warm but safe to touch)4. Cold metal object (e.g., metal spoon or block cooled with ice water)5. Safety gloves or cloth (optional, for handling hot or cold objects)Experimental Procedure:1. Preparation: Turn on the handheld infrared camera and allow it to calibrate. Set the display to a standard false-color temperature scale.2. Initial Observation: Aim the infrared camera steadily at the empty tabletop and observe the uniform temperature color, representing room temperature.3. Warm Object Placement: Place the warm ceramic mug onto the tabletop while keeping the camera aimed at the surface. Hold the camera steady to capture the change.4. Observation of Warm Object: Observe the mug appearing in high-temperature colors (e.g., yellow/red/white) compared to the tabletop. Note any warming of the contact area.5. Cold Object Placement: Place the cold metal object onto the tabletop at a different position.6. Observation of Cold Object: Observe the cold metal object appearing in low-temperature colors (e.g., blue/purple) and the cooler contact area on the tabletop.7. Conclusion: Remove the objects and observe the gradual return of the tabletop temperature toward uniformity.Observation of Experimental Phenomena:1. Initial State: The tabletop appears in a relatively uniform color, indicating room temperature.2. Warm Mug Placement: The ceramic mug appears significantly brighter or warmer in color than the tabletop, clearly standing out on the infrared display.3. Experiment Title: Using a Compact Disc as a Diffraction Grating2. Subject: Natural Science – Astrophysics & Astronomy (Optics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the diffraction and dispersion of white light using the microscopic track structure of a compact disc, understand how a diffraction grating separates light into its component colors, and learn how viewing angle affects observed spectra.II. Experimental EquipmentReflective compact disc (CD or DVD), white LED flashlight (continuous white light), dark room or darkened enclosure, flat surface or table, camera or smartphone with manual focus capability, tripod or stable support for camera (recommended).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Darken the room as much as possible to reduce ambient light. Place the compact disc flat on a table with the reflective side facing upward. Set the camera on a tripod and manually fix the focus on the CD surface.2. Illumination Setup: Hold or mount the white LED flashlight so that it shines steadily onto the CD surface from one side at a shallow angle. Keep the flashlight fixed throughout the experiment.3. Core Operation: Start recording or time-lapse photography. Slowly tilt one edge of the CD upward while keeping the flashlight stationary. Then gently rotate the CD around its center, maintaining slow and continuous motion.4. Observation Phase: Continue tilting and rotating the CD, allowing the camera to capture changes in the reflected light patterns. Avoid sudden movements to ensure clear observation of gradual changes.5. Completion: Stop recording. Return the CD to a flat position, turn off the flashlight, and restore room lighting.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: When the CD lies flat, reflected white light appears bright with limited color separation.2. During Tilting: As the CD is tilted, distinct rainbow-like bands of color (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet) appear on the CD surface or in the reflected light.3. During Rotation: Rotating the CD causes the colored bands to shift position and orientation smoothly, with different colors becoming more prominent at different angles.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleA compact disc has closely spaced spiral tracks that act as a diffraction grating. When white light from the LED flashlight strikes the CD, different wavelengths are diffracted at different angles according to the grating equation. As the viewing and incident angles change during tilting and rotation, constructive interference occurs for different wavelengths, producing visible rainbow spectra. This demonstrates the wave nature of light and the principle of diffraction and dispersion.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the flashlight remains fixed to maintain a clear cause–effect relationship. Perform movements slowly for stable observation. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Reaction of Ferric Chloride and Ferrous Sulfate with Sodium HydroxideSubject: Chemistry – Inorganic ChemistryObjective: To observe and compare the reactions of ferric ions and ferrous ions with hydroxide ions, and to understand the differences in properties between Fe3+ and Fe2+ through precipitation phenomena.II. Experimental EquipmentTest tubes (2), test tube rack, droppers (2), ferric chloride solution (FeCl3, yellow-brown), ferrous sulfate solution (FeSO4, pale green), sodium hydroxide solution (NaOH, colorless), safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Place two clean test tubes side by side on a test tube rack and wear safety goggles.2. Add about one-third volume of ferric chloride solution into the left test tube.3. Add about one-third volume of ferrous sulfate solution into the right test tube.4. Using a dropper, slowly add sodium hydroxide solution dropwise into the left test tube while gently shaking.5. Using another dropper, slowly add sodium hydroxide solution dropwise into the right test tube while gently shaking.6. Place both test tubes back on the rack and observe the changes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Left test tube (ferric chloride): Upon adding sodium hydroxide, a reddish-brown gelatinous precipitate forms immediately.2. Right test tube (ferrous sulfate): Upon adding sodium hydroxide, a pale green precipitate forms; after standing briefly in air, it gradually turns brown.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesFerric ions (Fe3+) react with hydroxide ions (OH−) to form insoluble ferric hydroxide, which appears as a reddish-brown precipitate: Fe3+ + 3OH− = Fe(OH)3↓. Ferrous ions (Fe2+) react with hydroxide ions to form ferrous hydroxide, a pale green precipitate: Fe2+ + 2OH− = Fe(OH)2↓. Ferrous hydroxide is unstable in air and is gradually oxidized by oxygen to ferric hydroxide, causing the color to turn brown. Experimental PrecautionsAdd sodium hydroxide slowly to avoid splashing; observe color changes promptly; dispose of waste solutions according to laboratory rules.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Electrical Discharge Streamers in a Plasma Globe2. Subject: Natural Science – Astrophysics & Astronomy3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand plasma globe electrical discharge streamers formed by accelerated electrons in a low-pressure gas, and to analyze how external electric fields caused by human touch influence plasma behavior.II. Experimental Equipment1. Plasma globe (commercially available, intact glass sphere)2. Power supply (integrated with plasma globe)3. Dark or dimly lit room4. Human participant (bare fingertip)5. Camera with tripod (capable of time-lapse recording, fixed focus)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the plasma globe on a stable surface in a dim room. Ensure the glass surface is clean and dry. Mount the camera on a tripod facing the plasma globe and fix the focus manually.2. Power Activation: Turn on the plasma globe and allow the internal plasma filaments to stabilize for several seconds.3. Core Operation: The participant gently touches the glass surface of the plasma globe with one fingertip. Keep the fingertip in contact and slowly move it along the surface in a continuous path.4. Recording: Start time-lapse or continuous recording with fixed focus while the fingertip moves. Maintain steady motion without lifting the finger.5. Completion: After sufficient observation, stop recording, remove the fingertip, turn off the plasma globe, and power down the camera.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Without touch, multiple thin, branching plasma filaments extend randomly from the central electrode to the inner glass surface.2. During Touch: When the fingertip touches the glass, several plasma filaments intensify, brighten, and converge toward the contact point.3. During Movement: As the fingertip moves slowly, the brightest plasma streamers follow the fingertip’s path along the glass surface.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA plasma globe contains a low-pressure noble gas. When powered, a high-voltage alternating electric field accelerates free electrons, ionizing the gas and forming visible plasma discharge streamers. When a human fingertip touches the glass, the body acts as a partial electrical ground, locally altering the electric field. This increases electron acceleration toward the contact point, causing plasma streamers to concentrate and follow the fingertip. The observed behavior demonstrates principles of plasma physics, electric fields, and electron acceleration.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not strike or apply excessive force to the glass sphere.2. Ensure hands are dry before touching the plasma globe.3. Avoid prolonged operation to prevent overheating.4. manual: Instructions for the Experiment "Reaction of Chlorine Water with Potassium Iodide"I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Reaction of Chlorine Water with Potassium Iodide and Carbon Tetrachloride Extraction2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Inorganic Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the oxidizing property of chlorine, verify that chlorine can displace iodine from potassium iodide solution, and use carbon tetrachloride to extract iodine for clear visual identification through color changes and liquid stratification.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tubes (2, clean and dry), test tube rack, dropper (2–3), potassium iodide solution (KI, colorless), chlorine water (light yellow-green), carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄, colorless, immiscible with water), glass stirring rod (optional), safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean test tubes side by side on the test tube rack and wear safety goggles.2. Adding Potassium Iodide: Use a dropper to add about 2–3 mL of potassium iodide solution into one test tube. The solution should be colorless and transparent.3. Adding Chlorine Water: Slowly add chlorine water dropwise into the potassium iodide solution. Gently shake the test tube to mix.4. Adding Carbon Tetrachloride: Add about 1–2 mL of carbon tetrachloride into the same test tube. Stopper or cover the tube and gently shake, then allow it to stand undisturbed.5. Stratification: Place the test tube back on the rack and allow the mixture to separate into layers for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Potassium iodide solution is colorless; chlorine water is pale yellow-green; carbon tetrachloride is colorless.2. After Adding Chlorine Water: The solution gradually turns yellow-brown, indicating the formation of iodine.3. After Adding Carbon Tetrachloride and Standing: Two distinct layers appear. The lower carbon tetrachloride layer turns violet or purple, while the upper aqueous layer becomes lighter in color.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Chlorine is a stronger oxidizing agent than iodine. When chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution, chlorine oxidizes iodide ions (I⁻) into iodine (I₂).2. Reaction Equation: Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂3. Iodine is only slightly soluble in water but is highly soluble in carbon tetrachloride, forming a violet solution. Due to the higher density and immiscibility of carbon tetrachloride, it forms the lower layer, making the iodine color more distinct. This extraction enhances visual identification of the reaction result.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Chlorine water is irritating; operate in a well-ventilated area and avoid inhalation.2. Carbon tetrachloride is toxic; avoid skin contact and inhalation.3. Gently shake the test tube to avoid leakage or splashing.4. Dispose of waste liquids according to laboratory safety regulations.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment ‘Effect of Electrolyte Concentration on the Rate of Visible Precipitation’I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of Electrolyte Concentration on the Rate of Visible Precipitation2. Subject: Chemistry – Inorganic Chemistry / Solution Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To compare the rate of visible precipitation when the same precipitating reagent is added to ionic solutions of different effective ion concentrations, and to understand how electrolyte composition influences reaction rate.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents1. Clear glass beakers (2 identical beakers, 100–150 mL)2. Pipette or dropper (1, capable of simultaneous addition by rapid alternation or split-stream)3. Sodium sulfate solution (Na2SO4, same concentration and volume for both beakers)4. Sodium nitrate solution (NaNO3)5. Barium chloride solution (BaCl2)6. Food coloring or labels: blue for left beaker, red for right beaker (for identification)7. Safety gogglesIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, clear beakers side by side on the bench. Label or tint the left beaker blue and the right beaker red for easy identification.2. Solution Setup: Add equal volumes of sodium sulfate solution to both beakers. Then add an appropriate amount of sodium nitrate solution only to the right (red) beaker and mix gently to obtain a clear solution.3. Initial Observation: Confirm that both beakers contain clear, transparent solutions with no precipitate before the reaction.4. Core Operation: Using a pipette, simultaneously add the same amount of barium chloride solution to both beakers. Ensure the addition starts at the same time and is completed as evenly as possible.5. Observation: Closely observe both beakers immediately after addition, focusing on the onset time and intensity of white precipitate formation.6. Conclusion and Cleanup: After the phenomenon is clearly observed, stop the reaction, record observations, dispose of waste solutions properly, and clean the apparatus.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers contain clear, colorless solutions.2. After Addition: A white precipitate forms in both beakers due to the reaction between barium ions and sulfate ions.3. Rate Difference: The left beaker (only sodium sulfate) shows faster and more obvious precipitation, while the right beaker (with added sodium nitrate) shows slower or less intense visible precipitation.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Core Reaction Equation: BaCl2(aq) + Na2SO4(aq) → BaSO4(s)↓ + 2NaCl(aq)2. Principle Analysis: Barium sulfate is a very insoluble white solid. When barium chloride is added, Ba2+ reacts with SO4^2− to form BaSO4 precipitate. Adding sodium nitrate increases the total ion concentration without providing sulfate ions, reducing the effective collision frequency between Ba2+ and SO4^2− per unit volume. As a result, the rate of visible precipitation is slower in the solution containing sodium nitrate.3. Key Concept: The rate of visible precipitation depends on effective ion concentration and collision probability, even when the final products are the same.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: the effect of electrolyte composition on the rate of visible precipitation in ionic reactions, assuming basic solubility rules and ion collision theory. Minimum assumptions include that BaSO4 is insoluble and forms immediately upon sufficient ion collisions.Phased storyline: (1) Establish two beakers side by side with clear solutions and distinct left–right identification; (2) show simultaneous addition of barium chloride; (3) reveal immediate formation of white precipitate in both beakers; (4) highlight the causal contrast—faster, denser precipitation in the sodium-sulfate-only beaker versus slower formation in the beaker containing additional sodium nitrate. Visibility requires a stable frontal view so both beakers and the timing difference can be directly compared.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Paper Chromatography of Black Marker Ink on Filter PaperI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Paper Chromatography of Black Marker Ink2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Separation Methods)3. Experiment Objective: To observe that black marker ink is a mixture of different pigments and to understand the principle of paper chromatography using water as the solvent.II. Experimental EquipmentWhite filter paper (strip shape), black water-based marker, clear transparent container (e.g., beaker or glass), clean water, clip or tape (optional), camera or mobile phone with fixed focus (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Cut the filter paper into a long strip. Using the black marker, draw a small solid dot about 1–2 cm from the bottom edge of the paper. Allow the ink to dry.2. Setup: Pour a small amount of clean water into the clear container, ensuring the water depth is below the ink dot height.3. Placement: Stand the filter paper upright in the container so that only the lower edge touches the water. Ensure the ink dot is above the water surface.4. Recording: Fix the camera focus and position, then start time-lapse recording.5. Development: Allow the water to slowly wick upward along the paper until clear color separation is observed.6. Completion: Stop recording when the solvent front nears the top or the color bands are clearly separated.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The filter paper is white, and the black ink dot is concentrated and unmoving.2. During the Experiment: Water rises upward through the paper by capillary action, carrying ink components with it.3. Final State: The original black dot separates into several colored bands (such as blue, green, or yellow) at different heights on the paper.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePaper chromatography separates mixtures based on differences in solubility and adsorption. Water acts as the mobile phase, moving upward through the paper by capillary action, while the paper is the stationary phase. Different pigments in the black ink dissolve to different extents and interact differently with the paper, causing them to travel at different speeds and separate into distinct color bands.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Calcium Chloride Dissolving in Water under Ice (Exothermic Heat Release)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Calcium Chloride Dissolving in Water under Ice (Exothermic Heat Release)2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Physical Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the heat release phenomenon when calcium chloride dissolves in water, understand the exothermic nature of the dissolution process, and visually verify heat transfer by observing ice melting around the container.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass beaker (250 mL), room-temperature water (about 150 mL), solid calcium chloride pellets (approximately 10–20 g), plastic or glass stirring rod, ice cubes, shallow tray or basin for holding ice, thermometer (optional), camera or smartphone fixed on a tripod for time-lapse photography, protective gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the shallow tray on a stable surface and evenly spread ice cubes inside it. Put the empty clear glass beaker in the center of the ice-filled tray. Fix the camera position and focus so that the beaker, water level, and surrounding ice are clearly visible.2. Adding Water: Pour room-temperature water into the beaker until it is about half full. Allow the setup to stand briefly so the initial state is clearly recorded.3. Core Operation: Slowly add solid calcium chloride pellets into the beaker. Use the stirring rod to gently stir the solution to help the pellets dissolve evenly.4. Observation and Recording: Continue stirring for several seconds, then stop and allow the camera to record the changes automatically using time-lapse. Do not move the beaker or tray during recording.5. Completion: After the visible changes are recorded, stop the camera. Dispose of the solution properly and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Ice cubes around the beaker remain solid; the water in the beaker is clear and calm.2. During Dissolution: Calcium chloride pellets gradually disappear as they dissolve; the water may show slight convection or movement.3. Heat Effect: Ice in direct contact with or near the beaker melts noticeably faster than ice farther away; water may form around the base of the beaker in the ice tray.4. Final State: Most calcium chloride is fully dissolved; surrounding ice shows clear melting compared with the initial state.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCalcium chloride dissolves in water through an exothermic dissolution process. When CaCl₂(s) dissolves, it dissociates into Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. The energy released from the hydration of these ions is greater than the energy required to break the ionic lattice, resulting in net heat release. This heat is transferred through the glass beaker to the surrounding ice, causing the ice to melt. The melting of ice serves as direct visual evidence of the exothermic nature of the process.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not touch the solution directly, as it may become warm.2. Add calcium chloride gradually to avoid splashing.3. Ensure the camera remains fixed to maintain consistent time-lapse recording.4. Dispose of chemicals according to laboratory safety rules.
