manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Copper Ions Producing Characteristic Color in a Flame TestI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Copper Ion Flame Test2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Inorganic Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the characteristic blue-green flame color produced by copper ions, understand the principle of flame tests, and demonstrate standardized flame test operation with stable holding for time-lapse recording.II. Experimental EquipmentBunsen burner, metal wire loop (nichrome or platinum), copper salt solution (e.g., copper(II) chloride solution), beaker, hydrochloric acid (for cleaning wire loop), safety goggles, laboratory bench, camera fixed on tripod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear safety goggles. Light the Bunsen burner and adjust to a non-luminous blue flame. Fix the camera focus and position for time-lapse recording.2. Cleaning the Wire Loop: Dip the wire loop into dilute hydrochloric acid, then place it in the flame until no color is observed, ensuring the loop is clean.3. Dipping in Copper Salt: Dip the clean wire loop into the copper salt solution so a small amount adheres to the loop.4. Flame Test Operation: Hold the wire loop steadily in the hottest part of the Bunsen burner flame (near the tip of the inner blue cone) for several seconds, keeping the hand stable.5. Completion: Remove the wire loop from the flame, turn off the burner after observation, and place equipment safely.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The Bunsen burner flame is colorless to pale blue; the wire loop shows no color.2. During Heating: When the copper salt is introduced, the flame changes to a distinct blue-green or emerald green color around the wire loop.3. End State: The green coloration fades as the copper ions are consumed or dispersed.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCopper ions are excited by thermal energy in the flame. When excited electrons return to lower energy levels, they emit light at characteristic wavelengths, producing a blue-green flame. This emission spectrum is unique to copper ions and forms the basis of flame test identification.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the wire loop is clean to avoid interference from other ions.2. Hold the wire loop steadily to clearly observe the flame color.3. Avoid touching the hot wire loop; allow it to cool before handling.4. Maintain a fixed camera focus to ensure clear time-lapse observation.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Glass Etching with Hydrofluoric AcidSubject: Chemistry – Materials ChemistryObjective: To demonstrate selective etching of glass by hydrofluoric acid using paraffin wax as a protective mask, and to observe surface changes through time-lapse imaging.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsGlass slide; paraffin wax; stylus or needle; hydrofluoric acid solution (dilute); plastic dropper; water for rinsing; beaker; forceps; protective gloves, goggles, lab coat; camera or microscope with time-lapse function.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Clean and dry the glass slide. Put on protective equipment.2. Wax Masking: Melt or soften paraffin wax and evenly coat one side of the slide. After cooling, use a stylus to draw a clear pattern by scraping away wax to expose the glass.3. Etching: Place the slide horizontally. Using a dropper, carefully add hydrofluoric acid solution to cover the patterned area. Allow the slide to stand for a short period.4. Washing: After etching, rinse the slide thoroughly with water. Remove remaining paraffin wax to fully expose the surface.5. Observation and Imaging: Focus the camera or microscope on the slide surface and record a time-lapse sequence showing the etched pattern and surface contrast.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Glass surface is smooth and transparent; wax-covered areas are opaque.During Etching: Exposed glass areas gradually lose transparency and become matte.After Washing: A clear contrast appears; etched regions are rough/frosted, wax-protected regions remain smooth.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleHydrofluoric acid reacts with silicon dioxide in glass to form soluble fluorosilicates, removing material from exposed areas. Paraffin wax acts as a physical barrier, preventing contact between acid and protected glass, resulting in selective etching.Core Reaction: SiO2 + 6HF → H2SiF6 + 2H2OVI. PrecautionsHydrofluoric acid is highly corrosive and toxic; handle only with proper protection and supervision. Dispose of waste according to safety regulations.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Formation of Deep Blue Copper(II)–Ammonia ComplexI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Formation of Deep Blue Copper(II)–Ammonia ComplexSubject: Chemistry – Coordination ChemistryExperiment Objective: To observe the color change of aqueous copper(II) sulfate upon coordination with ammonia ligands and understand ligand substitution and complex ion formation.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsClear glass beaker (100–250 mL), dropper or pipette, glass stirring rod (optional), aqueous copper(II) sulfate solution (light blue), aqueous ammonia solution, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clean, clear glass beaker on a stable surface and put on safety goggles. Pour an appropriate volume of light blue aqueous copper(II) sulfate solution into the beaker.2. Camera Setup (for demonstration): Fix the camera focus on the beaker to ensure the entire color change can be recorded clearly for time-lapse photography.3. Core Operation: Using a dropper, add aqueous ammonia dropwise into the copper(II) sulfate solution while gently swirling the beaker to ensure uniform mixing.4. Continue adding ammonia slowly until the solution becomes uniformly deep blue.5. Finish: Stop adding ammonia, place the beaker still, and observe the final color. Dispose of the solution properly after the demonstration and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The copper(II) sulfate solution is light blue and transparent.2. During Ammonia Addition: Upon adding a small amount of ammonia, a pale blue precipitate may briefly appear.3. With Further Addition: The precipitate dissolves, and the solution gradually turns an intense, uniform deep blue.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIn aqueous solution, Cu2+ initially exists as a copper(II) aqua complex. When ammonia is added, ammonia molecules act as ligands and replace water molecules around the Cu2+ ion, forming the tetraamminecopper(II) complex [Cu(NH3)4]2+. This coordination change alters the d-orbital energy levels of Cu2+, leading to a stronger absorption of visible light and the characteristic deep blue color.

Experiment Objective: To verify that bromoethane undergoes nucleophilic substitution with aqueous sodium hydroxide upon heating, producing bromide ions, and to confirm the presence of bromide ions by silver nitrate precipitation.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Electrolytic Refining of CopperI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Electrolytic Refining of CopperSubject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Electrochemistry)Experiment Objective: To understand the principle of electrolytic refining of copper by observing current flow and electrode changes in a copper sulfate electrolytic cell.II. Experimental EquipmentBeaker or electrolytic cell, copper sulfate solution (blue), crude copper plate, pure copper plate, DC power supply, connecting wires with clips, ammeter, support stand (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Pour an appropriate amount of copper sulfate solution into the electrolytic cell until both electrodes can be fully immersed. Check that the solution is clear and blue.2. Electrode Installation: Place the crude copper plate and the pure copper plate vertically into the solution, keeping them parallel and not touching.3. Circuit Connection: Connect the crude copper plate to the positive terminal of the DC power supply as the anode. Connect the pure copper plate to the negative terminal as the cathode. Connect the ammeter in series to measure current.4. Energizing: Switch on the power supply. Adjust voltage to allow a steady current and observe the ammeter pointer deflection.5. Observation and Recording: Keep the image focused on the electrolytic cell and ammeter. Use time-lapse photography to record gradual changes at the electrodes.6. Completion: After observation, turn off the power supply, disconnect the circuit, remove electrodes, and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Copper sulfate solution is blue; both electrodes have metallic luster; ammeter reads zero.2. After Energizing: Ammeter pointer deflects, indicating current flow. The crude copper anode gradually dissolves and becomes thinner; insoluble impurities may fall to the bottom as anode mud. The pure copper cathode gradually becomes thicker and smoother as copper deposits.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleElectrolytic refining of copper is based on redox reactions under an external electric field. At the anode, copper atoms lose electrons and enter the solution as Cu2+. At the cathode, Cu2+ ions gain electrons and are reduced to pure copper metal, depositing on the cathode. Impurities either remain in solution or fall as anode mud, resulting in purified copper.Anode reaction: Cu – 2e- = Cu2+Cathode reaction: Cu2+ + 2e- = Cu

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Sodium Acetate Crystallization – Rapid Snap vs Slow CoolingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Sodium Acetate Crystallization – Rapid Snap Crystallization vs Slow Cooling Crystallization2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Physical Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To compare rapid crystallization induced by crystal seeding with slow crystallization caused by undisturbed cooling, and to understand supersaturation and nucleation in sodium acetate solutions.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical glass beakers (100–150 mL), supersaturated sodium acetate solution (clear and hot-prepared), small sodium acetate crystal seed, shallow cooling bath (room-temperature water), heat-resistant gloves or sleeves (one red, one blue), stirring rod (optional), safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Prepare a clear supersaturated sodium acetate solution by heating sodium acetate in water until fully dissolved. Carefully pour equal volumes of the hot clear solution into two identical beakers. Allow them to cool slightly without disturbance.2. Placement: Place both beakers on a stable surface. Put the blue-sleeved beaker into a shallow water bath and leave it completely undisturbed.3. Crystal Seeding (Core Operation): Using a red-sleeved hand, gently touch a small sodium acetate crystal seed to the surface of the solution in the other beaker.4. Cooling Observation: Allow the blue-sleeved beaker to cool naturally in the water bath without shaking or touching.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers contain clear, colorless liquid with no visible solids.2. Red-Sleeved Beaker (Seeded): Upon contact with the crystal seed, the solution rapidly solidifies, forming visible crystalline structures that spread quickly through the beaker (snap crystallization).3. Blue-Sleeved Beaker (Undisturbed Cooling): The solution remains liquid for a period, then gradually forms crystals as cooling continues, with slower and less dramatic solidification.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe experiment demonstrates supersaturation and nucleation. Sodium acetate forms a supersaturated solution when hot and undisturbed. Introducing a crystal seed provides nucleation sites, triggering rapid exothermic crystallization. Without seeding, crystallization occurs slowly as cooling reduces solubility, leading to gradual crystal formation.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure solutions are clear before starting; avoid shaking the beakers; handle hot solutions carefully; wear eye protection throughout the experiment.

Minimum assumptions: sodium acetate forms a clear supersaturated solution when hot; crystallization requires nucleation via seeding or sufficient cooling. Phased Storyline: Phase 1 – two identical beakers with clear solution are shown; Phase 2 – red-sleeved hand introduces a crystal seed, immediately causing snap crystallization; Phase 3 – blue-sleeved beaker remains undisturbed in a shallow bath, showing delayed, gradual crystallization. Key causal transitions: crystal seed leads to immediate nucleation; undisturbed cooling leads to slow nucleation. Visibility constraints: both beakers must remain in frame, with clear visibility of crystal growth and color cues (red vs blue sleeves) to verify causality.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Adding Baking Soda Solution to Red Cabbage Indicator Causes a Blue-Green ColorI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Adding Baking Soda Solution to Red Cabbage Indicator Causes a Blue-Green Color2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To observe the color change of red cabbage indicator in an alkaline environment and understand how indicators reflect solution acidity and alkalinity through visible color changes.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo clear glass beakers (identical size), red cabbage indicator solution (purple), clear baking soda solution (sodium bicarbonate dissolved in water), stirring rods or gentle swirling by hand, flat tabletop, camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, clear beakers side by side on a flat tabletop. Label them left and right if necessary. Pour an equal volume of purple red cabbage indicator into each beaker.2. Initial Observation: Observe that both beakers contain the same purple-colored solution and remain still.3. Core Operation: While gently swirling both beakers, slowly pour a small amount of clear baking soda solution into only the right-hand beaker. Do not add any solution to the left-hand beaker.4. Recording: Keep the camera focus fixed and record the process using time-lapse photography to capture the gradual color change.5. Completion: Stop adding solution once a clear color change is observed. Allow both beakers to rest for comparison.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Distinct Flame Emissions of Calcium and Barium SaltsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Distinct Flame Emissions of Calcium and Barium Salts2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry – Inorganic Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare the characteristic flame colors produced by calcium and barium salts, understand the flame test method for identifying metal ions, and demonstrate the distinct emission characteristics of alkaline earth metals under identical experimental conditions.II. Experimental EquipmentBunsen burner (1), heat-resistant bench mat, identical metal wire loops (2, cleaned), ceramic dishes (2, left and right), calcium salt powder (e.g., CaCl2), barium salt powder (e.g., BaCl2), laboratory tongs or holders, safety goggles, camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse photography.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Put on safety goggles. Place two ceramic dishes on the bench, the left containing calcium salt powder and the right containing barium salt powder. Ensure both wire loops are clean and identical in size and material.2. Dipping: Dip one wire loop into the calcium salt powder and the other wire loop into the barium salt powder so that a small, similar amount of powder adheres to each loop.3. Ignition: Light the Bunsen burner and adjust it to obtain a steady, non-luminous blue flame. Fix the camera focus and angle to clearly capture the flame area for time-lapse recording.4. Core Operation: Insert the calcium-loaded wire loop into the hottest part of the Bunsen burner flame and observe the flame color. Then, under the same conditions, insert the barium-loaded wire loop into the same flame region.5. Completion: Remove the wire loops after observation, turn off the Bunsen burner, and allow equipment to cool. Clean the wire loops after use.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Calcium salt: When introduced into the flame, the flame shows a brick-red to orange-red coloration.2. Barium salt: When introduced into the flame, the flame shows a yellow-green to apple-green coloration.3. Comparison: Under identical flame conditions, the two salts produce clearly different and stable flame colors, suitable for side-by-side or sequential comparison in time-lapse images.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on the flame test principle. When calcium or barium salts are heated in a flame, their metal ions are excited as electrons absorb energy and move to higher energy levels. As the electrons return to lower energy levels, they emit light of specific wavelengths. Calcium ions emit light mainly in the red-orange region, while barium ions emit light mainly in the green region. These characteristic emissions allow qualitative identification of alkaline earth metal ions.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure wire loops are clean to avoid contamination and mixed flame colors.2. Use the same flame region and similar amounts of salt to ensure fair comparison.3. Do not look directly into very bright flames at close range; wear safety goggles at all times.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Reaction of 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine with Aldehydes and AlcoholsI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Identification of Carbonyl Compounds Using 2,4-DinitrophenylhydrazineSubject: Chemistry – Organic ChemistryExperiment Objective: To distinguish an aldehyde from an alcohol by observing the formation of a solid precipitate when reacting with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (DNPH), and to understand the characteristic reaction between carbonyl groups and DNPH.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsClear glass vials (2, identical), vial rack, droppers or pipettes (3), clear aldehyde sample (e.g., ethanal solution), clear alcohol sample (e.g., ethanol), 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine reagent solution (Brady’s reagent), safety goggles and gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, dry clear glass vials side by side on the rack. Put on safety goggles and gloves.2. Sample Addition: Using a dropper, add an equal small volume of the clear aldehyde to the left vial. Using a clean dropper, add the same volume of the clear alcohol to the right vial. Both liquids should be colorless and transparent.3. Reagent Addition: Using a third dropper, add several drops of 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine solution to each vial.4. Mixing: Gently swirl both vials to ensure thorough mixing without splashing.5. Observation: Allow the vials to stand briefly while observing any changes.6. Completion: Record observations, then dispose of waste according to laboratory safety rules and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both vials contain clear, colorless liquids with no solid present.After DNPH Addition: In the left vial containing the aldehyde, a yellow to orange solid precipitate gradually forms. In the right vial containing the alcohol, the solution remains clear with no precipitate.V. Summary of Experimental Principles2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine reacts specifically with carbonyl compounds (aldehydes and ketones) to form yellow or orange crystalline hydrazone precipitates. Aldehydes contain a carbonyl (C=O) group and therefore react positively with DNPH. Alcohols lack the carbonyl group and do not react under these conditions, so no precipitate forms. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Iodine–Thiosulfate Redox Titration with Starch IndicatorI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Iodine–Thiosulfate Redox Titration with Starch Indicator2. Subject: Chemistry – Analytical Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To observe the redox reaction between iodine and sodium thiosulfate using starch as an indicator, master the basic titration operation, and understand the principle of color change at the endpoint.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsConical flask (250 mL), burette (50 mL) with stand and clamp, iodine solution (known concentration), sodium thiosulfate solution, starch indicator solution, dropper, white background or tile, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Rinse the burette with sodium thiosulfate solution and fill it, removing air bubbles from the tip. Place the burette vertically on the stand. Put on safety goggles.2. Sample Setup: Pour a measured volume of iodine solution into a clean conical flask. Add 1–2 mL of starch indicator. The solution turns dark blue.3. Titration Operation: Place the conical flask under the burette on a white background. Start the camera and fix the focus for time-lapse recording. While gently swirling the conical flask, slowly add sodium thiosulfate solution from the burette, initially faster and then dropwise as the color lightens.4. Endpoint Judgment: Continue swirling and adding thiosulfate dropwise until the blue color disappears completely and the solution becomes colorless. Stop adding titrant immediately.5. Completion: Record the final burette reading. Stop the recording, dispose of waste solution properly, and clean the apparatus.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The iodine solution with starch indicator appears dark blue in the conical flask.2. During Titration: As sodium thiosulfate is added, the blue color gradually becomes lighter while the flask is continuously swirled.3. Endpoint: At the endpoint, the blue color suddenly disappears, leaving a clear and colorless solution.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on a redox titration. Iodine is reduced to iodide ions by sodium thiosulfate, while thiosulfate is oxidized to tetrathionate. Starch forms a blue complex with iodine, making the reaction visually detectable. When all iodine is consumed, the blue starch–iodine complex disappears, indicating the titration endpoint.Core Reaction Equation: I2 + 2S2O3^2− = 2I− + S4O6^2−VI. Experimental Precautions1. Add starch indicator in small amount to ensure a sharp endpoint.2. Swirl the conical flask continuously to ensure uniform reaction.3. Add sodium thiosulfate dropwise near the endpoint to avoid overshooting.4. Fix the camera focus before titration to ensure clear time-lapse recording.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Hydrogen Peroxide Decomposition With Yeast Catalyst vs No CatalystI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Decomposition of Hydrogen Peroxide Using Yeast as a Catalyst2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To compare the rate of hydrogen peroxide decomposition with and without a catalyst (yeast) through visual observation of bubble formation, and to understand the catalytic role of enzymes.II. Experimental Equipment and Materials- Clear glass beakers (2, identical)- Hydrogen peroxide solution (3%, equal volumes for both beakers)- Dry yeast or yeast suspension- Measuring cylinder- Stirring rod or spoon (optional)- Camera or smartphone (fixed position for time-lapse recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear beakers side by side on a flat surface. Ensure the background is uncluttered. Fix the camera on a tripod and lock focus and angle.2. Solution Addition: Measure equal volumes of hydrogen peroxide and pour them into each beaker. Confirm that liquid levels are the same.3. Initial Observation: Observe that both beakers are colorless and transparent, with no visible bubbles.4. Catalyst Addition (Core Operation): Add a small, equal amount of yeast to the left beaker only. Do not add anything to the right beaker, which serves as the control.5. Recording and Observation: Keep the camera steady and record continuously or via time-lapse. Do not move the beakers during the reaction.6. Completion: After sufficient observation, stop recording and dispose of the solutions according to safety guidelines.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Summary of Experimental PrincipleHydrogen peroxide decomposes into water and oxygen gas: 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2↑. This reaction occurs slowly without a catalyst. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Acid–Base Neutralization in a Beaker with Color IndicatorSubject: Chemistry – Acid–Base ReactionsObjective: To observe acid–base neutralization through color change of an indicator and understand the relationship between solution pH and indicator color.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsClear glass beaker (100–250 mL), glass stirring rod or swirling by hand, dropper, clear acidic solution (e.g., dilute hydrochloric acid), clear basic solution (e.g., dilute sodium hydroxide), acid–base indicator solution (e.g., phenolphthalein or universal indicator), safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clean, clear beaker on a stable surface. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Lucas Test Comparison of tert-Butanol and EthanolI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Lucas Test – Reaction Rate Comparison of tert-Butanol and Ethanol2. Subject: Chemistry – Organic Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To distinguish tertiary and primary alcohols by observing the rate of alkyl chloride formation in the Lucas test, and to demonstrate that tert-butanol reacts rapidly while ethanol reacts very slowly or not at room temperature.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tubes (2 identical tubes), test tube rack, dropper or Pasteur pipettes, glass rod or gentle swirling by hand, Lucas reagent (concentrated hydrochloric acid saturated with anhydrous zinc chloride), tert-butanol, ethanol, stopwatch or timer, camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording, safety goggles and gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, dry test tubes in a rack. Label the left tube as tert-butanol and the right tube as ethanol. Fix the camera focus and framing so both tubes are clearly visible.2. Addition of Reagent: Using a dropper, add an equal volume (about 2 mL) of Lucas reagent to each test tube.3. Addition of Alcohols: Add the same small volume (about 0.5 mL) of tert-butanol to the left tube and ethanol to the right tube.4. Mixing: Briefly swirl each test tube gently for 2–3 seconds to mix, then return both tubes to the rack.5. Standing and Recording: Leave the test tubes undisturbed at room temperature. Record continuously or by time-lapse, without refocusing the camera, to observe changes over time.6. Completion: After clear phenomena are observed, stop recording and dispose of the reaction mixtures according to laboratory waste rules.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both mixtures are colorless and transparent immediately after mixing.2. tert-Butanol Tube (Left): Within seconds to a few minutes, the solution becomes cloudy or milky due to the formation of insoluble tert-butyl chloride.3. Ethanol Tube (Right): The solution remains clear and transparent for a long time at room temperature, with no obvious turbidity during the observation period.4. Comparative Result: The left tube shows rapid cloudiness, while the right tube shows little or no change.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe Lucas test distinguishes alcohol classes based on their reaction with concentrated HCl in the presence of ZnCl2. Tertiary alcohols, such as tert-butanol, form stable carbocations and react rapidly via an SN1 mechanism to produce insoluble alkyl chlorides, causing immediate turbidity. Primary alcohols, such as ethanol, do not readily form carbocations and react very slowly at room temperature, so no cloudiness is observed within a short time.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use equal volumes of reagents to ensure a fair comparison.2. Swirl gently to avoid splashing and ensure uniform mixing.3. Keep the test tubes stationary during observation to clearly see turbidity formation.4. Handle Lucas reagent with care, as it is corrosive.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: The Lucas test differentiates tertiary and primary alcohols by reaction rate with ZnCl2/HCl, assuming SN1 reactivity for tertiary alcohols and negligible reaction for primary alcohols at room temperature. Expected storyline: Phase 1 – two clear test tubes with Lucas reagent are prepared and alcohols are added left (tert-butanol) and right (ethanol); Phase 2 – brief swirling initiates contact; Phase 3 – standing period shows rapid cloudiness forming only in the left tube while the right remains clear. Visibility constraints: both tubes must stay in frame with fixed focus so relative clarity and turbidity over time can be directly compared.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Effect of Temperature on Reaction Rate Using the Iodine Clock ReactionSubject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Chemical Kinetics)Objective: To demonstrate that increasing temperature increases reaction rate by comparing the time required for color change in identical iodine clock reactions placed in an ice bath and a warm water bath.II. Equipment and ReagentsTwo identical clear beakers; ice bath (ice and water); warm water bath (about 40–50 °C); stopwatch or timer; camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording; iodine clock reaction solutions: Solution A (e.g., potassium iodate, sodium thiosulfate, starch indicator) and Solution B (e.g., hydrogen peroxide and acid). Safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical beakers side by side. Add equal volumes of Solution A to each beaker. Ensure both solutions are colorless and identical.2. Temperature Setup: Place one beaker into the ice bath and the other into the warm water bath. Allow 1–2 minutes for temperature equilibration without mixing.3. Camera Setup: Fix the camera focus and framing so both beakers are visible. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.4. Reaction Start: Simultaneously add the same volume of Solution B (final reagent) to both beakers. Start timing immediately and do not disturb the beakers.5. Observation: Continue recording until both solutions undergo a sudden color change.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both beakers contain colorless solutions.After Addition: Solutions remain colorless for a short induction period.Color Change: The solution in the warm water bath turns blue-black first, while the solution in the ice bath changes color noticeably later.V. Experimental Principle SummaryThe iodine clock reaction involves competing reactions that delay the appearance of free iodine until a critical point, producing a sudden blue-black color with starch. According to chemical kinetics, increasing temperature raises the average kinetic energy of particles, increasing effective collision frequency and reaction rate. Therefore, the reaction in the warm water bath proceeds faster and reaches the color-change endpoint earlier than the reaction in the ice bath.VI. PrecautionsUse identical volumes and concentrations; add the final reagent simultaneously; keep camera fixed; avoid shaking or mixing after starting.

manual: Experiment Title: Bromine Water Test—Reactivity of Benzene vs CyclohexeneSubject: Chemistry—Organic ChemistryObjective: Compare the reactivity of an aromatic hydrocarbon (benzene) and an alkene (cyclohexene) with bromine water by visual observation.Apparatus and Reagents: Two clear flasks with stoppers, benzene (left flask), cyclohexene (right flask), bromine water (orange), droppers or pipettes, lab bench, safety goggles and gloves.Procedure: Place two clean, dry clear flasks side by side on the lab bench; label left as benzene and right as cyclohexene. Add equal volumes of benzene and cyclohexene to their respective flasks. Fix the camera focus for time-lapse recording. Using separate droppers, add equal amounts of orange bromine water to each flask. Stopper and gently swirl both flasks simultaneously for mixing.Observation: Initially, both flasks contain orange bromine water. Upon swirling, the cyclohexene flask rapidly loses the orange color and becomes colorless, while the benzene flask remains orange with no obvious change under room light and without catalyst.Principle Summary: Bromine adds across the C=C double bond of alkenes, so cyclohexene undergoes an addition reaction that consumes bromine, causing decolorization. Benzene is aromatic and stabilized by delocalized π electrons; it does not readily react with bromine water without a catalyst or UV light, so the color persists.Precautions: Avoid skin contact with bromine water; use separate droppers to prevent contamination; do not expose to strong light or add catalysts; dispose of wastes properly.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Differential reactivity of alkenes versus aromatic hydrocarbons with bromine water based on addition reactions and aromatic stability. Minimum assumptions: bromine water is orange; cyclohexene contains a C=C bond; benzene is aromatic and unreactive without catalyst/light. Phased storyline: (1) Static setup—two clear flasks side by side, left benzene, right cyclohexene; (2) Action—equal orange bromine water added and gentle swirling; (3) Causal transition—time-lapse shows rapid decolorization only in cyclohexene; (4) End state—cyclohexene flask colorless, benzene flask remains orange. Visibility constraints: fixed camera focus, clear view of color in both flasks, stable lighting to verify color change and left/right identity.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Boc-Protected Amine vs Free Amine Reacting with NinhydrinI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Ninhydrin Reaction Between Free Amine and Boc-Protected AmineSubject: Chemistry – Organic ChemistryObjective: To demonstrate that free amines react with ninhydrin to produce a characteristic purple color, while Boc-protected amines show little or no color change, thereby illustrating the effect of amine protection.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTwo small glass vials with caps (left: blue cap, free amine solution; right: red cap, Boc-protected amine solution), ninhydrin solution (0.2–0.5% in ethanol or acetone), droppers or micropipettes, water bath (60–90 °C), beaker, hot plate, vial holder or rack, gloves and safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, labeled glass vials side by side in a rack. Ensure the left vial contains the free amine solution and the right vial contains the Boc-protected amine solution. Put on safety goggles and gloves.2. Reagent Addition: Using a dropper, add an equal number of drops (2–3 drops) of ninhydrin solution to each vial. Gently swirl both vials to mix.3. Heating: Place both vials simultaneously into a preheated water bath (approximately 80 °C). Ensure the liquid levels are below the vial caps and that both vials experience the same heating conditions.4. Observation: Maintain heating for several minutes. Observe and record color changes in both vials. For demonstration, fix the camera focus and record the process as a short time-lapse.5. Completion: Remove the vials from the water bath using tongs, place them back in the rack, and allow them to cool. Dispose of waste according to laboratory guidelines.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both solutions are colorless or very pale before heating.During Heating: The free amine solution (blue-capped vial) gradually develops a deep blue–purple color. The Boc-protected amine solution (red-capped vial) remains colorless or shows only a very faint yellow coloration.Final State: A clear contrast is visible between the intensely colored free amine vial and the weakly colored or unchanged Boc-protected amine vial.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesNinhydrin reacts with free primary amines upon heating to form Ruhemann’s purple, a deep blue–purple compound. In Boc-protected amines, the amino group is blocked by the tert-butyloxycarbonyl group and cannot participate in the reaction. Therefore, little or no purple color forms. This experiment visually demonstrates the role of protecting groups in organic chemistry by suppressing characteristic functional group reactions.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Ninhydrin selectively reacts with free amines but not Boc-protected amines under identical heating conditions. Minimum assumptions: two correctly identified amine samples, ninhydrin reagent, and uniform heating. Expected phased storyline: (1) static setup with two labeled vials side by side; (2) simultaneous addition of ninhydrin; (3) placement into a water bath and heating; (4) time-lapse color development where only the free amine turns purple while the Boc-protected amine remains unchanged. Visibility constraints: fixed camera focus, clear view of vial colors, and consistent framing to verify contrast and causal sequence.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Nitration Reaction of BenzeneI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Nitration Reaction of BenzeneSubject: Chemistry – Organic ChemistryExperiment Objective: To observe the nitration of benzene by mixed acid and understand electrophilic substitution reactions of aromatic hydrocarbons.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube, test tube rack, dropper, water bath, thermometer, benzene, concentrated nitric acid, concentrated sulfuric acid, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, dry test tube in a rack and wear safety goggles.2. Addition of Reagents: Add a small amount of benzene into the test tube, then carefully add concentrated nitric acid, followed by concentrated sulfuric acid along the tube wall.3. Heating: Place the test tube in a water bath and heat gently, controlling the temperature at about 55℃ for a short time.4. Reaction Completion: Remove the test tube from the water bath and allow it to stand.5. Observation: Observe the appearance and layering of the liquid in the test tube.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitially, the mixture is colorless or slightly yellow. After heating, an oily yellow liquid appears, often forming a separate layer, indicating formation of nitrobenzene.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesUnder the catalysis of concentrated sulfuric acid, nitric acid generates the nitronium ion (NO2+), which acts as an electrophile. Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution to form nitrobenzene. This reaction demonstrates the typical nitration of aromatic hydrocarbons.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution (nitration) when heated with mixed acid at controlled temperature. Minimum assumptions include correct reagents, water bath heating, and safe laboratory context. Expected storyline: (1) reagents are combined in a test tube; (2) gentle heating in a water bath initiates reaction; (3) chemical change leads to formation of a yellow oily nitrobenzene layer. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Hydrogen Peroxide Decomposition Catalyzed by YeastI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Decomposition of Hydrogen Peroxide Using Yeast Catalyst2. Subject: Natural Science - Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To observe the catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide by enzymes in yeast, compare reaction rates with and without a catalyst, and understand the role of catalysts in chemical reactions.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass containers (2 identical), hydrogen peroxide solution (same concentration, equal volume in each container), moist baker’s yeast (a small spoonful), dropper or spoon, camera with fixed focus (for real-time or time-lapse recording), tray or bench mat.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear glass containers side by side on a stable surface. Pour equal volumes of hydrogen peroxide into each container. Ensure both liquids are colorless and transparent.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly in front of the containers, ensuring both are fully visible. Fix the focus and framing; do not adjust during recording.3. Core Operation: Add a small amount of moist baker’s yeast only to the left container. Do not add anything to the right container.4. Observation: Record the containers in real time or accelerated time-lapse, observing changes immediately after yeast addition.5. Completion: After clear phenomena are observed, stop recording. Dispose of the solutions safely and clean the containers.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both containers contain clear, colorless hydrogen peroxide with no visible bubbles.2. After Yeast Addition: The left container rapidly produces a large number of bubbles and foam, rising upward due to gas release. The right container shows little to no change.3. Comparison Result: Bubbling in the left container is vigorous and continuous, while the right container remains mostly still.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesYeast contains the enzyme catalase, which acts as a biological catalyst. Catalase accelerates the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen gas. The released oxygen forms visible bubbles and foam. The right container lacks a catalyst, so the decomposition is very slow and not visually obvious.Core Reaction: 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2 (gas)This experiment demonstrates how catalysts increase reaction rates without being consumed.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Effect of Different Ionic Salts on Ice Melting RateI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Ice Melting Rates with Calcium Chloride and Sodium ChlorideSubject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Physical Chemistry)Objective: To compare the melting rate of ice when sprinkled with different ionic salts (CaCl2 and NaCl), and to understand freezing point depression and heat effects during dissolution.II. Materials and EquipmentTwo identical ice trays with equal amounts of ice; calcium chloride (solid); sodium chloride (solid); two identical spoons; flat tray or table; camera or smartphone with tripod; timer.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical ice trays side by side on a flat surface. Ensure the amount, size, and initial temperature of ice in both trays are the same. Fix the camera position and focus to cover both trays.2. Salt Application: Sprinkle an equal amount of calcium chloride evenly over the ice in the left tray. Sprinkle an equal amount of sodium chloride evenly over the ice in the right tray.3. Observation: Start the timer and record the trays continuously or using time-lapse photography for several minutes without changing camera position.4. Completion: Stop recording after a clear difference in melting is observed. Clean the area and dispose of melted ice and salts properly.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial state: Both trays contain solid ice with no visible melting.After sprinkling: Ice under both salts begins to melt.During observation: The ice in the calcium chloride tray melts faster, producing more liquid water earlier, while the sodium chloride tray melts more slowly.V. Experimental Principle SummaryBoth calcium chloride and sodium chloride lower the freezing point of water (freezing point depression). Calcium chloride dissociates into more ions and releases heat when dissolving, enhancing melting. Therefore, CaCl2 causes ice to melt faster than NaCl under the same conditions.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Evaporation Rate Comparison of Water and Rubbing Alcohol DropletsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Evaporation Rate Comparison of Water vs Rubbing Alcohol on Glass2. Subject: Natural Science - Chemistry (Physical Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To compare the evaporation rates of water and rubbing alcohol under identical conditions through visual observation, understand that different liquids evaporate at different speeds, and relate evaporation rate to properties such as volatility and intermolecular forces.II. Experimental EquipmentClean horizontal glass pane (or glass slide), dropper or pipette (2 identical droppers or one used alternately), water, rubbing alcohol (ethanol or isopropyl alcohol), marker or tape (to label left/right positions), camera or smartphone with tripod, stable indoor room environment (no strong airflow).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Clean and dry the glass pane thoroughly to remove dust, grease, or residual liquid. Place it horizontally on a stable table. Mark the left position as water and the right position as rubbing alcohol.2. Setup for Recording: Fix the camera on a tripod directly above or at a slight angle to the glass pane. Adjust focus and exposure so both droplet positions are clearly visible. Lock focus to prevent refocusing during recording.3. Droplet Placement: Using identical droppers, simultaneously place one equal-sized droplet of water on the left side and one equal-sized droplet of rubbing alcohol on the right side of the glass pane. Ensure both droplets are similar in volume and placed at the same time.4. Observation and Recording: Start time-lapse or continuous recording immediately after placing the droplets. Do not disturb the glass pane or change environmental conditions during the observation.5. Completion: Continue recording until one droplet completely disappears and the other is nearly or fully evaporated. Stop recording and clean the glass pane after the experiment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both water and rubbing alcohol appear as transparent, dome-shaped droplets on the glass surface.2. During Evaporation: The rubbing alcohol droplet gradually becomes smaller at a faster rate, its diameter and height decreasing noticeably over time. The water droplet also shrinks but more slowly.3. Final State: The rubbing alcohol droplet evaporates completely first, leaving no visible residue, while the water droplet remains for a longer time before eventually evaporating.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesEvaporation is the process by which liquid molecules at the surface gain enough energy to escape into the gas phase. Rubbing alcohol evaporates faster than water because it has a lower boiling point and weaker intermolecular forces compared to water. As a result, alcohol molecules require less energy to escape from the liquid surface, leading to a higher evaporation rate under the same environmental conditions.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure equal droplet size for a fair comparison.2. Avoid air currents, direct sunlight, or heating sources during the experiment.3. Handle rubbing alcohol carefully and keep it away from flames.4. Fix camera focus and position to ensure consistent visual comparison.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Different liquids evaporate at different rates due to differences in volatility and intermolecular forces, assuming identical environmental conditions. Minimum assumptions: same surface material, equal droplet volume, same temperature and airflow, fixed camera perspective. Expected storyline: Phase 1 – setup shows clean horizontal glass with two equal droplets placed simultaneously (water left, alcohol right). Phase 2 – both droplets gradually shrink, with alcohol visibly decreasing faster. Phase 3 – alcohol disappears first while water remains briefly before further evaporation. Visibility constraints: stable overhead or angled view, fixed focus, clear contrast between droplets and glass to verify size changes and evaporation order.

manual: Experiment Title: Sealed Plastic Bag Vinegar–Baking Soda Reaction on a BalanceSubject: Chemistry – Basic Chemical Reactions and Conservation of MassI. Experiment ObjectiveTo observe the reaction between vinegar and baking soda in a sealed system, verify gas generation, and understand the law of conservation of mass by monitoring the balance reading during the reaction.II. Experimental EquipmentElectronic balance (1); transparent plastic zip-lock bag (1, intact and sealable); vinegar (acetic acid solution); baking soda (sodium bicarbonate); small measuring spoon or paper funnel; camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Turn on the balance and zero it. Place the empty sealed plastic bag on the balance to confirm stable reading.2. Loading Reactants: Pour a measured amount of vinegar into the bottom of the bag. Carefully add baking soda so that it does not contact the vinegar yet (e.g., hold it in a folded paper or separate corner of the bag).3. Sealing: Expel excess air and completely seal the bag to ensure a closed system.4. Initial Placement: Place the sealed bag flat on the center of the balance pan. Start time-lapse recording with the camera focus fixed.5. Mixing Reaction: Gently tilt or shake the bag so that baking soda mixes with vinegar inside the sealed bag.6. Observation: Keep the bag on the balance throughout the reaction until bubbling subsides and the bag inflation stabilizes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The sealed bag lies flat on the balance; vinegar is a clear liquid and baking soda is a white solid; balance reading is stable.2. During Reaction: After mixing, rapid bubbling occurs; gas is produced, and the bag gradually inflates and becomes taut.3. Final State: Bubbling slows and stops; the bag remains inflated. The balance reading before and after the reaction is essentially unchanged.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesVinegar (acetic acid) reacts with baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) to produce carbon dioxide gas, water, and sodium acetate. In a sealed system, although gas is generated and the bag inflates, no matter escapes. Therefore, the total mass measured by the balance remains constant, demonstrating the law of conservation of mass.Core Reaction: NaHCO3 + CH3COOH → CO2↑ + H2O + CH3COONa
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: chemical reaction in a closed system and conservation of mass. Minimum assumptions: vinegar is acetic acid solution, baking soda is sodium bicarbonate, the plastic bag is fully sealed, and the balance measures total mass of the system.Expected phased storyline: (1) Static setup phase—sealed transparent bag containing separated vinegar and baking soda placed on a balance with a stable reading. (2) Mixing phase—reactants combine, bubbling begins as CO2 forms, causing visible bag inflation. (3) Completion phase—reaction slows, bag remains inflated, and the balance reading remains unchanged. Visibility constraints: camera focus and framing remain fixed to continuously show the bag and balance display, enabling verification of reaction progression and mass conservation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Cobalt Chloride Equilibrium Color Shift After Adding Water or HeatI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Cobalt Chloride Equilibrium Color Shift After Adding Water or Heat2. Subject: Chemistry – Physical Chemistry / Chemical Equilibrium3. Experiment Objective: To observe the reversible color change of cobalt chloride solution under the influence of water addition and heating, and to understand the effect of concentration and temperature on chemical equilibrium.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass container or beaker (100–150 mL), cobalt chloride solution (moderate concentration), dropper or pipette, distilled water, hot plate, heat-resistant gloves, lab bench, camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear container with cobalt chloride solution on the lab bench. Fix the camera focus and angle to ensure the container remains centered throughout recording.2. Initial Observation: Observe and record the initial color of the cobalt chloride solution (typically blue or blue-purple).3. Water Addition: Using a dropper, slowly add a small amount of distilled water into the container without stirring violently. Continue recording as the solution color changes.4. Heating: Place the same container gently onto a hot plate and apply mild heating. Do not boil. Continue recording the color change during heating.5. Completion: Turn off the hot plate after a clear color change is observed. Allow the container to cool if needed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The cobalt chloride solution appears blue or blue-purple.2. After Adding Water: The solution gradually changes to pink, indicating increased hydration.3. During Heating: The pink solution gradually returns to blue as water molecules are released.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCobalt chloride exists in an equilibrium between blue anhydrous cobalt chloride complexes and pink hydrated cobalt chloride complexes. Adding water shifts the equilibrium toward the hydrated (pink) form, while heating drives off water and shifts the equilibrium back to the anhydrous (blue) form. This demonstrates Le Chatelier’s principle, showing how concentration and temperature affect chemical equilibrium.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: reversible chemical equilibrium demonstrated by cobalt chloride color change under water addition and heating, based on Le Chatelier’s principle. Minimum assumptions: cobalt chloride solution exhibits distinct blue (anhydrous) and pink (hydrated) states; water increases hydration, heat promotes dehydration.Expected phased storyline: (1) Stable initial blue solution in a clear container on a lab bench with fixed camera focus; (2) water is added, causing a gradual and visible shift to pink; (3) the same container is heated on a hot plate, causing a gradual return to blue. Key causal transitions must be visually continuous, with no camera refocus or container change, enabling verification of cause–effect relationships within a short, accelerated time-lapse.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Single Displacement Reaction of Zinc and Copper SulfateI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Zinc Displacing Copper from Copper Sulfate Solution2. Subject: Chemistry – Inorganic Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To observe a single displacement reaction, understand metal activity series, and record the reaction process using a fixed-focus time-lapse setup.II. Experimental EquipmentGlass beaker, copper sulfate solution (blue), zinc metal strip, tweezers or forceps, support stand (optional), camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clean glass beaker on a stable surface. Pour an appropriate amount of blue copper sulfate solution into the beaker (about half full). Set the camera facing the beaker and fix the focus.2. Core Operation: Using tweezers, slowly lower a clean zinc strip vertically into the copper sulfate solution, ensuring part of the strip is fully submerged.3. Recording: Keep the beaker and zinc strip still. Maintain fixed camera position and focus while recording the reaction in time-lapse mode.4. Completion: After sufficient reaction time, stop recording. Remove the zinc strip and dispose of solutions according to laboratory rules.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Copper sulfate solution is clear and blue; zinc strip is silver-gray.2. During Reaction: A red-brown solid gradually forms on the surface of the zinc strip; the blue color of the solution slowly becomes lighter.3. Final State: Zinc surface is partially covered with copper; solution color is noticeably paler than at the start.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates a single displacement reaction. Zinc is more chemically active than copper, so zinc atoms lose electrons and enter the solution as Zn2+, while Cu2+ ions gain electrons and are reduced to solid copper.Core reaction equation: Zn + CuSO4 = ZnSO4 + CuThe visible copper deposition and fading blue color directly reflect this redox process.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Wear safety goggles and avoid skin contact with copper sulfate solution.2. Ensure the zinc strip is clean to allow clear observation of copper deposition.3. Keep the camera fixed to ensure accurate time-lapse observation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Cobalt(II) Complex Ligand Exchange with Color ChangeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Ligand Exchange of Cobalt(II) Complexes (Water vs Chloride)2. Subject: Chemistry – Inorganic Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To observe the reversible color change of cobalt(II) complexes caused by ligand exchange between water and chloride ions, and to understand the equilibrium nature of coordination compounds through visual phenomena.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsClear glass beaker (100–250 mL), glass stirring rod, dropper or pipette, aqueous cobalt(II) chloride solution (dilute, pink), concentrated hydrochloric acid, distilled water, safety goggles, gloves. Camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, clear glass beaker on the bench. Pour an appropriate amount of dilute aqueous cobalt(II) salt solution into the beaker. The solution should appear pink. Fix the camera focus and position for time-lapse photography.2. Addition of Hydrochloric Acid: While gently stirring with a glass rod, slowly add concentrated hydrochloric acid dropwise to the beaker. Continue stirring to ensure uniform mixing.3. Observation During Acid Addition: Observe the gradual color change of the solution.4. Reversal with Water: After the color change is evident, slowly add distilled water to the beaker while stirring continuously.5. Final Observation: Observe the color change as water is added. Stop stirring once the color stabilizes. End the recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The cobalt(II) aqueous solution is pink and transparent.2. After Adding Concentrated HCl: The solution gradually changes from pink to blue.3. After Adding Water: The blue color gradually fades and the solution returns toward pink.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCobalt(II) ions form different coordination complexes depending on the ligands present. In water, cobalt(II) mainly exists as the pink hexaaquacobalt(II) complex [Co(H2O)6]2+. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Bromine Water Decolorization by an Alkyne (Electrophilic Addition)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Bromine Water Decolorization by an Alkyne Solution2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry – Organic Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that alkynes can undergo electrophilic addition reactions with bromine, leading to decolorization of bromine water; to compare the reaction result with an inert solvent as a control; to strengthen understanding of unsaturated hydrocarbons and qualitative tests for multiple bonds.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents- Test tubes: 2 clear glass test tubes of the same size- Test tube rack- Droppers or pipettes: 2- Bromine water: dilute bromine solution, orange in color- Alkyne solution: clear solution of an alkyne (e.g., ethyne solution or other suitable laboratory alkyne)- Inert solvent: same volume as alkyne solution (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or cyclohexane, non-reactive)- Labels or marker for left and right test tubes- Camera or recording device with fixed focus (for time-lapse recording)- Protective gloves and gogglesIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, dry, and identical test tubes side by side on a test tube rack. Label the left test tube as Alkyne and the right test tube as Inert Solvent. Put on protective goggles.2. Adding Bromine Water: Using a dropper, add the same volume (about 2–3 mL) of orange bromine water into each test tube. Ensure both solutions appear equally orange and transparent.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly in front of the two test tubes, ensuring both tubes are fully visible. Fix the focus and framing. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.4. Addition of Reagents: Using a clean dropper, add a measured equal volume of clear alkyne solution to the left test tube. Using another clean dropper, add the same volume of inert solvent to the right test tube.5. Mixing: Gently swirl both test tubes side by side at the same time to ensure uniform mixing, avoiding splashing.6. Observation: Place the test tubes back into the rack and observe the color changes over time while recording continues.7. Completion: After the color change is clearly observed, stop recording. Dispose of the solutions according to laboratory waste regulations and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both test tubes contain orange bromine water with identical color intensity.2. After Mixing: In the left test tube containing the alkyne, the orange color of bromine water gradually fades and eventually becomes colorless or significantly lighter. In the right test tube containing the inert solvent, the orange color remains largely unchanged.3. Final State: A clear contrast is observed between the two test tubes: the alkyne tube is decolorized, while the control tube remains orange.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesBromine water is orange due to dissolved bromine molecules (Br2). Alkynes contain carbon–carbon multiple bonds with high electron density, which can undergo electrophilic addition reactions. When bromine is added to an alkyne, bromine molecules add across the multiple bond, consuming Br2 and causing the solution to lose its orange color. In contrast, an inert solvent does not react with bromine under these conditions, so no decolorization occurs. This experiment demonstrates the characteristic chemical reactivity of unsaturated hydrocarbons and provides a qualitative test for multiple bonds.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Bromine water is corrosive and volatile; handle with care and avoid skin contact.2. Ensure equal volumes are added to both test tubes for a fair comparison.3. Swirl gently to prevent splashing and ensure consistent mixing.4. Keep the camera fixed to avoid visual misinterpretation of color changes.

Minimum assumptions: bromine water is initially orange; alkyne has a reactive multiple bond; inert solvent does not react. Experiment Title: Comparison of Catalase and Heat-Denatured Catalase in Decomposing Hydrogen Peroxide2. Subject: Natural Science - Chemistry (Biochemistry Basics)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the catalytic effect of the enzyme catalase on hydrogen peroxide decomposition and to understand the effect of heat denaturation on enzyme activity through direct visual comparison.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsTwo clear test tubes (same size), test tube rack, dropper or pipette, fresh catalase solution (e.g., yeast or potato extract), heat-denatured catalase solution (prepared by boiling catalase solution for several minutes and cooling), hydrogen peroxide solution (approximately 3%), safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, dry test tubes in a test tube rack side by side. Label the left test tube as Catalase and the right test tube as Heat-Denatured Catalase. Put on safety goggles.2. Sample Addition: Add an equal volume (about 2 mL) of fresh catalase solution into the left test tube. Add the same volume of heat-denatured catalase solution into the right test tube. Ensure both solutions are clear and at room temperature.3. Core Operation: Using a dropper, simultaneously add an equal volume (about 2 mL) of hydrogen peroxide into both test tubes.4. Observation: Immediately observe and compare the changes occurring in the two test tubes.5. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Iron Nail in Blue Copper Sulfate Solution (Iron Displaces Copper)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Iron Displaces Copper from Copper Sulfate Solution2. Subject: Natural Science - Chemistry (Inorganic Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: Place a clean iron nail in a clear glass beaker containing blue copper sulfate solution and observe the changes over time through fixed-focus time-lapse recording, so as to understand the metal activity series and displacement reactions.II. Experimental EquipmentClean iron nail (1), clear glass beaker (1, 100–250 mL), blue copper sulfate solution (CuSO4, moderate concentration, enough to submerge the nail), tweezers or thread (optional, for suspending the nail), camera or mobile device with tripod (for fixed-focus time-lapse photography), safety gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear safety goggles. Ensure the iron nail is clean and free of rust or oil. If necessary, lightly polish it with sandpaper and rinse with water.2. Solution Setup: Pour blue copper sulfate solution into the clear glass beaker until it is about half full. Ensure the solution is clear and uniformly blue.3. Placement of Iron Nail: Using tweezers or by gently holding it, slowly place the iron nail into the copper sulfate solution so that it is fully submerged and not touching the beaker wall.4. Recording Setup: Position the camera directly in front of the beaker, fix the focus, and start time-lapse recording. Keep the setup undisturbed.5. Observation Period: Leave the system undisturbed for a period of time (minutes to hours; accelerated in video), allowing the reaction to proceed naturally.6. Completion: Stop recording after clear changes are visible. Remove the iron nail if required, and dispose of the solution according to laboratory rules.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The copper sulfate solution is blue and transparent; the iron nail has a metallic gray appearance.2. During Reaction: After some time, a reddish-brown solid gradually forms on the surface of the iron nail. The blue color of the solution slowly becomes lighter, especially near the nail.3. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates a metal displacement reaction based on the metal activity series. manual: Instructions for the Comparative Experiment of Sodium Sulfate Solution Reacting with Potassium Chloride Solution and Barium Chloride SolutionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparative Experiment of Sodium Sulfate Solution Reacting with Potassium Chloride Solution and Barium Chloride Solution2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Inorganic Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: Through a comparative experiment, observe and compare the reaction phenomena of sodium sulfate solution with potassium chloride solution and barium chloride solution, understand the conditions for double displacement reactions, and recognize precipitation reactions involving sulfate ions.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents1. Equipment: Test tubes (2, same specification), test tube rack, droppers (2 or one cleaned between uses).2. Reagents: Sodium sulfate solution (Na2SO4, colorless), potassium chloride solution (KCl, colorless), barium chloride solution (BaCl2, colorless).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean test tubes on the test tube rack. Using a dropper, add 5 mL of colorless sodium sulfate solution into each test tube.2. Labeling: Mark the left test tube as A and the right test tube as B for distinction.3. Reaction Operation:   (1) Left test tube (A): Use a dropper to add several drops of potassium chloride solution into test tube A. Gently shake to mix.   (2) Right test tube (B): Use another dropper (or a cleaned one) to add several drops of barium chloride solution into test tube B. Gently shake to mix.4. Observation: Place both test tubes back on the rack and carefully observe the changes in the solutions.5. Completion: Record the observed phenomena, then pour the solutions into the designated waste container and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Test tube A (Na2SO4 + KCl): The solution remains colorless and transparent, with no precipitate formed.2. Test tube B (Na2SO4 + BaCl2): A white precipitate quickly forms, and the solution becomes turbid.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Sodium sulfate reacts with potassium chloride in solution without forming a precipitate because all possible products (K2SO4 and NaCl) are soluble in water; therefore, no observable reaction phenomenon occurs.2. Sodium sulfate reacts with barium chloride to produce barium sulfate, which is insoluble in water and appears as a white precipitate.3. Core reaction equation:   Na2SO4 + BaCl2 = BaSO4↓ + 2NaCl4. Principle Conclusion: Double displacement reactions in aqueous solutions only show obvious phenomena when an insoluble substance (precipitate), gas, or weak electrolyte is formed. The formation of insoluble barium sulfate is the key reason for the observed difference between the two test tubes.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Blue Bottle ReactionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Blue Bottle Reaction (Colorless–Blue–Colorless Cycle)2. Subject: Chemistry – Physical Chemistry / Redox Reactions3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate a reversible redox reaction through visible color changes, and to understand the role of oxygen in oxidation–reduction processes.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents1. Clear glass bottle with stopper or screw cap (250–500 mL)2. Glucose solution (approximately 5–10 g glucose dissolved in water)3. Sodium hydroxide solution (0.5–1.0 mol/L)4. Methylene blue solution (0.1–0.2%, a few drops)5. Distilled water6. Safety goggles and glovesIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear glass bottle on a lab bench. Add distilled water to about half the bottle volume.2. Reagent Addition: Add glucose solution, then sodium hydroxide solution, and finally add 2–3 drops of methylene blue solution. Gently swirl to mix.3. Sealing: Seal the bottle tightly with a stopper or cap to prevent leakage.4. Core Operation (Shaking): Shake the sealed bottle vigorously for several seconds.5. Resting: Place the bottle back on the lab bench and allow it to stand undisturbed.6. Repetition: After the solution becomes colorless again, shake the bottle once more to repeat the color change cycle.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The solution is colorless or very pale.2. After Shaking: The solution rapidly turns blue.3. During Resting: The blue color gradually fades and returns to colorless.4. Repetition: The colorless–blue–colorless cycle can be repeated multiple times by shaking and resting.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on a reversible redox reaction. In alkaline conditions, glucose acts as a reducing agent and reduces methylene blue to its colorless leuco form. When the bottle is shaken, oxygen from the air dissolves into the solution and oxidizes the leuco-methylene blue back to blue methylene blue. When the bottle is left standing, dissolved oxygen is gradually consumed by glucose, reducing the dye again and causing the solution to become colorless. The visible color changes reflect the oxidation–reduction cycle.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Sodium hydroxide is corrosive; avoid skin or eye contact.2. Ensure the bottle is well sealed before shaking to prevent leakage.3. Dispose of the solution according to laboratory waste guidelines.

Minimum mechanistic assumptions: glucose reduces methylene blue in alkaline solution; oxygen oxidizes reduced methylene blue back to its blue form.Expected phased storyline: (1) Static bottle on lab bench with colorless solution; (2) bottle is sealed and shaken, introducing oxygen; (3) solution visibly turns blue; (4) bottle is set down and left undisturbed; (5) blue color gradually fades to colorless; (6) cycle may repeat. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Oil and Water Separation in a Clear ContainerI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Oil and Water Separation in a Clear Container2. Subject: Natural Science - Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the phenomenon of oil and water separating into two liquid phases, recognize immiscible liquids, and relate macroscopic observations to molecular polarity differences.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass jar with lid (1), clean water (about 1/2 jar), edible oil (such as vegetable oil, about 1/4 jar), flat table surface, camera or mobile phone with tripod (for time-lapse photography).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear glass jar on a stable table. Ensure the jar is clean and transparent. Fix the camera on a tripod facing the jar, and adjust focus so the entire jar is clearly visible.2. Adding Liquids: Slowly pour clean water into the jar until it reaches about half the jar. Then gently add oil along the inner wall of the jar so that it forms a separate layer above the water.3. Shaking: Close the lid tightly. Hold the jar and gently shake it for 3–5 seconds to mix the oil and water temporarily.4. Resting and Recording: Place the jar back on the table. Do not disturb it. Start time-lapse recording and allow the jar to stand still.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before shaking, water and oil form two distinct layers, with oil floating on top of the water.2. After Shaking: Immediately after shaking, the liquid appears cloudy, with small oil droplets dispersed throughout the water.3. During Rest: Over time, the oil droplets gradually merge and rise upward. The liquid slowly becomes clear again, finally forming two clearly separated layers, oil on top and water below.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesOil and water are immiscible liquids due to differences in molecular polarity. Water is a polar substance, while oil is non-polar. Polar and non-polar molecules do not mix well. When shaken, oil is temporarily dispersed as small droplets, but due to density differences and intermolecular forces, oil droplets coalesce and float back to the top, forming two separate liquid phases.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Shake gently to avoid leakage or excessive bubbles.2. Keep the jar undisturbed during resting to clearly observe separation.3. Ensure stable camera focus throughout the recording process.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Iron(III) Ions Reacting with Thiocyanate to Form a Blood-Red Coordination ComplexI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Iron(III) Ions Reacting with Thiocyanate to Form a Blood-Red Coordination Complex2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Coordination Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the formation of a blood-red coordination complex when iron(III) ions react with thiocyanate ions, and to understand the basic concept of coordination reactions through visual observation.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass beaker (100–250 mL), dropper or pipette, aqueous iron(III) solution (e.g., FeCl3, light yellow), aqueous thiocyanate solution (e.g., KSCN or NH4SCN, colorless), stirring rod or gentle hand swirling, camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse recording), safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clean, clear beaker on a stable surface and put on safety goggles. Pour an appropriate amount of aqueous iron(III) solution into the beaker; the solution should appear light yellow and transparent.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera facing the beaker, adjust the framing to include the entire beaker, and fix the focus to avoid refocusing during the experiment.3. Core Operation: Using a dropper, add aqueous thiocyanate solution dropwise into the iron(III) solution while gently swirling the beaker to mix evenly.4. Observation: Continue adding drops until a clear color change is observed. Maintain gentle swirling to ensure uniform mixing.5. Completion: Stop adding thiocyanate once the color change is distinct. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Ligand Substitution Alters Solubility of Silver ChlorideI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Ligand Substitution Alters Solubility: Dissolution and Re-precipitation of Silver Chloride2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Inorganic Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To observe how ligand substitution changes the solubility of a precipitate by forming and breaking a complex ion; to understand the reversible dissolution and re-precipitation of silver chloride through visual phenomena.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents1. Clear glass beakers (2, 100 mL)2. Glass stirring rod (1)3. Dropper or pipette (2)4. Aqueous silver nitrate solution (for preparing AgCl, if needed)5. Dilute hydrochloric acid solution (for preparing AgCl, if needed)6. Cloudy white silver chloride suspension (AgCl, prepared in advance in both beakers)7. Aqueous ammonia solution (NH3·H2O, dilute)8. Dilute nitric acid solution (HNO3)9. Camera or recording device fixed on a tripod (for time-lapse recording)10. Safety goggles and glovesIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place two clean, clear glass beakers on a lab bench side by side. Each beaker contains an equal volume of cloudy white silver chloride suspension. Put on safety goggles and gloves. Fix the camera focus and position to cover both beakers clearly for time-lapse photography.2. Control Observation: Do not operate on the right beaker; it serves as a comparison. Observe that both beakers initially appear milky white due to suspended AgCl precipitate.3. Addition of Ammonia: Using a dropper, add aqueous ammonia dropwise to the left beaker while gently stirring with a glass rod. Continue adding slowly until a clear change is observed.4. Intermediate Observation: Stop adding ammonia once the cloudy white precipitate in the left beaker gradually dissolves and the solution becomes clear and colorless.5. Addition of Nitric Acid: After the solution in the left beaker becomes clear, use another dropper to add dilute nitric acid dropwise to the same beaker without changing the camera position.6. Final Observation: Continue adding nitric acid until a cloudy white precipitate reappears in the left beaker.7. End of Experiment: Stop the reaction, cease recording, and compare the final states of the two beakers. Dispose of waste according to laboratory regulations and clean the apparatus.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers contain a milky white, cloudy suspension of silver chloride.2. During Ammonia Addition: In the left beaker, the white precipitate gradually decreases and finally disappears, forming a clear, transparent solution. The right beaker remains unchanged.3. During Nitric Acid Addition: The clear solution in the left beaker gradually turns cloudy again, with a white precipitate reforming.4. Final State: The left beaker again contains cloudy white silver chloride, while the right beaker shows no change throughout the experiment.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSilver chloride is a sparingly soluble salt that forms a white precipitate in water. When aqueous ammonia is added, Ag+ ions react with NH3 to form a soluble complex ion [Ag(NH3)2]+, causing the AgCl precipitate to dissolve.Core Equations:1. AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag+(aq) + Cl−(aq)2. Ag+(aq) + 2NH3(aq) ⇌ [Ag(NH3)2]+(aq)When dilute nitric acid is added, NH3 is protonated to form NH4+, reducing the concentration of free NH3. The complex ion dissociates, releasing Ag+ ions, which recombine with Cl− ions to form AgCl precipitate again. This experiment demonstrates how ligand substitution can reversibly alter solubility.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Add reagents dropwise and stir gently to ensure clear observation of gradual changes.2. Do not add excessive ammonia or nitric acid at once to avoid splashing or masking intermediate phenomena.3. Ensure the camera focus and position remain fixed throughout the experiment for accurate time-lapse recording.4. Handle nitric acid and ammonia with care; avoid skin contact and inhalation.
