Expected phased storyline: (1) Initial frame shows two beakers with identical cloudy white AgCl. (2) Ammonia is added dropwise with stirring to the left beaker, causing gradual clearing while the right beaker remains unchanged. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Reaction Between Carbon and Copper OxideI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Reaction Between Carbon and Copper Oxide2. Subject: Chemistry – Inorganic Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To understand the redox reaction between carbon and copper oxide through heating, verify that carbon can reduce copper oxide to copper, and identify carbon dioxide by passing the produced gas into clear limewater.II. Experimental EquipmentHard test tube, test tube clamp and stand, alcohol blast lamp, rubber stopper with glass delivery tube, rubber tubing, clear limewater, beaker (for limewater), black carbon powder, copper(II) oxide powder, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Put on safety goggles. Mix an appropriate amount of black carbon powder and copper oxide powder evenly, and place the mixture into a clean, dry hard test tube.2. Assembly: Fix the test tube on the stand with the mouth slightly downward. Seal the mouth with a rubber stopper connected to a glass delivery tube, and lead the other end of the tube into a beaker containing clear limewater.3. Heating: Light the alcohol blast lamp and heat the bottom of the test tube evenly, moving the flame slowly to avoid local overheating.4. Gas Collection: Continue heating so that the generated gas exits from the test tube and passes through the delivery tube into the clear limewater.5. Ending the Experiment: After clear phenomena are observed, remove the delivery tube from the limewater first, then stop heating. Allow the test tube to cool naturally.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. In the test tube: The black mixture gradually shows red or reddish-brown metallic copper after heating.2. Gas observation: Gas is continuously released from the test tube during heating.3. In limewater: The originally clear limewater gradually becomes milky white and turbid.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhen heated, carbon reduces copper(II) oxide to copper, while carbon itself is oxidized to carbon dioxide. The produced carbon dioxide passes into clear limewater and reacts with calcium hydroxide to form calcium carbonate precipitate, causing turbidity.Core reaction equations:2CuO + C = 2Cu + CO2Ca(OH)2 + CO2 = CaCO3↓ + H2OVI. Experimental Precautions1. Use a hard test tube to withstand strong heating.2. Heat evenly to prevent cracking of the test tube.3. Remove the delivery tube from limewater before stopping heating to prevent backflow.4. Handle hot apparatus carefully and follow laboratory safety rules.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Reaction Between Carbon and Concentrated Sulfuric AcidI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Reaction Between Carbon and Concentrated Sulfuric Acid2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Inorganic Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the reaction between carbon and concentrated sulfuric acid under heating conditions, verify the strong oxidizing property of concentrated sulfuric acid, and identify sulfur dioxide gas through its decolorizing effect on fuchsine solution.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsHard glass test tube, test tube clamp and stand, alcohol lamp, rubber stopper with glass delivery tube, rubber tubing, beaker or test tube containing fuchsine solution (red or magenta), black carbon powder, concentrated sulfuric acid (colorless), dropper, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Put on safety goggles. Fix the hard test tube on the test tube stand with a clamp. Place a small amount of black carbon powder at the bottom of the dry test tube.2. Adding Reagent: Use a dropper to carefully add an appropriate amount of colorless concentrated sulfuric acid to the carbon powder, ensuring it wets the carbon but does not overflow.3. Apparatus Connection: Seal the test tube with a rubber stopper connected to a glass delivery tube. Connect the delivery tube to rubber tubing, and insert the outlet into the fuchsine solution, with the tube end below the liquid surface.4. Heating: Light the alcohol lamp and gently heat the bottom of the test tube evenly. Maintain steady heating to promote the reaction.5. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesConcentrated sulfuric acid acts as a strong oxidizing agent when heated with carbon. Carbon is oxidized, and sulfuric acid is reduced, producing sulfur dioxide gas. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Iodine Solution Penetrating a Starch-Filled Semi-Permeable MembraneI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Iodine Solution Penetrating a Starch-Filled Semi-Permeable Membrane2. Subject: Natural Science – Cell & Developmental Biology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate selective permeability of a semi-permeable membrane and diffusion of small molecules by observing iodine solution diffusing into dialysis tubing containing starch, and to record the process using fixed-focus side-view time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentDialysis tubing (pre-soaked, one segment, tied at both ends), starch solution (inside tubing), iodine solution (brown-yellow), clear glass beaker, string or clips for sealing tubing, tray or bench surface, camera or mobile device with tripod for fixed side recording.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Soak dialysis tubing in water until flexible; tie one end securely. Fill tubing with starch solution using a dropper, remove air bubbles, and tie the other end to form a sealed starch-filled bag.Setup: Pour iodine solution into a clear beaker to a level sufficient to fully submerge the tubing. Place the beaker on a stable surface.Core Operation: Gently place the sealed dialysis tubing into the iodine solution, ensuring full immersion. Do not stir or disturb the system.Recording: Position the camera at the side of the beaker, fix the focus and frame, and begin time-lapse recording.Completion: Leave the setup undisturbed for observation. After recording, remove tubing and dispose of solutions properly.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Iodine solution in the beaker is yellow-brown; starch solution inside tubing is milky white.2. Over Time: The iodine solution gradually penetrates the dialysis tubing. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates diffusion and selective permeability. The dialysis tubing acts as a semi-permeable membrane that allows small iodine molecules to pass through but restricts large starch molecules. Iodine diffuses down its concentration gradient into the tubing and reacts with starch to form a blue-black complex, providing visible evidence of molecular diffusion across a semi-permeable membrane.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure tubing is tightly sealed to prevent leakage; avoid disturbing the beaker during observation; use a fixed-focus camera to maintain consistent visual comparison.

Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Culture cells expressing GFP–glucocorticoid receptor in two identical dishes under the same conditions. Replace with fresh imaging medium before microscopy.2. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Osmotic Stress on Onion Epidermal Cells Causing PlasmolysisI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Osmotic Stress on Onion Epidermal Cells Causing Plasmolysis2. Subject: Natural Science – Cell & Developmental Biology3. Experiment Objective: To observe plasmolysis in plant cells under hypertonic conditions, understand the effect of osmotic stress on cell structure, and master the technique of preparing onion epidermal peels and perfusing solutions at the edge of a slide while observing under a light microscope with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsLight microscope with camera and time-lapse function, glass slides and cover slips, fresh onion bulb, forceps, scalpel or blade, dropper or pipette, absorbent paper or filter paper, distilled water, concentrated salt solution (e.g., 10–20% NaCl), staining solution (optional, e.g., iodine or methylene blue).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation of Specimen: Use forceps to peel a thin, transparent inner epidermis from the onion scale. Place the peel flat on a clean glass slide.2. Initial Mounting: Add one drop of distilled water onto the epidermal peel and gently lower a cover slip to avoid air bubbles. Place the slide on the microscope stage.3. Initial Observation: Under low power and then high power, focus clearly on the onion epidermal cells. Adjust and fix the microscope focus and camera settings to ensure stable imaging for time-lapse photography.4. Application of Osmotic Stress: Without moving the slide or changing focus, place one drop of concentrated salt solution at one edge of the cover slip. At the opposite edge, use absorbent paper to draw the solution underneath the cover slip, allowing the salt solution to diffuse across the cells.5. Time-lapse Observation: Continuously observe and record the cells as the salt solution diffuses. Keep the focus fixed and do not adjust magnification during recording.6. End of Experiment: After clear plasmolysis is observed, stop recording. Remove the slide, discard biological waste properly, and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Onion epidermal cells appear rectangular with a distinct cell wall; the cytoplasm and plasma membrane are closely appressed to the cell wall, and the vacuole is full.2. During Diffusion: As the concentrated salt solution reaches the cells, the cytoplasm begins to shrink, and the plasma membrane gradually detaches from the cell wall.3. Final State (Plasmolysis): The protoplast is clearly retracted toward the center of the cell, leaving a visible gap between the cell wall and the plasma membrane.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates osmosis in plant cells. When onion epidermal cells are exposed to a hypertonic salt solution, water moves out of the cells through the semi-permeable plasma membrane. The loss of water reduces turgor pressure, causing the plasma membrane and cytoplasm to shrink away from the rigid cell wall, a phenomenon known as plasmolysis. This process illustrates the principles of osmotic pressure, semi-permeable membranes, and the structural characteristics of plant cells.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use a thin and intact epidermal peel to ensure clear observation.2. Avoid air bubbles when placing the cover slip.3. Do not adjust focus during time-lapse recording to maintain spatiotemporal consistency.4. Handle blades and glassware carefully and dispose of biological materials properly.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: plasmolysis in plant cells caused by osmotic stress under hypertonic conditions. Expected phased storyline: (1) clear microscopic view of intact onion epidermal cells in water; (2) concentrated salt solution introduced at the edge of the cover slip and diffuses inward; (3) gradual shrinkage of cytoplasm and detachment of plasma membrane from the cell wall; (4) stable final plasmolyzed state. Visibility constraints: fixed microscope focus, constant field of view, and sufficient magnification to resolve cell walls and protoplast changes.

Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that a small-molecule inhibitor (ascorbic acid) slows an enzyme-catalyzed color-changing reaction, and to understand the principle of enzyme inhibition through visual comparison.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo clear glass beakers (same size), catechol solution, catechol oxidase solution, ascorbic acid solution, blue tape (for labeling), dropper or pipette, lab bench, camera or smartphone with tripod (for fixed-focus time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, clear beakers side by side on a lab bench. Ensure lighting is even. Mark the right beaker clearly with blue tape.2. Reagent Setup: Add equal volumes of catechol solution and catechol oxidase solution into each beaker. Gently swirl to mix; both solutions should initially appear clear or very lightly colored.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly in front of the beakers, ensuring both are fully in frame. Fix the focus and exposure, and start time-lapse recording.4. Core Operation: Using a dropper, add a measured amount of ascorbic acid solution only to the right beaker (marked with blue tape). Do not add anything to the left beaker.5. Conclusion: Stop recording once a clear difference in color development between the two beakers is observed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Effect of Light on Genetically Similar Seedlings (Etiolation vs Normal Growth)Subject: Natural Science – Genetics & GenomicsExperiment Objective: To demonstrate how environmental factors, specifically light, influence gene expression and plant phenotype by comparing genetically similar seedlings grown under light and darkness.II. Experimental MaterialsTwo identical seedling trays; genetically similar seeds (e.g., bean or Arabidopsis); potting soil; water source; grow light; opaque cover or box; labels; fixed camera or phone tripod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fill both trays with the same amount of soil. Plant the same number of genetically similar seeds at equal depth in each tray. Label trays as Light Group and Dark Group.2. Setup: Place both trays in the same room to ensure identical temperature and humidity. Position the Light Group under a grow light. Cover the Dark Group completely with an opaque box to block light.3. Camera Fixation: Set a camera on a tripod facing both trays. Fix focus, angle, and frame. Do not adjust during recording.4. Watering: Water both trays equally at the same time each day.5. Observation Period: Record growth over several days using time-lapse photography.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial Stage: Both trays show similar germination.Growth Stage: Light-grown seedlings develop green leaves, shorter stems, and sturdy structure. Dark-grown seedlings show etiolation: elongated stems, small leaves, and pale yellow color.V. Experimental Principle SummaryAlthough seedlings share the same genetic background, light acts as an environmental signal regulating gene expression. Light stimulates chlorophyll synthesis and normal photomorphogenesis, while darkness triggers etiolation. This demonstrates gene–environment interaction, where phenotype depends on both genetic information and external conditions.VI. PrecautionsEnsure equal watering; prevent light leakage to dark group; keep camera fixed; do not disturb trays during growth.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Effect of Increasing Anesthetic Drops on Brine ShrimpI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effects of Two Anesthetic Solutions on Brine Shrimp Activity2. Subject: Natural Science – Neuroscience3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare how increasing concentrations of two different anesthetic solutions affect neural activity as reflected by changes in brine shrimp movement.II. Experimental MaterialsLive brine shrimp (equal numbers), two shallow transparent dishes (one blue, one red), seawater, two different anesthetic solutions (A and B), two droppers, stopwatch or timer (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place equal numbers of active live brine shrimp into the blue and red dishes. Add enough seawater to cover the shrimp while keeping them clearly visible.2. Initial Observation: Observe and note baseline swimming activity in both dishes; shrimp should swim actively and randomly.3. Anesthetic Addition: Using separate droppers, add 1 drop of anesthetic solution A to the blue dish and 1 drop of anesthetic solution B to the red dish.4. Observation: Watch changes in shrimp movement for several seconds.5. Incremental Dosing: Continue adding drops one at a time at short intervals (e.g., every few seconds), observing after each addition.6. Termination: Stop adding drops once shrimp show明显 reduced movement or near immobilization.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initially, shrimp in both dishes swim actively.2. After a few drops, swimming slows; movement becomes less frequent and less coordinated.3. With increasing drops, shrimp may become nearly motionless.4. The rate and degree of immobilization differ between the two dishes, reflecting different anesthetic effects.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAnesthetic solutions act on the nervous system by reducing neural signal transmission. As concentration increases, neuronal activity decreases, leading to slower and eventually absent motor responses in brine shrimp. Different anesthetics vary in potency and onset, producing observable differences in behavioral suppression.VI. PrecautionsUse equal numbers of shrimp; avoid cross-contamination of droppers; observe humane handling and proper disposal.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Exposing Vascular Bundles in a Celery StalkI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Exposing Vascular Bundles in a Celery Stalk by Lengthwise Slicing2. Subject: Natural Science – Neuroscience (Plant Structure as an Analogy for Transport Systems)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the internal vascular bundle structure of a celery stalk by slicing it lengthwise and removing the outer fibrous tissue, and to visually understand plant transport structures through time-lapse observation.II. Experimental EquipmentFresh celery stalk (1), cutting board (1), kitchen knife (1), paper towels (optional), camera or smartphone with tripod, adequate lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the cutting board on a stable surface. Wash and dry the celery stalk. Set up the camera on a tripod facing the cutting board and fix the focus and framing for time-lapse photography.2. Positioning: Lay the celery stalk flat on the cutting board, aligning it lengthwise with the camera frame so the entire stalk is visible.3. Lengthwise Slicing: Using the knife, carefully slice the celery stalk lengthwise from one end to the other, applying steady pressure to create a clean cut.4. Removing Outer Tissue: Gently peel or trim away part of the outer fibrous tissue along the cut surface to better expose the interior structure.5. Observation and Recording: Keep the celery stationary and allow the camera to record the exposed interior structure, ensuring the vascular bundles remain clearly visible.6. Completion: Stop recording, clean the cutting board and knife, and dispose of or store the celery appropriately.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The intact celery stalk appears smooth and fibrous on the outside, with no internal structures visible.2. After Slicing: The interior of the celery becomes visible, showing lighter-colored strands arranged lengthwise.3. After Removing Outer Tissue: Distinct vascular bundles appear as string-like structures running parallel along the stalk.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCelery is a plant whose vascular bundles consist mainly of xylem and phloem tissues responsible for water and nutrient transport. These bundles run lengthwise through the stalk. By slicing the celery lengthwise and removing the outer fibrous tissue, the internal vascular bundles are exposed and can be directly observed. This experiment visually demonstrates the organized transport system in plants, which is conceptually analogous to bundled pathways in biological systems studied in neuroscience.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Handle the knife carefully to avoid injury.2. Ensure the camera focus is fixed before cutting to avoid refocusing during time-lapse recording.3. Use a fresh celery stalk to ensure the vascular bundles are clearly visible.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrating plant vascular bundle structure by mechanically exposing the interior of a celery stalk through lengthwise slicing. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: celery contains longitudinal vascular bundles; cutting and removing outer tissue reveals these structures; no chemical change is involved. Phased storyline: (1) stable setup with celery on cutting board and fixed camera view; (2) knife performs a clear lengthwise cut; (3) outer fibrous tissue is peeled or trimmed away; (4) interior vascular bundles become visibly distinct and remain stable in frame. Visibility constraints: camera must maintain fixed focus and angle, with sufficient lighting to distinguish the lighter vascular strands from surrounding tissue.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Plant Seedlings Grown Under Light vs Darkness (Etiolation vs Normal Growth)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Growth of Bean Seedlings Under Light and Darkness2. Subject: Natural Science - Genetics & Genomics (Plant Growth and Gene Expression)3. Experiment Objective: To compare the growth characteristics of bean seedlings grown under light and in darkness, observe etiolation, and understand how light regulates plant growth and development.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentTwo identical seedling trays, germinated bean seedlings of the same age and size, potting soil, bright grow lamp, ventilated light-blocking box, ruler, labels, fixed-position camera or smartphone, timer.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fill two identical trays with the same amount of soil. Transplant equal numbers of germinated bean seedlings into each tray, keeping spacing consistent. Label trays as Light Group and Dark Group.2. Setup: Place the Light Group tray under a bright grow lamp at a fixed distance. Place the Dark Group tray into a ventilated light-blocking box that allows air exchange but blocks light completely.3. Camera Fixation: Position the camera facing both trays simultaneously, ensuring a fixed focus and angle suitable for time-lapse recording. Do not move the camera during the experiment.4. Growth Recording: Turn on the grow lamp and begin time-lapse recording. Maintain the same watering schedule and temperature for both trays over several days.5. Completion: After sufficient growth differences appear, stop recording and remove the trays for direct observation and measurement.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both groups show similar short, pale-green seedlings with small cotyledons.2. After Growth Under Light: Seedlings in the Light Group grow relatively shorter and sturdier, with thicker stems and expanded green leaves.3. After Growth in Darkness: Seedlings in the Dark Group grow taller and thinner, with elongated stems, small unopened leaves, and pale yellow or white coloration (etiolation).V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesLight is a key environmental signal regulating plant gene expression and development. Under light conditions, genes related to chlorophyll synthesis and normal leaf development are activated, resulting in green, sturdy plants. In darkness, chlorophyll synthesis is suppressed, and plants exhibit etiolation, characterized by rapid stem elongation and pale color. This experiment demonstrates how environmental factors influence gene expression and plant morphology.VI. PrecautionsEnsure trays and seedlings are identical at the start; prevent light leakage into the dark box; keep watering and temperature consistent; avoid moving the camera during recording.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Calcium Imaging of a Neuron with Soma StimulationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Calcium Imaging of a Neuron with Activity Initiating in the Soma2. Subject: Natural Science – Neuroscience3. Experiment Objective: To observe intracellular calcium dynamics in a live cultured neuron, demonstrating that neuronal activity initiated at the soma propagates into neurites.II. Experimental EquipmentFluorescence microscope with time-lapse imaging capability, live cultured neurons on glass-bottom dish, calcium-sensitive fluorescent dye (e.g., Fluo-4 AM), perfusion medium, microelectrode and micromanipulator, electrical stimulator, computer with imaging software.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Culture neurons on a glass-bottom dish. Load cells with calcium-sensitive dye according to standard incubation and wash steps. Place the dish on the fluorescence microscope stage and maintain physiological conditions.2. Imaging Setup: Focus on a single healthy neuron. Identify the soma and major neurites. Begin continuous fluorescence time-lapse imaging to establish a stable baseline signal.3. Stimulation: Using a micromanipulator, position a microelectrode to gently contact or closely approach the soma. Deliver a brief electrical stimulus while imaging continues uninterrupted.4. Recording: Continue imaging for several seconds after stimulation to capture calcium signal changes and spatial spread.5. Termination: Stop imaging, remove the electrode, and save the time-lapse data for analysis.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Baseline: Before stimulation, fluorescence intensity is low and stable throughout the neuron.2. Immediately after stimulation: Fluorescence intensity increases sharply at the soma, indicating calcium influx.3. Propagation: The increased fluorescence spreads from the soma into dendrites and/or axon over time, gradually decaying back to baseline.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesNeuronal electrical stimulation opens voltage-gated calcium channels, allowing Ca2+ to enter the soma. Calcium-sensitive dyes increase fluorescence upon binding Ca2+, converting electrical activity into an optical signal. The observed soma-initiated fluorescence increase and its spread along neurites reflect intracellular calcium diffusion and signal propagation, demonstrating the spatial dynamics of neuronal activation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Soma-initiated neuronal activity visualized by calcium-sensitive fluorescence imaging. Minimum assumptions: a live cultured neuron expresses normal calcium dynamics; calcium dye fluorescence reliably reports intracellular Ca2+; microelectrode stimulation depolarizes the soma.Phased storyline: (1) Establish baseline fluorescence in a clearly visible neuron under a fluorescence microscope; (2) Apply a brief, localized microelectrode stimulus to the soma; (3) Observe an immediate fluorescence increase at the soma; (4) Observe subsequent spatial spread of fluorescence into neurites. Visibility constraints: soma, electrode tip, and fluorescence changes must be simultaneously visible in the same field of view, with continuous time-lapse perspective to verify causal order.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Red Blood Cell Agglutination Driven by Surface Glycoprotein AntigensI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Red Blood Cell Agglutination Test on a Glass Slide2. Subject: Natural Science – Biochemistry & Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that specific antibodies recognize red blood cell surface glycoprotein antigens and induce agglutination; to understand antigen–antibody specificity using a saline control comparison.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsGlass slide (clean and grease-free); human red blood cell suspension (isotonic, uniform); anti-blood-group serum (specific antibody); physiological saline; micropipette or dropper; microscope with camera; gloves and bio-safety materials.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clean glass slide on the microscope stage. Adjust the microscope and camera, and fix the focus before starting time-lapse recording.2. Sample Placement: Using a dropper, place two separate drops of human red blood cell suspension on the slide, spaced evenly left and right.3. Reagent Addition: Add one drop of anti-blood-group serum to the left red blood cell drop. Add one drop of physiological saline to the right drop as a control.4. Mixing: Gently rock the glass slide back and forth to allow uniform mixing without splashing or merging the two drops.5. Observation and Recording: Under the fixed-focus microscope camera, observe and record changes in both drops for a short period suitable for time-lapse photography.6. Completion: Stop recording after clear phenomena appear. Dispose of biological materials according to safety guidelines and clean the workspace.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesRed blood cell membranes contain specific glycoprotein antigens (such as ABO blood group antigens). When anti-blood-group serum containing corresponding antibodies is added, antigen–antibody binding occurs. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Differential Adherence of Cationic Dye to Cotton and Polyester FabricsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Differential Staining of Cotton and Polyester by a Cationic Dye2. Subject: Natural Science – Biochemistry & Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that cationic dyes preferentially adhere to negatively charged natural fibers by visually comparing dye uptake of cotton and polyester fabrics.II. Experimental MaterialsNatural cotton fabric swatch (1 piece), synthetic polyester fabric swatch (1 piece), beaker (250 mL), cationic dye solution (e.g., methylene blue, dilute aqueous solution), forceps or tweezers, running water source, gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place equal-sized cotton and polyester swatches side by side. Pour the cationic dye solution into a beaker.2. Dyeing: Using forceps, lower both fabric swatches simultaneously into the dye solution, ensuring they are fully submerged and positioned next to each other.3. Soaking: Allow the swatches to soak briefly (a few seconds) to ensure contact between fibers and dye.4. Lifting: Lift both swatches out of the dye solution at the same time using forceps.5. Rinsing: Rinse both swatches together under running water until excess dye is removed.6. Comparison: Place the rinsed swatches side by side for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both cotton and polyester swatches are unstained and similar in appearance.2. After Dyeing: Both swatches appear colored immediately after immersion.3. After Rinsing: The cotton swatch retains a noticeably deeper color, while the polyester swatch becomes much lighter or nearly colorless.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCationic dyes carry a positive charge. Natural cotton fibers are primarily composed of cellulose, which contains negatively charged groups that attract and bind cationic dyes through electrostatic interactions. Polyester fibers are largely hydrophobic and lack significant negative charges, resulting in weak dye adherence. Therefore, after rinsing, cotton retains more dye than polyester, demonstrating selective binding based on fiber chemistry.VI. PrecautionsUse equal-sized swatches for fair comparison; handle dye solutions carefully to avoid staining skin or surfaces; rinse both fabrics simultaneously to ensure consistent conditions.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Thermostable Catalase Activity After Heat ExposureI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Thermostable and Regular Catalase After HeatingSubject: Natural Science – Biochemistry & Molecular BiologyObjective: To demonstrate that thermostable catalase retains enzymatic activity after heat exposure, while regular catalase loses activity, by observing oxygen bubble production after adding hydrogen peroxide.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsClear glass beakers (2, identical); thermostable catalase solution (red, equal volume); regular catalase solution (blue, equal volume); hydrogen peroxide solution (3%, fresh); hot water bath (70–80°C); thermometer; dropper or pipette; beaker tongs; stopwatch; camera mounted on tripod (fixed focus).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, clear beakers side by side. Add equal volumes of red thermostable catalase to the left beaker and blue regular catalase to the right beaker. Label if necessary.2. Heating: Place both beakers together into the hot water bath at 70–80°C. Heat for the same duration (about 3–5 minutes) to ensure uniform heat exposure.3. Camera Setup: Fix the camera position and focus on both beakers simultaneously, ensuring the entire reaction area is visible. Do not change focus or angle afterward.4. Core Operation: Remove the beakers from the water bath and place them back side by side. Using two droppers, add an equal volume of hydrogen peroxide to both beakers at the same time.5. Observation: Record the reactions continuously using time-lapse or accelerated recording for about 10 seconds.6. Cleanup: After observation, dispose of solutions according to laboratory safety rules and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both solutions are colored liquids with no bubbles after heating.After Hydrogen Peroxide Addition: The red thermostable catalase rapidly produces visible oxygen bubbles that persist; the blue regular catalase produces few or no bubbles, or bubbles stop quickly.Comparative Result: Bubble production in the red solution is significantly stronger than in the blue solution.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCatalase catalyzes the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen (2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2↑). Heating denatures most enzymes by disrupting their protein structure. Thermostable catalase maintains its functional structure at high temperatures, so it continues to produce oxygen bubbles after heating. Regular catalase is denatured by heat, resulting in reduced or absent catalytic activity.

Visibility constraints: both beakers must remain in frame at all times with a stable perspective to verify simultaneity, comparative intensity, and causal sequence.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Capillary Rise of Water vs Oil in a Paper TowelI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Capillary Rise of Water in a Paper Towel Compared to Cooking Oil2. Subject: Natural Science – Biochemistry & Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To compare the capillary rise behavior of water and cooking oil in identical paper towels, observe differences in liquid movement over time, and understand the role of polarity and intermolecular forces in capillary action.II. Experimental MaterialsPaper towel strips (2 identical strips, same size and thickness), transparent containers or beakers (2), blue-dyed water, yellow cooking oil, ruler or scale (optional), tray or flat surface, camera or smartphone with tripod (for fixed-focus time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two transparent containers side by side on a flat surface. Pour equal volumes of blue water into the left container and yellow cooking oil into the right container.2. Setup: Cut two identical paper towel strips. Ensure they are the same length and width. Position them vertically.3. Operation: Simultaneously dip the lower ends (about 1–2 cm) of the left paper towel into the blue water and the right paper towel into the yellow oil. Ensure both strips touch only their respective liquids.4. Recording: Fix the camera focus and position so both paper towels and containers are clearly visible. Start time-lapse recording.5. Observation Period: Allow the liquids to move upward along the paper towels. For demonstration purposes, the process may be accelerated while maintaining correct order.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both paper towels are dry above the liquid level; blue water and yellow oil are stationary in their containers.2. During the Experiment: Blue water rapidly climbs upward along the fibers of the paper towel, forming a clear rising front. Yellow oil rises much more slowly and to a lower height.3. Final State: After a period of time, the height of blue water on the paper towel is noticeably higher than that of the oil.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCapillary action occurs due to the interaction between liquid molecules and the solid fibers of the paper towel. Water is a polar molecule and forms strong hydrogen bonds with the cellulose fibers, resulting in strong adhesion and efficient capillary rise. Cooking oil is nonpolar, has weaker intermolecular attraction to cellulose, and higher viscosity, leading to slower and lower capillary rise. Therefore, water climbs higher and faster than oil in the paper towel.VI. Precautions1. Use identical paper towel strips to ensure fair comparison.2. Keep the camera fixed to avoid affecting time-lapse observation.3. Avoid disturbing the setup during recording.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Capillary action driven by intermolecular forces, comparing polar (water) and nonpolar (oil) liquids in a fibrous medium. Minimum assumptions: paper towel fibers act as capillary channels; water has stronger adhesion to cellulose than oil; gravity is constant; camera perspective is fixed.Expected Phenomena Storyline: Phase 1 – Setup: two identical paper towels placed side by side, each dipped into differently colored liquids. Phase 2 – Initiation: liquids begin to wet the lower fibers. Phase 3 – Development: blue water visibly and continuously climbs upward faster, while yellow oil shows slower, limited rise. Phase 4 – Outcome: clear height difference between water and oil is established. Visibility constraints: both strips must remain in frame, color contrast must be clear, and time progression must be continuous for causal verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Ni-NTA Agarose Column Binding and Elution of a Blue His-Tagged ProteinI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Binding and Elution of a His-Tagged Protein Using a Ni-NTA Agarose Column2. Subject: Natural Science – Biochemistry & Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the affinity purification of a His-tagged protein using a Ni-NTA agarose column by visually observing binding, washing, and elution processes, and to record the process using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Principle SummaryNi-NTA agarose specifically binds polyhistidine (His) tags through coordination between nickel ions and histidine residues. When a His-tagged protein solution passes through the column, the target protein binds to the resin, while unbound impurities are removed during washing. Addition of an elution buffer containing imidazole competitively disrupts the Ni–His interaction, releasing the bound protein, which is collected in fractions.III. Experimental Equipment and Materials1. Vertical Ni-NTA agarose column (pre-packed or manually packed)2. Stand and clamp for vertical fixation of column3. Blue His-tagged protein solution4. Binding buffer5. Wash buffer (low imidazole concentration)6. Elution buffer (high imidazole concentration)7. Collection tubes (multiple, labeled sequentially)8. Pipette or peristaltic pump9. Waste container10. Camera mounted on tripod with fixed focus for time-lapse recordingIV. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Fix the Ni-NTA column vertically on a stand. Ensure the outlet is aligned over collection tubes. Prime the column with binding buffer to remove air bubbles. Fix the camera focus and field of view on the entire column and collection area.2. Loading Stage: Slowly load the blue His-tagged protein solution onto the top of the column. Allow the solution to flow through by gravity or controlled flow. Begin time-lapse recording.3. Binding Observation: Observe that the blue color becomes retained within the agarose bed, indicating binding of the His-tagged protein to the Ni-NTA resin. The flow-through collected in the tube appears lighter or colorless.4. Washing Stage: Add wash buffer to the column. Collect wash fractions sequentially. Observe that minimal blue color elutes, while the column remains visibly blue.5. Elution Stage: Add elution buffer to the column. Collect eluate into new labeled tubes. Observe the blue color moving down the column and appearing clearly in the collection tubes.6. Completion: Stop the flow once elution is complete. End time-lapse recording. Dispose of waste properly and clean the setup.V. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Column resin appears pale or colorless; protein solution is distinctly blue.2. During Loading: Blue color accumulates within the agarose bed; effluent is mostly clear.3. During Washing: Column remains blue; wash fractions show little or no blue color.4. During Elution: Blue band migrates downward; eluate fractions become visibly blue.VI. Experimental Notes and Precautions1. Maintain a steady flow rate to ensure clear visual separation of steps.2. Avoid disturbing the resin bed to preserve band clarity.3. Ensure camera focus remains fixed to avoid changes during time-lapse recording.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstration of affinity purification of a His-tagged protein using a Ni-NTA agarose column. Minimum assumptions: a vertically fixed column, gravity-driven or controlled buffer flow, and visible blue color as a proxy for protein location. Expected phased storyline: (1) Initial setup with clear column and fixed camera; (2) loading phase where blue protein enters and binds within the resin; (3) wash phase where column remains blue and effluent is mostly clear; (4) elution phase where blue band moves downward and appears in collection tubes. Visibility constraints: the entire column and collection area must remain in frame, with stable focus, to verify causal transitions and order of events.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Simple In Vitro Transcription with Fluorescent RNA AccumulationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Fluorescent RNA Accumulation During In Vitro Transcription2. Subject: Natural Science – Biochemistry & Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that RNA polymerase can synthesize RNA from a DNA template in vitro and that the RNA product accumulates over time, visualized by fluorescence under UV light.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentTwo microcentrifuge tubes (one with blue cap, one with red cap), tube rack, micropipette with tips, DNA template containing a transcription promoter, ribonucleotide mix (including a fluorescent RNA dye or aptamer system), RNA polymerase, transcription buffer, disposable gloves, UV transilluminator or UV lamp.III. Experiment Title: Airflow Containment Demonstration with Theatrical Smoke2. Subject: Natural Science – Biochemistry & Molecular Biology (Laboratory Safety)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate airflow direction and containment efficiency of a laboratory fume hood by observing the movement of theatrical smoke near the hood opening.II. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the fume hood is powered on and operating normally. Adjust the front sash to a partially open position (approximately 30–50 cm opening). manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Benedict’s Test for Glucose in Urine SampleI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Benedict’s Test for Glucose in Urine (Diabetes Screening)2. Subject: Natural Science – Biochemistry & Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To detect the presence of reducing sugar (glucose) in urine by observing color changes after heating with Benedict’s reagent, and to understand the biochemical basis of diabetes screening.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tubes (2, identical and transparent), test tube rack, water bath or beaker with hot water, heat source, dropper or pipette, Benedict’s reagent (blue solution), urine sample (test sample), distilled or clear water (control), test tube holder or tongs, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Put on safety goggles. Place two clean test tubes on the rack and label them as Test (Urine) and Control (Water).2. Sample Addition: Add an equal volume (about 2 mL) of urine sample to the Test tube and the same volume of clear water to the Control tube.3. Reagent Addition: Add an equal volume (about 2 mL) of Benedict’s reagent to each test tube. Gently shake to mix; both solutions should appear blue initially.4. Heating: Place both test tubes into a hot water bath, ensuring the liquid levels are below the rim. Heat for 3–5 minutes. Fix the camera focus and position for time-lapse recording during heating.5. Completion: Remove the test tubes from the water bath using tongs and place them back on the rack for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Control Tube: The Control (water) tube remains blue with no precipitate.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleBenedict’s reagent contains copper(II) sulfate. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Iodine Reaction with Linear Starch vs Branched GlycogenI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Iodine Reaction with Linear Starch vs Highly Branched Glycogen2. Subject: Natural Science - Biochemistry & Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To compare the color reactions of iodine with linear starch and highly branched glycogen, and to understand how polysaccharide structure affects iodine binding and color formation.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo clear glass beakers (100–150 mL), starch solution (1%, cloudy), glycogen solution (1%, clear), iodine solution (I2/KI), droppers, glass stirring rods, white background, camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean beakers side by side on a white background. Pour equal volumes of starch solution into the left beaker and glycogen solution into the right beaker.2. Initial Observation: Observe and record that the starch solution appears cloudy, while the glycogen solution is clear.3. Core Operation: Using a dropper, add 2–3 drops of iodine solution to the left beaker and then to the right beaker.4. Mixing: Gently swirl each beaker to ensure uniform mixing without splashing.5. Recording: Fix the camera focus and record the color changes using time-lapse photography.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Left beaker contains a cloudy starch solution; right beaker contains a clear glycogen solution.2. After Adding Iodine: The starch solution rapidly turns blue–black. The glycogen solution develops a much lighter reddish-brown or brownish-yellow color.3. Comparison: The color intensity in starch is significantly stronger than in glycogen.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIodine molecules insert into the helical structure of linear amylose in starch, forming a stable polyiodide complex that produces an intense blue–black color. Experimental PrecautionsUse equal concentrations and volumes of solutions; add iodine dropwise to avoid excess; swirl gently; maintain consistent lighting and fixed camera focus for clear comparison.

Subject: Natural Science - Biochemistry and Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that ATP is required for the luciferase-catalyzed oxidation of luciferin by visually comparing light emission in two identical reaction systems, and to understand the biochemical principle of enzyme-catalyzed bioluminescence.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentClear reaction vials (2, identical size and material), luciferase solution, luciferin solution, ATP solution, micropipette or syringe for ATP injection, vial caps (one red, one blue), camera capable of time-lapse recording, tripod, dark laboratory or dark box, gloves and basic lab safety equipment.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Label the two clear vials and cap one with a red cap and the other with a blue cap. Seal the vials.Setup Stage: Place the two vials side by side on a stable surface in a dark laboratory. Fix the camera on a tripod directly facing the vials. Adjust focus and exposure, then lock the focus to prevent changes during recording.Recording Stage: Start time-lapse or continuous video recording before any reaction is initiated.Core Operation: Using a micropipette or syringe, inject a measured amount of ATP solution only into the red-capped vial. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Universal pH Indicator Color Change with Acid and BaseI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Color Change of Universal pH Indicator upon Addition of Acid and Base2. Subject: Natural Science – Biochemistry & Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To observe how a universal pH indicator changes color in response to acidic and basic solutions and to understand the relationship between pH and indicator color.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass beaker, distilled water, universal pH indicator solution, dropper or pipette, clear dilute acidic solution (e.g., hydrochloric acid), clear dilute basic solution (e.g., sodium hydroxide), lab bench, camera fixed on tripod (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, clear glass beaker on the lab bench. Add an appropriate volume of distilled water.2. Indicator Addition: Add several drops of universal pH indicator to the water and gently swirl until the solution shows a uniform initial color (typically green, indicating near-neutral pH).3. Acid Addition: Using a dropper, slowly add clear acidic solution dropwise into the beaker while keeping the camera focus fixed. Allow the solution to mix naturally.4. Base Addition: After the acidic color change is stable, add clear basic solution dropwise into the same beaker, continuing to record.5. Completion: Stop adding reagents once a clear basic color is observed. End recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The indicator solution appears green, indicating neutral pH.2. After Acid Addition: The solution gradually changes color toward yellow, orange, or red, indicating an acidic environment.3. After Base Addition: The color shifts back through green and then toward blue or purple, indicating a basic environment.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesUniversal pH indicators are mixtures of dyes that change color depending on hydrogen ion concentration. Adding acid increases H+ concentration, lowering pH and shifting the indicator toward red hues. Adding base reduces H+ concentration, raising pH and shifting the indicator toward blue or purple hues. The observed color changes directly reflect changes in solution pH.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Title: Redox-Dependent Color Change of Cytochrome c2. Subject: Natural Science – Biochemistry & Molecular Biology3. Objective: To demonstrate that the heme iron in cytochrome c undergoes reversible redox changes, producing visible color changes upon reduction and oxidation.II. Materials and Reagents- Clear optical cuvette (1 cm path length)- Purified cytochrome c solution (oxidized, ~50–100 µM, buffered at pH ~7.0)- Mild reductant (e.g., sodium dithionite or ascorbate, dilute)- Oxidizing agent (e.g., potassium ferricyanide, dilute)- Two clean pipettes or micropipettes- Kimwipes or lint-free tissue- Gloves and eye protectionIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clean, dry cuvette in a holder. Add cytochrome c solution to fill ~2/3 of the cuvette. Observe and record the initial color.2. Reduction Step: Using the first pipette, add 1–2 drops of the mild reductant to the cuvette. Gently mix by pipetting up and down or by careful swirling.3. Observation After Reduction: Observe the immediate color change of the solution.4. Oxidation Step: Using a second pipette, add 1–2 drops of the oxidizing agent to the same cuvette. Gently mix again.5. Final Observation: Observe the color change following oxidation.6. Cleanup: Dispose of solutions according to laboratory rules; rinse the cuvette with water.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena- Initial State: Oxidized cytochrome c appears pale brownish or orange.- After Reduction: Upon addition of reductant and mixing, the solution rapidly turns bright pink to red.- After Oxidation: After adding oxidant, the red color fades and returns to the brownish/orange oxidized appearance.V. Experimental Principle SummaryCytochrome c contains a heme prosthetic group whose iron atom cycles between Fe3+ (oxidized) and Fe2+ (reduced) states. The electronic structure of the heme changes with redox state, altering light absorption and producing distinct visible colors. Addition of a reductant converts Fe3+ to Fe2+, intensifying the red color; addition of an oxidant reverses this process, demonstrating reversible biological redox chemistry.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Glucose Oxidase–Peroxidase Color Change with Glucose-Containing LiquidI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Glucose Oxidase–Peroxidase Color Change with Glucose-Containing Liquid2. Subject: Natural Science – Biochemistry & Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the specific enzymatic reaction of glucose using the glucose oxidase–peroxidase (GOD–POD) system through observable color change, and to understand enzymatic specificity and coupled oxidation–reduction reactions.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsClear vials (2, identical), vial rack or flat lab bench, dropper or micropipette, glucose oxidase–peroxidase color reagent, glucose solution (known glucose-containing liquid), non-glucose control liquid (such as distilled water), gloves and safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, dry, and transparent vials side by side on the lab bench. Label the left vial as Glucose and the right vial as Control.2. Reagent Addition: Using a dropper, add an equal volume of glucose oxidase–peroxidase reagent into both vials. Ensure the liquids are clear and at the same initial state.3. Sample Addition: Add a measured amount of glucose solution to the left vial. Add the same volume of non-glucose liquid to the right vial.4. Reaction and Observation: Allow the vials to stand briefly and observe the color changes without shaking excessively.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. manual: Instructions for the Experiment "Pill Bug Rolls into a Ball When Touched"I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Pill Bug Rolls into a Ball When Touched2. Subject: Natural Science – Ecology & Evolutionary Biology3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the defensive behavior of pill bugs (Armadillidium spp.) when gently stimulated, and to explain this behavior as an adaptive response to predators.II. Experimental MaterialsPill bug (1–2 individuals, alive and active), shallow observation container or Petri dish, moist soil or damp paper towel (to maintain humidity), clean human finger or soft cotton swab (for gentle touch), magnifying glass (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place moist soil or a damp paper towel evenly in the observation container to create a humid environment. Gently transfer a pill bug onto the surface and allow it to acclimate for about 10–20 seconds.2. Initial Observation: Observe and record the pill bug’s normal state, such as walking freely with its body extended and antennae moving.3. Core Operation: Using a clean finger, gently touch the pill bug on its back or side once, avoiding excessive force.4. Reaction Observation: Closely observe the pill bug’s immediate response after being touched.5. Recovery Observation: Stop touching and continue observing to see whether the pill bug gradually uncurls and resumes movement.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The pill bug is flat or slightly arched, walking slowly on the moist soil.2. Upon Touching: When gently touched, the pill bug quickly curls its segmented body inward, forming a tight ball, with legs and soft body parts hidden inside.3. After Stimulation Stops: After a short period without disturbance, the pill bug may slowly uncurl and resume crawling.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePill bugs exhibit a defensive behavior known as conglobation. When touched, they interpret the stimulus as a potential predator threat. Curling into a ball protects their soft underside and reduces exposed surface area, making them harder for predators to bite or swallow. This behavior is an evolutionary adaptation that increases survival in natural environments.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Keep the environment moist; pill bugs require humidity to survive.2. Touch gently to avoid harming the organism.3. Do not repeatedly disturb the pill bug for long periods; return it to its habitat after observation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Red Blood Cells Swelling and Bursting in Distilled WaterI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Red Blood Cells Swelling and Bursting in Distilled WaterSubject: Natural Science – Ecology & Evolutionary BiologyObjective: Observe osmotic effects on red blood cells by adding distilled water under a light microscope and recording the process with fixed focus time-lapse photography.II. Materials and EquipmentLight microscope with camera; prepared slide with red blood cells and coverslip; distilled water; dropper or micropipette; lens paper.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the red blood cell slide on the microscope stage. Select low to medium magnification and focus until red blood cells appear clearly.2. Focusing: Adjust fine focus to obtain sharp cell outlines. Fix the microscope focus and camera settings to avoid refocusing during recording.3. Recording Setup: Start time-lapse or continuous recording while keeping the field of view unchanged.4. Core Operation: Gently place 1–2 drops of distilled water at the edge of the coverslip using a dropper, allowing it to diffuse naturally into the field of view.5. Observation: Continue recording as distilled water diffuses; do not move the slide or adjust focus.6. Ending: Stop recording after clear swelling and bursting phenomena are observed.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial: Red blood cells appear as small, round biconcave discs with clear boundaries.During diffusion: As distilled water reaches the cells, they gradually swell and become more spherical.Final: Cell membranes rupture, and cells lose their distinct shape, indicating hemolysis.V. Experimental Principle SummaryThis experiment demonstrates osmosis. Distilled water is hypotonic relative to the cytoplasm of red blood cells. Water enters the cells through the semipermeable membrane, increasing internal pressure. Because red blood cells lack a rigid cell wall, excessive water influx causes swelling and eventual membrane rupture (hemolysis).

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Soil Aggregate Stability When Dropped into WaterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Soil Aggregate Stability When Dropped into Water (Crumbly vs Dispersing)2. Subject: Natural Science – Ecology & Evolutionary Biology3. Experiment Objective: To compare the stability of different soil aggregates by observing whether dry soil clods remain intact or disperse when dropped into still water, and to understand the ecological significance of soil structure.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical clear glass or plastic bowls, clean water (room temperature), one dry dark compact soil clod (aggregated soil), one dry light-colored loose soil clod (poorly aggregated soil), flat surface or lab bench, camera or smartphone with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two clear bowls side by side on a stable surface. Pour equal amounts of clean, still water into each bowl and allow the water to settle until completely motionless.2. Soil Selection: Prepare a dry, dark, compact soil clod and a dry, lighter, loose soil clod of similar size.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly in front of the bowls, ensuring both bowls are fully visible. Fix the focus and do not change the camera position during recording.4. Core Operation: Simultaneously drop the dark compact soil clod into the left bowl and the lighter loose soil clod into the right bowl from the same height.5. Recording: Continue recording or time-lapse photography for several seconds to capture the changes after the soils contact water.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both bowls contain clear, still water; both soil clods are dry before contact.2. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Ice Melting on Dark vs Light Surfaces (Albedo Effect)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Ice Melting on Dark vs Light Surfaces (Albedo Effect)2. Subject: Natural Science - Ecology & Evolutionary Biology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how surface color (albedo) affects heat absorption and melting rate of ice, and to understand the role of albedo in Earth’s energy balance.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical ice blocks (same size and shape), one dark matte surface (black paper or board), one white surface (white paper or board), overhead heat lamp or direct sunlight, flat table, camera or smartphone with tripod, timer or time-lapse function.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the dark matte surface and white surface side by side on a flat table. Ensure both surfaces are clean and dry.2. Placement of Ice: Put one identical ice block at the center of each surface at the same time.3. Heat Source Setup: Position a single heat lamp directly above the midpoint between the two ice blocks, or place the setup under direct sunlight, ensuring equal exposure.4. Camera Setup: Fix the camera on a tripod facing the ice blocks. Lock focus and exposure. Start time-lapse recording or continuous recording.5. Observation Phase: Turn on the heat lamp or begin exposure to sunlight and allow the ice to melt. Do not move the setup during the experiment.6. End of Experiment: Stop recording when a clear difference in melting between the two ice blocks is observed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both ice blocks are solid, clear or slightly cloudy, and equal in size.2. During Heating: Water appears around both ice blocks, but the ice on the dark surface melts faster, producing more liquid water.3. Later Stage: The ice block on the dark surface becomes significantly smaller or disappears earlier, while the ice on the white surface remains larger.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the albedo effect. Dark surfaces have low albedo and absorb more radiant energy, converting it into heat. White surfaces have high albedo and reflect more radiation. As a result, the dark surface warms faster and transfers more heat to the ice above it, causing faster melting. This principle helps explain phenomena such as faster melting of snow and ice on darker ground and the influence of surface color on Earth’s climate system.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure both ice blocks are identical and placed simultaneously. Keep the heat source centered and at a fixed height. Avoid airflow or shadows that could affect melting. Handle electrical equipment safely.

Basic InformationTitle: Diffusion of Ammonia and Hydrogen Chloride Vapors in a Glass TubeSubject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Diffusion)Objective: To observe gas diffusion and compare relative diffusion rates using the formation position of ammonium chloride.II. MaterialsHorizontal glass tube (about 1 m), two small cotton plugs, concentrated ammonia solution, concentrated hydrochloric acid, rubber stoppers or sealing film, gloves and goggles.III. Procedure1. Place the clean glass tube horizontally on a stable bench.2. Soak one cotton plug with ammonia solution and insert it into the left end of the tube.3. Soak the other cotton plug with hydrochloric acid and insert it into the right end of the tube.4. Immediately seal both ends to prevent air currents.5. Keep the tube undisturbed and observe.IV. ObservationInitially the tube is clear. After a short time, a white smoke/ring appears inside the tube, forming closer to the hydrochloric acid end.V. Principle SummaryAmmonia (NH3) and hydrogen chloride (HCl) gases diffuse from opposite ends. When they meet, they react to form solid ammonium chloride (NH4Cl), visible as a white ring. Because ammonia has a lower molar mass, it diffuses faster, so the ring forms closer to the HCl end.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Iodine Staining of a Leaf After Light ExposureI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Iodine Staining of a Leaf After Light Exposure2. Subject: Natural Science – Ecology & Evolutionary Biology (Plant Physiology)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that green leaves exposed to bright light produce starch through photosynthesis, and to verify starch accumulation in the leaf using iodine staining; to master the basic procedures of killing, decolorizing, staining plant leaves, and recording the process with fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentFresh green leaf (exposed to bright light for several hours), beaker, hot water bath, alcohol (95% ethanol), test tube or small beaker for alcohol heating, forceps, glass rod, white ceramic tile or petri dish, iodine solution (iodine–potassium iodide), dropper, heat source, camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse recording), protective gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Select a healthy green leaf that has been exposed to bright light. Set up the camera, fix the focus and framing on the experimental area, and start time-lapse recording.2. Killing the Leaf: Place the leaf into hot water (near boiling) for about 1–2 minutes to kill the cells and stop enzymatic reactions.3. Decolorization: Transfer the leaf into a test tube or beaker containing alcohol. Heat the alcohol in a hot water bath until the leaf loses its green color and becomes pale or whitish. Use forceps to handle the leaf safely.4. Rinsing and Flattening: Remove the leaf from alcohol, rinse briefly with warm water to soften it, and lay it flat on a white tile or petri dish.5. Iodine Staining: Use a dropper to add iodine solution evenly across the surface of the leaf, ensuring full coverage.6. Observation: Keep the leaf stationary and continue time-lapse recording as the color change develops.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before staining, the decolorized leaf appears pale yellow or nearly white.2. After Adding Iodine: Areas of the leaf that contain starch gradually turn blue-black, while areas without starch remain yellow-brown.3. Overall Result: Most regions of the light-exposed green leaf show blue-black staining, indicating starch accumulation.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePhotosynthesis in green leaves uses light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into organic matter, producing glucose that is stored as starch. Heating in hot water kills the leaf and stops metabolism, while alcohol removes chlorophyll so color changes can be clearly observed. Iodine reacts specifically with starch to form a blue-black complex. Therefore, the appearance of blue-black regions after iodine staining indicates starch accumulation resulting from photosynthesis under light exposure.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Alcohol is flammable; heating must be done in a hot water bath, not over direct flame.2. Handle hot liquids and glassware carefully to avoid burns.3. Ensure the leaf is fully decolorized for clear staining results.4. Avoid moving the camera after fixing focus to ensure consistent time-lapse recording.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Light-dependent photosynthesis leads to starch accumulation in green leaves, detectable by iodine staining. Minimum assumptions: the leaf is green, exposed to light, chlorophyll is removed before staining, and iodine specifically indicates starch.Phased Storyline: (1) Establish a green leaf previously exposed to light; camera framing is fixed. (2) Leaf is briefly heated in hot water to stop metabolism. (3) Leaf is heated in alcohol and visibly loses green color. (4) Pale leaf is laid flat on a white surface. (5) Iodine is added and blue-black coloration appears across starch-rich regions. Visibility constraints: close-up, stable view of the leaf surface is required to verify color transitions and causal sequence.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Wetland Plants Filtering Muddy WaterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Wetland Plants Filtering Muddy Water2. Subject: Natural Science - Ecology & Evolutionary Biology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the role of wetland plants and soil in filtering sediments from muddy water by comparing water clarity after flowing through planted and bare soil trays.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo shallow soil trays of the same size, garden soil, wetland plants (e.g., reeds or rushes), muddy water (soil mixed with water), two identical clear containers, water jug or beaker, stable table, camera fixed on tripod.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Place two identical shallow soil trays side by side on a table. Fill both with the same depth of soil. Plant wetland plants evenly in one tray; leave the other tray bare. Place a clear container at the drainage end of each tray.Camera Setup: Fix the camera position and focus so that both trays and containers are visible. Do not adjust focus during recording to allow time-lapse comparison.Core Operation: Pour the same volume of muddy water slowly and evenly onto the upper end of the planted tray. Repeat the same operation with the bare tray, keeping pouring speed and volume consistent.Collection: Allow water to flow through the soil and drain into the clear containers. Continue recording until drainage stops.Cleanup: Stop recording, dispose of muddy water properly, and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Muddy water is brown and opaque before entering both trays.2. During Flow: In the planted tray, water flows more slowly and visible sediment is trapped among plant roots and soil. In the bare tray, water flows faster with more sediment passing through.3. Final State: Water collected from the planted tray is visibly clearer than water collected from the bare tray.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleWetland plants and soil act as natural filters. Plant roots slow water flow and physically trap sediment, while soil particles further filter suspended matter. As a result, water passing through planted wetland soil contains fewer suspended particles and appears clearer than water passing through bare soil.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Food Dye Spreading in Warm Water vs Cold WaterI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Food Dye Spreading in Warm Water vs Cold WaterSubject: Natural Science - BiophysicsExperiment Objective: To observe how temperature affects the rate of diffusion in liquids by comparing the spreading speed of food dye in warm water and cold water.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical clear glass beakers, warm water (approximately 40–50°C), cold water (approximately 5–10°C), blue food dye, dropper or pipette, thermometer (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear beakers side by side on a flat surface. Pour equal volumes of warm water into one beaker and cold water into the other, ensuring both are clear and still.2. Core Operation: Using two droppers or the same dropper quickly, add one drop of blue food dye into the center of each beaker at the same time.3. Observation: Keep the beakers undisturbed and observe the spreading process of the dye in both beakers.4. Conclusion: After clear differences are observed, stop the experiment and record results.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers contain clear, colorless water; the blue dye is concentrated at the point of entry.2. During the Experiment: In the warm water beaker, the blue dye spreads rapidly throughout the water. In the cold water beaker, the dye spreads much more slowly and remains concentrated longer.3. Final State: The warm water becomes uniformly blue sooner than the cold water.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleDiffusion is the movement of particles from areas of higher concentration to lower concentration. Higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of water molecules, causing faster molecular motion and more frequent collisions. Therefore, diffusion occurs more rapidly in warm water than in cold water.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure beakers are identical and water volumes are equal to maintain experimental fairness.2. Add dye drops as simultaneously as possible.3. Avoid stirring or shaking the beakers during observation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Temperature affects diffusion rate due to changes in molecular kinetic energy; warm water molecules move faster than cold water molecules.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Liquids are transparent, dye behaves as a passive tracer, and higher temperature implies higher molecular motion.Phased Storyline: Phase 1 setup with two identical clear beakers side by side (warm vs cold); Phase 2 simultaneous addition of blue dye drops; Phase 3 visible divergence where dye rapidly disperses in warm water but slowly diffuses in cold water. Visibility Requirements: static camera, clear view of both beakers, no obstruction, and sufficient contrast to track dye spreading.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Heat-Tolerant vs Heat-Sensitive Seedlings Exposed to a Short HeatwaveI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Responses of Heat-Tolerant and Heat-Sensitive Seedlings to a Short Heatwave2. Subject: Natural Science – Ecology & Evolutionary Biology3. Experiment Objective: To compare the growth and survival responses of heat-tolerant and heat-sensitive seedlings when exposed to a short-term heatwave, and to understand how heat tolerance influences plant performance under thermal stress using time-lapse observation.II. Experimental Materials and Equipment1. Plant materials: Heat-tolerant seedlings (uniform size and age); Heat-sensitive seedlings (uniform size and age)2. Containers: Seedling trays; red pots and blue pots (used to distinguish plant types)3. Growth chamber with controllable temperature and light conditions4. Heat source integrated in growth chamber (for simulating heatwave)5. Fixed-position camera for time-lapse photography6. Labels and marker pens7. Watering equipment (spray bottle or watering can)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:- Select healthy heat-tolerant and heat-sensitive seedlings of similar size.- Plant heat-tolerant seedlings in red pots and heat-sensitive seedlings in blue pots, or place them in clearly labeled trays.- Ensure all seedlings are watered equally and allowed to acclimate in the growth chamber under normal temperature conditions for 24 hours.2. Arrangement in Growth Chamber:- Place trays, red pots, and blue pots side by side in the growth chamber so that all seedlings experience identical light and spatial conditions.- Adjust lighting to standard growth conditions.- Fix the camera on a stable mount, ensuring all seedlings are in the frame; lock focus and exposure settings.3. Heatwave Treatment:- Increase the temperature in the growth chamber to simulate a short heatwave (e.g., 40°C) for a defined period (e.g., several hours).- Start time-lapse photography at the beginning of the heatwave.- Do not move the plants or camera during heating.4. Recovery Stage:- After the heatwave period, turn off the heat and return the growth chamber to normal temperature.- Continue time-lapse photography to record post-heat recovery.- Maintain equal watering and light conditions for all seedlings.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before heating, both heat-tolerant and heat-sensitive seedlings appear upright, green, and healthy.2. During Heatwave: Heat-sensitive seedlings may show wilting, leaf drooping, or color fading; heat-tolerant seedlings show little or slower visible stress.3. After Heat Is Turned Off: Heat-tolerant seedlings gradually recover turgor and continue growing; heat-sensitive seedlings may recover slowly, remain wilted, or show leaf damage.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePlants differ in their physiological tolerance to high temperatures. Heat-tolerant seedlings possess adaptive traits such as stable cell membranes, heat-shock protein production, and efficient water regulation, allowing them to maintain function during heat stress. Heat-sensitive seedlings lack these traits and therefore suffer greater damage during a heatwave. By exposing both types to the same short-term heat stress and observing them side by side, differences in stress response and recovery directly demonstrate the ecological and evolutionary significance of heat tolerance.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure all seedlings receive identical conditions except for heat treatment.2. Do not adjust camera focus or angle once time-lapse recording begins.3. Avoid overwatering during the heatwave period.4. Handle seedlings gently to avoid mechanical damage that could affect results.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Differential plant responses to short-term heat stress based on heat tolerance. Minimum assumptions: seedlings are living plants with visible leaves; a growth chamber can simulate a heatwave; heat stress causes wilting or slowed growth. Phased storyline: Phase 1 – normal growth with healthy green seedlings side by side; Phase 2 – temperature rises, initiating heatwave, sensitive seedlings begin wilting while tolerant ones remain relatively stable; Phase 3 – heat turned off, recovery phase where tolerant seedlings regain normal posture faster than sensitive ones. Visibility constraints: fixed camera angle, consistent lighting, clear view of pot colors and leaf posture changes to verify causal transitions.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: GFP-Tagged Cells Glowing Under Blue Excitation LightSubject: Natural Science – BiophysicsObjective: To observe green fluorescent protein (GFP) fluorescence in living cells under blue excitation light and understand the excitation–emission principle using fixed-focus time-lapse imaging.II. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the petri dish containing GFP-expressing cells on a stable lab bench. Darken ambient light to enhance fluorescence visibility. Excitation: Switch on the blue excitation lamp aimed directly at the petri dish without moving the camera or dish.4.
