manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Gelatin Setting as It Cools2. Subject: Natural Science – Biophysics3. Experiment Objective: To observe how gelatin changes from a liquid to a gel as it cools, and to understand that cooling allows protein chains to form a three-dimensional gel network.II. Experimental Materials and Equipment- Gelatin powder- Warm water (about 50–60°C)- Two shallow transparent dishes (same size)- Refrigerator- Flat counter or tabletop at room temperature- Camera or smartphone with tripodIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Dissolve gelatin powder in warm water according to instructions, stirring until fully dissolved and clear.2. Pouring: Pour equal amounts of the warm gelatin solution into two identical shallow transparent dishes.3. Initial Recording: Place both dishes side by side, fix the camera focus and position, and start recording or time-lapse capture.4. Placement: Move one dish into the refrigerator; leave the other on the counter at room temperature.5. Time-Lapse Observation: Over time, record the gelatin in both locations. At intervals, gently tilt each dish to test fluidity, keeping camera position unchanged.6. End of Experiment: Stop recording once a clear difference in firmness between the two dishes is observed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both dishes contain clear, flowing liquid gelatin.2. During Cooling: The refrigerated gelatin gradually thickens and stops flowing when tilted, while the counter gelatin remains liquid for longer.3. Final State: The refrigerated dish forms a firm gel earlier; the counter dish may still flow or be softer at the same time point.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleGelatin is made of protein chains. When warm, these chains move freely in solution. As temperature decreases, the chains slow down and form a three-dimensional network that traps water, turning the liquid into a gel. Faster cooling in the refrigerator accelerates this network formation, so gelatin sets more quickly at lower temperatures.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Gelatin setting due to cooling-induced protein network formation. Minimum assumptions: gelatin behaves as a liquid when warm and forms a gel when cooled; lower temperature accelerates gelation.Expected phased storyline: (1) Warm gelatin poured into two identical transparent dishes, both clearly liquid; (2) One dish placed in refrigerator, one left on counter, camera fixed for time-lapse; (3) Over accelerated time, refrigerated gelatin visibly thickens first; (4) Gentle tilting reveals reduced or absent flow in cooled gelatin while the counter sample remains more fluid. Visibility constraints: dishes must remain in frame, transparency allows state observation, tilting motion must be visible to verify flow differences.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Plant Stem Water Transport Demonstrated by Colored Water UptakeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Plant Stem Water Transport Demonstrated by Colored Water Uptake2. Subject: Natural Science - Biophysics3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand how water is transported upward in plant stems through xylem by visualizing the movement of colored water; to learn basic methods of plant preparation, long-term observation, and time-lapse recording.II. Experimental EquipmentFresh white flower (such as carnation) or fresh celery stalk, sharp knife or scissors, clear glass or plastic container, water, edible food coloring or ink, camera or mobile phone with tripod, adequate lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Select a fresh white flower or celery stalk. Use a knife or scissors to cut the stem at an angle under normal conditions to ensure the cut surface is fresh and open.2. Solution Preparation: Fill the clear container with water and add a few drops of food coloring. Stir until the water is evenly colored and transparent.3. Setup: Immediately place the freshly cut stem into the colored water, ensuring the cut end is fully submerged.4. Recording: Position the camera in front of the setup, fix the focus and framing so that the stem and container are fully visible, and begin time-lapse or continuous recording.5. Observation Period: Leave the setup undisturbed for a period of time. For demonstration purposes, the process may be accelerated or condensed in the recording.IV. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesPlants transport water mainly through xylem vessels in their stems. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Temperature Change Shown by a Liquid Thermometer During Heating and CoolingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Temperature Change Shown by a Liquid Thermometer During Heating and Cooling2. Subject: Natural Science – Biophysics3. Experiment Objective: To observe how the liquid level in a glass thermometer changes during heating and cooling, understand thermal expansion and contraction of liquids, and learn to record temperature changes using fixed-focus time-lapse observation.II. Experimental EquipmentGlass liquid thermometer (alcohol or mercury type), beaker A (with room-temperature water), beaker B (with cool water), hot plate, thermometer clamp or holder, tripod-mounted camera (fixed focus), heat-resistant gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place beaker A with water on the hot plate. Set up the camera on a tripod, fix the focus on the thermometer scale, and start time-lapse recording.2. Heating Stage: Insert the glass thermometer vertically into beaker A so that the bulb is fully submerged without touching the beaker bottom. Turn on the hot plate and heat the water steadily.3. Observation During Heating: Observe and record the gradual rise of the liquid column in the thermometer as the water temperature increases.4. Cooling Stage: After the temperature rise is clearly observed, carefully remove the thermometer and quickly place it into beaker B containing cool water.5. Observation During Cooling: Observe and record the gradual fall of the liquid column as the thermometer cools.6. Completion: Turn off the hot plate, stop recording, and return all equipment after cooling.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The thermometer liquid column is stable at an initial scale reading.2. During Heating: As water is heated, the liquid column in the thermometer rises continuously.3. During Cooling: After transfer to cool water, the liquid column gradually falls and stabilizes at a lower reading.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on thermal expansion and contraction of liquids. When temperature increases, the liquid inside the thermometer expands and rises in the narrow glass tube. When temperature decreases, the liquid contracts and the level falls. The thermometer converts temperature change into visible liquid level change.VI. Precautions1. Handle the thermometer gently to avoid breakage.2. Ensure the thermometer bulb does not touch the beaker walls or bottom.3. Avoid sudden shaking during transfer to maintain clear observation.

manual: Experimental Instruction ManualI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Warming in Liquid Water and Gelatin Gel on a Hot PlateSubject: Natural Science – BiophysicsObjective: To visually compare the warming behavior of liquid water and a protein gel (gelatin) under identical heating conditions, and to understand how material state and internal structure affect heat transfer.II. Experimental EquipmentHot plate with flat heating surface; two identical transparent glass beakers (250 mL); liquid water (same volume in both beakers); gelatin gel prepared in advance (same volume as water); thermochromic dye (same concentration added to both samples); thermometer (optional, for calibration); camera or smartphone with tripod for fixed-focus time-lapse recording; heat-resistant gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the hot plate on a stable laboratory bench. Prepare two identical transparent beakers, ensuring they are clean and dry.2. Sample Loading: Pour an equal volume of liquid water into one beaker. Place an equal volume of pre-set gelatin gel into the other beaker. Add the same amount of thermochromic dye to both samples and gently mix (for gelatin, ensure dye is evenly distributed without breaking the gel structure).3. Placement: Position the two beakers side by side at equal distance from the center of the hot plate to ensure uniform heating conditions.4. Camera Setup: Fix the camera on a tripod directly in front of the beakers. Adjust focus and exposure, then lock focus to avoid changes during recording. Set the camera to time-lapse or continuous recording mode.5. Heating: Turn on the hot plate to a medium, constant power setting. Start recording simultaneously with heating.6. Observation Period: Allow heating for a short, accelerated duration suitable for time-lapse capture (e.g., until clear color differences appear).7. Completion: Turn off the hot plate. Stop recording. Allow beakers to cool before handling and clean up the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers show the same initial thermochromic dye color, indicating equal starting temperature.2. Early Heating: The liquid water begins to change color more uniformly throughout the beaker, while the gelatin shows localized color change near the bottom.3. Continued Heating: Water displays faster and more homogeneous color transition due to convection. Gelatin shows slower, layered or gradient color change, indicating limited internal movement.4. Final State: At the same heating time, water appears overall warmer (advanced color state) than gelatin.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesHeat transfer in materials depends on their physical state and internal structure. Liquid water allows convection currents, which distribute heat efficiently and lead to uniform temperature increase. Gelatin is a protein gel with a semi-solid network that suppresses convection; heat is transferred mainly by conduction, which is slower. Therefore, under identical heating conditions, water warms faster and more uniformly than gelatin.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure equal volumes and identical beakers; keep camera focus fixed; avoid overheating to prevent boiling or gel melting that could obscure observations.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Comparison of Fluorescent Specimen Mounted in Antifade Medium vs Plain GlycerolI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of Antifade Mounting Medium on Fluorescence Photobleaching2. Subject: Natural Science – Biophysics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate and compare fluorescence photobleaching of the same fluorescent specimen mounted in antifade mounting medium versus plain glycerol under continuous illumination, and to understand the biophysical mechanism of photobleaching and antifade protection.II. Experimental Equipment and Materials1. Fluorescence microscope with stable light source and camera2. Camera and time-lapse imaging software (focus-lock or manual fixed focus)3. Two microscope slides containing the same fluorescent specimen4. Antifade mounting medium (commercial or prepared)5. Plain glycerol mounting medium6. Coverslips7. Labels or markers for slide identificationIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   a. Prepare two slides using the same fluorescent specimen.   b. Mount one specimen in antifade mounting medium and the other in plain glycerol.   c. Apply coverslips and seal if necessary.   d. Clearly label each slide as antifade or glycerol.2. Microscope Setup:   a. Place both slides side by side on the microscope stage so they can be observed within the same field of view.   b. Select the appropriate excitation and emission filter set for the fluorophore.   c. Adjust illumination intensity to a constant level suitable for continuous observation.3. Imaging Operation:   a. Focus the microscope carefully on the fluorescent structures and fix the focus of the camera.   b. Begin continuous illumination without changing intensity.   c. Start time-lapse photography or continuous recording, ensuring no refocusing or repositioning occurs.4. Observation Period:   a. Continue illumination and recording for a sufficient duration to observe fluorescence decay.   b. Avoid touching the microscope or stage during recording.5. Completion:   a. Initial State: Both slides show bright and comparable fluorescence intensity at the start of illumination.2. During Continuous Illumination:   a. The slide mounted in plain glycerol shows a noticeable decrease in fluorescence intensity over time.   b. The experiment visually demonstrates the biophysical mechanism of photobleaching and the protective role of antifade reagents.VI. Experimental Precautions1. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Leaf Starch Iodine Test After Light ExposureI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Leaf Starch Iodine Test After Light Exposure2. Subject: Biology – Plant Physiology (Photosynthesis)3. Experiment Objective: To verify that starch is produced in green leaves only in areas exposed to light, and to understand the role of light in photosynthesis.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsFresh green leaf (broad leaf), opaque aluminum foil, strong light source or sunlight, beaker, hot water bath, ethanol (95%), forceps, white tray or tile, dropper, iodine solution.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Select a healthy green leaf. Cover the left half tightly with opaque foil, leaving the right half uncovered.2. Light Exposure: Place the leaf under bright light for sufficient time to allow photosynthesis.3. Killing and Decolorization: Remove the leaf and place it in hot water briefly to stop metabolic activity, then transfer it into hot ethanol in a water bath until the leaf becomes pale and chlorophyll is removed.4. Rinsing: Rinse the decolorized leaf in warm water to soften it.5. Iodine Test: Spread the leaf flat on a white tray. Using a dropper, evenly apply iodine solution over the leaf surface.6. Observation and Recording: Fix the camera focus and record the color change for time-lapse observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before iodine: The leaf appears pale after ethanol treatment.2. After iodine application: The uncovered (light-exposed) right half turns blue-black, while the foil-covered left half remains yellow-brown or lightly colored.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePhotosynthesis in green leaves produces starch only in the presence of light. The covered part of the leaf cannot receive light and therefore does not form starch. Ethanol removes chlorophyll so color changes are visible. Iodine reacts with starch to form a blue-black complex, demonstrating that starch is present only in the illuminated areas of the leaf.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Ionic Interaction Screening in Milk ColloidsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Milk Colloid Clumping After Salt Addition2. Subject: Biology – Natural Science (Colloids and Ionic Interactions)3. Experiment Objective: To observe how added salt screens ionic interactions in milk colloids, leading to aggregation, and to understand the stability of colloidal systems through visual comparison.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo transparent glasses of the same size, fresh milk (enough to fill both glasses equally), table salt (sodium chloride), spoon (1), flat table surface, camera or mobile phone fixed on a stand (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, transparent glasses side by side on a flat surface. Pour equal volumes of milk into each glass. Label the left glass as A and the right glass as B.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera position and focus so that both glasses are clearly visible in the same frame. Ensure lighting is stable.3. Core Operation: Leave glass A untouched. Add one spoonful of table salt to glass B and gently stir with the spoon until the salt is dispersed.4. Observation Stage: Stop stirring and keep both glasses still. Record or observe both glasses over a short period (time-lapse recommended).IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both glasses contain uniform, white, opaque milk with no visible clumps.2. After Salt Addition: In glass B, small clumps or curd-like aggregates gradually appear, and slight separation may be observed. Glass A remains uniformly milky with no visible change.3. Comparative Result: The difference between glass A and glass B becomes increasingly clear over time.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesMilk is a colloidal system in which protein particles are stabilized by electrical charges on their surfaces. When salt is added, ions from sodium chloride screen and reduce these surface charges. This weakens the repulsive forces between colloidal particles, allowing them to aggregate and form visible clumps. The untreated milk remains stable, demonstrating the role of ionic interaction screening in colloid stability.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use equal volumes of milk for accurate comparison.2. Do not add salt to the control glass.3. Avoid shaking the glasses after stirring.4. Ensure camera focus and position remain fixed throughout observation.

Minimum assumptions: milk is a stable colloid; added salt provides ions that reduce electrostatic repulsion among colloidal particles.Phased Storyline: (1) Initial stable state—two identical glasses of uniform milk side by side. (2) Intervention—salt added and stirred only in the right glass, left glass untouched. (3) Transition—after stirring stops, ions act to screen charges. (4) Outcome—gradual visible clumping or separation in the right glass while the left glass remains unchanged. Visibility constraints: both glasses must remain in the same frame, with fixed camera focus, allowing direct visual comparison over time.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Microscope Time-Lapse of Yeast Cells Shrinking and Recovering After Osmotic AdjustmentI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Microscope Observation of Osmotic Response in Yeast Cells2. Subject: Biology – Cell Biology3. Experiment Objective: To observe the osmotic behavior of live yeast cells under a light microscope by recording cell shrinkage in a hypertonic saline solution and recovery after returning to an isotonic solution, and to understand the principle of osmosis across the cell membrane.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsLight microscope (with 400× magnification capability), glass slide and coverslip, dropper or micropipette, live yeast suspension (in isotonic solution), hypertonic saline solution (e.g., 5–10% NaCl), isotonic solution (e.g., physiological saline or culture medium), absorbent paper.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean glass slide on the bench. Using a dropper, add one small drop of live yeast suspension onto the center of the slide.2. Mounting: Gently place a coverslip over the droplet to form a thin liquid layer without air bubbles. Place the slide on the microscope stage and focus until individual yeast cells are clearly visible.3. Initial Observation: Observe and record the initial state of yeast cells. Cells should appear plump, oval to round, with stable size in the isotonic environment.4. Hypertonic Treatment: At one edge of the coverslip, add a drop of hypertonic saline. Simultaneously place absorbent paper at the opposite edge to draw the solution under the coverslip, ensuring cells remain in view.5. Time-Lapse Observation: Continuously observe the same field of view. Over a short time, record yeast cells shrinking and becoming more compact as water leaves the cells.6. Isotonic Recovery: Add isotonic solution at one edge of the coverslip and use absorbent paper at the opposite edge to replace the hypertonic solution.7. Recovery Observation: Observe and record the gradual recovery of yeast cell volume as cells rehydrate and return toward their original shape.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Yeast cells are full, smooth, and stable in size.2. After Hypertonic Saline Introduction: Cells gradually shrink, with reduced volume and increased density; some cells may show clear plasmolysis.3. After Isotonic Solution Exchange: Cells slowly re-expand, regaining volume and approaching their original shape.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates osmosis across a selectively permeable cell membrane. In a hypertonic environment, the external solute concentration is higher than inside the yeast cell, causing water to move out of the cell and resulting in cell shrinkage. When the environment is returned to isotonic conditions, the solute concentration inside and outside the cell becomes balanced, allowing water to re-enter the cell and restore its volume. This reversible process illustrates the fundamental principles of cellular water balance and membrane permeability.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure solutions are introduced gently to avoid displacing the coverslip or washing cells out of view.2. Keep the same microscopic field of view throughout the experiment for accurate comparison.3. Use fresh, live yeast for clear osmotic responses.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Osmosis in living yeast cells observed under a light microscope. Minimum assumptions: yeast cells are alive, have semipermeable membranes, and change volume in response to external solute concentration.Phased storyline: (1) Initial phase – stable, plump yeast cells in an isotonic droplet under a light microscope; cells are clearly visible and stationary. (2) Hypertonic phase – introduction of hypertonic saline causes a causal transition where water exits cells, leading to visible, gradual shrinking while cells remain in view. Visibility constraints: fixed microscope perspective, consistent lighting, and continuous framing are required to verify size changes and causal order.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Yeast Producing Carbon Dioxide in Sugar SolutionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Yeast Producing Carbon Dioxide in Sugar-Rich Solution vs Plain Water2. Subject: Natural Science - Microbiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that yeast can use sugar as a nutrient source to carry out respiration and fermentation, producing carbon dioxide gas, and to compare the gas production in sugar-rich solution and plain water through visible balloon inflation and bubble formation.II. Experimental EquipmentClear plastic bottles (2 identical bottles, 500 mL recommended), balloons (2, light-colored and flexible), dry yeast (same brand and batch, 1 teaspoon per bottle), warm water (about 35–40 °C), granulated sugar (2 teaspoons), measuring spoon, funnel (optional), camera or mobile phone with tripod for fixed-focus time-lapse photography.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two empty clear bottles side by side on a stable surface. Label the left bottle Sugar Water and the right bottle Plain Water. Ensure the camera is fixed on a tripod, focused on both bottles, and will not move during recording.2. Solution Setup: Pour equal volumes of warm water into both bottles (about 300 mL each). Add 2 teaspoons of sugar only to the left bottle. Gently swirl until the sugar dissolves completely. Do not add sugar to the right bottle.3. Adding Yeast: Using the same measuring spoon, add 1 teaspoon of dry yeast into each bottle. Do not stir; allow the yeast to settle naturally.4. Balloon Placement: Carefully stretch a balloon over the mouth of each bottle, ensuring an airtight but loose seal so the balloon can expand upward.5. Observation and Recording: Leave both bottles undisturbed in a warm place. Start time-lapse recording with the fixed camera. Observe changes over time.6. Comparison: The difference between the two bottles becomes increasingly obvious, with significantly more gas production in the sugar water bottle.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesYeast is a living microorganism that requires sugar as an energy source. In warm sugar-rich conditions, yeast carries out respiration and fermentation, breaking down sugar to release energy and producing carbon dioxide gas as a byproduct. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Protein Precipitation by Salting Out in Cell-Free Microbial CultureI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Protein Precipitation Caused by High Salt Concentration2. Subject: Natural Science – Microbiology3. Experiment Objective: To observe protein precipitation from a cell-free microbial culture when ionic strength is increased by adding concentrated salt solution, and to understand the salting-out principle through visible settling phenomena.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass beaker (250 mL), magnetic stirrer or glass stirring rod, concentrated salt solution (e.g., saturated ammonium sulfate or sodium chloride), cell-free microbial culture supernatant (clear), pipette or dropping funnel, lab bench, camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear beaker containing the cell-free microbial culture on the lab bench. Ensure the solution is transparent and free of cells or debris. Fix the camera focus and framing toward the beaker.2. Stirring: Begin gentle stirring of the culture using a stirrer or rod, avoiding air bubbles.3. Salt Addition: Slowly add concentrated salt solution dropwise into the beaker while continuing gentle stirring, ensuring even mixing.4. Stop Stirring: After the planned volume of salt solution is added, stop stirring carefully without disturbing the liquid.5. Standing Observation: Leave the beaker undisturbed and continue time-lapse recording to capture changes over time.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The culture solution is clear and transparent with no visible solids.2. During Salt Addition: The solution gradually becomes cloudy; small white or pale aggregates appear.3. After Standing: Visible protein precipitates grow larger and slowly settle to the bottom of the beaker, forming a sediment while the upper liquid becomes clearer.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIncreasing salt concentration raises the ionic strength of the solution. Salt ions compete with protein molecules for water, reducing protein solubility. As hydration shells collapse, proteins aggregate and precipitate out of solution. Under gravity, these aggregates settle, forming visible solids. This process is known as salting out and is commonly used in protein purification.VI. Experimental PrecautionsAdd salt slowly to avoid local over-concentration; maintain gentle stirring; do not disturb the beaker during settling; handle concentrated salt solutions with care.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Bacteriophage Endpoint Dilution Showing Clearing vs TurbiditySubject: Natural Science – MicrobiologyObjective: To observe bacteriophage-induced lysis of bacteria at different phage concentrations, determine the endpoint dilution, and understand the relationship between phage titer and bacterial clearing.II. Serial Dilution: Add bacteriophage stock to the first tube. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: E. coli Transformed with GFP Plasmid Showing Green FluorescenceI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of GFP Expression in Transformed E. coli2. Subject: Natural Science - Microbiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that E. coli cells transformed with a GFP plasmid can express green fluorescent protein and emit green fluorescence under blue light, and to compare transformed bacteria with a non-transformed control.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentE. coli competent cells, GFP plasmid, LB agar plates (with appropriate antibiotic), water bath for heat shock, incubator (37°C), sterile spreaders, blue light source or transilluminator, marker for labeling plates, dark laboratory environment or darkened room.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Label two LB agar plates: Plate A as GFP-transformed and Plate B as non-transformed control.2. Transformation: Mix GFP plasmid with competent E. coli and perform heat-shock transformation according to standard protocol. Do not add plasmid to the control sample.3. Plating: Spread transformed cells onto Plate A and control cells onto Plate B using sterile technique.4. Incubation: Place both plates upside down in a 37°C incubator for sufficient time to allow colony growth.5. Observation Setup: After incubation, place the two agar plates side by side in a dark lab environment.6. Illumination: Shine blue light evenly onto both plates.IV. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe GFP plasmid carries the gene encoding green fluorescent protein. After heat-shock transformation, some E. coli cells take up the plasmid and express the GFP gene. This experiment visually demonstrates gene expression and the use of a control for comparison.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Follow aseptic techniques throughout the experiment.2. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Weak Acid Applied to Carbonate Fossil versus Silicate-Rich SedimentI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Reaction of Weak Acid with Carbonate Shell Fragment and Silicate-Rich Sediment2. Subject: Natural Science – Paleontology3. Experiment Objective: To distinguish carbonate fossils from silicate-rich sediments by observing their different reactions with a weak acid, and to understand the chemical basis for fossil identification.II. Experimental EquipmentLab bench, carbonate shell fragment (left), silicate-rich sediment sample (right), dilute weak acid (e.g., 5% acetic acid or dilute hydrochloric acid), two droppers, petri dishes or glass slides, camera or smartphone with fixed mount for time-lapse recording, protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the carbonate shell fragment on a petri dish on the left side of the lab bench and the silicate-rich sediment on a separate dish on the right. Ensure both samples are dry and clearly visible.2. Camera Setup: Mount the camera above the bench, adjust focus to include both samples, and fix the focus and position to avoid changes during recording.3. Acid Application: Fill two droppers with the weak acid. Simultaneously apply one drop of acid to the surface of the carbonate shell fragment (left) and one drop to the silicate-rich sediment (right).4. Recording: Continue recording for a short period (or use time-lapse) to capture the reactions.5. Completion: Stop recording after the main phenomena are observed. Neutralize and dispose of residues according to lab safety rules.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Carbonate Shell Fragment (Left): Immediately after acid application, small bubbles appear on the surface, indicating effervescence.2. Silicate-Rich Sediment (Right): No visible bubbling occurs; the surface remains largely unchanged.3. Comparison: The contrast between active bubbling on the carbonate and the inert silicate is clear and persistent.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCarbonate fossils contain calcium carbonate (CaCO3), which reacts with weak acids to produce carbon dioxide gas, water, and a soluble salt, resulting in visible effervescence. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: River vs. Lake Sediment Deposition Using Flowing vs. Still Water2. Subject: Natural Science – Paleontology (Sedimentology Basics)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how water movement affects sediment deposition, helping learners understand why river deposits are layered and sorted while lake deposits are finer and more uniform, a key concept for interpreting sedimentary rocks and fossils.II. Experimental Equipment- Clear plastic trays (2 identical trays)- Water source (tap or container)- Small pump or raised inlet to create gentle flowing water in one tray- Mixed sediment (sand, silt, small gravel; well mixed)- Measuring scoop (same size for both trays)- Camera or smartphone with tripod- Stable table and light sourceIII. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Place two clear trays side by side on a level table. Fill both trays with equal depths of water.2. Water Conditions: Keep one tray completely still (lake model). In the other tray, create gentle, continuous water flow from one end to the other (river model).3. Camera Fixing: Position the camera directly above or at a slight angle so both trays are fully visible. Fix focus and framing, and start time-lapse recording.4. Sediment Addition: Simultaneously pour one equal scoop of mixed sediment into the upstream end of the flowing tray and the center of the still tray.5. Observation Period: Allow sediment to settle while recording. Do not disturb the trays during deposition.6. End of Experiment: Stop recording after clear deposition patterns are visible. Turn off water flow.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Flowing Water Tray (River): Coarser gravel settles quickly near the entry point; sand deposits downstream; fine silt remains suspended longer and travels farther, forming visible layering.2. Still Water Tray (Lake): Most sediments fall nearly straight down; finer particles settle slowly, forming a more uniform, flat layer with minimal sorting.3. Over Time (Time-lapse): Differences in sediment sorting, spread, and layering become increasingly clear between the two trays.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSediment deposition depends on water energy. Flowing water has enough energy to carry fine particles farther while dropping heavier particles first, producing sorted, layered deposits typical of rivers. Still water lacks directional energy, so particles settle mainly by gravity, producing finer, evenly distributed layers typical of lakes. These patterns help paleontologists interpret ancient environments preserved in sedimentary rocks.VI. Experimental Precautions- Ensure both trays receive equal sediment amounts.- Keep water flow gentle and constant.- Avoid shaking the table during observation.- Fix camera focus to prevent visual bias in time-lapse comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Aquarium Tank Turbidity Current Flowing Down a Sloped BasinI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Aquarium Tank Turbidity Current Flowing Down a Sloped Basin2. Subject: Natural Science – Paleontology (Sedimentology and Stratigraphic Processes)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the formation, movement, and deposition behavior of a turbidity current by releasing a pulse of dark sediment-laden water into an aquarium tank with a sloped basin transitioning to a flat floor, and to understand how gravity-driven density flows transport and deposit sediments in ancient marine environments.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent aquarium tank (rectangular, clean);Adjustable sloped insert or basin ramp (one end elevated, smoothly transitioning to a flat bottom);Flat tank floor area at base of slope;Container or cup (for holding sediment-laden water);Fine dark sediment (e.g., clay, silt, or cocoa powder as proxy);Clear water;Camera or smartphone with tripod;Uniform background and side lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the sloped basin inside the aquarium so that it descends smoothly to a flat floor. Fill the tank with clear water until the slope and flat floor are fully submerged. Allow the water to settle until completely still.2. Sediment Mixture Preparation: In a container, mix fine dark sediment with water to create a visibly darker, denser suspension. Stir until uniform and free of clumps.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera at the side of the tank, perpendicular to the slope, ensuring the entire slope-to-floor transition is in frame. Fix the camera focus and exposure. Set the camera for continuous or time-lapse recording.4. Core Operation: Gently hold the container at the top of the slope, just above the water surface. Release a single pulse of the dark sediment-laden water into the tank without stirring the surrounding clear water.5. Observation and Recording: Continue filming as the sediment-laden flow moves downslope, spreads onto the flat floor, and gradually slows and deposits sediment.6. Completion: Stop recording after the flow ceases and the sediment has largely settled. Drain and clean the tank after observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Clear, still water fills the tank; the slope and flat floor are clearly visible with no suspended sediment.2. Downslope Flow: Upon release, the dark sediment-laden water sinks and forms a coherent turbidity current that accelerates downslope due to gravity.3. Transition Zone: At the slope-to-flat boundary, the flow decelerates, thickens, and spreads laterally across the flat floor.4. Deposition Stage: Sediment gradually settles from the flow, forming a darker layer on the flat floor, while the overlying water becomes progressively clearer.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis demonstration models turbidity currents, which are gravity-driven density flows caused by suspended sediment increasing water density. The denser sediment-laden water flows downslope beneath clearer, less dense water. As slope decreases, flow velocity drops, causing sediment deposition. Such processes are fundamental in forming graded bedding and deep-marine sedimentary layers observed in the paleontological and stratigraphic record.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Release the sediment mixture smoothly to avoid artificial turbulence.2. Ensure fine sediment is well mixed to maintain uniform density.3. Keep the camera fixed to preserve spatiotemporal consistency.4. Avoid external vibrations during filming.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Muddy Sediment Flow in a Clear Laboratory FlumeI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Observation of Muddy Sediment Transport in a Clear FlumeSubject: Natural Science – Paleontology (Sedimentology)Objective: To demonstrate how muddy sediment remains suspended under turbulent flow and begins to settle when flow rate is reduced, simulating natural river and depositional processes.II. Experimental EquipmentClear laboratory flume (transparent side walls), water circulation pump with adjustable flow rate, fine sediment or clay (brown), water reservoir, flow control valve, ruler or scale on flume wall (optional), fixed-focus camera mounted for side view, lighting source.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fill the flume with clean water and ensure side walls are transparent. Fix the camera at a side view, lock focus, and prepare for time-lapse recording.2. Sediment Introduction: Add a measured amount of fine sediment into the upstream section of the flume.3. High-Flow Stage: Turn on the pump and adjust to a higher flow rate to generate turbulent water. Allow sediment to mix and suspend uniformly.4. Flow Reduction Stage: Gradually reduce the flow rate using the control valve while continuing recording.5. Completion: Maintain low flow briefly, then stop the pump. End recording.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Clear water in the flume with visible sediment added.Turbulent Flow: Water becomes visibly muddy; sediment is suspended throughout the water column with swirling motion.Reduced Flow: Turbulence weakens; sediment concentration decreases in the upper water column, and particles begin to settle toward the flume bottom, forming a denser layer.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSediment transport depends on flow velocity and turbulence. High-energy turbulent flow provides upward forces that keep fine particles in suspension. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the flume is level and sealed; reduce flow gradually to avoid sudden disturbances; keep camera fixed to maintain consistent observation.

Experiment Title: Simulation of Asteroid Impact Crater Formation Using a Dropped Steel Sphere2. Subject: Natural Science – Paleontology3. Experiment Objective: To simulate and observe the basic process of asteroid impact crater formation, understand how impact energy affects surface materials, and recognize characteristic features of impact craters through visual observation.II. Experimental EquipmentShallow tray (flat-bottomed), fine dry sand or flour, sieve or straight ruler (for leveling), polished steel sphere (smooth, spherical), support or hand for releasing the sphere, camera or smartphone with tripod, stable light source.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the shallow tray on a stable, level surface. Pour fine sand or flour into the tray to a depth of about 2–3 cm.2. Bed Smoothing: Use a ruler or gently shake the tray to create a smooth, flat, and uniform surface without grooves or slopes.3. Camera Setup: Fix the camera directly above or at a slight angle to the tray. Lock focus and exposure. Start recording or set time-lapse mode.4. Core Operation: Hold the polished steel sphere directly above the center of the tray at a fixed height. Release it vertically without horizontal push so it falls freely under gravity.5. Observation: Allow the sphere to impact the surface and come to rest. Do not disturb the tray immediately after impact.6. Completion: Stop recording after visible sand/flour movement ceases. Carefully remove the sphere if needed for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The sand/flour surface is smooth, flat, and undisturbed.2. Impact Moment: Upon impact, material is rapidly displaced outward from the contact point.3. Immediate Result: A circular, bowl-shaped crater forms at the center, with a raised rim.4. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Sand and Gravel Moving Along the Bottom of a Shallow Stream FlumeI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Bedload Transport in a Shallow Stream FlumeSubject: Natural Science - PaleontologyObjective: To observe how flowing water in a shallow stream moves sand and gravel along the bed, helping explain sediment transport processes relevant to fossil deposition.II. Experimental EquipmentClear shallow stream flume or transparent tray; sand and small gravel; water source with adjustable flow; stand or blocks to create gentle slope; collection container.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear flume on a stable support and raise one end slightly to form a gentle downslope.2. Bed Setup: Evenly spread a thin layer of sand mixed with small gravel along the bottom of the flume.3. Water Introduction: Slowly introduce water at the higher end until a shallow, steady flow forms downslope.4. Core Operation: Adjust flow so water moves smoothly without splashing; maintain constant flow for observation.5. Observation: Watch sediment behavior along the bed during flow.6. Conclusion: Stop water flow, drain flume, and clean materials.IV. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesFlowing water exerts shear stress on the stream bed. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Stream Table Demonstration of Sediment DepositionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Stream Table Demonstration of Sediment Sorting and Deposition2. Subject: Natural Science – Paleontology / Earth Science3. Experiment Objective: To simulate river processes using a sloped laboratory stream table and observe how flowing water transports and deposits gravel, sand, and mud, illustrating sediment sorting related to flow energy.II. Experimental EquipmentSloped laboratory stream table (with adjustable incline), water inlet with steady-flow pump or reservoir, outlet drain, mixed sediments (gravel, sand, fine mud), collection tray, overhead or fixed-position camera for time-lapse recording, light source.III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Place the stream table on a stable surface and adjust it to a gentle, uniform slope. Ensure the outlet is lower than the inlet and unobstructed.2. Sediment Placement: Evenly spread a thin layer of mixed gravel, sand, and mud across the upper section of the stream table near the inlet.3. Camera Preparation: Fix the camera position and focus so the entire length of the stream table, from inlet to outlet, is visible. Do not adjust focus during recording.4. Water Flow Initiation: Turn on the water inlet to produce a steady, continuous flow toward the outlet.5. Core Operation: Allow water to flow across the sediments for a short, continuous period. Record the process using time-lapse or accelerated recording.6. Completion: Stop the water flow after clear deposition patterns form. Save the recorded footage.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Sediments are mixed and stationary on the sloped surface.2. During Flow: Water begins to transport sediments; gravel moves short distances and settles quickly near the inlet, sand travels farther, and fine mud remains suspended longer.3. Final State: Coarse gravel is deposited near the source area, sand forms mid-stream deposits, and fine mud settles in quieter water near the outlet.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesFlowing water has different energy levels along a stream. Near the source, higher energy allows transport of coarse materials, but they settle quickly as energy decreases. Finer particles remain suspended longer and are carried farther downstream before deposition. This process, known as sediment sorting, explains characteristic sedimentary patterns observed in ancient river deposits and the fossil record.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure water flow is steady, avoid disturbing sediments during operation, keep camera focus fixed, and clean the stream table after use.

Minimum assumptions include gravity-driven water flow on a sloped surface, mixed sediment sizes, and decreasing flow energy downstream.Phased Storyline: (1) Static setup showing sloped stream table with mixed sediments; (2) steady water flow initiated from inlet toward outlet; (3) active transport where gravel moves briefly and settles early, sand moves moderately, and fine mud remains suspended; (4) final deposition pattern with coarse material upstream and fine material downstream. Visibility constraints require a fixed camera angle capturing inlet-to-outlet continuity to verify causal sediment sorting.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Petrified Wood vs Modern Wood Sinking BehaviorI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Sinking Behavior of Petrified Wood and Modern Wood in Water2. Subject: Natural Science – Earth Science3. Experiment Objective: To compare the sinking behavior of petrified wood and modern wood in water, observe differences in buoyancy, and understand how fossilization changes material density.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical clear water containers, clean tap water, one similar-sized piece of petrified wood, one similar-sized piece of modern wood, flat stable table, camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clear containers side by side on a stable table and fill them with equal amounts of clear water.2. Setup: Position petrified wood above the left container and modern wood above the right container; adjust camera to cover both containers and lock focus.3. Core Operation: Release both wood samples into the water simultaneously and begin time-lapse recording.4. Observation: Allow the samples to move freely in the water without disturbance.5. Final State: Petrified wood rests at the bottom; modern wood remains near or at the surface.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePetrified wood has undergone mineral replacement during fossilization, greatly increasing its density above that of water, causing it to sink. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Copper Sulfate Dissolves in Water but Not in OilI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Copper Sulfate Dissolves in Water but Not in Oil2. Subject: Natural Science – Earth Science (Properties of Materials)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that copper sulfate is soluble in water but insoluble in vegetable oil by observing color changes after shaking and settling in a layered liquid system.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass jar with lid (1), clean water, vegetable oil, copper sulfate crystals (blue), small spoon or spatula, safety gloves (recommended).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear jar on a flat surface. Pour water into the jar to about one-half of its height.2. Layering: Slowly pour vegetable oil along the inner wall of the jar until it forms a clear upper layer above the water. Allow the layers to settle and separate clearly.3. Addition of Solute: Add a small amount of copper sulfate crystals into the jar so that the crystals pass through the oil layer and reach the water layer.4. Shaking: Close the lid tightly. Gently but thoroughly shake the jar for several seconds so that the copper sulfate contacts both liquids.5. Settling: Place the jar back on the table and leave it undisturbed until the oil and water layers separate again.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The bottom layer is colorless water, and the top layer is colorless or pale yellow vegetable oil.2. During Shaking: Copper sulfate crystals move throughout the jar, and blue color begins to appear mainly in the water.3. After Settling: The water layer at the bottom becomes blue due to dissolved copper sulfate, while the oil layer remains clear and unchanged.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCopper sulfate is an ionic compound that readily dissolves in polar solvents such as water but does not dissolve in non-polar substances such as vegetable oil. During shaking, copper sulfate comes into contact with both liquids, but only water can dissolve it. After settling, the denser water forms the bottom layer containing dissolved copper sulfate, while the oil remains on top without color change.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse a small amount of copper sulfate; avoid direct contact with skin; ensure the jar lid is secure before shaking; dispose of solutions according to safety guidelines.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Different-Sized Spheres Settling in a Clear Water ColumnI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Different-Sized Spheres Settling in a Clear Water Column2. Subject: Natural Science – Paleontology (Sedimentation Processes)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how particle size affects settling speed in water, helping to understand sediment sorting processes relevant to fossil formation and stratigraphy.II. Experimental EquipmentTall transparent water column (acrylic or glass), clear water (filled to at least 80% of column height), two smooth solid spheres of the same material but different diameters (e.g., glass or metal), release device or hand for simultaneous release, camera with fixed focus and stable mount.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Fill the transparent column with clear, still water and place it upright on a stable surface. Ensure no visible currents or bubbles are present. Fix the camera focus and frame the entire column.Core Operation: Hold the two smooth spheres at the same height just above the water surface. Release both spheres simultaneously without applying extra force.Recording: Use fixed-focus time-lapse or accelerated recording to capture the full settling process until both spheres reach the bottom.Completion: Stop recording after both spheres have settled; reset equipment if repeating the experiment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both spheres start from the same height and begin to sink simultaneously.2. During Settling: The larger sphere accelerates and moves downward faster than the smaller sphere, creating an increasing vertical separation.3. Final State: The larger sphere reaches the bottom first, followed by the smaller sphere.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment illustrates sedimentation principles governed by gravity, buoyancy, and fluid drag. Although both spheres are made of the same material, the larger sphere has a greater mass-to-surface-area ratio, experiencing relatively less drag per unit weight. This principle explains natural size-based sorting of sediments in water, which is important in understanding layered deposits and fossil burial environments.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure simultaneous release to avoid bias; keep water still before release; maintain a fixed camera position; use smooth spheres to minimize turbulence effects.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Elongated Shell Fragments Aligning in a Shallow Water Flume Under Steady CurrentI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Elongated Shell Fragments Aligning in a Shallow Water Flume Under Steady CurrentSubject: Natural Science - Paleontology (Sedimentology)Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how elongated shell fragments on a sandy bed become preferentially aligned under a steady unidirectional water current, and to understand the sedimentary processes that produce shell orientation patterns in the fossil record.II. Experimental EquipmentClear-sided shallow water flume (with adjustable flow control), clean fine sand, elongated shell fragments or shell-shaped analogs (length clearly greater than width), water supply and pump, flow straightener (optional), ruler or scale marker, video camera or smartphone with tripod, stable lighting source.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Place the flume on a level surface. Spread an even layer of fine sand (1–2 cm thick) on the bottom. Gently place elongated shell fragments randomly on the sandy bed, ensuring varied initial orientations.Camera Setup: Position the camera perpendicular to the clear side of the flume. Fix the focus and framing so the entire shell bed is visible. Do not adjust focus during recording.Initiating Flow: Start the water pump and gradually increase to a steady, low-energy unidirectional current that moves across the sandy bed without eroding it.Core Operation: Maintain a constant flow rate. Record continuously or use time-lapse photography as water flows over the shell fragments.Completion: After clear alignment is observed, stop the flow. Save the recorded footage for analysis.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Shell fragments lie flat on the sand with random orientations.During Flow: As water flows, shells begin to pivot, slide slightly, and rotate.Final State: Most elongated shell fragments become aligned with their long axes parallel to the current direction, forming a preferred orientation.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesElongated particles in a moving fluid experience uneven drag and lift forces. Under a steady unidirectional current, shells rotate until their long axes align parallel to flow, minimizing resistance and achieving hydrodynamic stability. This process explains preferred shell orientations observed in sedimentary rocks and fossil assemblages, providing clues about ancient current directions.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure flow is steady and not turbulent. Avoid strong currents that may bury or transport shells out of view. Keep camera focus fixed to allow accurate time-lapse comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Ion Exchange Resin Column Showing Color Front as Hard-Water Ions Replace SodiumI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Ion Exchange Resin Column Showing Color Front as Hard-Water Ions Replace Sodium2. Subject: Natural Science – Earth Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the softening of hard water by ion exchange, observe the replacement of sodium ions on a resin by calcium ions, and visually understand the process through a moving color front.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent vertical column with outlet valve; sodium-form cation exchange resin containing a color indicator; stand and clamp; beaker or flask; calcium-rich hard water (simulated CaCl2 solution); funnel; safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Secure the transparent column vertically on a stand. Ensure the outlet valve is closed. Wear safety goggles.2. Packing the Column: Use a funnel to fill the column with sodium-form ion exchange resin. Gently tap to remove air bubbles and ensure uniform packing.3. Initial State Check: Rinse the resin with a small amount of distilled water until the resin shows a uniform initial indicator color.4. Core Operation: Place a beaker under the outlet. Open the outlet slightly and pour calcium-rich hard water into the top of the column, allowing it to flow downward at a steady rate.5. Observation Stage: Continue the flow for a short time, keeping the column vertical and flow rate constant.6. Completion: Stop the inflow, close the outlet, and record observations. Dispose of solutions properly and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The resin bed shows a uniform initial color, indicating sodium-form resin.2. During Flow: As hard water flows downward, a distinct color front appears near the top of the resin bed.3. Progression: The color front gradually moves downward with the flowing water, separating reacted resin (Ca-form) from unreacted resin (Na-form).V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIon exchange resins contain fixed negative groups that hold exchangeable cations. In the sodium form, the resin releases Na+ ions into solution when contacted by hard water containing Ca2+ or Mg2+. Because Ca2+ has a stronger affinity for the resin, it replaces Na+. The built-in indicator changes color when the resin switches from Na-form to Ca-form, making the ion-exchange process visible as a moving color front.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Maintain a slow, steady flow to keep the color front clear.2. Avoid introducing air bubbles into the resin bed.3. Handle solutions carefully and follow laboratory safety rules.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: ion exchange softening of hard water using sodium-form resin, assuming basic aqueous flow, ion selectivity, and indicator-based color change. Phased storyline: (1) static initial state with uniformly colored resin in a transparent vertical column; (2) introduction of calcium-rich hard water flowing downward; (3) formation of a distinct color front at the top of the resin due to Ca2+ replacing Na+; (4) smooth downward movement of the color front with continued flow. Visibility constraints: the column must be transparent, the resin bed fully visible, and the color contrast strong enough to track the front and verify causal sequence.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Pine Cone Drying and Opening to Release Winged SeedsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Pine Cone Drying and Opening to Release Winged Seeds2. Subject: Natural Science – Paleontology (Plant Fossil and Reproductive Structure Analogy)3. Experiment Objective: To observe how environmental humidity and dryness affect the opening and closing of mature pine cones, and to understand the physical principle by which pine cones release winged seeds under dry conditions.II. Experimental EquipmentMature pine cones (2, similar size and maturity), desk lamp or heat lamp (warm, dry light source), spray bottle with clean water, shallow tray or table surface, hygrometer or humidity indicator (optional), camera or mobile phone with tripod, time-lapse photography software or mode.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Select two mature, closed or semi-open pine cones. Place them side by side on a flat surface, keeping their orientation consistent. Fix the camera on a tripod directly facing the pine cones and lock focus and framing.2. Dry Condition Setup: Position a warm, dry lamp approximately 20–30 cm above one pine cone to create a dry environment. Ensure no water contacts this pine cone.3. Humid Condition Setup: Regularly mist the second pine cone with water to maintain a humid surface. Do not place it under the lamp.4. Recording: Start time-lapse recording. Film continuously for several hours, or use accelerated time-lapse mode to condense the process into a short video while preserving the sequence of changes.5. Completion: Stop recording once a clear difference in cone scale opening is observed. Turn off the lamp and clean the workspace.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both pine cones appear similar in shape, color (brown), and scale arrangement.2. During the Experiment: The pine cone under the warm, dry lamp gradually opens its scales outward. Final State: A clear contrast is visible: the dry pine cone is open, while the humid pine cone is closed or significantly less open.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePine cone scales are composed of plant tissues that respond differently to moisture. In dry conditions, the tissues shrink unevenly, causing the scales to bend outward and open, allowing winged seeds to disperse. In humid conditions, the tissues absorb water and swell, keeping the scales closed. This is a physical, non-living hygroscopic response rather than active growth, illustrating how ancient and modern conifers use environmental conditions to control seed release.VI. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Mixing Calcium Chloride Solution with Sodium Carbonate to Form Calcium CarbonateI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Mixing Calcium Chloride and Sodium Carbonate Solutions to Form Calcium Carbonate2. Subject: Natural Science – Earth Science (Basic Chemistry in Earth Materials)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the formation of calcium carbonate precipitate through a double displacement reaction; understand how mineral precipitates can form from aqueous solutions; demonstrate the process using two clear solutions with time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Equipment- Clear glass beakers (2, identical, 100–250 mL)- Aqueous calcium chloride solution (CaCl2, colorless and transparent)- Aqueous sodium carbonate solution (Na2CO3, colorless and transparent)- Glass stirring rod (optional, minimal use)- Camera or mobile device with tripod (for fixed-focus time-lapse recording)- Protective gloves and safety gogglesIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   - Place two clean, dry, clear beakers on a flat laboratory bench.   - Pour equal volumes (about 50 mL) of calcium chloride solution into one beaker and sodium carbonate solution into the other. Both solutions should be colorless and transparent.   - Set up the camera on a tripod facing the beakers. Fix the focus and framing so both beakers and the pouring process are clearly visible. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.2. Core Operation:   - Slowly and steadily pour the sodium carbonate solution from one beaker into the beaker containing the calcium chloride solution.   - Do not shake the beaker; allow the solutions to mix naturally during pouring. Optional: gently stir once with a glass rod after pouring is complete.3. Observation Stage:   - Continue recording for several seconds after pouring to capture the full development of the reaction.4. Completion:   - Stop recording. Allow the precipitate to settle.   - Dispose of the reaction mixture according to laboratory waste guidelines and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both solutions are clear, colorless, and transparent, with no visible solid.2. During Mixing: As the solutions come into contact, a white, cloudy substance appears immediately at the interface.3. After Mixing: The mixture becomes visibly turbid, with fine white solid particles suspended in the liquid; some precipitate may gradually settle at the bottom.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Core Reaction Equation:   CaCl2(aq) + Na2CO3(aq) → CaCO3(s)↓ + 2NaCl(aq)2. Principle Explanation:   When calcium ions (Ca2+) from calcium chloride react with carbonate ions (CO3 2−) from sodium carbonate, insoluble calcium carbonate forms as a white precipitate. This process models how carbonate minerals can precipitate from aqueous environments in Earth systems. The remaining sodium chloride stays dissolved in water.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both solutions are clear before mixing; contaminated solutions may affect observation.2. Pour slowly to clearly observe the formation process of the precipitate.3. Keep the camera focus fixed to avoid changes in image clarity during time-lapse recording.4. Wear safety goggles and gloves to prevent contact with chemical solutions.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Water Percolation Through Sandstone Versus Dense RockI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Water Percolation Through a Sandstone Block Versus a Dense Rock2. Subject: Natural Science - Geology & Geophysics3. Experiment Objective: To compare the permeability of porous sandstone and dense rock by observing differences in water infiltration and runoff, and to understand how rock structure affects groundwater movement.II. Experimental EquipmentSandy sandstone block (1), smooth dense rock block such as granite or basalt (1), two shallow trays, graduated cup or beaker, clean water, stable table surface.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two trays side by side on a level table. Put the sandy sandstone block in one tray and the smooth dense rock in the other, ensuring both rocks are dry and similar in size.2. Core Operation: Measure equal amounts of water using the graduated cup. Simultaneously pour the water evenly onto the top surface of each rock.3. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Simulating Formation of Mold Fossils (Shell Mold)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Simulating Formation of Mold Fossils (Shell Mold)2. Subject: Natural Science - Earth Science3. Experiment Objective: To simulate the formation of a mold fossil using a seashell and plaster, understand how organisms leave imprints in sediments, and observe the formation process through focused, time-lapse observation.II. Experimental MaterialsBowl or shallow container, dry plaster powder, water, stirring stick or spoon, natural seashell (clean and dry), camera or mobile device (fixed position, time-lapse mode).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the bowl on a stable surface. Prepare the camera so it focuses directly on the inside of the bowl, centered on the area where plaster will be poured.2. Pouring: Slowly pour the wet plaster paste into the bowl, forming an even layer.4. Placing the Shell: Gently place the seashell into the wet plaster with the convex side facing downward. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Mohs Hardness Scratch Test: Quartz Scratching Glass and Softer MineralsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Mohs Hardness Scratch Test Using Quartz2. Subject: Natural Science - Geology & Geophysics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate relative mineral hardness by observing that quartz can scratch glass and softer minerals when the same scratching motion is applied.II. Experimental EquipmentSharp quartz crystal, glass plate, softer mineral specimen (e.g., calcite or gypsum), clean work surface, safety gloves or goggles (recommended).III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the glass plate and softer mineral flat on a stable surface. Ensure their surfaces are clean and dry.Operation Step 1: Hold the sharp edge of the quartz crystal firmly in one hand.Operation Step 2: Using the same hand motion and pressure, draw the quartz tip across the surface of the glass plate in a straight line.Operation Step 3: Using the same motion and pressure, draw the quartz tip across the surface of the softer mineral.Observation Step: After scratching, tilt each surface under light and observe whether visible scratch marks are present.Conclusion Step: Compare the scratch results on glass and the softer mineral, then return equipment to a safe position.IV. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Dyed Water Flow Through Sand Versus Clay ColumnsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Permeability Between Sand and Clay Using Dyed Water2. Subject: Natural Science - Geology & Geophysics3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare the permeability of coarse sand and compacted clay by observing the flow rate of dyed water through two identical columns, and to understand how grain size and pore structure affect groundwater movement.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical clear vertical columns (transparent plastic or glass), coarse sand (dry and clean), clay (moistened and compacted), fine mesh or filter paper, two graduated cylinders or measuring cups, dyed water (water mixed with food coloring), collection containers, stable stand, camera fixed on tripod (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a piece of mesh or filter paper at the bottom of each column to prevent material loss. Pack one column evenly with coarse sand. Pack the other column tightly with clay, compacting it to reduce pore spaces. Ensure both columns have the same height of material.2. Setup: Secure the two columns vertically side by side on a stand. Place collection containers beneath each column. Fix the camera position and focus to include both columns in the frame.3. Core Operation: Measure equal volumes of dyed water using graduated cylinders. Simultaneously pour the dyed water into the top of both columns at a steady rate.4. Observation: Allow the water to infiltrate while recording continuously or via time-lapse. Do not disturb the setup during flow.5. Conclusion and Cleanup: After flow stabilizes, stop recording. Compare the collected water volumes and flow times. Dispose of materials properly and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both columns are dry or slightly moist, with no dyed water present.2. During Flow: In the sand column, dyed water quickly infiltrates and emerges at the bottom, forming a steady outflow. In the clay column, dyed water infiltrates very slowly, often pooling at the top with little or delayed outflow.3. Final State: Significantly more dyed water passes through the sand column in the same time period compared to the clay column.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePermeability refers to the ability of a material to transmit fluids through its pore spaces. Coarse sand has larger, well-connected pores, allowing water to flow easily. Compacted clay has very small pores and low connectivity, greatly restricting water movement. This experiment demonstrates fundamental groundwater flow principles in geology.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure equal packing height and identical columns; pour equal water volumes simultaneously; keep camera fixed; avoid cracks in clay that may artificially increase permeability.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Mica Sheet Cleavage Peeling into Thin Flexible LayersI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Mica Sheet Cleavage Peeling into Thin Flexible Layers2. Subject: Natural Science – Geology & Geophysics3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the perfect basal cleavage of mica minerals by manually peeling a shiny mica sample into thin, flexible layers, and to demonstrate the layered crystal structure of mica through direct visual and tactile observation.II. Experimental Materials and Equipment1. Natural mica sample (e.g., muscovite or biotite), with a shiny surface and visible sheet structure2. Bare hands (no tools required)3. Flat, stable surface (optional, for placing the sample)4. Camera or smartphone with fixed focus capability5. Tripod or stable support for time-lapse photography (optional but recommended)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Select a clean, dry mica sample with a reflective, plate-like surface. Place the camera in a fixed position facing the mica sample, adjust focus manually, and lock the focus to avoid refocusing during recording. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.2. Holding the Sample: Hold the mica sample steadily with one hand, ensuring the shiny basal surface is visible to the camera.3. Initiating Cleavage: Using the fingernail of the other hand, gently pry up an edge or corner of the mica along its natural plane.4. Peeling Process: Slowly peel the lifted edge away from the main body. Continue separating the mica along the same plane, producing a thin, transparent or translucent sheet.5. Repetition: Repeat the peeling process to obtain multiple thin layers, showing that each layer remains flexible and intact.6. Completion: Hold the peeled thin layers up to the camera to show their flexibility and sheen, then stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The mica sample appears solid, shiny, and plate-like, with smooth, reflective surfaces.2. During Peeling: The mica separates easily along flat planes. Thin sheets detach smoothly without breaking, maintaining a uniform thickness.3. Final State: The peeled mica layers are flexible, slightly transparent, and can bend without cracking, while the remaining sample retains flat cleavage surfaces.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesMica minerals have a sheet silicate (phyllosilicate) crystal structure, where silicon–oxygen tetrahedral layers are bonded strongly within the sheet but weakly between sheets by ionic bonds. These weak interlayer forces result in perfect basal cleavage, allowing mica to split easily into thin, flexible layers. The observed peeling directly demonstrates the anisotropic bonding and layered crystal structure characteristic of mica minerals.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Peel gently to avoid tearing very thin layers.2. Keep hands dry to maintain grip and prevent slipping.3. Ensure the camera focus is fixed before peeling to maintain consistent visual documentation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate mica basal cleavage resulting from its layered crystal structure, assuming mica is a sheet silicate with weak interlayer bonding.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Applying gentle force at an edge overcomes weak interlayer bonds, causing separation along flat planes without breaking sheets.Phased Storyline: (1) Static shiny mica held by bare hands with fixed camera focus; (2) Fingernail pries an edge, initiating separation; (3) Thin sheet peels away smoothly; (4) Multiple layers shown as flexible and intact. Visibility Constraints: Camera remains fixed and close enough to resolve thin layers, edge separation, and bending of sheets for verification.

manual: Experiment Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: River Channel Shifting and Point Bar Deposition in a Stream Table2. Subject: Natural Science – Geology & Geophysics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how steady flowing water in a meandering river causes lateral channel migration, erosion on outer bends, and deposition of point bars on inner bends, using a clear stream table with sand and gravel, and to document the process with fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Equipment1. Clear stream table (transparent sides and base)2. Fine sand (light-colored) and small gravel3. Adjustable water supply with steady flow control (pump or elevated reservoir)4. Water collection basin and drain hose5. Camera or mobile device mounted on a fixed tripod (focus locked)6. Overhead light source (uniform illumination)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   - Place the stream table on a stable, level surface.   - Evenly spread a 3–5 cm thick layer of sand mixed with small gravel across the base.   - Gently carve a shallow, sinuous (meandering) channel from the upstream to downstream end.   - Set up the camera above the stream table, ensure the entire channel is visible, and lock focus and position.2. Initiating Flow:   - Start the water supply at a low, steady rate to avoid disturbing the sediment abruptly.   - Allow water to flow continuously through the pre-cut meandering channel.3. Core Observation Operation:   - Maintain a constant flow rate throughout the experiment.   - Do not touch or reshape the channel once flow begins.   - Record the process using time-lapse photography, capturing gradual changes in channel shape.4. Ending the Experiment:   - After clear channel migration and sediment deposition are observed, stop the water flow.   - Turn off the camera and save the time-lapse recording.   - Drain water, clean the stream table, and store equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Water flows smoothly within the original meandering channel; sand and gravel remain mostly stable.2. During Flow:   - Outer bends of meanders show erosion, with sediment being removed.   - Inner bends show accumulation of sand and gravel, forming visible point bars.   - The channel gradually shifts laterally over time.3. Final State:   - The meandering path has migrated compared to its initial position.   - Point bars are clearly developed on inner bends, while cut banks appear on outer bends.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates fluvial geomorphology principles. In meandering rivers, faster water flow along outer bends increases erosive power, removing sediment and causing bank retreat. Slower flow on inner bends reduces transport capacity, leading to sediment deposition and point bar formation. Continuous erosion and deposition cause lateral channel migration over time. The stream table simulates these natural river processes at a reduced scale.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Keep water flow steady; sudden changes may destroy the channel structure.2. Ensure camera focus and position remain fixed for valid time-lapse comparison.3. Avoid excessive flow rates that cause widespread sediment suspension instead of localized erosion and deposition.

Subject: Natural Science – Geology & Geophysics3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare mineral cleavage and fracture by lightly tapping a halite crystal and a quartz crystal under identical conditions.II. Experimental EquipmentWorkbench; cubic halite crystal (1); quartz crystal (1); small geological hammer (1); camera or smartphone fixed on a tripod for time-lapse or continuous recording; safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the workbench in a stable, well-lit area. Put on safety goggles. Fix the camera focus and position so both crystals are clearly visible throughout the experiment.2. Placement: Place the cubic halite crystal on the left side of the workbench and the quartz crystal on the right side, leaving sufficient space between them.3. Tapping Halite: Using the same small hammer, lightly tap the halite crystal once or twice from above. Avoid excessive force.4. Tapping Quartz: Using the same hammer and similar force, lightly tap the quartz crystal once or twice.5. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the low hardness of gypsum by observing whether a bare human fingernail can scratch its surface, and to visually record the process using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II.
