manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Mineral Fluorescence Under Ultraviolet LampI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Observation of Mineral Fluorescence Under Ultraviolet LightSubject: Natural Science – Geology & GeophysicsExperiment Objective: To observe and understand the fluorescence phenomenon of minerals such as calcite or fluorite under ultraviolet (UV) illumination, and to recognize the relationship between ultraviolet radiation and visible light emission.II. Experimental EquipmentCalcite or fluorite mineral specimen (1 piece), handheld ultraviolet lamp (long-wave UV recommended), table or flat surface, dark room or enclosed dark environment, camera with fixed focus and tripod (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the mineral specimen flat on the table. Set up the camera facing the mineral and fix the focus and position. Turn off ambient lights to darken the room.2. Initial Observation: With the ultraviolet lamp turned off, observe and record the appearance of the mineral in darkness.3. Core Operation: Turn on the handheld ultraviolet lamp and illuminate the mineral steadily. Maintain a fixed distance between the lamp and the mineral.4. Phenomenon Observation: Observe the color and intensity of light emitted by the mineral while illuminated by UV light.5. Lamp Off: Turn off the ultraviolet lamp and observe the immediate change in the mineral’s appearance.6. Repetition (Optional): Repeat switching the lamp on and off to confirm reproducibility of the phenomenon.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: In darkness without UV light, the mineral shows no visible glow and appears dim or colorless.2. Under UV Illumination: When exposed to ultraviolet light, the mineral emits visible fluorescent light, commonly blue, green, or orange, depending on its composition.3. After UV is Off: The visible glow disappears quickly once the ultraviolet lamp is turned off.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMineral fluorescence occurs when certain minerals absorb high-energy ultraviolet radiation and re-emit part of that energy as visible light. In calcite or fluorite, trace impurities and crystal lattice defects create energy levels that allow this conversion. When the UV source is removed, the excitation stops, and the visible emission ceases, demonstrating a direct cause-and-effect relationship between ultraviolet light and fluorescence.VI. Experimental PrecautionsAvoid direct eye exposure to ultraviolet light; do not point the UV lamp at skin or eyes; ensure the room is sufficiently dark to clearly observe fluorescence; keep camera focus fixed throughout recording.

Experiment Title: Mohs Hardness Scratch Test Comparing Quartz and Feldspar2. Subject: Natural Science - Geology and Geophysics3. Experiment Objective: To compare the relative hardness of quartz and feldspar using the Mohs scratch test, understand the concept of mineral hardness, and verify that a harder mineral can scratch a softer one.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentQuartz specimen (clear or white, clean surface)Pink feldspar specimen (flat surface preferred)Workbench or flat tabletopCamera or smartphone mounted on a fixed stand (for time-lapse recording)Protective gloves (optional)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the quartz and pink feldspar specimens side by side on a stable workbench with fresh, flat surfaces facing upward. Fix the camera position and focus so both minerals remain clearly visible throughout the experiment.2. First Scratch Test: Hold the quartz firmly in one hand. Using a consistent moderate force, drag the sharp edge of the quartz across the surface of the pink feldspar in a straight line.3. Observation Pause: Slightly tilt or adjust lighting (without moving specimens) to check for visible scratch marks on the feldspar surface.4. Second Scratch Test: Hold the pink feldspar and use it to scratch the surface of the quartz with similar force and motion.5. Final Observation: Examine the quartz surface for scratch marks and compare with the feldspar surface. Keep camera fixed to capture the full sequence as a time-lapse.IV. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the Mohs hardness scale, which ranks minerals by their ability to scratch others. Subject: Natural Science - Geology & Geophysics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate chemical weathering of limestone caused by weak acid, observe localized dissolution under continuous dripping, and understand the geological principle of carbonate rock weathering.II. Experimental EquipmentLimestone block (one flat surface exposed), weak acid solution (e.g., dilute acetic acid or carbonic acid solution), drip apparatus (dropper or burette with stand), collection tray or beaker, support stand for limestone, camera with tripod, timer or interval shooting mode, safety gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the limestone block on a stable support above a collection tray. Ensure one flat surface faces upward and is clean and dry.2. Drip Setup: Fix the drip apparatus above the limestone so that drops of weak acid fall continuously onto the same surface spot. Adjust to a slow, steady drip.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera facing the limestone block and runoff area. Fix focus, framing, and exposure. Set camera to time-lapse or continuous recording.4. Core Operation: Start acid dripping and simultaneously start camera recording. Allow the acid to drip continuously, flow across the limestone surface, and run off into the collection tray.5. Completion: After sufficient dripping time (or accelerated demonstration), stop the drip, stop recording, and safely dispose of the collected liquid.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Limestone surface appears solid, dry, and relatively smooth.2. During Dripping: The impact point remains wet; liquid flows downward along preferred paths. Final State: Compared with surrounding areas, the drip spot shows clearer signs of surface dissolution and roughening.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesLimestone is mainly composed of calcium carbonate (CaCO3). Weak acids react with calcium carbonate, producing soluble calcium bicarbonate, water, and carbon dioxide. Continuous acid contact at a fixed point enhances dissolution, demonstrating chemical weathering. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Formation of Black Copper Sulfide PrecipitateI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Formation of Black Copper Sulfide Precipitate by Adding Sulfide to Copper-Ion SolutionSubject: Natural Science – Geology & Geophysics (Geochemistry)Objective: To demonstrate that copper ions in solution react with sulfide ions to form an insoluble black copper sulfide precipitate, and to observe the reaction through side-by-side comparison and time-lapse recording.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsClear glass beakers (2, identical size); copper-ion solution (e.g., dilute copper(II) sulfate solution, blue); colorless sulfide solution (e.g., sodium sulfide solution, dilute); dropper or pipette; flat laboratory bench; camera or smartphone with fixed focus for time-lapse photography; protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, dry, clear beakers side by side on a stable bench. Pour equal volumes of blue copper-ion solution into each beaker, ensuring identical initial appearance.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly in front of the beakers. Fix focus, exposure, and angle. Start time-lapse recording.3. Core Operation: Using a dropper, slowly add the colorless sulfide solution dropwise into the left beaker only. Do not disturb the right beaker.4. Observation: Continue recording as the reaction proceeds. Do not stir vigorously; allow natural mixing.5. Completion: Stop adding sulfide once a clear precipitate is observed. End recording after the phenomenon stabilizes.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both beakers contain clear, blue copper-ion solution with no precipitate.During Addition: In the left beaker, black solid particles gradually appear and spread through the solution, causing it to darken and become turbid.Final State: The left beaker contains a visible black precipitate settled or suspended in the solution, while the right beaker remains blue and clear with no change.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCopper ions (Cu2+) react with sulfide ions (S2−) to form copper sulfide (CuS), an insoluble black solid. When sulfide is added to the copper-ion solution, a precipitation reaction occurs, removing Cu2+ from solution and producing black CuS. The right beaker serves as a control, confirming that the observed change is caused solely by sulfide addition.Core Reaction Equation: Cu2+ + S2− → CuS↓VI. PrecautionsUse dilute solutions to ensure clear observation; add sulfide slowly to avoid splashing; do not touch chemicals directly; dispose of waste according to laboratory safety guidelines.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Alignment of a Compass Needle with Earth’s Magnetic NorthI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Alignment of a Compass Needle with Earth’s Magnetic North after RotationSubject: Natural Science – Geology & GeophysicsExperiment Objective: To demonstrate that a freely rotating magnetic compass needle aligns with Earth’s magnetic north due to Earth’s magnetic field, and to observe the alignment process through time-lapse recording.II. Experimental EquipmentMagnetic compass (single, transparent housing preferred); flat tabletop (wood or non-magnetic material); human hand (operator); camera or smartphone with tripod; stable lighting environment.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the compass flat on the tabletop, away from magnetic interference (metal objects, electronic devices). Fix the camera above the compass, ensure the compass is centered in the frame, and lock the focus and exposure for time-lapse photography.2. Randomization: Use one hand to gently rotate the entire compass housing to disturb and randomize the needle orientation. Ensure the needle is visibly displaced from its original north-south direction.3. Release: Stop rotating and remove the hand completely, allowing the compass needle to move freely without external force.4. Recording: Continue time-lapse or continuous recording while the needle oscillates and gradually settles into a stable direction.5. Completion: Stop recording once the needle has clearly aligned and remains stable.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before rotation, the compass needle points approximately in a fixed north-south direction.2. After Rotation: Immediately after the housing is rotated and released, the needle is deflected and begins to swing back and forth.3. Alignment Process: The oscillation amplitude gradually decreases, and the needle slowly stabilizes.4. Final State: The needle comes to rest, aligning approximately along Earth’s magnetic north-south direction.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleEarth acts like a giant magnet, producing a magnetic field with magnetic north and south poles. The compass needle is a small magnet that experiences a torque in Earth’s magnetic field. When disturbed and then released, the needle rotates freely and aligns itself with the direction of the magnetic field, ultimately pointing toward Earth’s magnetic north. Damping due to friction and air resistance causes the oscillations to decrease until equilibrium is reached.

Phase 4 – Stabilization: Oscillations dampen over time, and the needle settles into a stable north-south alignment. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Deflection of a Magnetometer Needle by a Bar MagnetSubject: Natural Science – Geology & GeophysicsObjective: To demonstrate that a magnetic field produced by a bar magnet can deflect the needle of a handheld analog magnetometer, and that the direction of deflection depends on the magnet’s polarity and position.II. Experimental Equipment1. Handheld analog magnetometer with a clearly visible needle.2. Bar magnet with two clearly marked poles (red and blue ends).3. Flat tabletop.4. Camera or smartphone fixed on a tripod (focus locked for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the magnetometer flat on the tabletop, away from other magnetic objects. Ensure the needle is free to rotate and initially points steadily in one direction.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera above or at a slight angle to the tabletop so that both the magnetometer needle and the approaching magnet are clearly visible. Lock focus and exposure.3. Core Operation – Approach: Slowly bring the red end of the bar magnet toward the side of the magnetometer, keeping the magnet at the same height as the instrument.4. Core Operation – Withdrawal: Gradually pull the magnet away from the magnetometer to its starting position.5. Polarity Change: Flip the bar magnet end-for-end so the opposite (blue) end faces the magnetometer.6. Repeat: Again approach from the side and then pull away. Repeat the approach–withdraw–flip cycle once more for clear comparison.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The magnetometer needle is steady and aligned with the ambient magnetic field.2. Magnet Approaches: As the bar magnet moves closer, the needle deflects noticeably toward or away from the magnet, depending on polarity.3. Magnet Withdraws: When the magnet is pulled away, the needle gradually returns toward its original direction.4. Summary of Experimental PrincipleA magnetometer needle is itself a small magnet that aligns with the surrounding magnetic field. When a bar magnet approaches, its magnetic field combines with the ambient field, producing a torque on the needle that causes deflection. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Salinity-Driven Density Layering Using Dyed Saltwater and FreshwaterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Salinity-Driven Density Layering Demonstration2. Subject: Natural Science – Marine Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how differences in salinity create density stratification in water, helping learners understand vertical layering phenomena in oceans and estuaries through clear visual observation and time-lapse recording.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass tank or aquarium (rectangular, transparent); blue-dyed saltwater (prepared in advance, visibly blue); clear freshwater (colorless); small tilted pouring container or beaker; camera or smartphone with tripod; stable table or lab bench.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear glass tank on a stable surface. Ensure the camera is fixed on a tripod facing the tank, with focus locked and framing centered on the water column for time-lapse recording.2. Initial Setup: Slowly pour blue-dyed saltwater into the tank until it reaches approximately half the height of the tank. Allow the water to become completely still.3. Core Operation: Tilt the pouring container and very slowly pour clear freshwater from above along the inner wall of the tank, minimizing turbulence. Continue pouring until a visible freshwater layer forms above the saltwater.4. Recording: Keep the camera fixed and continue recording (or time-lapse) during and shortly after pouring to capture the layering process.5. Completion: Stop pouring, allow the system to rest undisturbed, and end the recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The lower half of the tank contains uniformly blue saltwater; the upper half is empty or filled with air.2. During Pouring: Clear freshwater enters from above and spreads gently over the surface of the blue saltwater without immediately mixing.3. Final State: Two distinct layers are visible: clear freshwater on top and blue saltwater below, with a relatively stable boundary between them. Mixing is minimal over a short time scale.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates salinity-driven density layering. Saltwater has a higher density than freshwater due to dissolved salts. When clear freshwater is gently poured on top of denser saltwater, gravity and density differences cause the freshwater to remain above, forming a stratified water column. This principle explains natural phenomena such as ocean stratification and estuarine circulation.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Pour freshwater slowly to avoid turbulence and mixing.2. Ensure the tank and water are still before pouring.3. Fix camera focus and position to avoid visual inconsistency during time-lapse recording.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Laser Beam Through Clear Water vs Milk-Diluted Water (Tyndall Scattering)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Laser Beam Through Clear Water vs Milk-Diluted Water (Tyndall Scattering)2. Subject: Natural Science – Marine Science (Light Scattering in Seawater)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the Tyndall scattering effect by comparing the visibility of a laser beam in clear water and in water containing fine suspended particles (milk-diluted water), and to understand how particle concentration affects light propagation in marine environments.II. Experimental Equipment1. Transparent rectangular tanks (2 identical tanks)2. Clear water (sufficient to fill one tank)3. Milk-diluted water (clear water with a small, well-mixed amount of milk)4. Narrow-beam green laser pointer (low power, safe for demonstration)5. Stable platform or table6. Camera or smartphone with tripod (fixed focus and position)7. Darkened room or shaded environment (recommended)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical transparent tanks side by side on a stable table. Fill one tank with clear water and the other with milk-diluted water to the same height.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera in front of the tanks, ensuring both tanks are fully in frame. Fix the focus and exposure; do not adjust during recording or time-lapse.3. Laser Alignment: Hold or mount the green laser so that the beam enters both tanks horizontally at the same height above the bottom.4. Core Operation: Turn on the laser and slowly sweep the beam horizontally through both tanks, keeping the height and direction constant.5. Recording: Record continuously or as a short time-lapse, ensuring the laser path in both tanks is clearly captured.6. Completion: Turn off the laser, stop recording, and safely store the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. In clear water: The laser beam path inside the water is faint or nearly invisible; only the entry and exit points may be seen.2. In milk-diluted water: The laser beam path appears as a bright, continuous green line clearly visible throughout the tank.3. Comparison: At the same height and time, the beam is significantly more visible in the milk-diluted water than in clear water.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the Tyndall scattering effect. Clear water contains very few suspended particles, so light passes through with minimal scattering and the beam path is not visible. Milk-diluted water contains fine particles that scatter light in multiple directions, making the laser beam visible from the side. In marine science, this principle explains why light beams and underwater visibility change with plankton, sediments, or other suspended matter in seawater.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not shine the laser into eyes; use low-power lasers suitable for teaching.2. Ensure milk is well mixed to avoid clumps that may distort results.3. Keep camera settings fixed to allow fair visual comparison.4. Clean tanks after the experiment to avoid residue.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Tyndall scattering—visibility of a light beam increases when fine suspended particles scatter light. Minimum assumptions: two identical transparent tanks, equal water height, one clear and one with uniformly suspended milk particles; a narrow green laser entering both tanks horizontally at the same height; fixed camera viewpoint and focus. Phased storyline: (1) Static setup shows two identical tanks side by side with different water clarity; (2) Laser is turned on and aligned horizontally; (3) As the beam sweeps through both tanks, it remains nearly invisible in clear water but becomes a bright visible line in milk-diluted water due to scattering; (4) Stable comparison is maintained without camera or alignment changes, allowing direct visual verification of the causal link between particles and light scattering.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment CO₂ Bubbling into Seawater Causes pH Indicator Color ShiftI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: CO₂ Bubbling into Seawater Causes pH Indicator Color Shift2. Subject: Natural Science - Marine Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how dissolved carbon dioxide lowers the pH of seawater through visual observation of a pH indicator color change, and to understand the basic process of ocean acidification.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass tank (aquarium or glass container), natural or artificial seawater, liquid pH indicator suitable for seawater (e.g., universal indicator or bromothymol blue), carbon dioxide gas source (CO₂ cylinder or generator), flexible tube or glass delivery tube, tube holder or clip, camera on tripod (fixed focus), adequate lighting.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Pour seawater into the clear glass tank to a stable level. Add a small, appropriate amount of liquid pH indicator and gently stir until the color is uniform. Place the tank on a stable surface with good lighting.Equipment Setup: Insert one end of the tube into the seawater, fixing it near the bottom without touching the tank walls. Connect the other end to the CO₂ source. Set the camera in front of the tank, fix the focus, and ensure the entire tank is in frame for time-lapse recording.Core Operation: Start the camera recording. Slowly and steadily introduce carbon dioxide so that a continuous stream of small bubbles rises through the seawater.Observation and Completion: Allow CO₂ to bubble for a set period until a clear color change is observed. Stop the CO₂ flow, end recording, and safely disconnect equipment. Dispose of or store seawater according to guidelines and clean all apparatus.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Seawater with pH indicator shows its initial color, corresponding to near-neutral or slightly alkaline seawater.2. During CO₂ Bubbling: As carbon dioxide dissolves, bubbles rise continuously and the indicator color gradually shifts toward colors representing lower pH.3. Final State: The seawater reaches a stable, more acidic indicator color, showing a clear contrast with the initial state.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCarbon dioxide dissolves in seawater to form carbonic acid, which partially dissociates into bicarbonate ions and hydrogen ions. The increase in hydrogen ion concentration lowers the pH of seawater, causing the pH indicator to change color. This experiment visually models the basic chemical process behind ocean acidification.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the CO₂ flow is slow and steady to avoid splashing. Use an indicator appropriate for seawater pH range. Fix the camera focus before bubbling begins. Handle CO₂ equipment safely and ensure good ventilation.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Swapping Red, Green, and Blue Optical Filters While Filming the Same SeaI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of Red, Green, and Blue Optical Filters on Sea Imaging2. Subject: Natural Science - Marine Science3. Experiment Objective: To observe how different optical filters (red, green, blue) affect the recorded appearance of the same sea scene, and to understand the principle of selective wavelength transmission in light and marine observation.II. Experimental EquipmentTripod-mounted digital camera (with manual focus capability), stable tripod, red optical filter, green optical filter, blue optical filter, clear outdoor sea viewpoint, timing device (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Set up the camera securely on a tripod facing a fixed sea scene. Adjust framing and manually fix the focus to ensure it remains unchanged throughout the experiment.2. Initial Recording: Begin filming or time-lapse photography without any filter to confirm stable image composition (optional baseline).3. Red Filter Operation: Carefully place the red optical filter over the camera lens without moving the camera. Record the sea scene for a short, consistent duration.4. Green Filter Operation: Remove the red filter and place the green optical filter over the lens. Continue recording the same sea scene.5. Blue Filter Operation: Remove the green filter and place the blue optical filter over the lens. Record the sea scene for the same duration.6. Completion: Stop recording and remove the filter. Ensure the camera remains fixed until the end of the experiment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. With the red filter, the sea image appears dominated by red tones, while green and blue components are suppressed.2. With the green filter, the sea appears greener, with reduced red and blue components.3. With the blue filter, the sea appears predominantly blue, with enhanced blue tones and reduced red and green.4. Throughout the experiment, the sea’s shape, waves, and position remain unchanged; only color appearance varies.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesOptical filters selectively transmit light of specific wavelength ranges while absorbing or blocking others. Red, green, and blue filters primarily transmit red, green, and blue light respectively. This principle is fundamental in marine observation, imaging, and remote sensing.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the camera is firmly fixed to prevent movement.2. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Coastal Wind-Driven Upwelling DemonstrationSubject: Natural Science - Marine ScienceExperiment Objective: To demonstrate the basic mechanism of coastal wind-driven upwelling by observing the upward movement of cold bottom water under steady surface wind forcing.II. Experimental EquipmentClear rectangular water tank; clean room-temperature water; cold water dyed blue; small electric fan; thermometer (optional); towel or tray for spill protection.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the clear rectangular tank on a stable table. Gently pour blue-dyed cold water into the tank so it settles at the bottom, forming a distinct blue layer. Slowly add clear room-temperature water on top to avoid mixing, creating a clear upper layer.Setup: Position the small fan at one long side of the tank, aimed horizontally across the water surface toward the opposite long side.Core Operation: Turn on the fan to produce a steady, uniform airflow across the surface. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates coastal wind-driven upwelling. Experiment Title: Paraffin Wax Injected Underwater to Mimic Lava Extrusion2. Subject: Natural Science - Marine Science3. Initial State: Seawater is clear with a stable initial indicator color corresponding to slightly alkaline seawater.2. During CO2 Bubbling: Continuous streams of small bubbles rise from the air stone. The indicator color gradually shifts toward a more acidic color (for example, from blue-green to yellow-green).3. After CO2 is Turned Off: Bubbling immediately stops. The color change slows and then stabilizes at a new, more acidic color without further visible change.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCarbon dioxide dissolves in seawater to form carbonic acid, which partially dissociates to release hydrogen ions, lowering pH. The pH indicator changes color in response to this decrease in pH. When CO2 bubbling stops, gas dissolution decreases and the seawater reaches a temporary equilibrium, so the indicator color stabilizes. This experiment models the basic process of ocean acidification caused by increased atmospheric CO2.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Control the CO2 flow rate to avoid violent bubbling or splashing.2. Use a pH indicator appropriate for seawater pH range.3. Ensure good ventilation when working with CO2.4. Observe only; do not taste or touch the seawater during or after the experiment.

Basic InformationExperiment Title: Cooling and Crystallization of Supersaturated Sodium Acetate (Hot Ice)Subject: Natural Science – Marine Science (Mineral Precipitation Analogy)Objective: To demonstrate mineral precipitation by observing rapid crystallization of a supersaturated sodium acetate solution triggered by a seed crystal, suitable for time-lapse recording.II. Experiment Title: Estuary-Style Saltwater–Freshwater Mixing in a Clear Flume2. Subject: Natural Science – Marine Science3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate estuary-style mixing between freshwater and saltwater using dye tracing, and to understand density-driven flow interaction and diffusion processes in estuaries.II. Experimental EquipmentClear acrylic flume (rectangular, transparent), freshwater reservoir and pump, saltwater reservoir and pump, blue dye (water-soluble), tubing for inflow, flow control valves, collection outlet or drain, camera with tripod, lighting source.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear flume on a level surface and ensure it is clean and transparent. Inlet Arrangement: Connect the freshwater pump to one end of the flume and the blue-dyed saltwater pump to the opposite end. Adjust tubing so inflows enter smoothly along the flume axis.4. Core Operation: Start both pumps simultaneously at steady, low flow rates. Allow freshwater and blue-dyed saltwater to flow toward each other until they meet in the central region of the flume.5. Recording: Begin time-lapse photography with the camera focus fixed. Continue pumping for a short period to capture the mixing and spreading process.6. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Salt Added to Muddy Clay Water Causes Clump Formation and SettlingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of Salt on the Settling of Muddy Clay Water2. Subject: Natural Science – Marine Science3. Experiment Objective: To observe how dissolved salt promotes the aggregation (flocculation) and settling of fine clay particles in muddy water, simulating sediment processes in marine and estuarine environments.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo clear glass jars of the same size, muddy clay water (prepared by mixing fine clay or soil with water), table salt (sodium chloride), small spoon or spatula, stirring rod or spoon, camera or smartphone with tripod for fixed-focus time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clear glass jars side by side on a stable surface. Pour equal volumes of muddy clay water into each jar so that both appear uniformly turbid.2. Salt Addition: Add a small, equal spoonful of salt only to the right jar. Do not add salt to the left jar (control).3. Stirring: Briefly and gently stir both jars for the same amount of time to evenly mix their contents.4. Resting and Recording: Stop stirring and leave both jars completely undisturbed. Fix the camera focus and position, and record the jars using time-lapse photography.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both jars contain uniformly muddy, opaque water with suspended fine particles.2. After Salt Addition and Stirring: In the right jar, small clumps of particles begin to appear.3. During Resting: The clumps in the salt jar grow larger and settle toward the bottom more quickly, forming a clearer upper layer. The left jar remains more uniformly turbid, with much slower settling.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesFine clay particles in water usually carry electric charges that keep them dispersed. When salt is added, dissolved ions reduce the repulsive forces between particles, allowing them to stick together and form larger clumps (flocculation). These larger clumps are heavier and settle faster under gravity. This principle explains why seawater promotes sediment settling compared with freshwater and is important in marine and estuarine sedimentation processes.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure both jars contain the same amount of muddy water; stir both jars equally; avoid disturbing the jars during settling; use a fixed camera to clearly compare changes over time.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment "Color Attenuation with Depth in Water (Red Fades First)"I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Color Attenuation with Depth in Water (Red Fades First)2. Subject: Natural Science – Marine Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how different wavelengths of light are absorbed by water at different rates, resulting in color attenuation with increasing depth. Through visual observation, students understand why red light fades first, followed by green, while blue penetrates deepest in water.II. Experimental Equipment1. Clear rectangular water tank (transparent glass or acrylic, allowing side view)2. Clean clear water (filled to at least 30–40 cm depth)3. Overhead white light source (simulating sunlight, fixed directly above the tank)4. Vertical rod or lowering mechanism (marked with depth scale)5. Three identical objects or plates colored red, green, and blue (same size and material)6. Fixed camera on tripod (side view of the tank, focus locked)7. Dark or neutral background (to improve color contrast)III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup Preparation: Place the clear water tank on a stable surface. Fill it with clear water, ensuring no bubbles or turbidity. Position a white light source directly above the tank to illuminate the water vertically.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera on a tripod facing the side of the tank. Adjust focus and exposure, then lock the focus and keep the camera stationary for time-lapse recording.3. Object Preparation: Attach the red, green, and blue objects evenly spaced along the vertical rod, ensuring they are aligned and face the camera.4. Initial State Recording: Begin recording with all colored objects just above the water surface, clearly visible and brightly colored.5. Core Operation: Slowly and steadily lower the vertical rod so that the colored objects descend deeper into the water together. Maintain a constant lowering speed to ensure comparable depth changes.6. Depth Observation: Continue lowering until the deepest object reaches near the bottom of the tank, then stop the motion.7. End Recording: Stop recording. Carefully remove the rod and drain or cover the tank if needed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. At the Surface: Red, green, and blue objects all appear bright and vivid under the overhead light.2. Shallow Depth: The red object begins to darken and lose saturation first, while green and blue remain relatively clear.3. Medium Depth: The red object becomes very dim or nearly black; the green object starts to fade; the blue object remains the most visible.4. Greater Depth: The green object becomes faint, while the blue object is still visible, though slightly darker.5. Overall Trend: With increasing depth, colors disappear in the order of red first, then green, with blue persisting the longest.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Core Principle: Water absorbs light selectively based on wavelength. Longer wavelengths (red) are absorbed more quickly, while shorter wavelengths (blue) penetrate deeper.2. Scientific Explanation: Sunlight or white light contains multiple wavelengths. As light travels through water, red light (long wavelength, low energy) is absorbed within shallow depths, green light at intermediate depths, and blue light (short wavelength, higher energy) penetrates deepest.3. Marine Science Significance: This principle explains why deep ocean environments appear blue and why red-colored marine organisms appear dark or black at depth.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the water is clear; turbidity will affect color visibility.2. Keep the light source fixed and vertical to avoid uneven illumination.3. Use objects of identical size and material to avoid brightness bias.4. Do not adjust camera focus or angle during recording to maintain consistency.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: White Light Passing Through a Glass Prism Producing a Rainbow FanI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: White Light Passing Through a Glass Prism Producing a Rainbow Fan2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science (Optics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the dispersion of white light by a glass prism, understand how different wavelengths refract at different angles, and recognize the formation of a visible spectrum similar to a natural rainbow.II. Experimental EquipmentNarrow-beam white light source (flashlight with slit or collimated lamp), clear triangular glass prism, flat table, blank white wall or screen, prism holder or soft pad, camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse), darkened room.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the triangular glass prism flat on the table. Darken the room to enhance visibility of light. Fix the camera position and focus so the prism and wall are both in frame.2. Light Alignment: Direct a narrow beam of white light horizontally toward one face of the prism so that it enters the glass cleanly.3. Core Operation: Slowly rotate the prism around its vertical axis while keeping the light source and camera fixed.4. Projection: Allow the emergent light from the prism to project onto the blank wall opposite the prism.5. Recording: Maintain slow, continuous rotation for clear observation while the camera records or captures time-lapse images.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: White light enters the prism and exits as a slightly bent beam.2. During Rotation: The exiting light spreads into a fan-shaped band of colors.3. Final Observation: A clear spectrum appears on the wall, arranged continuously from red through orange, yellow, green, blue, to violet. The angle and spread of the spectrum change smoothly as the prism rotates.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhite light is composed of multiple wavelengths. When it enters and exits a glass prism, each wavelength refracts by a different amount because the refractive index of glass depends on wavelength. Shorter wavelengths (violet) bend more than longer wavelengths (red), causing the light to separate into a visible spectrum. This phenomenon is called dispersion and explains the formation of natural rainbows in the atmosphere.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the prism is clean and transparent.2. Rotate the prism slowly to avoid losing the spectrum.3. Avoid direct eye exposure to intense light sources.4. Keep camera focus fixed to ensure consistent visual comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Crushing an Aluminum Can by Steam CondensationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Crushing an Aluminum Can by Steam Condensation and Air Pressure2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how heating water to produce steam and then rapidly cooling it causes a pressure difference, allowing external air pressure to crush an aluminum can.II. Experimental EquipmentEmpty aluminum soda can (1), water (10–20 mL), heat source (hot plate or stove), tongs or heat-resistant gloves, shallow bowl with cold water, stable heat-resistant surface, camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Rinse the empty aluminum can and add a small amount of water (just covering the bottom). Place the can upright on the heat source. Fix the camera focus and framing.2. Heating: Heat the can until the water boils and visible water vapor steadily escapes from the can opening.3. Inversion: Using tongs, quickly and carefully invert the hot can mouth-down into the shallow bowl of cold water.4. Observation: Keep the camera recording as the can undergoes rapid deformation.5. End: After the can cools, stop recording and safely dispose of the can.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before heating: The can retains its original shape; water is liquid.2. During heating: Steam escapes continuously from the can opening.3. After inversion: The can is suddenly crushed inward with a sharp deformation as it contacts cold water.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleHeating causes water to vaporize, filling the can with steam and pushing out most of the air. When the can is inverted into cold water, the steam rapidly condenses into liquid, sharply reducing internal pressure. Experimental PrecautionsUse heat protection when handling the hot can; invert quickly; keep face and hands away from the can opening; ensure stable camera placement.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Rotating Tank Model Showing Coriolis Deflection with Dyed WaterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Rotating Tank Model Demonstrating Coriolis Deflection2. Subject: Natural Science – Marine Science3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the Coriolis effect in a rotating reference frame by observing the deflection of dyed water released near the center of a rotating water tank.II. Experimental EquipmentClear cylindrical water tank, rotating turntable with adjustable steady speed, clean water, bright food dye or tracer dye, dropper or syringe, camera or observer at a fixed position, optional ruler or marker for reference.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear cylindrical tank at the center of the turntable and fill it with water to a moderate depth. Ensure the water surface is calm.2. Establish Rotation: Turn on the turntable and allow it to rotate steadily for sufficient time so that the water rotates uniformly with the tank.3. Dye Release: Using a dropper, gently release a small amount of bright dye from a fixed point near the center of the water surface without disturbing the water.4. Observation: Keep the camera or observer fixed relative to the rotating tank and observe the motion of the dye as it spreads outward.5. Completion: Stop the turntable after observation and allow the water to settle before cleaning the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIn a rotating reference frame, moving fluids experience an apparent force known as the Coriolis force. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure steady rotation before dye release; release dye gently to avoid turbulence; use small amounts of dye for clear trajectories; keep observation perspective fixed relative to the tank.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Saltwater Density Separation of Plastic and SandI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Saltwater Density Separation of Plastic and Sand2. Subject: Natural Science - Marine Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate density-based separation in a marine environment by observing that plastic particles float while sand sinks in saltwater, and to understand how salinity affects the vertical distribution of materials in seawater.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass jar with lid (1), saltwater (prepared by dissolving table salt in water until fully dissolved, transparent), mixed beach sand (natural sand with visible grains), colored plastic fragments (small, lightweight pieces), stirring rod or spoon, camera or smartphone with fixed focus and time-lapse function, stable surface.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear glass jar on a stable, well-lit surface. Fill the jar with saltwater to about 80% capacity, ensuring the solution is clear and fully dissolved.2. Adding Materials: Gently add a small amount of mixed beach sand and several colored plastic fragments into the saltwater.3. Stirring: Use the stirring rod to briefly and gently stir the mixture for 3–5 seconds so that sand and plastic are fully mixed throughout the water column.4. Settling and Recording: Stop stirring and remove the rod. Do not disturb the jar. Fix the camera focus and start time-lapse photography, recording the jar as it remains undisturbed.5. Completion: Allow the jar to stand until the separation phenomenon is clearly visible. Stop recording once the system reaches a stable state.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Immediately after stirring, sand grains and plastic fragments are suspended throughout the saltwater.2. During Settling: Over time, sand particles gradually sink to the bottom of the jar, forming a visible sediment layer.3. Final State: Colored plastic fragments float and remain near the water surface, while sand is clearly separated at the bottom, with clear saltwater in between.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on density separation in marine science. Saltwater has a higher density than freshwater. Sand has a density greater than saltwater, so gravity causes it to sink. Most plastics have a density lower than saltwater, so buoyant force exceeds their weight, causing them to float. This principle is widely used in marine pollution studies to separate microplastics from sediments.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure salt is fully dissolved to avoid crystals affecting observations.2. Stir gently to avoid breaking plastic fragments or creating bubbles that interfere with settling.3. Keep the jar undisturbed during observation to maintain clear separation results.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: density separation in marine science, assuming gravity, buoyancy, and stable saltwater conditions. Minimum assumptions include a transparent container, dissolved saltwater, and materials with contrasting densities (sand > saltwater > plastic). Expected phenomena storyline: (1) initial mixed suspension immediately after brief stirring; (2) transition phase where gravity causes denser sand to move downward while buoyant plastic rises; (3) final stable separation with sand settled at the bottom and colored plastic floating at the surface. Visibility requirements: a fixed camera angle, clear jar walls, and sufficient lighting to track vertical movement and final layered distribution over time.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Balloon on a Bottle Expands in Warm Water and Contracts in Cold WaterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Balloon Expansion and Contraction Due to Air Temperature Change2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To observe how air expands when heated and contracts when cooled by placing a balloon-fitted glass bottle in warm and cold water, and to understand the relationship between temperature and air volume.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass bottle (1), deflated rubber balloon (1), red bowl with warm water, blue bowl with cold water, thermometer (optional), camera or phone with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the balloon is completely deflated and stretch it gently. Secure the balloon tightly over the mouth of the clear glass bottle to prevent air leakage.2. Warm Water Stage: Place the bottle upright into the red bowl filled with warm water. Ensure the water level surrounds the lower part of the bottle without entering it. Start recording with the camera focus fixed.3. Observation in Warm Water: Keep the bottle still and observe the balloon gradually inflating.4. Cold Water Stage: Carefully transfer the same bottle into the blue bowl filled with cold water, maintaining the camera position and focus.5. Observation in Cold Water: Observe the balloon gradually shrinking or deflating.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The balloon is deflated when the bottle is at room temperature.2. In Warm Water: After a short time in warm water, the balloon slowly expands and becomes visibly inflated.3. In Cold Water: When moved to cold water, the balloon gradually contracts and partially or fully deflates.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAir inside the bottle expands when heated and contracts when cooled. In warm water, the temperature of the air inside the bottle rises, causing the air molecules to move faster and occupy more space, pushing air into the balloon and inflating it. In cold water, the air temperature decreases, molecular motion slows, and the air volume decreases, causing the balloon to contract. This demonstrates the basic atmospheric science principle that air volume changes with temperature.

Experiment Title: Condensation of Water Droplets from Warm Moist Air in a Transparent Box2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the condensation process of water vapor when warm moist air is cooled, and to visually demonstrate how clouds or dew form due to temperature decrease.II. Experimental Equipment- Clear sealed plastic box (transparent on all sides, with lid)- Electric kettle (to produce warm moist air)- Tray filled with ice cubes or crushed ice- Camera or smartphone with time-lapse function- Tripod or stable stand for camera- Heat-resistant gloves (optional, for safety)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the tray of ice on a stable table. Ensure the ice fully covers the tray surface. Set up the camera on a tripod facing the side of the plastic box, and fix the focus manually to avoid refocusing during recording.2. Filling with Warm Moist Air: Carefully open the plastic box lid. Use the kettle to introduce warm moist air (steam mixed with air) into the box for several seconds until the interior air appears warm and humid. Quickly seal the box tightly.3. Cooling Operation: Immediately place the sealed plastic box onto the tray of ice, ensuring the bottom and lower sides are in direct contact with the cold surface.4. Recording: Start the camera time-lapse recording. Do not move the box or camera during the process.5. Observation Period: Allow the box to remain on the ice for a short period while condensation develops on the inner walls and bottom.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Nitrogen Dioxide–Dinitrogen Tetroxide Equilibrium (Color Change with Temperature)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Temperature-Dependent Equilibrium between Nitrogen Dioxide and Dinitrogen Tetroxide2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the temperature-dependent chemical equilibrium between nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and dinitrogen tetroxide (N2O4), and to understand the reversible monomer–dimer structural change through color variation under different thermal conditions.II. Experimental EquipmentSealed transparent glass tube containing nitrogen dioxide gas, ice bath (ice + water), warm water bath (about 40–60 °C), transparent containers for baths, thermometer (optional), camera or smartphone with tripod, stable light source, heat-resistant gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the sealed glass tube containing NO2 on the bench. Fix the camera on a tripod, adjust the focus once to clearly capture the tube, and keep the focus unchanged for the entire experiment.2. Initial Observation: Record the initial color of the gas in the tube at room temperature.3. Cooling Stage: Gently place the sealed tube into the ice bath. Ensure the tube is stable and fully visible to the camera. Continue recording.4. Observation during Cooling: Observe and record the gradual color change of the gas.5. Heating Stage: Remove the tube from the ice bath and transfer it into the warm water bath. Keep recording continuously.6. Observation during Heating: Observe and record the color change as the temperature rises.7. Repetition (Optional): Alternately place the tube into the ice bath and warm water once more to confirm reversibility.8. Completion: Remove the tube, stop recording, and allow all equipment to return to room temperature.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. At room temperature: The gas in the tube appears brown.2. In the ice bath: The brown color gradually fades and becomes light brown or nearly colorless.3. In the warm water bath: The gas darkens again, returning to a deeper brown color.4. Reversibility: The color change is repeatable and reversible with alternating temperature conditions.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesNitrogen dioxide (NO2) exists in a temperature-dependent equilibrium with its dimer, dinitrogen tetroxide (N2O4):2 NO2 (g) ⇌ N2O4 (g) + heat.NO2 is a brown gas, while N2O4 is colorless. Lower temperatures favor the formation of N2O4, causing the gas to become lighter in color. Higher temperatures favor the dissociation into NO2, deepening the brown color. This experiment demonstrates Le Chatelier’s principle and the monomer–dimer structural change relevant to atmospheric nitrogen oxides.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Temperature-dependent chemical equilibrium between NO2 and N2O4, assuming a sealed system, constant pressure, and visible color differences between species. Expected storyline: (1) Initial brown gas at room temperature; (2) cooling in ice bath causes gradual fading toward colorless as N2O4 forms; (3) heating in warm water deepens brown color as NO2 increases; (4) repeated alternation confirms reversibility. Visibility requirements: fixed camera focus, unobstructed view of the tube, clear contrast of gas color across temperature stages.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Cold Surface Plate with Warm Humid Air Forming a Visible Fog LayerI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Condensation Fog Formation on a Cold Metal Plate2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how warm, humid air forms a visible fog layer when it encounters a cold surface, and to understand the condensation process relevant to atmospheric phenomena such as fog and dew.II. Experimental EquipmentFlat metal plate (aluminum or stainless steel), refrigerator or ice bath (for chilling the plate), table or flat support, source of warm humid air (human breath or humidifier), thermometer (optional), camera with fixed focus and tripod (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the metal plate in a refrigerator or on ice for several minutes until it is clearly colder than room temperature.2. Setup: Remove the chilled plate and place it flat on a table. Position the camera on a tripod facing the plate and fix the focus and framing.3. Core Operation: Gently blow warm, humid air across the surface of the cold plate, or direct a small humid airflow over it.4. Recording: Keep the camera fixed and record continuously or in time-lapse mode as the air flows across the plate.5. Completion: Stop the airflow after clear fog formation is observed. Allow the plate to gradually warm and observe changes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The metal plate appears dry and clear immediately after placement on the table.2. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Tabletop Cold-Plate Temperature Inversion DemonstrationSubject: Natural Science – Atmospheric ScienceObjective: To demonstrate a temperature inversion and reduced vertical mixing by observing incense smoke remaining layered above a chilled metal plate.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Flashlight Beam Through Clean Air vs Air with Candle SootI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Flashlight Beam Through Clean Air vs Air with Candle Soot2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how suspended particles in air scatter light, making a light beam visible, and to understand the role of aerosols in atmospheric light scattering.II. Experimental EquipmentFlashlight (1, constant brightness), transparent boxes (2 identical clear boxes with lids), candle (1), lighter or matches, dark room, black background or wall, camera or smartphone with manual focus, tripod (recommended).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Darken the room as much as possible. Place two identical transparent boxes side by side on a table, facing a wall or screen. Ensure both boxes are initially filled with clean air.2. Soot Introduction: Light the candle and carefully hold it near the opening of the right box so that candle soot enters the box. Gently close the lid to trap soot particles inside. Keep the left box clean and untouched.3. Optical Setup: Place the flashlight at the same distance from both boxes, aimed horizontally so the beam passes through both boxes toward the wall.4. Camera Setup: Position the camera facing the boxes and the wall. Fix the focus manually and keep all camera settings constant. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.5. Core Operation: Turn on the flashlight and maintain a steady beam through both boxes for the duration of recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before adding soot, the flashlight beam in clean air is barely visible from the side.2. After Soot Addition: In the right box, the flashlight beam becomes clearly visible as a bright path due to scattered light from soot particles. The left box remains mostly dark, with only the illuminated spot visible on the wall.3. Comparison: The wall shows similar brightness from both boxes, but only the soot-filled box reveals the beam path in air.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates light scattering by atmospheric particles. Clean air contains very few particles, so light passes through with minimal scattering and the beam path is not visible. Candle soot consists of fine solid particles that scatter light in many directions, making the beam visible from the side. This principle explains phenomena such as visible sunbeams in dusty air or haze in polluted atmospheres.VI. Experimental PrecautionsAvoid inhaling candle soot; ventilate the room after the experiment. Handle fire carefully. Ensure camera focus and flashlight position remain fixed throughout the experiment.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: IR Temperature Sensor Triggering LED BrightnessI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: IR Temperature Sensor Triggering LED Brightness as a Hot Object ApproachesSubject: Natural Science – Atmospheric ScienceObjective: To demonstrate non-contact infrared temperature sensing by observing how an IR temperature sensor controls LED brightness as a heated metal block moves closer and farther; to understand the relationship between infrared radiation, temperature, and sensor output.II. Experimental EquipmentIR temperature sensor module, LED, current-limiting resistor, microcontroller or analog driver circuit, connecting wires, power supply (5V), metal block, heat source (hot water or heater), insulated gloves, tabletop, camera on tripod with fixed focus.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the IR temperature sensor and LED circuit securely on a tabletop. Wire the sensor output to control LED brightness. Fix the camera focus and position for time-lapse recording.2. Heating the Object: Heat the metal block using hot water or a heater. Wear insulated gloves and avoid direct contact after heating.3. Core Operation: Hold the heated metal block in front of the IR sensor without touching it. Slowly move the block closer to the sensor, pause, then slowly move it farther away.4. Observation and Recording: Record the entire process with the fixed-focus camera, ensuring the LED and sensor remain in frame.5. Completion: Remove the metal block, turn off the power, and allow components to cool.IV. Summary of Experimental PrincipleHot objects emit infrared radiation. PrecautionsAvoid touching hot metal directly; maintain non-contact sensing; ensure stable wiring and fixed camera focus throughout recording.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Cloud-in-a-Bottle Pressure Release Causing CondensationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Cloud-in-a-Bottle Pressure Release Causing Condensation2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how a rapid decrease in air pressure causes cooling and condensation of water vapor, simulating cloud formation in the atmosphere, and to learn basic observation and explanation of atmospheric physical processes.II. Experimental EquipmentClear plastic bottle with cap (1, flexible type), small amount of clean water (about 5–10 mL), hands for squeezing, optional light source, camera or phone with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Pour a small amount of clean water into the clear plastic bottle. Cap the bottle tightly to ensure it is sealed. Gently shake once so the inner wall becomes moist, forming water vapor inside. Place the bottle in front of the camera and fix the camera focus.Core Operation: Hold the bottle with one or both hands and squeeze it firmly for 1–2 seconds, increasing the internal air pressure. Then suddenly release the bottle completely.Observation and Recording: Keep the bottle still and observe the changes inside immediately after release. Continue recording for several seconds to capture the formation and dissipation of the cloud-like mist.Conclusion and Reset: The bottle may be squeezed and released again to repeat the phenomenon. After finishing, open the cap and pour out the water.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The bottle is transparent, and the air inside is mostly clear with slight moisture on the walls.2. During Squeezing: No obvious cloud appears; the inside remains clear.3. Immediately After Release: A white, cloud-like mist suddenly forms inside the bottle.4. After a Short Time: The mist gradually disappears, and the inside becomes clear again.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSqueezing the sealed bottle increases the air pressure and temperature slightly. When the bottle is suddenly released, the internal pressure drops rapidly, causing the air to cool. Cooler air can hold less water vapor, so excess water vapor condenses into tiny droplets, forming a visible cloud. This process is similar to cloud formation in the atmosphere caused by rising air and pressure decrease.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the bottle is well sealed before squeezing.2. Do not overfill with water; only a small amount is needed to provide water vapor.3. Fix the camera focus to clearly capture the condensation process.4. Avoid excessive force that could damage the bottle.

Visibility requirements: transparent bottle, fixed camera focus, clear view of hand action and internal mist formation.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Formation of Rime Ice on a Cold Metal RodI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Rime Ice Formation on a Metal Rod in Supercooled MistSubject: Natural Science – Atmospheric ScienceExperiment Objective: To observe and understand the formation of rime ice when supercooled liquid-water droplets carried by airflow impact a below-freezing solid surface.II. Experimental EquipmentBelow-freezing environmental chamber (≤ –5 °C), cylindrical metal rod (aluminum or steel, diameter 5–10 mm), rod holder or clamp (to keep rod stationary), fine mist generator or atomizer producing liquid-water droplets, airflow source (fan or ducted flow), thermometer, time-lapse camera with fixed focus and tripod, protective gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Set the environmental chamber to a stable temperature below 0 °C. Mount the metal rod horizontally on a holder so it remains stationary and fully exposed to airflow.2. Camera Setup: Place the camera outside or inside a viewing window of the chamber. Fix focus, framing, and exposure. Enable time-lapse mode.3. Mist and Airflow Setup: Position the mist generator on one side of the rod so a steady stream of fine liquid-water droplets is blown across the rod from a single direction.4. Core Operation: Start airflow and mist generation simultaneously, then begin time-lapse recording. Maintain constant temperature, mist density, and airflow.5. Completion: After visible ice growth is recorded, stop mist and airflow. End recording and allow the chamber to warm before removing equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The metal rod surface is clean and dry, with no visible ice.During Exposure: Fine droplets strike the windward side of the rod and freeze immediately upon contact.Later Stage: A white, opaque, porous ice structure grows outward from the rod, extending into the airflow direction, showing a feathery or spiky texture characteristic of rime ice.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesRime ice forms when supercooled liquid-water droplets in mist collide with a surface whose temperature is below freezing. Upon impact, droplets freeze almost instantly, trapping air and creating a porous, opaque ice structure. Continuous airflow supplies more droplets, causing the ice to grow outward on the windward side. This process is common in cold-cloud environments and on exposed structures such as aircraft wings and mountain instruments.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure stable subfreezing temperature throughout the experiment. Keep the rod stationary and avoid touching icy surfaces with bare hands. Maintain consistent mist and airflow to ensure clear, interpretable results.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Rime ice formation due to supercooled liquid-water droplets freezing on impact with a below-freezing solid surface.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Air temperature below 0 °C; mist consists of liquid droplets (not snow); metal rod temperature is below freezing; airflow delivers droplets from one side; droplets freeze instantly upon contact.Phased Storyline: (1) Establish cold chamber and stationary metal rod; (2) introduce steady one-sided mist and airflow; (3) droplets impact rod and freeze; (4) white, porous rime ice accumulates and grows outward on the windward side over time. Visibility Constraints: Fixed camera focus and stable framing are required so outward ice growth and directional asymmetry can be clearly verified in time-lapse.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: CO2 from Exhaled Air Changes the Color of Bromothymol BlueI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of Exhaled Carbon Dioxide on Bromothymol Blue Indicator2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that carbon dioxide in exhaled air dissolves in water to form an acidic solution, lowering pH and causing a visible color change in bromothymol blue; to understand the role of CO2 in air and its interaction with aqueous systems.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo clear plastic or glass cups; bromothymol blue indicator solution (blue, weakly alkaline); drinking straw; lab bench or flat surface; camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording (optional for demonstration).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear cups on a lab bench, labeled left and right. Pour equal volumes of blue bromothymol blue solution into each cup.2. Initial Observation: Confirm both cups show the same blue color, indicating similar initial pH.3. Core Operation: Insert a straw into the left cup. A person exhales gently and continuously through the straw into the solution for several seconds. Do not disturb the right cup.4. Control Setup: Keep the right cup untouched throughout the experiment as a comparison.5. Recording (optional): Keep the camera fixed and record the process using time-lapse or continuous video.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both cups contain clear blue bromothymol blue solution.2. During Exhalation: Bubbles appear in the left cup as air is blown in; the blue color gradually shifts to green and then yellow.3. Final State: The left cup shows a clear color change toward green/yellow, while the right cup remains blue with no obvious change.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesHuman exhaled air contains a high concentration of carbon dioxide. When CO2 dissolves in water, it forms carbonic acid, which lowers the pH of the solution. Bromothymol blue is a pH indicator that is blue in alkaline conditions, green near neutral, and yellow in acidic conditions. Therefore, the introduction of CO2 through exhalation causes the indicator in the left cup to change color, while the untouched right cup serves as a control.VI. Experimental PrecautionsExhale gently to avoid splashing; do not inhale through the straw; ensure equal solution volumes in both cups; clean up solutions after the experiment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Carbon dioxide in exhaled air dissolves in water to form carbonic acid, lowering pH and causing bromothymol blue to change color.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Exhaled air contains CO2; CO2 dissolves in aqueous solution; bromothymol blue responds predictably to pH changes; the right cup functions as an unchanged control.Expected Phenomenon Storyline: Phase 1 – Stable initial state with two blue solutions. Phase 2 – Exhalation through a straw introduces CO2 into the left cup, producing bubbles. Phase 3 – Gradual, unidirectional color transition in the left cup from blue to green/yellow while the right cup remains blue. Visibility requires a fixed camera angle showing both cups simultaneously for comparison.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Cooling Humid Air vs Dry Air Causes Earlier Condensation2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that humid air reaches saturation and condenses earlier than dry air under the same cooling conditions, and to visually compare condensation processes using two identical clear sealed chambers.II. Experimental Equipment1. Two identical clear sealed chambers (transparent, airtight)2. Red band (for left chamber identification)3. Blue band (for right chamber identification)4. Steam source (hot water or steam generator)5. Cooling source (ice packs or refrigerated cooling plate)6. Thermometer or temperature probe (optional)7. Camera with tripod (fixed focus, time-lapse mode)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear sealed chambers side by side on a flat surface. Mark the left chamber with a red band and the right chamber with a blue band. Ensure both chambers are initially clear and dry inside.2. Humidification: Open the red-banded left chamber briefly and inject visible steam until the air inside becomes humid, then seal it immediately. Do not introduce steam into the blue-banded right chamber; keep its air dry.3. Setup for Recording: Position the camera directly facing both chambers. Fix the focus and framing so both chambers remain fully visible. Start time-lapse recording.4. Cooling Operation: Apply the same cooling method to both chambers simultaneously (e.g., place ice packs evenly around them or put both on a cooling surface).5. Observation Period: Continue cooling while recording until condensation phenomena are clearly observed in one or both chambers.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both chambers appear clear and transparent; no visible droplets on inner walls.2. During Cooling: As temperature decreases, fine water droplets appear earlier on the inner wall of the red-banded chamber.3. Comparative Result: The blue-banded dry chamber shows delayed condensation or significantly fewer droplets compared with the red chamber.4. Final State: The red chamber has obvious fogging or droplet accumulation, while the blue chamber remains clearer under the same cooling conditions.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Humid air contains more water vapor than dry air.2. When air is cooled, its capacity to hold water vapor decreases.3. Humid air reaches saturation sooner, causing water vapor to condense into liquid droplets earlier than in dry air.4. Therefore, under identical cooling conditions, condensation appears earlier and more明显 in the humid (red) chamber than in the dry (blue) chamber.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both chambers are identical and sealed to avoid air exchange.2. Apply cooling uniformly to both chambers.3. Fix camera focus and position to ensure reliable time-lapse comparison.4. Avoid shaking or moving chambers during observation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Heated Surface Creating Vertical Convection Columns Visualized with SmokeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Heated Surface Creating Vertical Convection Columns Visualized with Smoke2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand thermal convection in air by visualizing rising warm air currents above a heated surface using incense smoke.II. Experimental EquipmentClear enclosure (glass or acrylic box), flat metal plate, electric heater or hot plate (placed below the metal plate), incense stick or smoke source, lighter or igniter, stable support frame, camera with tripod (fixed focus, time-lapse mode), heat-resistant gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Place the flat metal plate horizontally inside the clear enclosure. Position the heater directly beneath the plate. Fix the camera outside the enclosure, adjust framing, and lock focus.2. Heating: Turn on the heater to warm the metal plate evenly from below. Allow a short preheating period.3. Smoke Release: Light the incense stick and gently introduce smoke just above the center of the heated plate without disturbing the air.4. Observation and Recording: Start time-lapse recording. Keep the enclosure closed and undisturbed while heating continues.5. Completion: After clear smoke patterns are recorded, turn off the heater, remove the incense, and allow the setup to cool.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitially, smoke drifts slowly and irregularly. After heating, smoke above the plate rises vertically, forming narrow upward columns. These columns may appear regularly spaced and persist as long as heating continues.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesHeating the metal plate warms the air above it, reducing air density. The warmer, less dense air rises while cooler surrounding air sinks, forming vertical convection columns. Incense smoke acts as a tracer, making otherwise invisible air motion visible.VI. PrecautionsEnsure even heating; avoid external air disturbances; handle hot equipment carefully; keep camera focus fixed throughout the experiment.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Increasing Fog Density Reduces Transmitted LightI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Increasing Fog Density Reduces Transmitted LightSubject: Natural Science – Atmospheric ScienceObjective: To demonstrate that increasing fog density between a light source and a camera reduces transmitted light intensity due to scattering and absorption, using time-lapse observation.II. Experimental EquipmentBright lamp (continuous light source), digital camera with tripod, fog machine with water-based fog fluid, darkened room, power supply, ruler or markers (optional for distance reference).III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Place the bright lamp at one end of the room. Fix the camera on a tripod directly facing the lamp at a constant distance. Lock focus, exposure, and white balance to prevent automatic changes.2. Fog Placement: Position the fog machine midway between the lamp and the camera, ensuring fog will pass through the optical path.3. Initial Recording: Start time-lapse or continuous recording with no fog present, capturing the lamp at full brightness.4. Core Operation: Turn on the fog machine and release fog steadily and continuously. Do not move the camera, lamp, or fog machine during recording.5. Completion: Continue recording until the fog density is visibly high and the lamp appears significantly dimmer or blurred, then stop recording and turn off equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The lamp appears bright and clearly defined with high contrast.During Fog Release: As fog density increases, the lamp gradually appears dimmer, edges become blurred, and overall contrast decreases.High Fog Density: The lamp’s light is strongly attenuated and diffused, appearing faint and hazy.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleFog consists of tiny water droplets suspended in air. As fog density increases, more droplets scatter and absorb light passing through them. This demonstrates atmospheric attenuation of light due to increased particle concentration.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Supercooled Bottled Water Freezing Instantly When TappedI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Supercooled Bottled Water Freezing Instantly When Tapped2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To observe the phenomenon of supercooled water rapidly freezing when disturbed, understand the metastable state of supercooled liquids, and demonstrate ice nucleation caused by mechanical disturbance.II. Experimental EquipmentClear sealed plastic bottle of purified water (unopened), refrigerator or freezer capable of maintaining about −5°C, cold countertop or metal surface, thermometer (optional), camera with fixed focus or tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Place the sealed bottle of purified water upright in a freezer for 2–3 hours. Ensure the temperature is below 0°C but the water remains liquid and clear, indicating a supercooled state.Setup Stage: Carefully remove the bottle without shaking it and place it gently on a cold countertop. Set up the camera with fixed focus aimed at the bottle.Core Operation: Using one hand, tap the side or top of the bottle once with moderate force.Conclusion: Continue observing the bottle for several seconds after the tap to record the freezing process.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The water in the bottle appears completely clear and liquid despite being below the normal freezing point.2. After Tapping: Immediately after the tap, ice crystals begin forming at the point of disturbance and rapidly spread throughout the bottle.3. Final State: Within seconds, most or all of the water becomes solid ice, often with a cloudy or crystalline appearance.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSupercooled water is a metastable liquid state where water remains liquid below 0°C due to the absence of nucleation sites. Mechanical disturbance from tapping provides energy and nucleation points, triggering rapid ice crystal formation. This demonstrates the relationship between temperature, phase change, and nucleation in atmospheric science, relevant to cloud ice formation and freezing rain processes.VI. Experimental PrecautionsAvoid shaking the bottle before tapping. Do not open the bottle during the experiment. Handle cold surfaces carefully to prevent frostbite.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate the metastable nature of supercooled water and the role of mechanical disturbance in triggering phase change.
