Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Laser Beam Refraction in a Horizontally Stratified Sugar-Water TankSubject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science (Optics and Refraction)Objective: To demonstrate how light propagates and refracts in a medium with vertically varying refractive index, analogous to atmospheric stratified refraction, by observing a horizontal laser beam passing through layered sugar-water.II. Experimental EquipmentRectangular transparent tank (glass or acrylic); sugar-water solutions of different concentrations; measuring cup or syringe; spoon or stirrer; narrow green laser pointer; tripod-mounted camera or smartphone; darkened background; stable table.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation of Layers: Prepare several sugar-water solutions with increasing sugar concentration. Carefully pour them into the rectangular tank from highest concentration at the bottom to lowest at the top, using slow pouring along the wall to maintain clear horizontal layers.2. Stabilization: Allow the tank to rest until the interfaces between layers become stable and horizontal, with minimal mixing.3. Laser Setup: Position the green laser so that it shines horizontally through one side wall of the tank at approximately mid-height. Ensure the beam is narrow and level.4. Camera Setup: Place the camera perpendicular to the tank, viewing from the side. Fix focus, exposure, and position to enable time-lapse or continuous recording without refocusing.5. Observation and Recording: Turn on the laser and record the beam path through the layered liquid. Maintain a darkened environment to enhance beam visibility.6. Completion: After recording sufficient footage, turn off the laser and safely empty and clean the tank.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The tank shows clear, horizontal liquid layers with no visible motion; the laser enters as a straight horizontal line.During Observation: As the laser passes through successive layers, its path bends slightly at each interface or curves gradually, producing a segmented or smoothly refracted trajectory.Overall Effect: The beam appears deflected due to changes in refractive index between layers, while the layers themselves remain stationary.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSugar concentration affects the refractive index of water: higher concentration corresponds to higher refractive index. When a laser beam passes through a medium with vertically stratified refractive indices, it refracts at each horizontal interface according to Snell’s law. This setup models atmospheric stratified refraction, where light bends due to vertical gradients in air density, temperature, or humidity.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure layers are poured slowly to avoid mixing; never look directly into the laser; fix the camera focus before recording; keep the tank and table stable throughout the experiment.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Frost Crystals Growing on a Supercooled Glass Plate in Humid AirSubject: Natural Science - Atmospheric ScienceExperiment Objective: To observe and understand the formation and growth of frost crystals on a supercooled surface under humid airflow conditions using time-lapse photography.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Copper–Iron Thermocouple Heated by CandleI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Copper–Iron Thermocouple Junction Heated by Candle2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science (Thermal and Electrical Effects)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the thermoelectric effect by heating a copper–iron thermocouple junction and detecting the induced current with an analog galvanometer; to understand the relationship between temperature difference and electrical response.II. Experimental EquipmentCopper wire, iron wire (joined to form a thermocouple junction), analog galvanometer (zero-centered preferred), connecting leads, candle, lighter or matches, heat-resistant stand or clamp, lab bench, camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the thermocouple on the lab bench. Ensure the copper–iron junction is exposed and securely connected to the analog galvanometer. Adjust the galvanometer to zero. Fix the camera focus and framing so the junction, candle position, and galvanometer needle are clearly visible.2. Initial Observation: Without heating, observe and record the initial state of the galvanometer needle (at or near zero).3. Heating Operation: Light the candle and slowly move the flame close to the copper–iron junction without touching it. Keep the flame steady to heat the junction.4. Observation During Heating: Observe the galvanometer needle as the junction temperature rises.5. Cooling Operation: After a clear deflection is observed, move the candle away from the junction and extinguish it safely.6. Observation During Cooling: Continue observing the galvanometer needle as the junction cools and the temperature difference decreases.7. End: Stop recording, allow equipment to cool, and tidy the lab bench.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The galvanometer needle remains at zero or the central position.2. During Heating: As the candle heats the copper–iron junction, the galvanometer needle gradually deflects to one side, indicating an induced current.3. After Removing the Candle: When the flame is removed, the needle slowly returns toward the zero position as the junction cools.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates the Seebeck effect. When a temperature difference exists between the junctions of two different metals (copper and iron), a thermoelectric potential is generated, driving a current in the circuit. Heating the junction increases the temperature difference, causing galvanometer deflection; removing the heat reduces the temperature difference, so the induced current decreases and the needle returns toward zero.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Avoid direct contact between flame and wires to prevent damage.2. Ensure firm electrical connections to avoid false readings.3. Handle the candle carefully and follow fire safety rules.4. Keep the camera fixed to ensure consistent time-lapse observation.

Heating: Turn on the heat lamp and allow both soil surfaces to heat simultaneously for a short period.4. Smoke Introduction: Light the incense stick and hold it upwind so that smoke drifts horizontally across both soil surfaces while the lamp remains on.5. Experiment Title: Formation of Ammonium Chloride Particulate by Gas Diffusion2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that when ammonia vapor and hydrogen chloride vapor diffuse and meet in air, they react to form fine ammonium chloride particulate, simulating secondary aerosol formation in the atmosphere.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Limewater Test with Ambient AirI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Limewater Test Using Ambient Air2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that ambient air contains carbon dioxide by bubbling air from a small pump through calcium hydroxide solution and observing the formation of turbidity over time.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass container (beaker or jar), clear limewater (calcium hydroxide solution), small air pump, flexible plastic or rubber tube, support stand (optional), camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Pour clear, colorless limewater into the glass container to about one-third of its volume. Ensure the solution is transparent and free of sediment.2. Setup: Connect one end of the tube to the small air pump and place the other end into the limewater, with the tube opening submerged but not touching the container wall or bottom.3. Camera Adjustment: Position the camera facing the container, fix the focus, and keep the field of view unchanged for the entire experiment to allow time-lapse observation.4. Operation: Turn on the air pump so that ambient air is steadily bubbled through the limewater.5. Observation: Allow bubbling to continue while recording. Observe changes in the clarity of the solution over time.6. Completion: After sufficient observation, turn off the pump, remove the tube from the solution, and stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The limewater is clear, colorless, and transparent.2. During Bubbling: Small air bubbles rise continuously through the solution.3. After Bubbling for Some Time: The solution gradually becomes cloudy or milky white due to the formation of fine solid particles.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAmbient air contains carbon dioxide. When air is bubbled through calcium hydroxide solution, carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate, which appears as a white precipitate and causes turbidity.Core reaction: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3↓ + H2O.The increasing turbidity over time visually confirms the presence of carbon dioxide in air.VI. Experimental NotesEnsure the limewater is clear before starting. Maintain steady airflow. Keep the camera fixed to clearly record gradual changes.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Incense Smoke Moving Upslope over a Sun-Heated Inclined Board (Anabatic Flow)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Incense Smoke Moving Upslope over a Sun-Heated Inclined Board (Anabatic Flow)2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate anabatic (upslope) wind formation caused by surface heating, and to observe how warm air rises and flows along a heated slope using incense smoke as a tracer.II. Experimental EquipmentInclined board (wood or metal, dark-colored preferred), support stand or books to raise one end of the board, incense stick and holder, sunlight source (direct sunlight or strong lamp), lighter or matches, calm indoor or outdoor environment.III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Place the board at an incline of about 20–30°, with the lower end accessible. Position it so sunlight directly heats the upper surface.2. Heating Stage: Allow the board to be heated by sunlight for several minutes so the surface becomes noticeably warm.3. Incense Placement: Fix the incense stick upright at the lower end of the inclined board, close to the surface.4. Ignition: Light the incense and allow it to burn steadily, producing continuous smoke.5. Observation: Observe the direction and motion of the smoke along the surface of the board.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before heating, incense smoke rises nearly vertically or disperses randomly.2. After Heating: Smoke bends toward the board and flows upward along the inclined surface, moving from the lower end toward the upper end.3. Sustained Heating: As long as the board remains warm, the upslope smoke flow remains clear and continuous.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSunlight heats the inclined board, warming the air in contact with its surface. The warmed air becomes less dense and rises. Because the surface is sloped, the rising warm air flows upslope, forming an anabatic wind. Incense smoke acts as a visible tracer, revealing the direction and strength of this thermally driven airflow.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure a calm environment with minimal background wind; avoid touching the hot board; secure the incense to prevent tipping; perform the experiment safely with fire precautions.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Food Dye Adsorption by Activated CarbonI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Food Dye Adsorption by Activated Carbon in Water2. Subject: Natural Science - Environmental Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the adsorption ability of activated carbon by comparing the color change of food-dyed water with and without activated carbon, and to understand the role of adsorption in water purification.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical clear glass beakers, clean water, activated carbon powder or granules, liquid food dye, stirring rods or spoons, measuring cup or dropper, camera or mobile phone with fixed support (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear beakers side by side on a stable surface. Pour the same volume of clean water into each beaker, ensuring equal water levels.2. Setup: Add a measured amount of activated carbon into the left beaker only. Do not add anything to the right beaker, which serves as the control group.3. Adding Dye: Prepare food-dyed water of uniform color and concentration. Pour the same volume of this dyed water into both beakers at the same time.4. Stirring: Use separate stirring rods to gently stir both beakers for the same duration to evenly mix the dye and, in the left beaker, to allow contact between dye and activated carbon.5. Recording: Fix the camera focus and position so that both beakers remain in frame. Record the process using time-lapse photography or accelerated video.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers contain uniformly colored dyed water; the left beaker also contains visible black activated carbon particles.2. During Observation: Over time, the color of the water in the left beaker gradually becomes lighter and clearer, while the activated carbon remains dark. The right beaker retains its original color with little or no change.3. Final State: A clear contrast is observed: the left beaker shows明显 fading of color, whereas the right beaker remains strongly colored.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesActivated carbon has a large surface area with many micropores, allowing it to adsorb dye molecules from water. This is a physical adsorption process driven by intermolecular forces. As dye molecules attach to the surface of activated carbon, their concentration in the water decreases, causing the color to fade. In the control beaker without activated carbon, no adsorption occurs, so the dye concentration and color remain largely unchanged.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use identical beakers and equal volumes to ensure fair comparison.2. Stir gently to avoid splashing or loss of material.3. Keep the camera fixed to ensure reliable comparison over time.4. Recording: Keep the camera fixed on both beakers and record the process using time-lapse photography to capture gradual changes.5. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Land Ice and Sea Ice Melting and Sea-Level Change2. Subject: Natural Science – Environmental Science3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate and understand the difference between sea ice (floating ice) and land ice (ice above water) melting, and their respective impacts on sea-level change.II. Experimental Equipment1. Two identical clear containers (transparent plastic or glass)2. Clean water3. Ice cubes of similar size and mass4. A small raised platform or stand (waterproof, stable)5. Overhead heat source (lamp or sunlight)6. Camera or smartphone with fixed focus and tripod (for time-lapse recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup Preparation: Place two clear containers side by side on a flat surface. Ensure both containers are at the same height and visible in the camera frame.2. Water Filling: Pour equal volumes of water into both containers, marking the initial water level on each container.3. Ice Placement:   (1) Left container (Sea Ice Model): Gently place ice cubes into the water so they float freely.   (2) Right container (Land Ice Model): Place ice cubes on a raised platform above the water surface, ensuring melted water can drip into the container.4. Camera Setup: Fix the camera focus and position to capture both containers simultaneously. Do not adjust the camera during the experiment.5. Heating Process: Apply the same overhead heat source to both containers. Begin time-lapse recording as the ice starts to melt.6. Completion: Continue heating until all ice in both containers has completely melted. Stop recording and observe final water levels.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both containers have the same water level; ice is solid and clearly visible.2. During Melting:   (1) Left container: Floating ice gradually shrinks while remaining afloat; water level changes very little.   (2) Right container: Ice on the platform melts, and meltwater drips into the container, causing a noticeable rise in water level.3. Final State: After complete melting, the left container’s water level is nearly unchanged, while the right container shows an increased water level.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Sea Ice Principle: Floating ice displaces an amount of water equal to its weight. When it melts, it occupies the same volume as the displaced water, so sea level does not significantly rise.2. Land Ice Principle: Ice resting on land does not displace water. When it melts, the resulting water adds to the container, causing sea-level rise.3. Environmental Significance: This experiment models why melting glaciers and ice sheets on land contribute to global sea-level rise, while melting sea ice does not.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both containers are identical and water volumes are equal for fair comparison.2. Use a stable platform to prevent ice from falling directly into the water prematurely.3. Keep the camera fixed to maintain spatiotemporal consistency in time-lapse recording.4. Handle heat sources carefully to avoid burns or container deformation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: The experiment demonstrates the environmental science principle that melting land ice raises sea level, while melting sea ice does not. Minimum assumptions: ice density is lower than water, floating ice displaces water, and melted ice conserves mass. Phased storyline: (1) Initial setup shows two identical clear containers with equal water levels and different ice positions; (2) overhead heat is applied equally while the camera remains fixed; (3) ice gradually melts—floating ice shrinks without water-level rise, elevated ice produces dripping meltwater; (4) final comparison shows unchanged level on the left and increased level on the right. Visibility constraints: both containers must remain in frame, water levels must be clearly visible, and no camera movement should occur.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Bacterial Viability Fluorescent Staining Detection (FDA Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Bacterial Viability Fluorescent Staining Detection Using FDA2. Subject: Natural Science - Environmental Science (Microbial Analysis)3. Experiment Objective: To determine bacterial viability by adding FDA fluorescent dye to a bacterial suspension, staining in the dark for 10 minutes, and observing fluorescence differences between live and dead bacteria under a fluorescence microscope.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentBacterial suspension (mixed live/dead or treated control), FDA fluorescent dye solution, sterile microcentrifuge tubes, micropipette and tips, aluminum foil or dark box, glass slide and coverslip, fluorescence microscope (blue-light excitation), timer.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place an appropriate volume of bacterial suspension into a sterile tube.2. Staining: Add a small volume of FDA dye to the suspension, mix gently to ensure uniform distribution.3. Dark Incubation: Cover the tube with aluminum foil and incubate in the dark for 10 minutes at room temperature.4. Slide Preparation: After staining, place one drop of the stained suspension onto a clean glass slide and gently apply a coverslip.5. Microscopic Observation: Place the slide on the fluorescence microscope stage, select the appropriate excitation wavelength, and adjust focus.6. Time-lapse Observation: Observe and record the fluorescence field over a short time sequence, maintaining focus.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Bacterial suspension shows no visible fluorescence to the naked eye.2. Under Fluorescence Microscope: Live bacteria emit bright green fluorescence; dead bacteria show weak or no fluorescence.3. Time-lapse: Fluorescent signal remains stable in live cells during observation.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleFDA (fluorescein diacetate) is a non-fluorescent compound that can penetrate bacterial cell membranes. In live bacteria, intracellular esterases hydrolyze FDA into fluorescein, which emits green fluorescence under blue-light excitation. Dead bacteria lack esterase activity or membrane integrity, so they show little or no fluorescence. Therefore, fluorescence intensity reflects bacterial viability.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Chemical Garden Experiment Forming Mineral Chimney StructuresI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Chemical Garden Experiment Forming Mineral Chimney Structures2. Subject: Natural Science – Marine Science (Ocean Chemistry and Hydrothermal Analogues)3. Experiment Objective: To simulate the formation of mineral chimney structures similar to deep-sea hydrothermal vents by observing the reaction between metal salt crystals and sodium silicate solution; to understand osmotic pressure, precipitation reactions, and self-organized mineral growth; to master basic skills of solution preparation, gentle solid addition, and long-term observation using time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentGlass tank or transparent beaker (capacity 500–1000 mL, clean and colorless), sodium silicate solution (clear, approximately 5–10% by mass), metal salt crystals (e.g., copper sulfate, cobalt chloride, iron(II) sulfate; dry and crystalline), tweezers or spatula, measuring cylinder, distilled water, protective gloves and goggles, stable table surface, camera or smartphone with tripod (for fixed-focus time-lapse photography).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the glass tank on a stable, vibration-free surface. Put on protective gloves and goggles. Prepare a clear sodium silicate solution and slowly pour it into the glass tank to a depth of about 5–8 cm, ensuring the solution is transparent and free of bubbles.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera in front of the glass tank, adjust framing so the entire liquid column is visible, fix focus and exposure, and start time-lapse or continuous recording. Do not move the camera afterward.3. Core Operation: Using tweezers, gently drop a small amount (1–3 crystals) of metal salt crystals into the solution. Allow the crystals to sink naturally to the bottom of the tank. Do not stir, shake, or disturb the solution.4. Observation Stage: Leave the system undisturbed. Continue recording as structures gradually form and grow upward from the crystals.5. Completion and Cleanup: After sufficient observation, stop recording. Dispose of the solution according to laboratory waste guidelines, rinse the tank with water, and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The sodium silicate solution is colorless and transparent; metal salt crystals rest at the bottom without immediate large-scale change.2. Early Stage: A thin, semi-transparent membrane forms around each crystal; small bubbles or colored solution may appear near the crystal surface.3. Growth Stage: Tubular or chimney-like structures emerge from the crystal, extending upward. The tubes are often hollow, fragile, and colored according to the metal salt (e.g., blue for copper sulfate).4. Later Stage: The chimneys may branch, curve, or collapse slightly as growth slows; overall structure resembles miniature mineral chimneys.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on precipitation reactions, osmotic pressure, and density differences. When metal salt crystals dissolve in sodium silicate solution, a semi-permeable membrane of metal silicate precipitate forms around the crystal. Water enters the membrane due to osmotic pressure, increasing internal pressure until the membrane ruptures. The metal salt solution jets out and reacts with silicate ions, forming solid precipitate that builds upward tubular structures. This self-organized process is analogous to the formation of mineral chimneys at deep-sea hydrothermal vents, where mineral-rich fluids meet seawater.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the sodium silicate solution is clear before starting; cloudy solution may affect observations.2. Drop crystals gently to avoid mixing or turbulence.3. Keep the setup completely still during observation to allow orderly structure formation.4. Wear protective equipment and handle chemical waste properly.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Simulation of mineral chimney formation via a chemical garden reaction in a marine science context. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: a clear sodium silicate solution, solid metal salt crystals, no external disturbance, and precipitation-driven self-organization.Phased storyline: (1) Static setup with clear solution and crystals resting at the bottom; fixed camera view. (2) Formation of a thin precipitate membrane around crystals. (3) Rupture and upward jetting leading to tubular, chimney-like growth. (4) Slowing or stabilization of growth. Visibility requirements: side view of the tank, clear contrast between solution and colored structures, continuous time-lapse perspective to verify causal and temporal continuity.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment "Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2) Photolysis in a Sealed Glass Tube under UV Light"I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2) Photolysis under UV Illumination2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science (Photochemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the photolysis behavior of nitrogen dioxide under ultraviolet light, observe color changes caused by photochemical reactions, and understand the role of solar radiation in atmospheric nitrogen oxide chemistry. The experiment also demonstrates time-lapse recording with a fixed-focus camera.II. Experimental EquipmentSealed glass tube containing nitrogen dioxide gas (light brown), UV lamp (wavelength 300–400 nm), lab bench, retort stand or holder for glass tube, digital camera or smartphone with tripod, UV protective goggles, lab gloves, dark background board (optional, for contrast).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:- Place the sealed glass tube containing NO2 horizontally or vertically on the lab bench using a stable holder.- Ensure the tube is intact and fully sealed; do not open it.- Put on UV protective goggles and gloves.2. Camera Setup:- Mount the camera on a tripod facing the glass tube.- Adjust the frame so the entire tube is clearly visible.- Manually fix the focus and exposure to prevent automatic changes during recording.- Set the camera to time-lapse or continuous video mode.3. Illumination Operation:- Turn on the UV lamp and position it at a fixed distance (about 10–20 cm) from the glass tube.- Ensure the UV light uniformly illuminates the tube.- Start recording with the camera.4. Observation Stage:- Keep the UV lamp on for a short period (accelerated for demonstration, e.g., several seconds).- Observe the change in color intensity of the gas inside the tube.5. Completion:- Turn off the UV lamp.- Stop recording.- Store the equipment properly and keep the sealed tube in a safe location.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The nitrogen dioxide gas in the sealed tube appears uniformly brown.2. During UV Illumination: The brown color gradually becomes lighter or fades, indicating a decrease in NO2 concentration.3. After UV is Turned Off (optional observation): The brown color may slowly deepen again due to recombination reactions in the sealed system.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleNitrogen dioxide is a key atmospheric pollutant that undergoes photolysis under ultraviolet radiation. When exposed to UV light, NO2 absorbs photons and dissociates:NO2 + hv → NO + OThe produced atomic oxygen can further participate in atmospheric reactions, while the reduction in NO2 concentration leads to a visible fading of the brown color. In a sealed glass tube, when UV illumination stops, NO and O can recombine or equilibrate back to NO2, partially restoring the color. This experiment models fundamental photochemical processes occurring in the Earth’s atmosphere under sunlight.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not open the sealed glass tube; NO2 is toxic.2. Avoid direct exposure of skin and eyes to UV light; always wear protective goggles.3. Keep the UV lamp at a stable position to ensure consistent illumination.4. Fix camera focus and exposure to ensure accurate time-lapse comparison.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Photolysis of atmospheric nitrogen dioxide under ultraviolet radiation. Minimum assumptions: NO2 is sealed in a transparent glass tube, UV light provides sufficient photon energy, and the system is safe and closed. Expected phased storyline: (1) Initial static scene with a uniformly brown NO2-filled tube on a lab bench; (2) UV lamp turns on, illuminating the tube; (3) gradual, visible fading of the brown color as photolysis occurs, captured by a fixed-focus camera; (4) optional stabilization or slight recovery after UV is off. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Comparison of Warming and Cooling of Bare Soil and Plant-Covered SoilI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Bare Soil vs Plant-Covered Soil Warming and Cooling under the Same Light Source2. Subject: Natural Science – Environmental Science3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare how bare soil and soil covered with dense green plants warm up and cool down under the same light conditions, and to understand the role of vegetation in regulating surface temperature.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo shallow trays of equal size; garden soil; dense green plants (e.g., grass or small seedlings); heat lamp (single lamp); thermometer or thermal camera (optional); video camera or smartphone; tripod; dark background (optional for contrast).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fill both trays with the same depth of soil. Leave one tray as bare soil. Plant dense green plants evenly in the other tray. Place both trays side by side on a flat surface.2. Setup: Position one heat lamp above the midpoint of the two trays so both receive equal light. Fix the camera on a tripod, lock focus and exposure, and frame both trays clearly.3. Heating Stage: Turn on the heat lamp and begin time-lapse or continuous filming. Maintain lighting for a short, accelerated period suitable for video demonstration.4. Observation during Heating: Observe surface changes; if using a thermal view, occasionally switch to an overhead thermal perspective to record temperature differences.5. Cooling Stage: Turn off the heat lamp while continuing to film. Record the cooling process of both trays.6. End and Cleanup: Stop filming after clear differences in cooling are observed. Turn off equipment and restore materials.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both trays start at similar temperatures.2. Heating Phase: Bare soil warms up faster and reaches a higher surface temperature. Plant-covered soil warms more slowly.3. Cooling Phase: After the lamp is turned off, bare soil cools rapidly, while plant-covered soil cools more slowly and remains relatively stable.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesBare soil absorbs and releases heat quickly due to low heat capacity and lack of shading. Plant-covered soil is shaded by leaves, has higher moisture content, and loses heat through transpiration, which moderates temperature changes. Vegetation therefore reduces extreme surface warming and cooling, helping stabilize the local environment.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure equal lamp distance and exposure for both trays; keep camera focus fixed; avoid disturbing soil or plants during filming; prevent overheating or drying of plants.

Experiment Title: Visualization of Inequality Transitivity on a Number Line2. Subject: Mathematics – Natural Science3. Experiment Objective: To visually verify the transitive property of inequalities by placing numbers on a number line and observing that if a<b and b<c, then a<c.II. Experimental MaterialsWhite background (paper or digital canvas), horizontal number line marked from -5 to 5, red dot (for a), blue dot (for b), green dot (for c), text labels.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Set a white background and draw a horizontal number line with evenly spaced tick marks labeled from -5 to 5.2. Marking a: Place a red dot at position x=1 and label it a=1.3. Marking b: Place a blue dot at position x=3 and label it b=3, adding the text label a<b near a and b.4. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Benzo(a)pyrene Detection in Water by Fluorescence MethodI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Detection of Benzo(a)pyrene in Water by Fluorescence Spectrophotometry2. Subject: Natural Science – Environmental Science3. Experiment Objective: To detect the presence of benzo(a)pyrene in a water sample extract using fluorescence characteristics, and to understand the principle that polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons emit fluorescence under specific ultraviolet excitation.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsFluorescence spectrophotometer; quartz cuvette (1 cm optical path); micropipette (1 mL range) with tips; water sample extract containing benzo(a)pyrene; laboratory wipes; protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Turn on the fluorescence spectrophotometer and allow it to warm up. Set the excitation wavelength to 365 nm. Ensure the instrument is in fluorescence measurement mode.2. Sample Loading: Use a micropipette to accurately transfer 1 mL of the prepared water sample extract into a clean quartz cuvette. Avoid introducing bubbles.3. Cuvette Handling: Wipe the outer surfaces of the cuvette with laboratory wipes to remove fingerprints or droplets. Ensure the optical faces are clean and transparent.4. Measurement: Place the quartz cuvette into the sample holder of the fluorescence spectrophotometer, aligning it correctly. Close the sample chamber lid.5. Observation: Start the measurement and observe the fluorescence signal or visual fluorescence emission indicated by the instrument display.6. Completion: After measurement, remove the cuvette, dispose of the sample according to laboratory waste regulations, and clean the cuvette.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The water sample extract in the quartz cuvette appears clear or slightly colored, with no visible luminescence under normal light.2. Under Excitation: When excited at 365 nm, the sample containing benzo(a)pyrene produces a characteristic blue fluorescence signal, displayed as an emission peak or intensity increase on the instrument.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleBenzo(a)pyrene is a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon with a conjugated aromatic structure. When irradiated with ultraviolet light at an excitation wavelength of 365 nm, its electrons are promoted to an excited state. Upon returning to the ground state, part of the absorbed energy is released as fluorescence in the visible region. The presence and intensity of this fluorescence are used to qualitatively or quantitatively detect benzo(a)pyrene in environmental water samples.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Quartz cuvettes must be used, as glass absorbs ultraviolet light.2. Avoid touching the optical surfaces of the cuvette.3. Ensure correct excitation wavelength setting before measurement.4. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Parallelogram Law Demonstration of Vector AdditionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Parallelogram Law Demonstration of Vector Addition2. Subject: Mathematics - Vector Geometry3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate vector addition using the parallelogram law in a Cartesian coordinate system, and to understand how the resultant vector is obtained from two given vectors.II. Experimental MaterialsWhite background (paper or digital canvas), Cartesian coordinate system with x- and y-axes, drawing tools (pen or digital drawing tool), color markers: blue, red, and green.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Set up a Cartesian coordinate system on a white background, clearly marking the origin and axes with uniform scale.2. Drawing Vector a: From the origin, draw vector a=(2,1) using a blue arrow, pointing 2 units along the x-axis and 1 unit along the y-axis. Label it clearly as a.3. Drawing Vector b: From the origin, draw vector b=(1,2) using a red arrow, pointing 1 unit along the x-axis and 2 units along the y-axis. Label it clearly as b.4. Parallelogram Construction: From the head of vector a, draw a line parallel and equal in length to vector b. From the head of vector b, draw a line parallel and equal in length to vector a, forming a parallelogram.5. Drawing the Resultant Vector: Draw the green arrow from the origin to the opposite vertex of the parallelogram. Label it as a+b.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Vectors a and b originate from the same point and point in different directions.2. The constructed parallelogram has opposite sides parallel and equal.3. The green resultant vector extends from the origin to the far vertex of the parallelogram, visually representing the sum of the two vectors.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe parallelogram law of vector addition states that when two vectors originate from the same point, their sum is represented by the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by these vectors. In this experiment, vector a=(2,1) and vector b=(1,2) combine to form the resultant vector a+b=(3,3), which is shown geometrically by the green diagonal vector.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Water COD Rapid Detection (Potassium Dichromate Colorimetric Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Rapid Detection of Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD) in Water by Potassium Dichromate Colorimetric Method2. Subject: Natural Science – Environmental Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the rapid qualitative detection of COD in a water sample by oxidation with potassium dichromate under acidic conditions, observe color changes after heating, and understand the basic principle of COD determination.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents1. Test tube (1 tube, clean and dry, 15×150 mm)2. Test tube rack3. Graduated pipette or dropper (2 mL scale)4. Boiling water bath (beaker with water placed on a heating device)5. Heat source (electric hot plate or alcohol lamp)6. COD-containing water sample (unknown COD level)7. Potassium dichromate–sulfuric acid reagent (orange solution)8. Test tube holder or clamp9. Safety goggles and glovesIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clean test tube on the test tube rack. Put on safety goggles and gloves. Ensure the water bath is prepared and heated to boiling.2. Sampling: Use a pipette to measure 2 mL of the COD-containing water sample and carefully add it into the test tube.3. Reagent Addition: Use another pipette to measure 2 mL of potassium dichromate–sulfuric acid reagent. Slowly add it into the test tube containing the water sample. Gently mix without splashing.4. Heating: Hold the test tube with a test tube holder and place it into the boiling water bath, ensuring the liquid level in the test tube is below the water level of the bath. Heat for approximately 2 minutes.5. Observation and Recording: During heating, focus the camera on the test tube and use time-lapse photography to record the color change of the solution.6. Completion: After heating, remove the test tube from the water bath and place it back on the rack. Allow it to cool naturally. Dispose of the waste solution according to laboratory safety regulations.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The potassium dichromate–sulfuric acid reagent is orange; the water sample is colorless or slightly colored.2. After Mixing: The mixed solution appears orange.3. During Heating: As heating proceeds, the orange color gradually weakens.4. Final State: After about 2 minutes of heating, the solution changes from orange to green or yellow-green, depending on the COD level. A more obvious green color indicates higher COD.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Core Principle: COD represents the amount of oxygen required to oxidize organic matter in water. In this method, potassium dichromate (Cr2O7^2−) acts as a strong oxidizing agent in a sulfuric acid medium.2. Reaction Explanation: Organic substances in the water sample are oxidized during heating, while hexavalent chromium (Cr(VI), orange) is reduced to trivalent chromium (Cr(III), green).3. Phenomenon–Principle Relationship: The observed color change from orange to green reflects the reduction of potassium dichromate and indicates the presence and relative level of oxidizable organic matter in the water sample.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Handle sulfuric acid-containing reagents carefully to avoid burns.2. Do not directly heat the test tube with a flame; always use a boiling water bath.3. Ensure accurate volume measurement (2 mL + 2 mL) for reliable observation.4. Experimental waste must be collected and disposed of according to environmental and laboratory safety rules.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Rapid qualitative COD detection using potassium dichromate oxidation under acidic heating conditions. Minimum assumptions: a test tube-scale experiment, fixed volumes (2 mL sample + 2 mL reagent), boiling water bath heating, and visible color change as evidence of redox reaction. Phased storyline: (1) Initial setup—clear water sample and orange reagent measured and combined in a test tube; (2) Causal action—test tube placed into boiling water bath, heating accelerates oxidation; (3) Observable transition—orange solution gradually shifts toward green during time-lapse; (4) Final state—stable green/yellow-green solution indicating COD presence. Visibility constraints: camera remains focused on the test tube, color change is clearly visible, and step order is unambiguous.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Scaling Transformation Demonstration of Scalar MultiplicationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Scaling Transformation Demonstration of Scalar Multiplication2. Subject: Mathematics – Natural Science3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the geometric meaning of scalar multiplication of a vector by observing how a vector changes in length while maintaining direction in a Cartesian coordinate system.II. Experimental MaterialsWhite background or canvas, Cartesian coordinate grid, drawing tools or software capable of drawing vectors in different colors, labeling tool.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Set a white background and draw a clear Cartesian coordinate system with x-axis and y-axis intersecting at the origin (0,0).2. Drawing the Original Vector: From the origin, draw a blue vector a pointing to the coordinate (1,2). Add an arrowhead and label it a=(1,2).3. Drawing the Stretched Vector: From the same origin, draw a red vector in the same direction as vector a, with endpoint at (2,4). Label it 2a.4. Drawing the Shortened Vector: From the origin, draw a green vector in the same direction as vector a, with endpoint at (0.5,1). Label it 0.5a.5. Final Check: Ensure all vectors start from the origin, arrows are clear, colors are correct, and labels are readable.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The blue vector a=(1,2) serves as the reference vector.2. The red vector 2a has the same direction as a but is twice its length.3. The green vector 0.5a has the same direction as a but is half its length.4. All vectors are collinear and originate from the same point, clearly showing scaling effects.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesScalar multiplication of a vector by a positive number changes the vector’s magnitude while keeping its direction unchanged. Multiplying by a factor greater than 1 stretches the vector proportionally, while multiplying by a factor between 0 and 1 shortens it. In coordinates, each component of the vector is multiplied by the scalar, producing the observed geometric scaling in the Cartesian plane.

Experiment Objective: To visually understand the vertex and axis of symmetry of an upward-opening quadratic function by plotting y = x² − 2x + 1 on a Cartesian coordinate system, and to relate the algebraic form of the function to its geometric features.II. Experimental Tools and MaterialsWhite background canvas or screen, Cartesian coordinate system template, plotting software or drawing tools, color settings (purple solid line, red points, blue dashed line), text labels.III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Prepare a white background and draw a Cartesian coordinate system with x-axis range [-4,4] and y-axis range [-1,8]. Label axes clearly.2. Plotting the Function: Using a purple solid line, plot the quadratic function y = x² − 2x + 1 smoothly across the given x-range, ensuring the parabola opens upward.3. Identifying the Vertex: Determine the vertex by calculation or observation, and mark the point (1,1) with a red dot. Label its coordinates clearly.4. Drawing the Axis of Symmetry: Draw a blue dashed vertical line through x = 1 to represent the axis of symmetry of the parabola.5. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Triangle Similarity Transformation (Homothety, Scale Factor 2)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visualization of Triangle Similarity Transformation by Homothety (Scale Factor 2)2. Subject: Natural Science – Mathematics (Geometry)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate a triangle similarity transformation using homothety with a scale factor of 2, understand the role of the homothetic center, and verify that corresponding vertices, connecting lines, and side ratios satisfy the properties of similar triangles.II. Experimental Materials and Environment1. White background coordinate plane.2. Black triangle ABC with labeled vertices: A(1,1), B(2,1), C(1,2).3. Red dot indicating the homothetic center O(0,0).4. Blue triangle A"B"C" as the image after homothety.5. Green dashed lines connecting corresponding vertices A–A", B–B", C–C".6. Yellow text label: Homothety Ratio 2 (enlarged).III. Experimental Operation Process1. Preparation: Display a white background coordinate plane. Mark the origin (0,0) clearly with a red dot as the homothetic center O.2. Original Figure Construction: Draw triangle ABC in black, with vertices A(1,1), B(2,1), and C(1,2). Label each vertex with its coordinate.3. Transformation Operation: Apply a homothety centered at O with a scale factor of 2. Determine the image points A", B", and C" by doubling the coordinates of A, B, and C relative to the origin.4. Image Figure Construction: Draw triangle A"B"C" in blue using the transformed coordinates and label each vertex.5. Correspondence Illustration: Draw green dashed lines connecting A to A", B to B", and C to C". Ensure all dashed lines pass through the red center point O.6. Annotation: Add yellow text on the figure indicating Homothety Ratio 2 (enlarged).IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Only the black triangle ABC and the red center O are visible on the white background.2. After Transformation: A larger blue triangle A"B"C" appears, maintaining the same shape and orientation as triangle ABC.3. Correspondence Features: Each dashed green line connects a vertex of ABC to its corresponding vertex of A"B"C" and passes through O.4. Quantitative Relationship: The distances OA", OB", and OC" are exactly twice OA, OB, and OC respectively.V. Summary of Experimental Principle1. Core Principle: Homothety is a similarity transformation that enlarges or reduces a figure from a fixed center by a constant ratio.2. Mathematical Expression: For a homothety centered at O(0,0) with ratio k=2, any point P(x,y) maps to P"(2x,2y).3. Similarity Conclusion: Triangle ABC and triangle A"B"C" are similar; corresponding angles are equal, corresponding sides are in the ratio 1:2, and corresponding vertices lie on straight lines passing through the homothetic center.VI. Experimental Notes1. Vertex coordinates must be labeled clearly to verify the numerical relationship.2. Colors should remain consistent: black for original triangle, blue for image triangle, red for center, green dashed for correspondence lines.3. The dashed lines must visually pass through the center to correctly reflect the homothety property.

manual: 实验名称：2×2矩阵加法可视化演示一、基本实验信息学科：数学（自然科学）实验目标：通过可视化方式演示2×2矩阵加法的运算过程，理解矩阵加法中对应元素相加的基本规则。二、实验材料与环境1. 白色背景显示界面。2. 矩阵A=[[1,2],[3,4]]（绿色，黑色文字，黑色实线边框）。3. 矩阵B=[[5,6],[7,8]]（绿色，黑色文字，黑色实线边框）。4. 结果矩阵C（蓝色，黑色文字，黑色实线边框）。三、实验操作过程1. 初始展示：在白色背景上，将绿色的2×2矩阵A和矩阵B左右并排显示，二者之间保持约1cm间距，在中间放置一个黑色“+”号。2. 等待阶段：保持A和B静止显示约1秒，强调即将进行矩阵加法运算。3. 运算演示：按照矩阵加法规则，将A与B中位置相同的元素进行相加。4. 结果呈现：生成蓝色的2×2结果矩阵C，并清晰标注其元素数值。四、实验现象观察1. 初始状态：仅显示两个绿色矩阵A和B及中间的“+”号。2. 运算后：出现一个新的蓝色矩阵C，其元素分别为：C11=1+5=6，C12=2+6=8，C21=3+7=10，C22=4+8=12。3. 矩阵边框均为黑色实线，元素文字为黑色，布局清晰。五、实验原理总结矩阵加法的基本原理是：只有行数和列数相同的矩阵才能相加；相加时，对应位置的元素分别相加，所得结果构成新的矩阵。该实验通过颜色和空间布局直观展示了“对应元素相加”的核心数学思想。
high_level_evaluation_guide: 目标概念：2×2矩阵加法。最小机制假设包括：矩阵具有固定行列结构；仅同位置元素可相加；结果矩阵维度不变。分阶段叙事：第一阶段展示A和B（白底、绿色、并列）；第二阶段静止约1秒作为因果过渡；第三阶段触发逐元素相加；第四阶段生成蓝色结果矩阵C。验证约束：视角保持正视、无旋转；矩阵位置前后保持一致；时间顺序严格为“先A+B，后C”，以便清晰检验因果与结果。

Experiment Title: Full Permutation of 3 Elements (A, B, C) Visualization2. Subject: Natural Science - Mathematics (Combinatorics)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the concept of full permutation using three distinct elements A, B, and C, and to help learners understand how all possible ordered arrangements are generated and organized in lexicographical order.II. Experimental MaterialsWhite background canvas or slide, text rendering tool, standard font, color setting tool (red and black).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Set the canvas background to pure white. Ensure no additional graphics or colors are present.2. Title Display: At the top center of the canvas, add red text reading Elements: A, B, C.3. Permutation Construction: Determine all possible permutations of A, B, and C (total of six).4. Layout Arrangement: Arrange the six permutations into three vertical columns below the title, following strict lexicographical order.5. Final Check: Verify that all permutations are included, non-repeating, and clearly legible.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The background remains uniformly white throughout.2. The title Elements: A, B, C appears in red and is visually distinct from the permutations.3. Below the title, three columns clearly display the six permutations in correct lexicographical order.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleA full permutation refers to all possible ordered arrangements of a set of distinct elements. For three elements A, B, and C, the number of permutations is 3! = 6. Displaying these permutations in lexicographical order helps learners systematically understand the structure and completeness of permutation sets.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Visualization of 2x2 Matrix SubtractionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visualization of 2x2 Matrix Subtraction2. Subject: Natural Science – Mathematics3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the concept of 2x2 matrix subtraction, help learners understand element-wise subtraction, and connect symbolic calculation with visual representation.II. Experimental MaterialsWhite background canvas (digital or physical), graphical representation tools (or animation software), two green 2x2 matrices labeled A and B, minus sign symbol, one blue 2x2 result matrix C, black text labels, solid black matrix borders.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Set a white background. Prepare matrix A=[[5,6],[7,8]] and matrix B=[[1,2],[3,4]] with green fill color and solid black borders. Label all elements with black text.2. Display Stage: Place matrix A on the left and matrix B on the right with approximately 1 cm spacing. Insert a clear black minus sign between them, centered vertically.3. Operation Stage: Keep the two matrices static for about 1 second to allow observation of the subtraction setup.4. Result Generation: After 1 second, display a blue 2x2 matrix C with a solid black border to represent the subtraction result A−B.5. Labeling: Fill matrix C with black text showing the computed values.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Two green 2x2 matrices A and B appear side by side on a white background with a minus sign between them.2. Transition: After a short pause, a new blue matrix appears.3. Final State: The blue matrix C displays values [[4,4],[4,4]], corresponding to element-wise subtraction of B from A.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMatrix subtraction is performed element by element for matrices of the same order. For matrices A and B, the result matrix C=A−B is defined by c_ij = a_ij − b_ij. In this experiment, each element of B is subtracted from the corresponding element of A, producing C=[[5−1,6−2],[7−3,8−4]]=[[4,4],[4,4]].
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: element-wise subtraction of two 2x2 matrices of equal order. Minimum assumptions: matrices are static, same dimensions, clearly labeled, and subtraction is visually implied without symbolic overload. Phased storyline: (1) white background with two green matrices A and B aligned horizontally and a centered minus sign; (2) brief pause to establish the operation context; (3) appearance of a blue result matrix C showing correct subtraction outcomes. Key causal transition: the subtraction operation directly causes the values in C. Visibility constraints: fixed camera, no zoom, stable layout so element correspondence is easily verified.

Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate scalar multiplication of a matrix, helping learners understand that multiplying a matrix by a scalar means multiplying each element of the matrix by that scalar.II. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Graph Visualization of the Ellipse Equation x²/9 + y²/4 = 12. Subject: Natural Science - Mathematics (Analytic Geometry)3. Experiment Objective: To visually understand the standard form of an ellipse equation, identify the major and minor axes, verify vertex positions, and connect algebraic parameters a and b with geometric features.II. Experimental Materials and ToolsCoordinate grid or graphing software (or graph paper), Cartesian coordinate system with x∈[-4,4], y∈[-3,3], drawing tools (or plotting tool), color markers (red, blue, green).III. Experimental Operation Process1. Preparation: Set a white background and establish a Cartesian coordinate system. Draw x- and y-axes with labeled scales covering x∈[-4,4] and y∈[-3,3].2. Axis Identification: Mark the major axis along the x-axis and the minor axis along the y-axis using blue dashed lines.3. Vertex Plotting: Plot the vertices of the major axis at (3,0) and (-3,0), and the vertices of the minor axis at (0,2) and (0,-2).4. Ellipse Drawing: Using the vertices as constraints, draw a smooth red ellipse centered at the origin that intersects the axes only at the plotted vertices.5. Annotation: Add green text near the ellipse stating: Ellipse x²/9 + y²/4 = 1 (a=3, b=2).IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The ellipse is symmetric about both the x-axis and y-axis.2. The longest diameter lies along the x-axis with total length 6, and the shortest diameter lies along the y-axis with total length 4.3. The ellipse passes exactly through (±3,0) and (0,±2) and does not exceed these bounds.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. The standard ellipse equation x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 represents all points whose distances satisfy this relationship.2. Here, a²=9 and b²=4, so a=3 and b=2.3. The value of a determines the semi-major axis along the x-direction, and b determines the semi-minor axis along the y-direction.4. The graph visually confirms the correspondence between algebraic parameters and geometric structure.VI. Experimental NotesEnsure equal scaling on both axes; incorrect scaling will distort the ellipse. Keep colors consistent to clearly distinguish axes, ellipse, and text.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Matplotlib Bar Chart for Categorical DataI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Drawing a Categorical Bar Chart Using Matplotlib2. Subject: Natural Science - Statistics & Data Science3. Experiment Objective: To learn how to use Python with numpy and matplotlib to visualize categorical data by drawing a bar chart, understand how categorical variables are mapped to bars, and interpret the relationship between data values and visual elements.II. Experimental Environment and ToolsComputer with Python installed, Python IDE or Jupyter Notebook, numpy library, matplotlib library.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Turn on the computer and open a Python IDE or Jupyter Notebook. Ensure numpy and matplotlib are available.2. Import Libraries: In the code editor, type and run code to import numpy and matplotlib.pyplot.3. Define Data: Define five category names (such as A, B, C, D, E) and corresponding numerical values within the range 0–10.4. Write Plotting Code: Use matplotlib to create a bar chart, setting the bar color to blue, assigning categories to the x-axis and values to the y-axis.5. Label Axes: Add x-axis labels for category names and a y-axis label indicating the value range.6. Display Chart: Run the code to display the bar chart on the screen with a white background.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The computer screen shows Python code with library imports and defined data.2. After Execution: A new window or output area pops up displaying a bar chart.3. Chart Features: Five blue rectangular bars appear, each corresponding to one category; the x-axis shows category names, and the y-axis shows numerical values from 0 to 10; the background is white and uncluttered.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on data visualization principles in Statistics & Data Science. Matplotlib maps categorical variables to discrete positions along the x-axis and numerical values to bar heights along the y-axis. The bar chart visually encodes magnitude through height, allowing intuitive comparison between categories. Python serves as the computational tool, while matplotlib translates numerical data into graphical form.VI. Notes and PrecautionsEnsure the correct order of code execution; confirm that values are numeric; avoid overcrowding the chart; verify that bar colors and labels are clearly visible.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Finding the Median of Eight Ordered Data PointsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Finding the Median of Eight Ordered Numeric Values2. Subject: Natural Science - Statistics & Data Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how to find the median of an even-numbered dataset by arranging eight numeric values in ascending order, identifying the 4th and 5th values, computing their average, and marking this value as the median on a number line.II. Experimental MaterialsWhiteboard or paper, marker or pen, ruler (optional for number line).III. Experimental Procedure1. Data Preparation: Write eight numeric values in ascending order on the board or paper, ensuring the numbers are clearly spaced and readable.2. Identifying Middle Values: Count the ordered values from left to right and clearly point out or circle the 4th and 5th values.3. Core Operation: Use basic arithmetic to calculate the average of the 4th and 5th values by adding them together and dividing the sum by two.4. Representation: Draw a simple number line that includes the 4th and 5th values, and mark the calculated average exactly between them. Label this point as the median.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The eight values appear in strictly increasing order.2. The 4th and 5th values are visually identified as the two middle data points.3. The calculated average lies numerically and visually between these two values.4. The median point is marked on the number line between the 4th and 5th values.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleFor an even number of ordered data points, there is no single middle value. The median is defined as the average of the two middle values. In this experiment, with eight ordered numbers, the 4th and 5th values represent the center of the dataset. Their average lies exactly between them and represents the median, reflecting the central tendency of the data.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: The median of an even-sized dataset is the average of the two middle ordered values. Minimum assumptions: numbers can be ordered, basic arithmetic averaging is valid, and a number line can represent numerical position. Phased storyline: (1) Present eight ordered numbers; (2) Identify the 4th and 5th as middle values; (3) Compute their average; (4) Visually place and label the median between them on a number line. Key causal transition: averaging the two middle values leads to a point exactly between them, justifying its identification as the median. Visibility constraints: all numbers, calculations, and the number line must be clearly visible and sequentially shown.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Geometric Mean as the Central Symmetry Point in Log-Log PlotsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Geometric Mean and Symmetry in Logarithmic Coordinates2. Subject: Natural Science – Statistics & Data Science3. Experiment Objective: To plot several positive data points on logarithmic x-y axes, compute the geometric mean of x and y values, mark it on the log-log plot, and verify that it is the central symmetric point of the data in log space.II. Experimental ToolsComputer with data analysis software (e.g., Python with matplotlib/numpy, spreadsheet software, or graphing tool), sample positive dataset (x_i, y_i with x_i > 0, y_i > 0).III. Experimental Procedure1. Data Preparation: Prepare several pairs of positive data points.2. Plotting: Set both x-axis and y-axis to logarithmic scale and plot the data points as a scatter plot.3. Calculation: Compute the geometric mean of x values and y values separately: Gx = (product of x_i)^(1/n), Gy = (product of y_i)^(1/n).4. Marking: Plot the point (Gx, Gy) on the same log-log graph using a distinct color or marker.5. Verification: Visually inspect the plot in log space and compare distances of data points around the geometric mean.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The data points appear uneven in linear space but more symmetrically distributed in log-log coordinates.2. The geometric mean point lies near the visual center of the cluster in log space.3. For pairs of points that are multiplicative inverses around the mean, their log distances to the geometric mean are equal and opposite.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Logarithmic transformation converts multiplicative relationships into additive ones.2. The geometric mean corresponds to the arithmetic mean in log space.3. Therefore, in log-log coordinates, the geometric mean acts as the central point of symmetry for multiplicatively distributed positive data.VI. Experimental Notes1. All data must be positive to allow logarithmic scaling.2. Axis labels and scale indicators should be clearly shown.3. Focus on relative positions in log space rather than linear distances.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: The geometric mean as the center of symmetry in logarithmic coordinate systems. Minimum assumptions include positive data values, correct use of log-log axes, and correct geometric mean computation.Phased Storyline: (1) Display positive data points on log-log axes; (2) Compute and introduce the geometric mean; (3) Mark the geometric mean distinctly; (4) Reveal symmetry by comparing log-space distances of points around the mean. The viewpoint should keep axes fixed and labels visible to verify scale and symmetry.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Comparing Arithmetic Mean and Harmonic MeanI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparing Arithmetic Mean and Harmonic Mean on a Number Line2. Subject: Natural Science – Statistics & Data Science3. Experiment Objective: To verify through calculation and visualization that for two positive numbers, the harmonic mean is always lower than the arithmetic mean, and to understand the relationship between numerical computation and graphical representation.II. Experimental MaterialsPaper or digital worksheet, pen or stylus, calculator (optional), ruler or simple chart/number line drawing tool.III. Experimental Procedure1. Data Preparation: Select two positive numbers, for example a = 2 and b = 8. Record them clearly in a two-row table.2. Calculation of Arithmetic Mean: Write the formula AM = (a + b) / 2. Substitute the values and calculate step by step: (2 + 8) / 2 = 10 / 2 = 5.3. Calculation of Harmonic Mean: Write the formula HM = 2ab / (a + b). Substitute the values and calculate step by step: 2 × 2 × 8 / (2 + 8) = 32 / 10 = 3.2.4. Chart Construction: Draw a horizontal number line or simple chart with a clear numerical scale covering the range of values.5. Plotting Means: Mark the arithmetic mean (5) as a point on the number line, label it AM. Mark the harmonic mean (3.2) as another point, label it HM.6. Comparison: Observe the relative positions of the two points on the same chart.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The arithmetic mean point appears to the right (higher value) on the number line.2. The harmonic mean point appears to the left (lower value) on the same number line.3. The harmonic mean is clearly below the arithmetic mean when both are plotted using the same scale.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleFor two positive numbers, the arithmetic mean is the simple average, while the harmonic mean gives greater weight to smaller values. Because of this weighting, the harmonic mean is always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean, and strictly less when the two numbers are unequal. The graphical comparison on a number line visually confirms this statistical principle.VI. Notes and Precautions1. Ensure both numbers are positive; negative or zero values invalidate the harmonic mean.2. Use the same scale for plotting both means to ensure a fair visual comparison.3. Perform calculations step by step to avoid arithmetic errors.

Experiment Objective: To visualize and compare binomial distributions with different numbers of trials under the same probability p=0.5, and to verify that as n increases, the distribution becomes more symmetric and closer to a bell-shaped curve.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Comparing Strong and Weak Negative Correlation Scatter PlotsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visual Comparison of Strong and Weak Negative Correlation2. Subject: Natural Science - Statistics & Data Science3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare strong and weak negative correlations using scatter plots, understand how point dispersion affects correlation strength, and observe how trend lines reflect the underlying relationship.II. Experimental EquipmentCoordinate axes (x-y plane), dataset A (strong negative correlation), dataset B (weak negative correlation), plotting tool or software capable of scatter plotting and linear trend line fitting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Draw or display a set of x-y axes with fixed scale and labels.2. Strong Negative Correlation Plot:   a. Sequentially add data points from dataset A onto the axes.   b. Observe that points appear close to a downward-sloping line.   c. Fit a linear trend line after most points are added.3. Weak Negative Correlation Plot:   a. Clear only the data points while keeping the same axes.   b. Sequentially add data points from dataset B.   c. Observe that points are widely scattered with only a slight downward tendency.   d. Fit a linear trend line after point addition.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. In the strong negative correlation plot, points cluster tightly around a clear downward trend line.2. In the weak negative correlation plot, points are far from the trend line, and the downward trend is less obvious.3. The fitted trend line in both cases slopes downward, but its visual explanatory power differs significantly.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCorrelation measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables. A strong negative correlation occurs when data points lie close to a downward-sloping line, indicating a consistent inverse relationship. A weak negative correlation occurs when points are widely scattered, so the inverse relationship exists but is obscured by variability. Trend lines summarize the overall tendency but do not indicate correlation strength alone; point dispersion around the line is critical.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Visual Verification of the Mean as a Balance PointSubject: Natural Science - Statistics & Data ScienceObjective: To draw a 2D line chart with five discrete, left-right symmetric data points, calculate and mark the mean value, and visually verify that the mean acts as the balance point of the data above and below.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Comparing Line Charts with Different Coefficients of VariationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Line Charts with Coefficient of Variation 2 and 0.22. Subject: Natural Science – Statistics & Data Science3. Experiment Objective: To simulate two numeric datasets with different relative variability, construct line charts on the same scale, and verify that a dataset with coefficient of variation (CV) = 2 shows wide fluctuations and a relatively low mean line, while a dataset with CV = 0.2 shows small fluctuations and a stable mean.II. Experimental Materials and ToolsComputer with Python (or spreadsheet software), numerical simulation environment (NumPy/Excel), plotting tool (Matplotlib/Excel charts), graphing interface with axis control.III. Experimental Procedure1. Data Simulation:   (1) Set the sample size n = 50 for both datasets.   (2) Dataset A: Choose a small mean value (e.g., mean = 10) and a large standard deviation (e.g., SD = 20) so that CV = SD/mean = 2.   (3) Dataset B: Choose a mean value (e.g., mean = 10) and a small standard deviation (e.g., SD = 2) so that CV = 0.2.   (4) Generate random values using a normal distribution for both datasets.2. Calculation:   (1) Compute the sample mean and standard deviation for each dataset.   (2) Verify the CV values are approximately 2 and 0.2.3. Plotting:   (1) Create two line charts using the same x-axis (index 1–50) and the same y-axis scale.   (2) Plot Dataset A and Dataset B separately or in aligned subplots.   (3) Add a horizontal mean reference line to each chart.4. Comparison:   (1) Visually compare the amplitude of fluctuations.   (2) Compare the position and stability of the mean lines.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Dataset A (CV = 2): The line chart shows large up-and-down fluctuations, with values spreading widely around the mean; the mean line appears relatively low compared with extreme values.2. Dataset B (CV = 0.2): The line chart shows small, smooth fluctuations; data points cluster closely around the mean line, which appears stable.3. Under the same scale, Dataset A is visually much more volatile than Dataset B.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe coefficient of variation (CV = SD/mean) measures relative variability independent of units. A larger CV indicates greater dispersion relative to the mean, leading to wider visual fluctuations in a chart. A smaller CV indicates more stable data relative to its mean, producing smoother lines. manual: Instructions for the Experiment "Interaction of Two Charged Pith Balls"I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Interaction of Two Charged Pith Balls2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics (Electrostatics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe electrostatic interaction between two identically charged objects, understand the law of electric charges (like charges repel), and relate distance changes to observable motion. The experiment is recorded using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentPith balls (2, lightweight and identical), insulating threads (2, equal length), adjustable supports or stands (2, with horizontal adjustment), rubbed rod (plastic or glass rod with silk/wool), insulating handle, ruler or scale (optional), camera with tripod (fixed focus, time-lapse mode).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Suspend two pith balls from equal-length threads on separate adjustable supports. Ensure the balls hang freely, are at rest, and initially touch or are very close.2. Camera Setup: Place the camera facing the pith balls. Fix focus, frame both balls and supports clearly, and set time-lapse recording.3. Charging Operation: Rub the rod with silk or wool to charge it. Touch the rod gently to each pith ball in turn, ensuring both receive charge from the same rod.4. Observation with Fixed Supports: Release the balls and observe them moving apart due to repulsion until reaching a stable separation.5. Support Adjustment – Closer: Slowly move the two supports closer together without touching the balls. Observe the balls’ relative motion as they adjust their separation.6. Support Adjustment – Farther Apart: Gradually move the supports farther apart. Observe how the distance between the balls changes as they continue to repel each other.7. Conclusion: Stop recording after the balls reach new equilibrium positions. Reset the apparatus if needed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The two uncharged pith balls hang vertically and remain in contact or very close.2. After Charging: Once charged by the same rubbed rod, the balls repel each other and separate symmetrically.3. Supports Moving Closer: As the supports move closer, the balls still repel and adjust their positions, maintaining separation rather than touching.4. Supports Moving Farther Apart: As supports move apart, the distance between the balls increases correspondingly, with smooth, continuous motion.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates electrostatic interaction. When both pith balls are charged by the same rubbed rod, they acquire the same type of electric charge. According to the law of electric charges, like charges repel each other. The repulsive force acts along the line joining the balls and competes with gravity and thread tension, leading to a stable separation distance. Adjusting the supports changes geometric constraints but does not change the nature of the repulsive force.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure threads are insulating and of equal length.2. Charge both balls with the same rod and method.3. Move supports slowly to avoid external disturbances.4. Keep camera focus fixed to ensure reliable time-lapse comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Three Sequential Polarizers with a Light SourceI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Light Transmission Through Three Sequential Polarizers2. Subject: Physics – Optics (Polarization of Light)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how inserting and rotating a third polarizer between two fixed polarizers changes transmitted light intensity, and to understand polarization and Malus’ law through visual observation.II. Experimental EquipmentCollimated light source (LED with collimator or laser with diffuser), three linear polarizing sheets or mounted polarizers, optical bench or stable mounts, screen or camera sensor, camera with fixed focus (tripod-mounted), rotation mount for the middle polarizer.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Mount the light source to produce a collimated beam. Fix the camera on a tripod facing the output screen and lock the focus and exposure.Initial Alignment: Place Polarizer A and Polarizer C in the beam path. Rotate them so their transmission axes are perpendicular (crossed), producing minimal light on the screen.Insertion of Middle Polarizer: Insert Polarizer B midway between A and C with its axis initially aligned with A.Core Operation: Slowly rotate Polarizer B through 0–90 degrees while keeping A and C fixed. Record continuously or via time-lapse.Removal: After one full rotation, stop and remove Polarizer B from the beam, returning to the initial two-polarizer setup.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: With two crossed polarizers, the screen appears very dark.2. During Rotation: As the middle polarizer rotates, transmitted light intensity increases from dark to brighter, reaching a maximum at intermediate angles, then decreases.3. After Removal: Removing the middle polarizer returns the system to the dark state.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesLinearly polarized light passing through a polarizer follows Malus’ law: I = I0 cos^2θ. Two crossed polarizers block light. Inserting a third polarizer allows the polarization direction to rotate in two steps, enabling partial transmission even though the first and last are crossed.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure polarizers are clean and fixed; keep camera focus and exposure constant; rotate the middle polarizer smoothly; avoid stray light.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Electron Beam in a CRT Deflected by a Bar MagnetI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Deflection of an Electron Beam in a CRT by a Bar Magnet2. Subject: Physics – Electromagnetism3. Experiment Objective: To observe the deflection of an electron beam in a cathode ray tube caused by an external magnetic field and understand the magnetic force acting on moving charges.II. Experimental EquipmentCathode ray tube (CRT) with power supply, bar magnet, dark laboratory environment, camera on tripod (focus fixed), safety gloves (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the CRT securely on the bench, connect the power supply, and darken the laboratory so the electron beam is clearly visible. Fix the camera focus and position for time-lapse or continuous recording.2. Initial Observation: Turn on the CRT and observe the straight electron beam path on the fluorescent screen.3. Core Operation: Slowly bring the bar magnet close to the side of the CRT without touching it. Observe the beam deflecting from its original path.4. Rotation: Keeping the magnet at a similar distance, rotate the bar magnet by 180 degrees and observe the change in beam deflection direction.5. End: Move the magnet away, turn off the CRT, and restore the lab lighting.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMoving electrons in the CRT experience a magnetic (Lorentz) force when subjected to an external magnetic field.
