manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Cluster of Magnets Repelling Each Other on a Smooth SurfaceI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Cluster of Magnets Repelling Each Other on a Smooth Surface2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics (Magnetism)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand magnetic repulsion between like poles by releasing a tight cluster of identical disc magnets on a smooth low-friction surface and recording the process using time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentIdentical disc magnets (6–10 pieces, same size and material), smooth low-friction tabletop (glass, polished wood, or acrylic), optional shallow tray to limit movement, camera or smartphone with tripod, time-lapse or fixed-focus recording mode.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Clean the tabletop to reduce friction and remove debris. Fix the camera on a tripod above or at an oblique angle to the tabletop. Set focus manually and lock it to avoid refocusing during recording.2. Magnet Arrangement: Identify the poles of the disc magnets. Place all magnets on the tabletop so that like poles face each other. Push them gently together so they are touching, forming a tight cluster at the center of the field of view.3. Recording Setup: Start video or time-lapse recording while keeping the camera completely still.4. Core Operation: Release all magnets simultaneously by removing your hands at the same time, without applying extra force.5. Completion: Allow the magnets to move freely until they come to rest. Stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The disc magnets are touching in a compact cluster and remain momentarily still.2. Release Moment: Immediately after release, the magnets begin to push away from one another.3. Movement Process: Each magnet moves outward from the center of the cluster, separating radially; speed is fastest at first and gradually decreases.4. Final State: The magnets stop at separated positions, no longer touching, forming a loose ring or scattered pattern.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesLike magnetic poles repel each other due to magnetic force. When identical disc magnets with like poles facing are forced into contact, magnetic potential energy is stored in the system. Upon release on a low-friction surface, this potential energy converts into kinetic energy, causing the magnets to move apart. The repulsive force decreases with increasing distance, so the magnets slow down and eventually stop when magnetic force and friction balance.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use identical magnets to ensure uniform interaction.2. Ensure the surface is smooth to clearly observe repulsion.3. Release magnets simultaneously to avoid introducing directional bias.4. Keep electronic devices and magnetic-sensitive objects away from strong magnets.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Magnetic repulsion between like poles of identical disc magnets on a low-friction surface. Minimum assumptions: magnets are identical, like poles face each other, surface friction is low, and motion results only from magnetic forces and friction.Expected Phenomena Storyline: Phase 1 – Static cluster: magnets touch in a tight group with no motion. Phase 2 – Release: hands withdraw simultaneously, triggering repulsive forces. Phase 3 – Expansion: magnets move radially outward from the center, fastest initially. Phase 4 – Rest: motion slows and stops as forces balance. Visibility constraints: stable camera, fixed focus, clear view of magnet shapes and separation paths.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Coin Resting on Card over Glass (Inertia Demonstration)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Coin Resting on Card over Glass (Inertia Demonstration)2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the property of inertia by observing the motion of a coin when the supporting card is flicked away quickly.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent glass (1), flat stiff card (1, slightly larger than the glass rim), coin (1), flat table, camera or mobile phone (for fixed-focus time-lapse or slow-motion recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the glass upright on a stable table. Lay the flat card horizontally across the rim of the glass.2. Setup: Place the coin at the center of the card directly above the opening of the glass. Adjust the camera so that the entire setup is in view and fix the focus.3. Core Operation: Using one hand, flick the card sharply and horizontally to the side in one swift motion, without lifting upward.4. Completion: Allow the coin to fall and come to rest; stop recording after the motion ends.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The coin is stationary on the card above the glass.2. During Flick: The card moves rapidly sideways and leaves the glass rim.3. Result: The coin does not move sideways with the card but drops almost vertically into the glass.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates inertia. The coin tends to remain in its original state of rest. When the card is flicked quickly, the frictional force and action time on the coin are very small, so the coin does not gain significant horizontal velocity. Once the support is removed, gravity causes the coin to fall straight down into the glass.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Attraction of Hanging Threads by a Long Charged RodI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Long Charged Rod Attracting Hanging Threads to Form Cylindrical SymmetrySubject: Physics – ElectrostaticsObjective: To observe electrostatic attraction and induction, and to understand the electric field distribution around a long charged rod.II. Experimental EquipmentLong plastic rod (e.g., PVC or acrylic), dry cloth or wool for charging; horizontal bar or support stand; lightweight threads (silk or cotton), evenly spaced and hanging freely; insulating stand; dry indoor environment.III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Fix the horizontal bar on a stand. Suspend multiple lightweight threads from the bar, ensuring equal spacing and free vertical hanging.2. Charging: Rub the plastic rod with a dry cloth to give it a static electric charge.3. Approach: Hold the charged rod parallel to the horizontal bar and slowly bring it close to the hanging threads without touching them.4. Sliding Motion: While keeping the distance small and constant, slide the charged rod smoothly along the length of the bar.5. End: Slowly move the rod away and observe the threads returning to their original vertical positions.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Threads hang vertically and are evenly spaced, showing no interaction.2. When the rod approaches: Threads near the rod are attracted and deflect toward it.3. Sliding the rod: As the rod moves along the bar, the attraction region moves with it; threads bend inward around the rod, forming an approximately cylindrical symmetric pattern.4. After removal: Threads gradually return to their original vertical positions.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleA charged plastic rod creates an electric field around it. When brought near neutral threads, electrostatic induction occurs: charges within the threads redistribute, resulting in a net attractive force toward the rod. Because the rod is long, the electric field around it is approximately cylindrically symmetric, leading to symmetric attraction of surrounding threads.VI. PrecautionsEnsure threads are lightweight and dry; avoid air currents; do not touch the threads with the rod; perform in a dry environment for clearer effects.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Zinc Plate on Electroscope Responding to Ultraviolet vs Visible LightI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Photoelectric Effect Demonstration with a Zinc-Plate Electroscope2. Subject: Physics – Natural Science (Modern Physics Basics)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that ultraviolet/violet light can cause a charged zinc plate to emit electrons and discharge a gold-leaf electroscope, while red visible light cannot; to observe and compare electroscope responses under different illumination.II. Experimental EquipmentGold-leaf electroscope with a clean zinc plate attached on top; charging rod (glass or plastic rod with silk/fur); ultraviolet/violet lamp; red visible-light lamp; insulating stand; camera or smartphone on tripod (focus fixed for time-lapse recording); darkened room (recommended).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the electroscope on an insulating stand. Clean the zinc plate to remove grease or oxide. Fix the camera on a tripod, adjust framing, and lock focus and exposure.2. Charging the Electroscope: Use the charging rod to give the electroscope a negative charge. Observe that the gold leaves diverge clearly and remain stable.3. Red Light Illumination: Turn on the red visible-light lamp and illuminate the zinc plate for several seconds while recording. Keep distance and angle constant.4. Observation under Red Light: Observe the gold leaves and record any change.5. Ultraviolet/Violet Illumination: Switch off the red lamp, then turn on the ultraviolet/violet lamp to illuminate the zinc plate under the same conditions.6. Observation under UV/Violet Light: Observe and record the change in gold-leaf divergence until a clear effect appears.7. End of Experiment: Turn off lamps, stop recording, and discharge the electroscope safely.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: After charging, the gold leaves are clearly diverged and stationary.2. Under Red Visible Light: The divergence of the gold leaves shows little or no change; the electroscope remains charged.3. Under Ultraviolet/Violet Light: The gold leaves gradually move closer together, indicating discharge of the electroscope.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates the photoelectric effect. Ultraviolet/violet light has sufficiently high photon energy to eject electrons from the surface of the zinc plate. When electrons are emitted, the negative charge on the electroscope decreases, causing the gold leaves to collapse. Red visible light has lower photon energy and cannot overcome the work function of zinc, so no electrons are emitted and the electroscope remains charged.VI. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Flame Emission Spectroscopy of Sodium (Yellow Flame Test)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Flame Emission Spectroscopy of Sodium Producing Yellow Light2. Subject: Natural Science - Physics (Atomic Spectra and Light Emission)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the characteristic yellow flame color produced by sodium salts in a flame; to understand that excited sodium atoms emit light of specific wavelengths due to electronic transitions; to master the basic operation of a flame test using a Bunsen burner and a wire loop.II. Experimental EquipmentBunsen burner (1), gas supply and striker, nichrome or platinum wire loop, sodium salt (such as sodium chloride, solid or solution), beaker with distilled water, concentrated hydrochloric acid (for cleaning the wire loop, optional), test tube or watch glass for holding sodium salt, safety goggles, lab bench with dim lighting conditions.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Darken the laboratory environment as much as safely possible to enhance visibility of flame color. Put on safety goggles. Check that the Bunsen burner is connected securely to the gas supply.2. Burner Adjustment: Ignite the Bunsen burner using a striker. Adjust the air hole to obtain a steady, non-luminous blue flame with a clear inner cone.3. Cleaning the Wire Loop: Dip the wire loop into distilled water and then into hydrochloric acid. Place the loop into the blue flame until no color is observed, ensuring the loop is clean and free from contamination.4. Loading the Sample: Dip the clean wire loop into the sodium salt (or sodium salt solution) so that a small amount adheres to the loop.5. Core Operation: Introduce the wire loop into the hottest part of the Bunsen burner flame (just above the inner blue cone). Hold it briefly, then withdraw it. Repeat the introduction and withdrawal several times.6. Ending the Experiment: After observation, remove the wire loop from the flame, turn off the gas supply, and allow equipment to cool. Clean the wire loop and return all apparatus to their proper places.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The Bunsen burner flame is blue and nearly colorless, and the wire loop shows no distinct flame color when clean.2. During the Test: When the sodium salt on the wire loop is placed into the flame, a bright, intense yellow light is immediately observed.3. Repetition: The yellow flame appears each time the sodium-coated wire loop is introduced into the flame and fades when it is withdrawn.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on flame emission spectroscopy. When sodium salt is heated in a flame, thermal energy excites the outer electrons of sodium atoms to higher energy levels. As the excited electrons return to lower energy states, they emit light of a specific wavelength, predominantly around 589 nm, which is observed as a bright yellow flame. The characteristic flame color is unique to sodium and can be used for qualitative identification of sodium ions.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the wire loop is thoroughly cleaned before testing to avoid interference from other elements.2. Do not touch the wire loop immediately after heating; it remains hot.3. Observe the flame color in a dim environment for better contrast.4. Handle acids and open flames carefully, following standard laboratory safety rules.

Visibility constraints: the scene must be dim enough to clearly distinguish the yellow emission against the blue flame, and the camera perspective should keep the burner flame and wire loop continuously in view to verify causal transitions.

Experiment Objective: To observe that the center of mass of a rotating object follows a parabolic trajectory under gravity while the object simultaneously undergoes free rotation; to understand the independence of translational and rotational motion.II. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand how a magnetic field affects ferrofluid, demonstrating the transition from a uniform liquid surface to spike-like structures as magnetic field strength increases.II. Experimental EquipmentShallow transparent dish (glass or plastic), black ferrofluid (small volume, evenly covering the bottom of the dish), strong round permanent magnet, vertical adjustable stage (for lifting the magnet), stable platform for the dish, camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording, gloves and protective covering for the workspace.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the shallow transparent dish on a stable horizontal platform. Setup: Mount the round magnet on a vertical stage directly below the center of the dish, leaving a small gap so the magnet does not touch the dish. Position the camera above or at a slight angle, and fix the focus to avoid refocusing during recording.3. Initial Observation: Start time-lapse recording. Observe and record the initial state of the ferrofluid, which should appear smooth and uniformly black.4. Core Operation: Slowly raise the magnet upward using the vertical stage, reducing the distance between the magnet and the dish in a controlled and continuous manner.5. manual: Experiment Instruction Manual: Hand-Pushed Magnet Resisting Motion Inside a Conducting CoilI. Basic InformationTitle: Resistance of a Moving Magnet in a Conducting CoilSubject: Physics – Electromagnetic InductionObjective: To observe the resistance encountered by a moving magnet inside a conducting copper coil and understand electromagnetic induction and Lenz’s law.II. Experimental Equipment1. Bare copper coil (several turns, not connected to a power source)2. Neodymium bar magnet3. Flat table4. Human hand (for manual operation)III. Experimental Procedure1. Place the bare copper coil flat on the table, with its central axis horizontal.2. Hold the neodymium bar magnet along the same axis as the coil.3. Slowly push the magnet into the center of the coil by hand.4. After the magnet passes through the coil, pull it back out along the same axis.5. Repeat the push–pull motion at different speeds for comparison.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. When the magnet is stationary relative to the coil, no obvious force is felt.2. When the magnet is pushed into the coil, a noticeable resisting force opposes the motion.3. When the magnet is pulled out, resistance is again felt, opposite in direction to the pull.4. Faster motion of the magnet results in stronger resistance.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleWhen the magnet moves relative to the conducting copper coil, the magnetic flux through the coil changes, inducing an electric current. According to Lenz’s law, the induced current creates a magnetic field that opposes the change in magnetic flux. This opposing magnetic interaction produces a resistive force against the motion of the magnet. The effect exists only during motion and increases with speed.VI. Precautions1. Ensure the coil is bare copper and not connected to any external circuit.2. Keep the magnet aligned with the coil axis to clearly feel the resistance.3. Avoid sudden release of the magnet to prevent it from snapping back abruptly.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Electromagnetic induction and Lenz’s law, demonstrated by resistive force on a moving magnet in a conducting coil. Minimum assumptions: a conductive copper coil, a strong bar magnet, and hand-driven linear motion along a shared axis.Phased Storyline: (1) Initial state: coil rests on table, magnet aligned and stationary. (2) Action phase: hand pushes magnet through coil center; induced current arises. (3) Effect phase: visible slowing or resistance during motion. (4) Reverse action: magnet pulled back along same axis with opposite-direction resistance. Visibility constraints: coil opening, magnet orientation, and hand motion must be clearly visible to verify axial alignment and causal resistance.

Experiment Title: Thermal Effect of Infrared Rays (Thermometer Temperature Measurement)2. Subject: Physics – Natural Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the thermal effect of infrared radiation and understand that different surface colors absorb infrared radiation differently by comparing temperature changes of two identical thermometers.II. Placement: Place both thermometers side by side at the same distance and height under the infrared lamp, ensuring bulbs face the lamp equally.4. Irradiation: Turn on the infrared lamp and start timing. Begin time-lapse photography, focusing the camera on the temperature scales of both thermometers.5. Summary of Experimental PrincipleInfrared rays carry energy and produce a thermal effect when absorbed by objects. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Induction Coil and Analog Galvanometer Showing Needle Kick on Switch On/OffI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Induced Current Using an Induction Coil and Analog Galvanometer2. Subject: Physics – Electromagnetism3. Experiment Objective: To observe the transient induced current produced when the current in a circuit changes, and to understand the basic phenomenon of electromagnetic induction through the deflection of an analog galvanometer needle.II. Experimental EquipmentBattery (1.5–3 V DC), induction coil (primary and secondary coils), switch (knife switch or push switch), analog galvanometer (center-zero preferred), connecting wires, tabletop experimental base.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place all components on the tabletop. Check that the galvanometer needle rests at zero when no current flows.2. Circuit Connection: Connect the battery, switch, and primary coil of the induction coil in series to form a closed circuit. Connect the secondary coil terminals to the analog galvanometer.3. Initial Check: Keep the switch open. Observe that the galvanometer needle remains at zero.4. Core Operation: Quickly close the switch by hand, then keep it closed briefly.5. Second Operation: Open the switch again by hand.6. Repeat: Perform several cycles of closing and opening the switch to confirm repeatability of the phenomenon.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. When the switch is closed, the galvanometer needle deflects briefly to one side and then quickly returns to zero.2. While the switch remains closed, the needle stays at zero with no continuous deflection.3. When the switch is opened, the needle deflects briefly to the opposite side and then returns to zero.4. Repeated switching produces repeated, momentary needle kicks.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleWhen the switch is closed or opened, the current in the primary coil changes, causing a change in magnetic flux through the secondary coil. According to Faraday’s law of electromagnetic induction, this changing magnetic flux induces a transient electromotive force and current in the secondary circuit, which is detected as a brief deflection of the galvanometer needle. The opposite directions of deflection correspond to increasing versus decreasing magnetic flux.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Electromagnetic induction caused by a change in current, observed via transient galvanometer deflection. Minimum assumptions: a correctly wired battery–switch–primary coil circuit, a secondary coil connected to an analog galvanometer, and a hand-operated switch producing rapid current changes. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) Initial steady state with switch open and needle at zero; (2) switch is closed by hand, causing a rapid change in current and a brief needle kick; (3) steady closed state with needle returning to zero; (4) switch is opened, causing an opposite change in current and an opposite needle kick. Visibility constraints: tabletop perspective with clear view of switch action and galvanometer needle; needle motion must be temporally aligned with switch on/off actions for causal verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Visible Spectrum Color Mixing (Red + Blue)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visible Spectrum Color Mixing Experiment (Red + Blue)2. Subject: Natural Science - Physics (Optics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the additive color mixing phenomenon by overlapping red and blue laser beams on a white screen, understand the basic rule of visible light additive color mixing, and recognize the color produced in the overlapping region.II. Experimental EquipmentRed laser light source (low-power, visible), blue laser light source (low-power, visible), optical mounts or stands (2), adjustable mirrors or beam alignment tools (optional), white screen or white paper screen (1), darkened room or shaded environment, safety goggles for laser use.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Place the white screen vertically on a stable surface. Fix the red and blue laser light sources on optical mounts so that they can be adjusted in direction and height. Darken the room to enhance visibility of laser spots. Put on laser safety goggles.Initial Observation: Turn on the red laser only and project it onto the white screen. Observe and confirm that a clear red light spot appears. Turn it off. Then turn on the blue laser only and confirm a clear blue light spot appears on the screen.Core Operation (Beam Overlap): Turn on both the red and blue lasers simultaneously. Carefully adjust the positions and angles of the laser sources (or mirrors) so that the red and blue light spots gradually move closer together on the white screen. Continue fine adjustment until the two spots overlap as much as possible.Observation: Observe the color of the overlapping area on the white screen and compare it with the non-overlapping red-only and blue-only regions.Conclusion and Shutdown: After observation, turn off the laser sources in sequence. Restore the room lighting and return all equipment to their proper places.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: When only one laser is on, a single-color light spot appears on the white screen (red or blue respectively).2. During Overlap: As the red and blue light spots overlap, the overlapping region shows a mixed color different from pure red or pure blue.3. Final Phenomenon: The overlapping area appears magenta (purple), while the non-overlapping areas remain red and blue respectively.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates additive color mixing of visible light. Red light and blue light are two primary colors of light. When they overlap on a white screen, their light intensities add together and stimulate the human eye’s photoreceptors simultaneously, producing the perception of magenta. This shows that, unlike pigment mixing, light mixing follows the additive color principle, where overlapping colored lights create new colors.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use low-power laser sources and never shine lasers into eyes or reflective surfaces.2. Adjust beams slowly to avoid sudden reflections.3. Ensure the screen is matte white to avoid glare or misleading reflections.4. Turn off lasers immediately after the experiment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: additive color mixing of visible light using red and blue lasers. Minimum assumptions: two distinct colored laser beams propagate in straight lines and project onto a matte white screen. Phased storyline: (1) show red-only and blue-only spots separately; (2) gradually adjust optical paths so spots approach; (3) beams overlap on the screen; (4) a magenta region appears at overlap while red and blue remain visible outside. Visibility constraints: camera must clearly capture the screen and color changes; overlap region must be centered and unobstructed for verification.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Soap Film Illuminated by White Light Showing Shifting Color BandsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Soap Film Illuminated by White Light Showing Shifting Color Bands2. Subject: Physics – Optics (Thin-Film Interference)3. Experiment Objective: To observe color bands produced by thin-film interference in a soap film, understand how film thickness affects interference colors, and relate drainage and tilting of the film to changes in observed colors.II. Experimental EquipmentRectangular wire frame (clean and smooth), soap solution (water with detergent or glycerin soap solution), shallow tray or beaker for soap solution, steady white light source (lamp or LED), dark or neutral background, support stand or hand grip, paper towels.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Prepare a uniform soap solution in a tray. Place the white light source so it can illuminate the frame evenly from the front. Ensure the background is dark to enhance color visibility.2. Forming the Soap Film: Dip the rectangular wire frame completely into the soap solution and slowly lift it out to form a continuous soap film covering the frame.3. Vertical Setup: Hold or mount the frame vertically so gravity causes the film to drain downward. Keep the frame steady at first.4. Illumination: Illuminate the soap film with steady white light. Do not change the light intensity or position during observation.5. Core Observation Operation: Observe the film as it slowly drains. After clear color bands appear, gently tilt the frame by a small angle and continue observing the changes in the color pattern.6. Completion: After observation, allow the film to break naturally or gently wipe the frame clean. Clean and store the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Immediately after lifting the frame, the soap film appears mostly transparent with faint or uniform colors.2. During Drainage: As the film drains under gravity, horizontal or curved color bands appear and gradually shift position. Different regions display different colors.3. During Tilting: When the frame is gently tilted, the color bands move and rearrange, showing clear changes corresponding to thickness redistribution in the film.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Core Principle: Thin-film interference of white light.2. Principle Explanation: The soap film has two reflective surfaces (front and back). White light reflecting from these surfaces interferes. Depending on the local thickness of the film, certain wavelengths undergo constructive interference and appear as visible colors.3. Thickness Relation: As the film drains, its thickness varies with height, causing different colors to appear at different positions. Tilting the frame changes the thickness distribution, leading to shifting color bands.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use steady white light; changing light conditions will affect color observation.2. Avoid shaking the frame; gentle tilting is sufficient.3. Ensure the wire frame is clean to form a uniform film.4. Perform the experiment away from strong air currents.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Thin-film interference in a draining soap film under white light. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: a continuous soap film forms on a rectangular wire frame; gravity causes gradual thickness variation; white light reflects from both surfaces of the film, producing interference colors dependent on thickness.Phased storyline for verification: (1) Setup phase – a vertical rectangular wire frame with a fresh soap film is illuminated by steady white light against a dark background; (2) Drainage phase – as time progresses, the film drains downward, and distinct colored bands emerge and slowly shift, indicating thickness changes; (3) Interaction phase – the frame is gently tilted, causing a visible redistribution of colors and movement of the bands. Visibility constraints: the camera should face the film directly, with stable lighting and sufficient contrast to clearly resolve color bands and their motion.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment "Two Identical Balls Collide and Bounce Apart"I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Collision of Two Identical Balls on a Horizontal Table2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics (Mechanics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the collision process of two identical smooth balls rolling toward each other on a horizontal table, and to verify that after collision both balls immediately bounce in opposite directions without any stationary state, demonstrating the characteristics of elastic collision between identical objects.II. Experimental Equipment1. Two identical smooth balls (same size, mass, color, and material; e.g., glass marbles or steel balls)2. A smooth, horizontal table or flat surface3. Ruler or visual center mark on the table (optional, for alignment)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Clean the table surface to reduce friction. Check that the table is level. Select two identical smooth balls and confirm they are free of deformation.2. Placement: Place the two balls on the table facing each other along the same straight line, with a clear distance between them. Mark the midpoint of the distance as the expected collision point (optional).3. Alignment: Adjust the balls so their centers lie on the same straight line, ensuring they will roll directly toward each other.4. Release: Use both hands to release the two balls simultaneously, applying similar gentle pushes so that they roll toward each other at approximately the same speed.5. Collision Observation: Allow the balls to collide naturally at the center of the table without external interference.6. Completion: Let the balls roll apart after collision until they come to rest. Repeat the experiment if necessary to confirm consistency.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before collision: Both balls roll smoothly toward each other along a straight line at similar speeds.2. At the moment of collision: The balls make brief contact at the center point; no ball remains stationary.3. After collision: Immediately after contact, both balls bounce back and roll away in opposite directions along the same straight line, with similar speeds to those before collision.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates the characteristics of an elastic collision between two identical objects. When two identical balls with equal mass collide head-on at similar speeds on a horizontal surface, momentum is conserved. Because the balls are identical and the collision is approximately elastic, they exchange velocities during the collision. As a result, each ball reverses its direction of motion immediately after impact, and no stationary state occurs. This visual phenomenon reflects the conservation of momentum and the basic laws of motion in physics.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the balls are identical to avoid asymmetrical motion after collision.2. Release both balls as simultaneously as possible to achieve a clear central collision.3. Avoid tilting the table or introducing external forces during the experiment.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Reaction Between Aluminum and Dilute Hydrochloric AcidI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Reaction Between Aluminum and Dilute Hydrochloric Acid2. Subject: Natural Science - Chemistry (Inorganic Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the chemical reaction between aluminum and dilute hydrochloric acid, understand the activity of metals and hydrogen generation, and master basic operations of adding solids to acids and observing gas-producing reactions.II. Experimental EquipmentTest tube (1, about 15×150 mm), test tube rack, dropper or measuring cylinder, dilute hydrochloric acid (colorless, about 5 mL), small piece of aluminum sheet (silvery white), tweezers, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the test tube rack and put on safety goggles.2. Adding Acid: Use a dropper or measuring cylinder to add about 5 mL of colorless dilute hydrochloric acid into the test tube.3. Adding Aluminum: Use tweezers to take a small piece of silvery white aluminum sheet and slowly put it into the test tube containing the hydrochloric acid.4. Observation: Keep the test tube upright and closely observe the changes in the aluminum sheet and the solution.5. Ending the Experiment: After the reaction weakens, place the test tube back on the rack. Dispose of the solution according to laboratory rules and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The hydrochloric acid solution is colorless and transparent; the aluminum sheet is silvery white and solid.2. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAluminum is an active metal that can react with dilute hydrochloric acid. Experimental Precautions1. Use dilute hydrochloric acid only; concentrated acid is dangerous.2. Add aluminum carefully to avoid splashing of acid.3. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Toy Car Driven Forward with Constant Sideways ForceI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Motion of a Toy Car Under a Constant Sideways Force2. Subject: Natural Science – Astrophysics & Astronomy (Classical Mechanics / Motion)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that when an object moving at constant forward speed is subjected to a constant sideways force, its motion becomes deflected sideways while maintaining forward motion, illustrating the principle of independent components of motion and constant acceleration due to force.II. Experimental EquipmentToy car (battery-powered or pull-back, capable of approximately constant forward speed), smooth horizontal tabletop or track, side desk fan with adjustable speed, tape or markers (to mark trajectory), camera or smartphone fixed on a tripod (focus fixed, time-lapse or continuous recording mode), ruler or grid paper (optional, for trajectory reference).III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Place the tabletop or track on a stable surface. Position the camera directly above or at an oblique angle so the full path of the toy car is visible; fix the focus and do not move the camera during recording.2. Initial Motion: Place the toy car at the starting line. Turn on the car so it drives straight forward at an approximately constant speed with the desk fan turned off.3. Recording Start: Begin recording or time-lapse photography while the car moves straight.4. Applying Sideways Force: When the car reaches the middle of the visible path, switch on the side desk fan so that airflow blows perpendicular to the car’s original direction of motion, applying a roughly constant sideways force.5. Continued Observation: Allow the car to continue moving under the combined forward motion and sideways force until it exits the frame or reaches the end of the track.6. End and Reset: Stop recording. Optionally mark the observed trajectory on the tabletop for clarity.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before the fan is switched on: The toy car moves in a straight line at nearly constant speed.2. After the fan is switched on: The toy car continues moving forward, but its path gradually curves or shifts sideways in the direction of the airflow.3. Overall trajectory: The forward motion persists while a sideways displacement increases with time, producing a deflected or gently curved path rather than an abrupt change in direction.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the independence of motion components and Newton’s second law. The toy car has an initial forward velocity. When the side fan is switched on, a constant sideways force acts on the car, producing a sideways acceleration while the forward velocity remains approximately unchanged. The resulting motion is the superposition of uniform forward motion and accelerated sideways motion, leading to a curved or diagonally deflected trajectory. This principle is analogous to projectile motion and to objects in space experiencing forces perpendicular to their velocity.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the tabletop surface is smooth to reduce frictional irregularities.2. Keep the fan speed constant once switched on to approximate a constant sideways force.3. Fix the camera position and focus to maintain spatiotemporal consistency in the recorded video.4. Keep hands and loose objects away from the moving car and fan during operation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: An object’s motion can be decomposed into independent components; a constant sideways force produces sideways acceleration without canceling forward motion. Minimum assumptions: the toy car maintains approximately constant forward speed; the desk fan provides a steady lateral airflow; friction and air resistance are secondary. Expected phased storyline: Phase 1 – car moves straight at constant speed with fan off; Phase 2 – fan switches on midway, introducing a lateral force; Phase 3 – car continues forward while gradually drifting sideways, forming a curved or deflected path. Visibility constraints: the full trajectory must remain in frame, camera position and focus fixed, with clear view of the fan direction relative to the car to verify causality.

Experiment Title: Iron Filings Aligning Around a Bar Magnet in a Transparent Spherical Shell2. Subject: Natural Science – Astrophysics & Astronomy (Magnetism as an analogy for field structures)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the three-dimensional distribution of magnetic field lines around a bar magnet by observing the alignment of iron filings on a transparent spherical surface.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent spherical shell (clear plastic or glass, separable if needed), bar magnet (standard rectangular magnet), iron filings (fine and dry), flat tabletop, small tray or paper sheet (to collect excess filings).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the tabletop in a stable, well-lit environment. Ensure the spherical shell is clean and dry.2. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Effect of Temperature on Yeast Catalase ActivityI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of Temperature on Yeast Catalase Foam Height2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Biochemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To investigate how temperature affects the activity of catalase in yeast by observing foam height produced from hydrogen peroxide decomposition over time.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentThree identical clear containers (beakers or cups), yeast suspension (same concentration and volume for each container), hydrogen peroxide solution (same concentration and volume), cold water bath (ice water), room-temperature environment, warm water bath (about 35–40°C), thermometer (optional), stopwatch or timer, camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Pour equal volumes of yeast suspension into three clear containers. Label them Cold, Room, and Warm.2. Temperature Setup: Place the Cold container in the cold water bath, leave the Room container in ambient air, and place the Warm container in the warm water bath. Allow 2–3 minutes for temperature equilibration.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera facing all three containers. Fix focus and framing to include foam height changes clearly. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.4. Reaction Start: Simultaneously add equal volumes of hydrogen peroxide to each container.5. Observation: Observe and record foam formation and height changes over time in each container.6. Completion: After foam growth stabilizes, stop recording and safely dispose of solutions.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Yeast suspensions are uniform liquids with little to no foam.2. During Reaction: Foam forms as bubbles rise; the warm container shows the fastest and highest foam formation, the room-temperature container shows moderate foam, and the cold container shows slow and minimal foam.3. Final State: Foam height stabilizes, with clear differences among temperature conditions.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleYeast contains the enzyme catalase, which decomposes hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen gas. The released oxygen forms bubbles, creating foam. Experimental PrecautionsUse equal volumes and concentrations for fairness; avoid excessively hot water that could denature catalase; keep camera fixed; handle hydrogen peroxide carefully.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Silver Mirror Reaction of AcetaldehydeI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Silver Mirror Reaction of AcetaldehydeSubject: Chemistry – Organic ChemistryObjective: To demonstrate the reducing property of aldehydes by observing the silver mirror reaction when acetaldehyde reacts with Tollens reagent under mild heating.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsClean test tube, test tube rack, dropper, water bath (with thermometer), beaker, heating device, Tollens reagent (freshly prepared ammoniacal silver nitrate solution), acetaldehyde solution, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wash and dry the test tube thoroughly to ensure the inner wall is clean and grease-free. Place it on the test tube rack and wear safety goggles.2. Reagent Addition: Add about 2 mL of freshly prepared Tollens reagent into the clean test tube.3. Substrate Addition: Using a dropper, add 3–5 drops of acetaldehyde solution into the test tube and gently shake to mix.4. Heating: Place the test tube in a water bath and heat to approximately 50℃, keeping the temperature stable for a short time.5. Observation: Remove the test tube and observe the inner wall.IV. Experiment Objective: To detect the presence of protein by observing the formation of a white ring at the interface between concentrated nitric acid and a protein solution, and to understand protein denaturation by strong acids.II. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube vertically in a test tube rack. Wear protective goggles and gloves.2. Addition of Acid: Using a dropper, add 2–3 mL of concentrated nitric acid into the bottom of the test tube. Keep the test tube steady.3. Layering of Protein Solution: Hold the test tube at a slight angle. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Tollens’ Test Comparison: Aldehyde vs KetoneI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Tollens’ Test Comparison of Aldehyde and KetoneSubject: Chemistry – Organic ChemistryObjective: To compare the reactivity of aldehydes and ketones with Tollens’ reagent and verify that aldehydes produce a silver mirror while ketones show no visible reaction.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsClear test tubes (2, identical), test tube rack, water bath (50–60°C), dropper or pipette, Tollens’ reagent (freshly prepared ammoniacal silver nitrate solution), colorless aldehyde solution (e.g., glucose or ethanal solution), colorless ketone solution (e.g., acetone), glass rod or gentle swirling by hand, safety goggles and gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, dry test tubes side by side in a test tube rack. Put on safety goggles and gloves. Prepare a warm water bath and place the test tubes in it to maintain gentle heating.2. Adding Reagent: Using a dropper, add an equal volume of freshly prepared Tollens’ reagent to each test tube.3. Adding Samples: To the left test tube, add a small amount of the colorless aldehyde solution. To the right test tube, add an equal amount of the colorless ketone solution.4. Mixing: Gently swirl both test tubes to mix the solutions, keeping them in the warm water bath.5. Observation: Fix the camera focus and record using time-lapse photography. Observe the inner walls of both test tubes during heating.6. Completion: After clear phenomena appear, remove the test tubes from the water bath. Dispose of waste according to laboratory regulations and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both test tubes contain colorless, transparent solutions.Left Test Tube (Aldehyde): After gentle heating and swirling, a bright silver mirror or gray–silver metallic deposit gradually forms on the inner wall of the test tube.Right Test Tube (Ketone): No visible change occurs; the solution remains colorless and transparent, and no silver deposit is observed.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesTollens’ reagent contains [Ag(NH3)2]+ ions, which act as a mild oxidizing agent. Aldehydes can be oxidized to carboxylic acids and, in the process, reduce silver ions to metallic silver, forming a silver mirror on the test tube wall. Ketones generally cannot be oxidized under these conditions and therefore do not reduce silver ions, resulting in no visible reaction.Core Reaction (for aldehyde): R–CHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]+ + 3OH− → R–COO− + 2Ag↓ + 4NH3 + 2H2OVI. Experimental Precautions1. Tollens’ reagent must be freshly prepared and should not be stored.2. Test tubes must be clean to ensure proper silver mirror formation.3. Gentle heating is sufficient; avoid boiling.4. Dispose of silver-containing waste according to safety regulations.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Decomposition of Hydrogen Peroxide With and Without Manganese Dioxide CatalystI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Hydrogen Peroxide Decomposition With and Without a Catalyst2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To observe the catalytic effect of manganese dioxide on the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide by comparing reaction rates in two identical beakers, and to understand the role of catalysts in chemical reactions.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical clear glass beakers, hydrogen peroxide solution (3%–6%), manganese dioxide powder (small amount), spatula, tray or lab bench mat, safety goggles, camera fixed on a tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear beakers side by side on a stable lab bench. Put on safety goggles. Ensure the camera is positioned in front of the beakers and the focus is fixed.2. Adding Reactant: Pour equal volumes of hydrogen peroxide into each beaker. The liquid in both beakers should be colorless and transparent.3. Catalyst Addition: Using a spatula, add a small amount of manganese dioxide powder to the left beaker only. Do not add anything to the right beaker.4. Observation and Recording: Start time-lapse recording. Keep the setup undisturbed and observe the changes in both beakers over time.5. Completion: After clear differences are observed, stop recording. Dispose of the reaction mixture according to laboratory waste guidelines and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers contain colorless, transparent hydrogen peroxide with no visible bubbles.2. After Catalyst Addition: The left beaker immediately produces a large number of bubbles, forming vigorous effervescence. The right beaker shows little to no bubbling, or only very slow bubble formation.3. Over Time: Bubbling in the left beaker continues intensely, while the right beaker remains largely unchanged.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesHydrogen peroxide decomposes into water and oxygen gas. This reaction is slow under normal conditions. Manganese dioxide acts as a catalyst, lowering the activation energy and greatly increasing the reaction rate without being consumed. The comparison demonstrates that a catalyst changes the speed of a reaction but not the final products.Core reaction equation: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂↑VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use low-concentration hydrogen peroxide suitable for demonstrations.2. Do not touch manganese dioxide with bare hands.3. Keep the camera fixed to ensure accurate comparison.4. Clean up and dispose of chemicals properly after the experiment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide and comparative reaction rates. Minimum assumptions: hydrogen peroxide is colorless, manganese dioxide is a solid catalyst, oxygen evolution is visible as bubbles, and the catalyst is not consumed.Phased storyline: (1) Two identical beakers with equal, clear hydrogen peroxide are shown side by side under a fixed camera; (2) manganese dioxide is added only to the left beaker; (3) immediate and vigorous bubbling begins in the left beaker while the right remains mostly unchanged; (4) time-lapse shows sustained contrast in reaction rates. Visibility constraints: both beakers must remain in frame, with stable focus and clear view of bubble formation for direct comparison.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Forming a Stable Oil–Water Emulsion by ShakingSubject: Chemistry – Physical Chemistry (Colloids)Objective: To observe how an emulsifier and mechanical shaking enable oil and water to form a stable, uniform emulsion.II. Experimental MaterialsClear glass jar with lid (1), water, vegetable oil, emulsifier (e.g., dish soap or lecithin), measuring cup or dropper.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the glass jar is clean and dry. Pour water into the jar until it is half full.2. Layering: Gently add vegetable oil on top of the water to form a clear oil layer.3. Adding Emulsifier: Add a small amount of emulsifier (2–3 drops) to the jar.4. Sealing: Tightly seal the jar with the lid to prevent leakage.5. Core Operation: Hold the jar with both hands and shake it vigorously for about 5–10 seconds.6. Observation: Place the jar on a flat surface and observe the liquid inside.IV. Summary of Experimental PrincipleOil and water are immiscible due to differences in polarity. Vigorous shaking breaks oil into tiny droplets dispersed in water. PrecautionsEnsure the jar is tightly sealed before shaking. Avoid overfilling. Clean the jar after the experiment.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Effect of Catalyst Surface Area on Reaction Rate (Crushed vs Intact MnO2)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of Catalyst Surface Area on the Decomposition of Hydrogen Peroxide2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that increasing the surface area of a solid catalyst increases the reaction rate, by comparing intact manganese dioxide pellets with crushed manganese dioxide powder in the catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical beakers (one blue, one red), manganese dioxide (MnO2) pellets, mortar and pestle (for crushing MnO2), hydrogen peroxide solution (same concentration), measuring cylinder, spatula, camera or smartphone with tripod, safety goggles, gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear safety goggles and gloves. Place the blue and red beakers side by side on a flat surface within the camera frame. Fix the camera focus and position for time-lapse recording.2. Catalyst Placement: Using a spatula, place an equal mass of intact MnO2 pellets into the blue beaker. Crush an equal mass of MnO2 pellets into fine powder using a mortar and pestle, then transfer the powder into the red beaker.3. Reactant Addition: Measure the same volume of hydrogen peroxide using a measuring cylinder. Simultaneously pour the hydrogen peroxide into both beakers.4. Observation: Start or continue time-lapse recording. Observe the formation of bubbles in both beakers without moving the camera or containers.5. Completion: After sufficient observation, stop recording. Dispose of reaction mixtures according to laboratory waste guidelines and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers contain dark MnO2 solids with clear, colorless hydrogen peroxide.2. After Addition: Bubbles of gas appear in both beakers.3. Comparison: The red beaker with crushed MnO2 shows faster, denser, and more vigorous bubbling, while the blue beaker with intact pellets shows slower and less intense bubbling.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesManganese dioxide acts as a catalyst in the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen (2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2↑). Crushing MnO2 increases its surface area, providing more active sites for the reaction. As a result, the reaction rate is higher and oxygen is released more rapidly in the beaker containing the crushed catalyst.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure equal amounts of catalyst and hydrogen peroxide are used. Add hydrogen peroxide simultaneously to ensure a fair comparison. Avoid touching chemicals directly and keep the camera fixed to maintain consistent observation conditions.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Oxygen Production by Heating Potassium ChlorateI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Oxygen Production by Heating Potassium Chlorate2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To understand the laboratory method for preparing oxygen by heating potassium chlorate with manganese dioxide as a catalyst, and to observe the related experimental phenomena and reaction principles.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsTest tube, test tube clamp and stand, alcohol lamp, potassium chlorate (white solid), manganese dioxide (black solid, catalyst), wooden splint (for oxygen test), safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Put on safety goggles. Mix a small amount of potassium chlorate with a small amount of manganese dioxide to form a uniform solid mixture, and place it into a dry test tube (about one-third full).2. Setup: Fix the test tube on the stand with the mouth slightly downward to prevent backflow. Check that the bottom of the test tube is exposed for heating.3. Heating: Light the alcohol lamp and gently heat the bottom of the test tube. Heat evenly and continuously.4. Gas Collection/Testing: As heating continues, gas is released. Insert a glowing wooden splint near the mouth of the test tube to test the gas.5. Ending the Experiment: After observation, remove the alcohol lamp first, then allow the test tube to cool before disassembly.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The mixture in the test tube is solid, mainly white with dark specks of manganese dioxide.2. During Heating: Colorless gas is gradually released from the test tube.3. Oxygen Test: The glowing wooden splint placed near the mouth of the test tube reignites, indicating the presence of oxygen.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhen potassium chlorate is heated, it decomposes to produce potassium chloride and oxygen. Manganese dioxide acts as a catalyst, lowering the decomposition temperature and speeding up the reaction.Chemical Equation: 2KClO3 → 2KCl + 3O2 (MnO2, heating)VI. Experimental Precautions1. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Acid–Base Titration with Indicator Color ChangeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Acid–Base Titration with Phenolphthalein Indicator2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Analytical Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the color change of an indicator during acid–base titration, understand the principle of neutralization reactions, and master the standard operation of titration using a burette and a conical flask. The experiment also serves as a visual demonstration suitable for fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsBurette (50 mL) with stand and clamp; conical flask (250 mL); funnel (for filling burette); white tile or paper (background for color observation); dropper; phenolphthalein indicator solution; standard sodium hydroxide solution (base, in burette); acidic solution such as dilute hydrochloric acid or acetic acid (in flask); distilled water; safety goggles and lab coat.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear safety goggles and lab coat. Rinse the burette with distilled water, then rinse it with a small amount of sodium hydroxide solution. Fill the burette with sodium hydroxide solution using a funnel, remove air bubbles from the tip, and adjust the liquid level to zero or a recorded initial reading.2. Sample Setup: Rinse the conical flask with distilled water. Add a measured volume (e.g., 25 mL) of acidic solution into the conical flask. Add 2–3 drops of phenolphthalein indicator; the solution remains colorless.3. Positioning for Observation: Place the conical flask on a white tile or paper under the burette. Fix the camera focus on the flask and burette tip to allow clear recording of the color change during time-lapse photography.4. Titration Operation: Open the burette stopcock to allow the base to flow slowly into the conical flask while gently swirling the flask continuously by hand to mix the solution evenly.5. Approaching Endpoint: As the endpoint nears, reduce the addition rate to drop by drop. Continue swirling the flask after each drop.6. Endpoint Judgment: Stop adding base immediately when a faint pink color appears in the solution and persists for about 30 seconds during swirling.7. Completion: Record the final burette reading. Dispose of the solution according to laboratory rules, clean all glassware, and return equipment to its proper place.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The acidic solution with phenolphthalein in the conical flask is colorless and transparent.2. During Titration: As sodium hydroxide is added and the flask is swirled, the solution remains colorless but may briefly show pink swirls that disappear upon mixing.3. At Endpoint: A uniform, faint pink color appears throughout the solution and does not fade within approximately 30 seconds of swirling.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the neutralization reaction between an acid and a base. When sodium hydroxide is gradually added to the acidic solution, hydrogen ions react with hydroxide ions to form water. Phenolphthalein is an acid–base indicator that is colorless in acidic and neutral solutions but turns pink in weakly basic conditions (pH above about 8.2). At the equivalence point of the titration, the acid has been neutralized, and a slight excess of base causes the indicator to change color, signaling the endpoint.Core reaction example: HCl + NaOH = NaCl + H2OVI. Experimental Precautions1. Swirl the conical flask continuously to ensure uniform mixing and accurate endpoint detection.2. Add the base slowly, especially near the endpoint, to avoid overshooting.3. Observe the color change against a white background for clarity.4. Handle acids and bases carefully to avoid skin contact or splashing.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: acid–base titration using phenolphthalein to indicate the neutralization endpoint. Minimum mechanistic assumptions include the presence of an acidic solution in a conical flask, a basic solution in a burette, gradual dropwise addition, continuous swirling for mixing, and an indicator that changes color only after slight excess base. Expected phenomena storyline: Phase 1 – initial colorless acidic solution under a fixed camera view; Phase 2 – base added drop by drop while the flask is swirled, with no lasting color change; Phase 3 – near endpoint, brief pink swirls appear and fade; Phase 4 – endpoint reached with a uniform faint pink persisting. Visibility constraints: the burette tip, liquid level changes, and flask interior color must remain clearly visible, and the camera focus should remain fixed to verify causal and temporal continuity.

Experiment Title: Reaction Between Iodine and Zinc (Water as Catalyst)2. Subject: Chemistry – Chemical Reactions3. Experiment Objective: To observe the reaction between iodine and zinc triggered by a small amount of water, understand the catalytic role of water, and recognize exothermic reaction phenomena such as heat release and smoke generation.II. Experimental EquipmentMortar and pestle (dry and intact), iodine powder (dark gray–purple), zinc powder (gray), dropper, clean water, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Put on safety goggles. Ensure the mortar is dry and undamaged.2. Mixing: Place a small amount of iodine powder and zinc powder into the mortar. Principle Analysis: Zinc and iodine can react directly, but the reaction starts slowly under dry conditions due to surface barriers. The heat causes iodine to sublime, producing visible purple-brown smoke. Water is not consumed in the overall reaction.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use only one drop of water to avoid splashing or excessive reaction.2. Do not touch the reacting mixture or residue with bare hands.3. Perform the experiment in a well-ventilated area.4. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Sodium Reacts with WaterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Sodium Reacts with Water2. Subject: Natural Science - Chemistry (Inorganic Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and verify that sodium metal floats on water and reacts vigorously, melting into a rapidly moving ball with abundant bubbles, and to understand the basic reaction principle of alkali metals with water.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent container (glass beaker), clear water, small sodium metal block (pea-sized), tweezers, filter paper, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Pour clear water into the transparent container to about half its volume and place it on a stable surface. Put on safety goggles.2. Sodium Handling: Use tweezers to pick up a small, dry sodium block. Briefly blot excess oil with filter paper if present.3. Core Operation: Gently place the sodium block onto the surface of the clear water using tweezers. Release it and withdraw the tweezers immediately.4. Observation: Keep the camera focused on the water surface and sodium block, recording the entire interaction process.5. Completion: After the reaction ends, stop recording and ensure the container is left undisturbed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The sodium block is silvery and solid; the water is clear and colorless.2. During Reaction: Sodium floats on the water surface, rapidly moves around, produces a large number of bubbles, and gradually melts into a small spherical ball.3. Final State: The sodium disappears completely, leaving clear solution with residual bubbles dissipating.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSodium is a low-density alkali metal, so it floats on water. When sodium contacts water, an exothermic chemical reaction occurs, producing sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas. The heat released melts the sodium into a ball, while the escaping hydrogen gas causes vigorous bubbling and propels the sodium to move rapidly across the water surface.Core reaction equation: 2Na + 2H2O = 2NaOH + H2↑VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse very small sodium pieces; always use tweezers; wear eye protection; keep distance during reaction.

Basic InformationExperiment Title: Observation of Oxygen Bubble Formation in Elodea Leaves During PhotosynthesisSubject: Natural Science – Cell & Developmental BiologyObjective: To observe photosynthesis in living plant cells by detecting oxygen bubbles released from Elodea chloroplasts under light, and to understand the relationship between light and photosynthetic activity.II. Experiment Objective: To verify that oxygen supports combustion by observing the relighting of a glowing wooden splint when inserted into a bottle filled with oxygen gas.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Starch Solution versus Simple Sugar Solution Mixed with Iodine (Contrast Reaction)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Contrast Reaction of Starch Solution and Simple Sugar Solution with Iodine2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Organic Chemistry Basics)3. Experiment Objective: To distinguish starch from simple sugar solutions through iodine reaction; understand the specific interaction between iodine and starch, and master basic methods of comparative observation.II. Experimental EquipmentBeakers (2 clear beakers, identical size), starch solution (cloudy, prepared), simple sugar solution such as glucose solution (clear), iodine solution (iodine–potassium iodide), droppers (1–2), glass rod or gentle swirling by hand, lab bench, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, clear beakers side by side on the lab bench. Put on safety goggles.2. Solution Placement: Pour an equal volume (about 50 mL) of cloudy starch solution into the left beaker and the same volume of clear simple sugar solution into the right beaker.3. Initial Observation: Observe and note the initial appearance of both solutions: starch solution is cloudy, sugar solution is clear and transparent.4. Iodine Addition: Use a dropper to add 2–3 drops of iodine solution into the left beaker, then add the same amount of iodine solution into the right beaker.5. Mixing: Gently swirl each beaker to mix the iodine evenly with the solution.6. Final Observation: Observe and compare the color changes in the two beakers.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before iodine addition: Left beaker contains a cloudy, colorless starch solution; right beaker contains a clear, colorless simple sugar solution.2. After iodine addition and swirling:- Left beaker (starch solution): The solution rapidly turns blue-black.- Right beaker (simple sugar solution): The solution remains yellow-brown (the color of iodine) with no blue-black change.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIodine can form a blue-black complex with starch due to iodine molecules entering the helical structure of amylose in starch. This specific interaction causes a distinct color change. Simple sugars such as glucose do not have this helical polymer structure, so they do not react with iodine and show no blue-black color. Therefore, iodine can be used as a qualitative reagent to identify starch.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure beakers are clean and transparent for clear observation.2. Add the same amount of iodine to both solutions for a fair comparison.3. Swirl gently to avoid splashing and ensure uniform mixing.4. Dispose of solutions according to laboratory waste guidelines after the experiment.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Swelling and Shrinking of Red Blood Cells in Hypotonic vs Hypertonic SolutionsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Swelling and Shrinking of Red Blood Cells in Different Tonicity Solutions2. Subject: Natural Science – Cell & Developmental Biology3. Experiment Objective: To observe, under a light microscope, the osmotic responses of red blood cells in hypotonic (distilled water) and hypertonic (concentrated saline) environments, and to understand the principle of osmosis through direct visual comparison.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsLight microscope with camera interface, microscope slides and coverslips, dropper or micropipette, fresh red blood cell suspension (e.g., diluted mammalian blood), distilled water, concentrated saline solution (stained faint blue for identification), absorbent paper.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Turn on the light microscope, adjust illumination, and pre-focus using a blank slide. Ensure the camera focus will remain fixed during recording.2. Slide Setup: Place a clean microscope slide on the bench. Using a dropper, place two small droplets of red blood cell suspension adjacent to each other, leaving a small gap between them.3. Solution Addition: Add an equal volume of distilled water to the first droplet. Add an equal volume of faintly blue concentrated saline to the second droplet. Do not mix the droplets together.4. Mounting: Carefully place a coverslip over the droplets to spread them evenly and avoid air bubbles.5. Observation and Recording: Place the slide on the microscope stage. Adjust focus once so that red blood cells are clearly visible, then fix the focus and camera position. Start time-lapse recording and leave the slide undisturbed.6. Completion: After sufficient observation, stop recording and remove the slide. Dispose of biological materials according to safety guidelines.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Red blood cells in both droplets appear as normal biconcave discs with clear outlines.2. Distilled Water Droplet (Hypotonic): Over time, red blood cells gradually swell, lose their biconcave shape, become spherical, and some may rupture (hemolysis), making the field appear clearer.3. Concentrated Saline Droplet (Hypertonic): Red blood cells gradually shrink, develop wrinkled or spiky edges (crenation), and appear smaller and darker.4. Comparative Result: The two adjacent droplets show opposite morphological changes under identical observation conditions.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates osmosis across the semi-permeable red blood cell membrane. In hypotonic distilled water, water enters the cells due to a higher external water potential, causing swelling and possible hemolysis. In hypertonic concentrated saline, water exits the cells due to lower external water potential, causing cell shrinkage and crenation. The differing behaviors directly reflect the osmotic balance between the cell interior and its surrounding solution.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Osmotic behavior of red blood cells in hypotonic vs hypertonic environments. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: red blood cell membranes are semi-permeable; water moves across membranes according to osmotic gradients; cell volume changes reflect net water movement. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) Fixed light-microscope view with two adjacent droplets; (2) initial identical red blood cell morphology in both droplets; (3) progressive divergence over time—cells in distilled water swell and may lyse, while cells in concentrated saline shrink and crenate; (4) changes occur smoothly without camera movement, suitable for accelerated time-lapse. Visibility constraints: clear cell outlines, distinguishable droplet colors, stable field of view enabling side-by-side comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment UV-Induced Fluorescence of Chlorophyll Extract in a Clear VialI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: UV-Induced Fluorescence of Chlorophyll ExtractSubject: Natural Science - BiophysicsExperiment Objective: To observe UV-induced fluorescence of chlorophyll and understand the relationship between excitation light intensity and fluorescence emission.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass vial (1), chlorophyll extract (green solution, filling about 1/2 vial), handheld UV lamp (long-wave UV preferred), darkened room or shaded environment, safety goggles.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the clear glass vial containing green chlorophyll extract upright on a stable surface. Dim ambient light to enhance visibility of fluorescence. Put on safety goggles.Operation: Turn on the handheld UV lamp. First hold the lamp about 20–30 cm away from the vial and illuminate the solution.Core Demonstration: Slowly move the UV lamp closer to the vial while continuously illuminating it, then gradually move it farther away again, keeping the lamp directed at the solution.Completion: Turn off the UV lamp after observation and restore normal lighting.IV. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Houseplant Shoot Bending Toward a Side Light Source (Phototropism)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Houseplant Shoot Bending Toward a Side Light Source2. Subject: Natural Science - Ecology & Evolutionary Biology3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand phototropism by demonstrating how a houseplant shoot gradually bends toward a unilateral light source over several days.II. Experimental EquipmentPotted houseplant with an upright green shoot, table or flat surface, single bright desk lamp or grow light, darkened room or shaded environment, camera or notebook for recording observations, ruler or visual reference (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Select a healthy potted houseplant with a straight, upright shoot. Place the pot at the center of a table in a room where other light sources can be minimized.2. Light Setup: Position a single bright lamp at the same height as the shoot, approximately 30–50 cm from the plant, on realizing only one side of the plant.3. Initial Recording: Record or photograph the initial position of the plant shoot, noting that it is upright and not bent toward the lamp.4. Core Observation: Keep the lamp on continuously (or for a fixed daily period). At regular intervals (e.g., every 12 or 24 hours), record the position of the shoot without moving the plant or lamp.5. Completion: After several days, stop the observation once a clear bending of the shoot toward the light source is visible.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The plant shoot is upright or randomly oriented, with no clear bending toward the lamp.2. Intermediate Stage: After one to two days, the shoot tip begins to curve slightly toward the light source.3. Final Stage: After several days, the shoot shows a明显 bending toward the lamp, with the tip facing the light direction.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates phototropism, a growth response of plants to light. Light causes an uneven distribution of auxin, a plant growth hormone, in the shoot. Auxin accumulates on the shaded side of the shoot, promoting greater cell elongation there. As a result, the shaded side grows faster than the illuminated side, causing the shoot to bend toward the light source.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure only one light source is present; do not rotate the pot during the experiment; maintain normal watering and temperature conditions; record observations from a consistent angle.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Cobalt Chloride Equilibrium Color Change with Heating and CoolingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Color Change of Aqueous Cobalt Chloride under Heating and Cooling2. Subject: Natural Science – Biophysics / Physical Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To observe the reversible color change of aqueous cobalt chloride when alternately heated and cooled, and to understand the effect of temperature on chemical equilibrium.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent test tube (1), test tube rack, beaker with hot water (about 70–80 °C), beaker with cold water or ice water, aqueous cobalt chloride solution (pink at room temperature), thermometer (optional), safety gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the transparent test tube on the rack and add cobalt chloride solution to about one-third of the tube volume. Observe its initial color at room temperature.2. Heating Operation: Carefully place the test tube into the hot water bath, ensuring the solution level is below the water surface. Keep the tube transparent and visible.3. Observation during Heating: Observe the color change of the solution while heating until a stable color appears.4. Cooling Operation: Remove the test tube from the hot water bath and immediately place it into the cold water bath.5. Observation during Cooling: Observe the solution color change as it cools. The test tube may be alternately moved once more between hot and cold baths to verify reversibility.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The cobalt chloride solution is pink at room temperature.2. In Hot Water Bath: The solution gradually changes from pink to blue.3. In Cold Water Bath: The blue solution gradually returns to pink.4. Reversibility: Repeated heating and cooling cause corresponding reversible color changes.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCobalt chloride exists in equilibrium between different hydrated cobalt complexes in aqueous solution. At lower temperatures, the pink hydrated complex predominates. Heating shifts the equilibrium toward the blue complex. Cooling shifts the equilibrium back toward the pink form. This demonstrates Le Châtelier’s principle, where temperature changes shift chemical equilibrium.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Handle hot water carefully to avoid burns.2. Ensure the test tube is transparent and clean for clear observation.3. Do not shake the test tube vigorously during heating or cooling.4. Dispose of cobalt chloride solution according to laboratory safety regulations.

Phase 2 (Heating): Placement into hot water bath causes a gradual color change to blue. Phase 3 (Cooling): Transfer into cold water bath causes the solution to revert from blue to pink. Key causal transition is temperature change driving equilibrium shift. Visibility constraint: the solution color must remain clearly visible throughout transfers.
