manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Food Coloring Diffusion in Thin vs Thick Gelatin LayersI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Food Coloring Diffusion in Thin vs Thick Gelatin Layers2. Subject: Biology – Natural Science3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare the diffusion rate of food coloring in thin and thick gelatin layers, and understand how medium thickness affects molecular diffusion.II. Experimental MaterialsTwo clear shallow dishes, prepared gelatin (one thin layer, one thick layer), blue food coloring, dropper, flat stable table, camera or smartphone with tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Prepare two clear dishes of gelatin in advance. One dish should contain a thin gelatin layer, and the other a visibly thicker layer. Allow both to fully solidify.2. Setup: Place the two dishes side by side on a flat surface under the camera. Adjust the camera so both dishes are fully in frame, and fix the focus and position.3. Core Operation: Using a dropper, simultaneously drip equal amounts of blue food coloring onto the exact center of each gelatin surface.4. Observation: Do not disturb the dishes. Start time-lapse recording and allow diffusion to occur.5. Completion: After sufficient time-lapse footage is captured, stop recording and compare the diffusion patterns.IV. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Chalk Block Compressed Under a Hydraulic Press to Model Compaction FragmentationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Compaction Fragmentation of Chalk Under Compression2. Subject: Natural Science – Paleontology (Sediment Compaction Modeling)3. Experiment Objective: To model and observe how brittle sedimentary materials fracture and fragment under increasing overburden pressure, simulating compaction processes relevant to sedimentary rock formation.II. Experimental EquipmentWhite chalk block (dry, rectangular), hydraulic press, two flat metal compression plates, stable workbench, camera with tripod (time-lapse mode), protective goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the hydraulic press on a stable surface. Clean the metal plates to ensure flat, even contact. Put on safety goggles.2. Setup: Place the lower metal plate on the press base. Position the white chalk block upright at the center of the plate. Place the upper metal plate flat on top of the chalk block.3. Camera Arrangement: Fix the camera on a tripod facing the chalk block from the side. Lock focus and exposure. Enable time-lapse recording.4. Core Operation: Slowly and steadily apply downward pressure using the hydraulic press, ensuring compression is vertical and uniform.5. Observation and Recording: Continue compression until visible cracking and fragmentation occur. Stop the press once clear fragmentation is observed.6. Completion: Release pressure gradually, stop recording, and safely remove fragments.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Chalk block is intact, white, and angular with smooth surfaces.2. Early Compression: Minor deformation and faint surface cracks appear.3. Continued Compression: Cracks propagate; the chalk fractures into smaller pieces, producing powder and fragments.4. Final State: Chalk is compacted into fragmented debris between the plates.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesChalk is a brittle, porous material analogous to carbonate sediments. Under increasing compressive stress, it cannot deform plastically and instead fractures. This experiment models sediment compaction fragmentation, where overburden pressure causes grain breakage and reduction of pore space, a key process in sedimentary rock formation.VI. Experimental PrecautionsApply pressure slowly to avoid sudden failure; keep hands clear of plates; ensure camera stability throughout the experiment.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Alcohol Decolorization in Gram StainingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Alcohol Decolorization Showing Selective Dye Loss in Gram-Negative Cells2. Subject: Natural Science - Microbiology3. Experiment Objective: To observe the selective removal of the crystal violet–iodine complex from Gram-negative bacteria during the alcohol decolorization step of Gram staining using a light microscope, and to understand the structural basis of differential staining.II. Experimental EquipmentLight microscope (oil immersion capable), clean glass slides with heat-fixed mixed bacterial smear (Gram-positive and Gram-negative), crystal violet–iodine treated smear, 95% ethanol or acetone-alcohol decolorizer, dropper or wash bottle, immersion oil, camera mounted on microscope for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the slide containing a mixed bacterial smear that has already been stained with crystal violet and iodine onto the microscope stage. Switch to oil immersion objective and adjust illumination.2. Focusing: Carefully adjust coarse and fine focus until bacterial cells are sharp. Fix the camera focus and microscope settings to avoid changes during recording.3. Core Operation (Decolorization): While observing through the microscope, gently apply clear alcohol so that it flows across the smear from one side to the other. Do not refocus during this step.4. Timing Control: Allow alcohol to contact the smear briefly (a few seconds), then stop the flow to prevent over-decolorization.5. Observation: Continuously observe and record changes in cell coloration during alcohol exposure.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both Gram-positive and Gram-negative cells appear dark purple due to the crystal violet–iodine complex.2. During Alcohol Flow: As alcohol passes over the smear, Gram-negative cells gradually lose the purple color and become colorless or faint, while Gram-positive cells remain purple.3. End State: A clear contrast is visible between purple Gram-positive cells and decolorized Gram-negative cells within the same field of view.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe alcohol decolorization step exploits structural differences in bacterial cell walls. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer that retains the crystal violet–iodine complex when exposed to alcohol. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane rich in lipids; alcohol dissolves these lipids, increasing permeability and allowing the dye complex to escape. This results in selective dye loss from Gram-negative cells.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the smear is properly heat-fixed before staining.2. Do not over-apply alcohol, as excessive decolorization may remove dye from Gram-positive cells.3. Keep microscope focus fixed during observation to ensure consistent time-lapse recording.4. Handle alcohol carefully and follow laboratory safety guidelines.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Mixed Sand–Silt–Gravel Settling in a Clear Water ColumnI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Mixed Sand–Silt–Gravel Settling in a Clear Water Column2. Subject: Natural Science – Geology & Geophysics3. Experiment Objective: To observe the settling behavior of gravel, sand, and silt in still water after shaking, and to understand how particle size affects settling velocity and sediment layering.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent graduated cylinder with tight-fitting seal or stopper (1), clear water, mixed sediments (gravel, sand, silt), rubber stopper or cap, paper towel.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the graduated cylinder upright on a stable surface. Add clear water until the cylinder is about 2/3 full.2. Adding Sediments: Add a small, visible mixture of gravel, sand, and silt into the cylinder.3. Sealing: Seal the cylinder tightly with the stopper to prevent leakage.4. Shaking: Hold the sealed cylinder firmly and shake it vigorously for several seconds until all sediments are fully suspended and the water becomes uniformly cloudy.5. Settling: Immediately place the cylinder upright on the table and stop all movement.6. Observation: Observe the settling process from bottom to top over a short time period.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State After Shaking: Water appears cloudy; all particles are suspended.2. Early Settling: Large gravel particles quickly sink and accumulate at the bottom.3. Intermediate Settling: Sand particles settle next, forming a layer above the gravel.4. Late Settling: Fine silt remains suspended the longest, then slowly settles to form the topmost sediment layer; water gradually becomes clearer.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates sediment settling controlled by particle size and mass. According to sedimentation principles, larger and heavier particles experience greater gravitational force and settle faster, while finer particles experience more resistance from water and settle more slowly. This process explains natural sediment layering in rivers, lakes, and oceans.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the cylinder is tightly sealed before shaking; place it upright gently after shaking to avoid remixing; observe without moving the cylinder.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: particle-size-controlled sediment settling in geology. Minimum assumptions: gravity acts downward, water is initially still after shaking, and sediments differ mainly by particle size. Phased storyline: (1) sealed transparent cylinder with clear water and mixed sediments; (2) vigorous shaking causes uniform suspension and cloudy water; (3) cylinder placed upright and motion stops; (4) rapid settling of gravel, followed by sand, then slow settling of silt while water clears. Key causal transitions: stopping motion leads to gravity-driven settling; larger particles settle faster. Visibility requirements: clear side view of the transparent cylinder, stable camera, and sufficient contrast to distinguish layers forming from bottom to top.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Steel Nail Briefly Magnetized by Rubbing with a MagnetI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Temporary Magnetization of a Steel Nail2. Subject: Natural Science - Geology & Geophysics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that a steel nail can be temporarily magnetized by rubbing it with a bar magnet and can attract small iron filings after magnetization.II. Experimental EquipmentSteel nail (1, clean and dry), bar magnet (1), iron filings (small amount), white paper or tray (for visibility).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the steel nail flat on a table or hold it steadily over a white paper or tray. Ensure the nail is not initially attracting iron filings.2. Magnetizing Operation: Use one pole of the bar magnet to rub along the length of the steel nail from one end to the other in a single direction. Lift the magnet away after each stroke and repeat the rubbing 5–10 times. Do not rub back and forth.3. Magnet Removal: After rubbing, completely remove the bar magnet from the vicinity of the nail.4. Attraction Test: Bring loose iron filings close to the steel nail and gently shake or tap the paper/tray to allow the filings to move freely.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesRubbing a steel nail with a bar magnet aligns some of the magnetic domains inside the steel in one direction, temporarily magnetizing the nail. Once magnetized, the nail produces a magnetic field that attracts ferromagnetic materials such as iron filings. Because the alignment is incomplete and unstable, the magnetism is temporary.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Always rub in one direction; back-and-forth rubbing reduces the magnetizing effect.2. Keep iron filings away from the magnet during the test to avoid interference.3. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Cold, Salty Water Sinking Due to Increased DensityI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Cold, Salty Water Sinking in Freshwater2. Subject: Natural Science – Marine Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that cold, salty water has a higher density than room-temperature freshwater and therefore sinks, helping learners understand density-driven circulation in the ocean.II. Experimental Equipment1. Clear transparent tank (glass or acrylic)2. Room-temperature freshwater (enough to fill the tank)3. Salt (sodium chloride)4. Cold water or ice bath (to chill saltwater)5. Blue food dye6. Narrow tube or thin plastic tubing7. Small container for preparing saltwater8. Camera or smartphone with fixed focus (for time-lapse photography)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fill the clear tank with room-temperature freshwater and allow it to stand until the water is still. Place the tank on a stable surface with good lighting.2. Saltwater Preparation: In a small container, dissolve salt in cold water to make a concentrated saltwater solution. Add a few drops of blue food dye and mix evenly. Keep the solution chilled.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera facing the side of the tank. Fix the focus and start time-lapse or continuous recording.4. Core Operation: Insert the narrow tube just below the water surface on one side of the tank. Gently release the blue-dyed chilled saltwater, keeping the flow slow to avoid strong mixing.5. Observation Stage: Continue recording as the blue saltwater enters the tank and moves within the freshwater.6. Completion: Stop the release after a clear sinking pattern is observed. End recording and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The freshwater in the tank is clear and still, with no visible currents.2. During Release: The blue-dyed chilled saltwater enters near the surface and forms a visible blue plume.3. Key Phenomenon: The blue saltwater sinks downward through the freshwater and spreads along the bottom of the tank instead of floating.4. Final State: A layered or pooled blue region is visible near the bottom, with limited mixing above.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCold, salty water has a higher density than room-temperature freshwater because both lower temperature and higher salinity increase water density. When the denser blue-dyed saltwater is introduced into the tank, gravity causes it to sink beneath the less dense freshwater. This experiment models density-driven processes such as thermohaline circulation in the ocean, where differences in temperature and salinity drive vertical and horizontal water movement.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Release the saltwater slowly to avoid turbulence.2. Ensure the tank water is still before starting.3. Fix the camera focus to prevent visual shifts during recording.4. Clean the tank and tools after the experiment.

manual: Experiment Title: Ice-Seed-Induced Freezing of Supercooled Bottled WaterSubject: Natural Science – Atmospheric ScienceObjective: To demonstrate that supercooled liquid water freezes rapidly when an ice crystal provides a nucleation seed.Equipment: Two identical clear plastic water bottles (sealed), freezer or ice-salt bath, small ice crystal (ice chip), clean tweezers, table, thermometer (optional), camera with fixed focus for time-lapse.Procedure: (1) Place sealed bottles upright in a freezer or ice-salt bath until cooled to about −1 to −5°C without freezing. (2) Carefully remove and place both bottles on a table; avoid shaking. (3) Fix the camera focus and start recording/time-lapse. (4) Open only the right-hand bottle. (5) Using tweezers, drop a small ice crystal into the right-hand bottle; do not touch the left bottle. (6) Observe both bottles without disturbance.Observed Phenomena: Initially, both bottles contain clear liquid water. Immediately after the ice crystal enters the right bottle, ice rapidly forms and spreads through the water, often starting at the contact point and moving upward. Experiment Title: Sediment Stirred into Clear Water Reducing Light Beam Visibility2. Subject: Natural Science – Marine Science3. Experimental Equipment1. Clear glass aquarium or rectangular glass tank2. Clean, clear water3. Fine sediment (e.g., clean sand, silt, or clay powder)4. Flashlight or narrow-beam torch5. Preparation: Place the clear glass aquarium on a stable surface and fill it with clean water until it appears transparent and free of particles. Sediment Addition: Slowly add a small amount of fine sediment into the water near the top of the aquarium.6. Completion: Stop stirring and continue recording briefly to observe the stabilized turbid state.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Fine Mist vs Coarse Spray in Backlit AirI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Fine Mist and Coarse Spray in Backlit Air2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare the behavior of fine mist and coarse spray droplets in air under backlighting, and to understand how droplet size affects suspension time and light scattering.II. Experimental Equipment1. Hand mister (produces fine mist)2. Trigger spray bottle (produces coarse spray)3. Clean water4. Dark room or dim indoor space5. Strong backlight source (lamp or window light placed behind the spray area)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Darken the room as much as possible. Place the light source behind the spraying area so that the light shines toward the camera, creating a backlit condition.2. Positioning: Stand facing the camera. Hold the hand mister in the left hand and the trigger spray bottle in the right hand, keeping both at similar heights and distances from the light source.3. Spraying Action: Simultaneously or sequentially spray water from the hand mister on the left and the trigger spray bottle on the right into the air in front of the backlight.4. Pause and Observation: Stop spraying and remain still. Allow the droplets to hang and move naturally in the air for a short time.5. End: After observation, turn off the light and clean up any water residue.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The hand mister produces a fine, cloud-like mist that appears bright and dense under backlighting.2. The fine mist droplets remain suspended in the air for a longer time and drift slowly downward.3. The trigger spray bottle produces larger, heavier droplets that appear as brighter streaks or beads.4. The coarse droplets fall quickly and disappear from the illuminated area sooner than the fine mist.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates how droplet size influences aerosol behavior in air. Fine mist consists of very small droplets with low mass and large surface-area-to-volume ratios, resulting in slower settling speeds and stronger light scattering, making them highly visible in backlit air. Coarse spray consists of larger droplets with greater mass, which are more strongly affected by gravity and therefore fall quickly. This principle is fundamental in atmospheric science, helping to explain phenomena such as fog, haze, and spray dispersion.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Laser Pointer Scattering in a Milk–Water TankI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Laser Pointer Scattering in a Milk–Water Tank with Increasing Particle Concentration2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science (Light Scattering and Aerosols)3. Experiment Objective: To simulate atmospheric particle scattering using a milk–water mixture, observe how increasing particle concentration enhances light scattering, and understand the relationship between particle density and visibility of a laser beam. The experiment also trains students to conduct controlled additions, uniform mixing, and fixed-focus time-lapse observation.II. Experimental Equipment- Transparent rectangular tank or clear glass aquarium (1)- Clean water (enough to fill the tank)- Milk (small volume, used as scattering particles)- Dropper or measuring spoon (for controlled milk addition)- Red laser pointer (continuous beam)- Camera or smartphone with tripod (focus lock enabled)- Stirring rod or spoon- Darkened room or shaded background (recommended for clear observation)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   Place the transparent tank on a stable table and fill it with clean water until about 3/4 full. Ensure the water is clear and free of bubbles. Darken the surrounding environment if possible. Mount the camera on a tripod facing the long side of the tank and fix the focus manually so it does not change during the experiment.2. Laser Alignment:   Turn on the red laser pointer and adjust its position so that the beam shines horizontally through the water, entering from one side of the tank and exiting the opposite side at mid-height. Ensure the beam is level and steady.3. Initial Observation:   Record or observe the tank before adding milk. The laser path should be faint or barely visible in the clear water.4. Controlled Milk Addition:   Using a dropper, add a very small amount of milk (e.g., 1–2 drops) into the water. Gently stir to ensure uniform mixing without creating bubbles. Continue recording.5. Repeated Addition and Mixing:   Repeat the process of adding small amounts of milk and mixing evenly. After each addition, pause briefly to observe and record changes in the visibility of the laser beam.6. Completion and Cleanup:   After the laser beam becomes clearly visible throughout the tank, stop adding milk. Turn off the laser, stop recording, and clean the equipment. Dispose of the milk–water mixture properly.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: In clear water, the red laser beam is difficult to see from the side, with only the entry and exit points visible.2. Low Particle Concentration: After adding a small amount of milk, the laser path becomes faintly visible as a thin red line inside the water.3. Increasing Particle Concentration: With more milk added, the laser beam becomes brighter and more clearly defined, and scattered light is visible throughout the tank.4. High Particle Concentration: At higher milk concentrations, the beam appears thick and strongly illuminated, and the water looks uniformly cloudy, with intense scattering along the entire beam path.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates light scattering by suspended particles, analogous to aerosol scattering in the atmosphere. Milk contains tiny fat and protein particles that remain suspended in water, acting as scattering centers. As particle concentration increases, more light from the laser is scattered in different directions, making the beam path visible from the side. This phenomenon is similar to the Tyndall effect and helps explain atmospheric visibility, haze, and why light beams are visible in fog or polluted air.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not look directly into the laser beam or point it at eyes.2. Add milk gradually to avoid sudden over-clouding that obscures intermediate stages.3. Stir gently to ensure uniform particle distribution without bubbles.4. Keep the camera focus fixed to ensure consistent time-lapse comparison.

Minimum assumptions include: milk particles remain suspended in water; a red laser emits a straight, continuous beam; increased particle concentration causes increased side scattering.Phased Storyline: (1) Initial clear-water phase where the laser beam is barely visible from the side; (2) Early addition phase where small amounts of milk create faint beam visibility; (3) Growth phase where repeated additions and mixing cause progressively brighter and thicker visible beam; (4) High-concentration phase where the tank appears cloudy and the beam is strongly illuminated. The camera perspective should remain fixed and side-on to verify changes purely due to particle concentration, not focus or viewpoint changes.

Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that cooled air becomes denser and sinks beneath warmer air by visually observing smoke movement in a transparent chamber.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent chamber or box (airtight or semi-airtight), metal ice tray, ice cubes, smoke source (incense or smoke generator), camera with tripod (fixed focus), dark background (optional for contrast).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the transparent chamber on a stable table. Ensure the chamber is clean and dry. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Smoke is evenly distributed inside the chamber with no strong directional movement.2. Final State: A downward flow of smoke is clearly visible beneath the ice tray, while relatively warmer air remains above.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAir temperature affects air density. The smoke acts as a tracer, making the otherwise invisible air movement visible. This demonstrates the atmospheric principle that cold air sinks while warm air rises.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Avoid excessive smoke, which can obscure airflow details.2. Ensure the camera remains fixed to allow accurate time-lapse comparison.3. Handle ice and metal tray carefully to prevent water dripping into the chamber.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Chemical Raw Material Moisture Detection (Karl Fischer Colorimetric Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Moisture Detection of Methanol by Karl Fischer Colorimetric Method2. Subject: Natural Science – Environmental Science (Analytical Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To qualitatively determine the presence of trace water in methanol by observing the color change after adding Karl Fischer reagent, and to understand the basic principle of the Karl Fischer moisture determination reaction.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsDry test tube (1 tube), test tube rack, calibrated dropper or pipette, methanol sample, Karl Fischer colorimetric reagent, safety goggles, gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the test tube is completely dry. Place it upright on a test tube rack and wear safety goggles and gloves.2. Sampling: Use a pipette to accurately transfer 1 mL of methanol into the dry test tube. Observe that the liquid is colorless and transparent.3. Reagent Addition (Core Operation): Using a dropper, add 2 drops of Karl Fischer reagent into the methanol sample.4. Mixing and Observation: Gently swirl the test tube to mix the contents evenly and immediately observe the color change of the solution.5. Completion: After observing the color, place the test tube back on the rack. Dispose of the waste liquid according to laboratory regulations.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Methanol in the test tube is colorless and transparent.2. After Reagent Addition: Upon adding Karl Fischer reagent, the solution shows a color change. If water is present, the brown color of the reagent fades and turns to a stable light yellow endpoint after mixing.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe Karl Fischer colorimetric method is based on the specific chemical reaction between water and Karl Fischer reagent. Water reacts with iodine and sulfur dioxide in the presence of a base and alcohol. When water is present in methanol, iodine is consumed, causing the color to change from brown to light yellow. The appearance of a stable yellow color indicates that the reaction has reached the endpoint, confirming the presence of water in the sample.VI. Experimental Precautions1. The test tube and methanol must be dry to avoid introducing external moisture.2. Add the reagent dropwise and observe carefully to avoid excess addition.3. Handle Karl Fischer reagent with care, as it is corrosive and volatile.4. Dispose of chemical waste properly after the experiment.

(2) Action phase: a dropper adds exactly two drops of Karl Fischer reagent into the test tube. (3) Reaction phase: gentle mixing occurs, followed by a visible color transition from brownish to stable light yellow. (4) Endpoint phase: the color remains stable, indicating completion. Visibility constraints: the camera should clearly show the liquid color and the order of actions from reagent addition to color stabilization for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Dioxin Detection (Immunochromatographic Test Paper Simulation)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Dioxin Detection by Immunochromatographic Test Paper SimulationSubject: Natural Science – Environmental ScienceObjective: To demonstrate the basic operation and result interpretation of immunochromatographic test paper for detecting dioxins in water by immersing the sample end, standing, and observing line changes.II. Experimental MaterialsImmunochromatographic test paper (dioxin-specific), water sample (simulated environmental water), clean beaker, timer or stopwatch, flat clean surface.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the water sample in a clean beaker. Remove one test paper and identify the sample end.2. Immersion: Vertically immerse only the sample end of the test paper into the water sample for 5 seconds, ensuring the liquid level does not exceed the marked limit line.3. Standing: Remove the test paper and place it upright on a clean flat surface. Allow it to stand undisturbed for 2 minutes. For demonstration, use time-lapse photography to compress this period.4. Observation: Focus the camera on the detection area of the test paper and record the gradual appearance of lines.IV. Experimental Principle SummaryThis experiment is based on immunochromatographic competitive binding. Dioxins in the water sample compete with labeled antigens on the test paper for specific antibodies. Capillary action drives the sample along the paper. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Rising of Warm Dyed Water Parcel in a Convection TankSubject: Natural Science – Atmospheric ScienceExperiment Objective: To simulate atmospheric convection by demonstrating how a warm, less-dense fluid parcel rises in a still fluid environment, helping students understand buoyancy and vertical motion of air parcels.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent convection tank filled with clear, still water; warm water dyed red; syringe or injector with thin tubing; thermometer (optional); support stand; paper towels.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the transparent convection tank on a level surface and fill it with clear water. Allow the water to stand until all motion stops, forming a still environment.2. Injection Setup: Draw warm red-dyed water into the syringe. Carefully insert the injector tip to the bottom center of the tank, avoiding disturbance of the surrounding water.3. Core Operation: Slowly inject a small amount of warm red-dyed water at the bottom. After injection, gently stop applying pressure and release the parcel so it is no longer forced by the syringe.4. Observation: Keep the tank undisturbed and observe the motion of the red-dyed water parcel.5. Completion: After the parcel has risen and begun to spread, end the observation and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The tank water is clear and motionless; the red-dyed warm water forms a compact blob at the bottom.2. During the Process: Once released, the red-dyed water rises upward in a plume-like shape through the surrounding clear water.3. Later Stage: As it rises, the parcel gradually slows, spreads, and mixes with the surrounding water.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates buoyancy and convection. Warm water has lower density than the surrounding cooler water. When the warm red-dyed water is released at the bottom of a still tank, the density difference creates an upward buoyant force, causing the parcel to rise. This process is analogous to warm air parcels rising in the atmosphere, forming the basis of atmospheric convection.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the tank water is still before injection; inject slowly to avoid forced jets; use a small volume of dyed water for clear parcel observation.

manual: Experiment Title: 2D Vector Subtraction (v−w) VisualizationSubject: Mathematics – VectorsExperiment Objective: To visually demonstrate 2D vector subtraction v−w in a Cartesian coordinate system, and to understand its geometric meaning.Experimental Environment and Tools: White background; Cartesian coordinate system with x∈[-5,5], y∈[-5,5]; drawing or animation tools capable of plotting vectors with arrows and colors.Experimental Procedure:1. Draw a Cartesian coordinate system on a white background, marking the x- and y-axes with ranges from −5 to 5.2. From the origin (0,0), draw vector v=(3,2) as a black arrow pointing to the coordinate (3,2).3. From the origin (0,0), draw vector w=(1,1) as a red arrow pointing to the coordinate (1,1).4. Construct vector −w by reversing the direction of w while keeping the same magnitude.5. Place −w with its tail at the head of v, following the head-to-tail rule of vector addition.6. Draw the resulting green vector from the origin to the end of the head-to-tail construction; label it v−w.Observation of Experimental Phenomena:1. Initially, two vectors v (black) and w (red) originate from the origin with different directions and lengths.2. After reversing w, the vector −w points in the opposite direction.3. Geometrically, this is achieved by reversing vector w to obtain −w and then adding it to vector v using the head-to-tail method. Algebraically, v−w=(3−1, 2−1)=(2,1), which matches the endpoint of the green vector in the visualization.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: 2D Vector Head-to-Tail Addition VisualizationI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: 2D Vector Head-to-Tail Addition VisualizationSubject: Mathematics – Natural ScienceObjective: To visually demonstrate 2D vector addition using the head-to-tail method in a Cartesian coordinate system and understand how component-wise addition determines the resultant vector.II. Experimental ToolsWhite background canvas; Cartesian coordinate grid with x-axis and y-axis labeled from -5 to 5; drawing tools for arrows; color coding: red, blue, green; text labels for coordinates.III. Experimental Procedure1. Draw a Cartesian coordinate system on a white background with clear grid lines; label x-axis and y-axis from -5 to 5.2. From the origin (0,0), draw a red arrow vector to the point (1,2); label it (1,2).3. From the endpoint of the red vector at (1,2), draw a blue arrow vector to the point (4,3), representing vector (3,1); label it (3,1).4. Draw the resultant green vector from the origin (0,0) directly to the final endpoint (4,3); label it (4,3).5. Ensure all vectors have clear arrowheads and coordinate labels.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitially, only the coordinate grid is visible. After drawing the red vector, its endpoint is at (1,2). The blue vector begins exactly at this endpoint and ends at (4,3). The green resultant connects the origin to (4,3), visually completing a triangle that confirms head-to-tail addition.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleVector addition in two dimensions follows the head-to-tail rule: placing the tail of the second vector at the head of the first. The resultant vector represents the total displacement. In Cartesian form, vectors add component-wise: (1,2) + (3,1) = (4,3). The green vector therefore correctly represents the sum of the red and blue vectors.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Sine Function y=sinx Graph VisualizationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Sine Function y=sinx Graph Visualization2. Subject: Mathematics – Trigonometric Functions3. Experiment Objective: To visualize the graph of y=sinx, understand its periodic and oscillatory nature, identify its amplitude, period (2π), vertices, and zeros through a clear Cartesian coordinate system.II. Experimental ToolsWhite background or digital canvas, Cartesian coordinate system with x-axis and y-axis, drawing tool or plotting software, color settings (blue, red, green).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Set a white background and draw a Cartesian coordinate system. Mark the x-axis from 0 to 2π and the y-axis from -1 to 1 with uniform scale.2. Axis Labeling: Label the x-axis with 0, π/2, π, 3π/2, and 2π; label the y-axis with -1, 0, and 1.3. Curve Drawing: Using a blue color, draw the curve y=sinx smoothly from x=0 to x=2π, ensuring a continuous and periodic oscillation.4. Key Point Marking: Mark the vertices (π/2,1) and (3π/2,-1) with red dots. Mark the zeros (0,0), (π,0), and (2π,0) with red dots.5. Text Annotation: Add green text near the curve reading y=sinx (period 2π).6. Final Check: Ensure the curve is smooth, symmetric, and confined within y∈[-1,1].IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The curve starts at (0,0), rises smoothly to a maximum at (π/2,1), then decreases to cross the x-axis at (π,0).2. The curve continues downward to a minimum at (3π/2,-1), then rises back to (2π,0).3. The entire graph shows smooth, continuous, and periodic oscillation with period 2π and amplitude 1.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe sine function y=sinx is a basic trigonometric function describing periodic motion. Its amplitude is 1, so values are restricted to [-1,1]. Its period is 2π, meaning the graph repeats every 2π units along the x-axis. Zeros occur where sinx=0, and vertices occur at maximum and minimum values, reflecting the function’s inherent oscillatory and periodic properties.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: visualization of the sine function y=sinx with correct period, amplitude, and key points. Minimum assumptions: a fixed Cartesian coordinate system, standard trigonometric definitions, and a white background for clarity. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) establish axes and ranges; (2) draw a smooth blue sine curve from 0 to 2π; (3) highlight zeros and extrema with red points; (4) annotate the function and period in green text. Key causal transitions: correct axis setup enables correct curve shape; correct curve shape reveals periodic oscillation. Visibility constraints: axes, points, colors, and labels must remain clearly visible and stable throughout for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Scatter Plot of Speed vs Time with Fixed DistanceI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Scatter Plot of Speed vs Time with Fixed Distance2. Subject: Natural Science - Statistics & Data Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate data collection and visualization for an experiment with fixed distance, record several pairs of time and corresponding speed, and verify through a scatter plot that all points lie on a single straight line, indicating a linear relationship.II. Experimental Materials and Tools1. Measuring tape or marked track (fixed distance, e.g., 10 meters)2. Stopwatch or timer3. Moving object (toy car or walking person)4. Data recording sheet or notebook5. Calculator6. Computer or graph paper for plottingIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Measure and mark a fixed distance (e.g., 10 m) on a straight path. Ensure the distance remains unchanged throughout the experiment.2. Data Collection: Move the object across the fixed distance at different speeds. For each trial, use the stopwatch to record the time taken to travel the fixed distance.3. Calculation: For each trial, calculate speed using speed = distance ÷ time.4. Recording: Record each pair of time and corresponding speed in a table.5. Plotting: Plot a scatter plot with time on the x-axis and speed on the y-axis. Mark all recorded data points.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The recorded times vary between trials while the distance remains constant.2. Calculated speeds change proportionally with the recorded times.3. On the scatter plot, all plotted points align along a single straight line without deviation.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleWhen distance is fixed, speed is directly proportional to time according to the relationship speed = distance ÷ time. Plotting speed against time under a fixed distance condition produces a linear relationship, which is visually confirmed when all data points align on one straight line in the scatter plot.VI. Experimental Notes1. Ensure the distance is strictly fixed for all trials.2. Record time accurately to reduce measurement error.3. Use multiple trials to clearly show the linear trend.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrate a linear relationship between speed and time under a fixed-distance condition using data collection and a scatter plot. Experiment Title: Comparison of Strong and Weak Negative Correlation Using Scatter Plots2. Subject: Natural Science – Statistics & Data Science3. Experiment Objective: To understand and compare strong and weak negative correlations by visualizing scatter plots, and to observe how data dispersion affects the clarity of a trend line.II. Experimental EquipmentComputer or tablet, statistical plotting software (e.g., Python with matplotlib, Excel, or similar), sample numerical datasets (one with strong negative correlation, one with weak negative correlation).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Open the plotting software and prepare two datasets. Dataset A should show a strong negative correlation; Dataset B should show a weak negative correlation.2. Plotting Strong Negative Correlation: Create a scatter plot using Dataset A. Ensure axes are set consistently. After plotting points, add a fitted linear trend line.3. Plotting Weak Negative Correlation: Clear the canvas or move to a new plot. Create a scatter plot using Dataset B, where points are widely scattered. Then add a fitted linear trend line.4. Sequence Completion: Ensure the plots are shown in sequence, first strong then weak correlation, each followed by its fitted line.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. In the second plot, data points are dispersed and do not closely align, and the fitted line shows a less obvious downward trend.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCorrelation describes the direction and strength of a relationship between two variables. A weak negative correlation occurs when data points are more scattered, making the downward trend less obvious even after fitting a line.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Matplotlib Normal Distribution PDF DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Matplotlib Normal Distribution PDF Demonstration2. Subject: Natural Science - Statistics & Data Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how to use Python with numpy, scipy, and matplotlib to generate and visualize the probability density function (PDF) of a standard normal distribution, and to understand the meaning of mean and standard deviation through graphical observation.II. Experimental Equipment and Environment1. Computer with Python installed2. Python libraries: numpy, scipy, matplotlib3. Integrated Development Environment (IDE) or terminal (e.g., Jupyter Notebook)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Open the Python environment and ensure numpy, scipy, and matplotlib are available. Prepare a blank Python script or notebook cell.2. Code Input: Import required libraries (numpy, scipy.stats, matplotlib.pyplot). Use numpy to generate a sequence of x-values evenly spaced from -3 to 3.3. Core Operation: Use scipy.stats.norm to calculate the probability density values corresponding to the x-values, setting mean μ=0 and standard deviation σ=1.4. Visualization: Use matplotlib to plot the PDF as a smooth blue curve. Set the x-axis range to [-3,3] and the y-axis range to [0,0.4]. Add axis labels and annotate the plot with μ=0 and σ=1. Keep the background white.5. Execution: Run the code and observe the plotted output appearing on the screen.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Only Python code is visible on the computer screen.2. After Execution: A smooth, continuous, blue bell-shaped curve appears.3. Graph Features: The curve is symmetric about x=0, peaks near y=0.4, with x-axis labeled from -3 to 3 and y-axis from 0 to 0.4. Mean (μ=0) and standard deviation (σ=1) are clearly annotated.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. The normal distribution is a fundamental continuous probability distribution in statistics.2. The probability density function is defined as f(x) = (1/(σ√(2π))) * exp(-(x-μ)²/(2σ²)).3. For a standard normal distribution, μ=0 and σ=1, producing a symmetric bell-shaped curve.4. The visualization links abstract statistical parameters to concrete graphical features, helping to understand how mean and standard deviation affect distribution shape.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Drawing Binomial Distribution Charts (n=10 vs n=100)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Binomial Distributions with Different Trial Numbers2. Subject: Natural Science – Statistics & Data Science3. Experiment Objective: Using computer-based plotting, generate and compare two binomial distributions with probability p=0.5. By drawing bar charts for n=10 and n=100 under identical scales, observe that the distribution with n=100 is closer to a bell-shaped symmetric form, while the distribution with n=10 shows stronger discreteness.II. Experimental Environment and ToolsComputer with standard plotting software (e.g., Python with matplotlib, R, or similar statistical software), screen display for charts.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Open the plotting software and create a new script or workspace. Ensure the random or theoretical binomial distribution function is available.2. Parameter Setting (Case 1): Set probability p=0.5 and number of trials n=10.3. Data Generation (n=10): Generate the binomial probability distribution for all possible outcomes (0 to 10 successes).4. Plotting (n=10): Draw a bar chart of the distribution. Label the horizontal axis as Number of Successes and the vertical axis as Probability. Fix the axis ranges to cover 0–100 on the horizontal axis and an appropriate probability range on the vertical axis.5. Parameter Setting (Case 2): Keep p=0.5 and change the number of trials to n=100.6. Data Generation (n=100): Generate the binomial probability distribution for outcomes from 0 to 100 successes.7. Plotting (n=100): Draw a bar chart using the same horizontal and vertical scales as in the n=10 chart.8. Display and Comparison: Display both charts side by side or sequentially on the same screen for direct visual comparison.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. For n=10: The bar chart shows a small number of distinct bars. The distribution is clearly discrete, with noticeable gaps and limited smoothness.2. For n=100: The bar chart contains many bars that form a smooth, symmetric shape centered around 50. The overall appearance is close to a bell-shaped curve.3. Comparison: Under identical scales, the n=100 distribution appears much smoother and more symmetric than the n=10 distribution.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe binomial distribution describes the probability of a given number of successes in n independent Bernoulli trials with probability p. When p=0.5, the distribution is symmetric around n/2. As n increases, the number of possible outcomes increases and the distribution becomes smoother. According to the normal approximation to the binomial distribution, when n is large, the binomial distribution approaches a bell-shaped (normal) distribution. This experiment visually demonstrates the effect of increasing n on the shape and continuity of the binomial distribution.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Phycoerythrin Fluorescence in Red AlgaeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Red Fluorescence in Red Algae under Blue-Green Light2. Subject: Natural Science – Marine Science3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand how phycoerythrin pigment in red algae absorbs blue-green light and emits red fluorescence, and to compare this phenomenon with green algae under the same lighting conditions.II. Experimental EquipmentDark aquarium or tank with clear seawater; live red marine algae; live green marine algae; overhead lamp capable of switching between white light and blue-green light; power switch or programmed light controller.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the aquarium in a dark environment to minimize external light interference. Fill with clear seawater.2. Placement: Position red marine algae and green marine algae side by side at the bottom of the aquarium, ensuring equal distance from the overhead lamp.3. Initial Lighting: Turn on the overhead lamp with white light and allow both algae to be illuminated evenly.4. Light Cycling: Switch the lamp from white light to blue-green light. Maintain the blue-green light for several seconds, then switch back to white light. Repeat the cycle at least once.5. Observation: Observe the color and brightness changes of both algae during each lighting condition.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Under white light: Both red and green algae appear in their natural colors, with no fluorescence.2. Under blue-green light: Red algae emits a visible red fluorescence, appearing brighter or glowing red, while green algae shows little to no red fluorescence and remains relatively dark or green.3. When returning to white light: The red fluorescence disappears, and both algae return to their original appearance.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesRed algae contain phycoerythrin, a photosynthetic pigment that strongly absorbs blue-green light. After absorption, phycoerythrin re-emits part of the energy as red fluorescence. Green algae lack significant amounts of phycoerythrin, so they do not show red fluorescence under blue-green light. This difference demonstrates pigment adaptation of marine algae to underwater light conditions.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Iodine Reaction with Starch vs CelluloseI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Iodine Reaction with Starch and CelluloseSubject: Chemistry – Organic Chemistry / PolymersObjective: To compare the reaction of iodine with starch and cellulose, and understand how polymer structure affects molecular binding.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo clear glass beakers, starch suspension, cellulose fibers (e.g., filter paper pulp or cotton fibers), iodine solution, dropper, stirring rod, camera or phone fixed on tripod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, clear beakers side by side. Add equal volumes of starch suspension to one beaker and cellulose fibers suspended in water to the other.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera focus and position to ensure both beakers remain fully visible for time-lapse recording.3. Core Operation: Using a dropper, add the same number of drops of iodine solution into each beaker simultaneously or sequentially.4. Observation: Do not stir excessively. Observe and record the color changes over a short period.5. Completion: Stop recording after the color changes stabilize; clean and store equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers contain colorless or white suspensions.2. After Iodine Addition: The starch suspension rapidly turns blue-black, while the cellulose suspension remains yellow-brown or shows no obvious color change.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleStarch contains helical amylose chains that can bind iodine molecules to form a blue-black complex. Cellulose has a linear polymer structure with strong hydrogen bonding between chains, preventing iodine from entering and forming the complex. Therefore, iodine reacts differently with starch and cellulose, demonstrating the effect of polymer structure on binding behavior.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse equal amounts of iodine for fair comparison; ensure clear labeling of beakers; avoid shaking that may obscure color observation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: polymer structure affects iodine binding; starch forms a helical iodine complex, cellulose does not. Minimum assumptions: iodine solution causes visible color change only when complexed with starch; both samples are comparable in amount and visibility. Expected phased storyline: (1) two clear beakers with different polysaccharide samples are shown side by side; (2) iodine is added to both under fixed camera focus; (3) starch beaker rapidly darkens to blue-black while cellulose remains largely unchanged; (4) final stable contrast is clearly visible. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Incense Smoke Forming a Convection Plume Above a Warm SurfaceI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Incense Smoke Forming a Convection Plume Above a Warm Surface2. Subject: Natural Science - Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate thermal convection in air by observing incense smoke rising as a plume above a gently heated metal plate, and to understand how temperature differences drive air movement.II. Experimental EquipmentIncense stick (1), lighter or matches, flat metal plate, electric hot plate or other gentle heat source, heat-resistant stand, camera with tripod (for time-lapse), well-ventilated but still room.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the metal plate on the heat source and warm it gently; ensure the room has minimal air movement. Set the camera on a tripod, frame the area above the plate, and fix the focus.2. Heating: Turn on the heat source to keep the plate warm but not glowing or smoking.3. Core Operation: Light the incense stick. Hold it steadily a few centimeters above the center of the warm plate without touching the plate.4. Recording: Start time-lapse or continuous recording while maintaining the incense position for several seconds.5. Completion: Extinguish the incense, turn off the heat source, and allow equipment to cool.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Incense smoke drifts slowly in still air.2. Above the Warm Plate: Smoke is drawn upward, forming a narrow, continuous rising plume directly above the plate.3. Sustained Observation: The plume remains stable as long as the plate stays warm and the air remains still.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleHeating the metal plate warms the air above it, causing the air to expand and decrease in density. The warmer, less dense air rises, creating an upward convection current. Incense smoke acts as a tracer, making the otherwise invisible air motion visible as a convection plume. This process illustrates atmospheric thermal convection driven by temperature differences.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Thermal convection in air visualized by incense smoke above a warm surface. Minimum assumptions: still indoor air, gentle heating sufficient to warm air without combustion effects, fixed camera viewpoint. Phased storyline: (1) Static setup with warm plate and fixed camera; (2) incense is lit and positioned above plate; (3) smoke initially diffuses, then is entrained upward as air warms; (4) a stable vertical plume forms and persists. Visibility constraints: side-on or slight angled view to clearly see vertical smoke motion; stable framing to verify continuous causal progression from heating to rising plume.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Orbital Decay in a Central Gravity Well ModelSubject: Natural Science - Astrophysics & AstronomyObjective: To model orbital motion and orbital decay using an elastic gravity well, and to observe how different initial speeds affect spiral trajectories toward a central mass.II. EquipmentCircular rigid frame with elastic fabric stretched tightly; heavy central ball (dark-colored, high mass); two smaller balls of equal size and color; flat support table.III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Place the circular frame horizontally on the table. Stretch the elastic fabric evenly and place the heavy center ball at the middle, forming a visible depression.2. Preparation: Place two small balls at the edge of the fabric at similar heights but at different starting points along the rim.3. Release A (slow speed): Gently push the first small ball tangentially along the edge with a low initial speed.4. Release B (fast speed): Gently push the second small ball tangentially with a noticeably higher initial speed.5. Observation: Allow both balls to roll freely until they spiral inward and reach the center.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Fabric is flat except for a deep central depression caused by the heavy ball.2. Motion: Both small balls follow curved paths around the center.3. Comparison: The slower ball spirals inward quickly, with a rapidly shrinking orbit; the faster ball maintains a wider orbit for a longer time.4. Final State: Both balls eventually spiral into the center and collide with the heavy ball.V. Experimental Principle SummaryThe elastic fabric represents curved spacetime around a massive object. The heavy center ball creates a gravity well by deforming the fabric. Rolling balls follow curved paths due to this deformation. With energy loss (rolling friction), their orbits decay, causing inward spirals. Higher initial speed provides greater angular momentum, delaying orbital decay, analogous to astrophysical orbital motion around massive bodies.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Orbital decay in a gravity well analogy, assuming curved spacetime is modeled by elastic fabric and friction represents energy loss.Expected Phenomena Storyline: Phase 1—static setup with visible central depression; Phase 2—two balls released tangentially from the edge at different speeds; Phase 3—both balls follow spiral paths, with the slower ball decaying faster; Phase 4—both reach the center. Visibility requires a top-down or angled view showing trajectories and relative speeds clearly.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Water Freezes and ExpandsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Water Turns from Liquid to Solid and Its Volume Expands2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics3. Experiment Objective: To observe the freezing process of water, understand the phase change from liquid to solid, and verify that water expands in volume when it freezes.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent container with lid (plastic or glass, heat-resistant), clean water, refrigerator or ice bath (with ice and salt), marker pen or tape (for marking water level), camera or mobile phone for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Pour clean water into the transparent container until about 80–90% full to allow space for expansion. Mark the initial water level on the container. Seal the container loosely (do not fully tighten if rigid).2. Placement: Place the container upright and keep it still inside a refrigerator freezer or an ice bath. Ensure the container is clearly visible to the camera.3. Recording: Set the camera to record a time-lapse video over approximately 24 hours (or accelerated representation for demonstration).4. Cooling and Freezing: Allow the water to cool gradually and freeze completely without disturbing the container.5. Observation: After freezing, remove the container and observe the internal state of the ice and the change in water level or container shape.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Water is colorless, transparent, and liquid, with a flat surface at the marked level.2. During Cooling: Small ice crystals begin forming, usually from the edges or surface, gradually spreading inward.3. After Freezing: The entire water body becomes solid ice. The ice level is higher than the original water level, or the container shows outward expansion.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhen water cools to 0°C, it changes from liquid to solid. During freezing, water molecules arrange into a stable hexagonal crystal structure with more empty space, causing ice to occupy a larger volume than liquid water. This is why water expands when it freezes, unlike most substances.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not overfill the container to prevent cracking or bursting.2. Use a transparent container for clear observation.3. Avoid disturbing the container during freezing.4. Handle frozen containers carefully after removal.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Water undergoes a phase change from liquid to solid when cooled, and uniquely expands in volume upon freezing due to its molecular structure. Minimum assumptions: presence of liquid water, a transparent container, a cooling environment below 0°C, and uninterrupted freezing.Expected phenomena storyline: Phase 1 – Initial state: transparent container with still, colorless liquid water at a marked level. Phase 2 – Cooling: container placed in refrigerator or ice bath; time-lapse shows gradual formation of ice from edges or surface. Phase 3 – Solidification: water fully freezes into solid ice. Phase 4 – Result observation: ice level higher than initial mark or container slightly expanded, visible through the transparent walls. Visibility constraints: camera must maintain a stable view of the container interior and water/ice level to verify freezing and expansion.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Incandescent Bulb Filament Heating from Dark to White-HotI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Incandescent Bulb Filament Heating from Dark to White-Hot2. Subject: Physics - Electricity and Thermal Radiation3. Experiment Objective: Observe how a tungsten filament heats and emits light as electrical power increases; understand the relationship between electric current, temperature, and light emission.II. Experimental EquipmentClear old-style incandescent bulb (tungsten filament visible), variable power supply (or dimmer), connecting wires and socket, darkened room, camera with tripod (fixed focus), safety gloves.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the bulb in its socket in a dim room; connect it to the variable power supply; set the camera on a tripod and fix focus and framing on the filament.Power Increase: Turn on the power supply at zero or minimum; gradually increase voltage/current smoothly over time.Core Operation: Continue increasing power steadily while recording time-lapse video; do not change camera position or focus.Completion: Stop increasing power before exceeding the bulb rating; turn off power and allow the bulb to cool.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Filament is dark and not glowing.Low Power: Filament begins to glow dull red.Medium Power: Filament becomes brighter, changing to orange/yellow.High Power: Filament appears bright yellow-white (white-hot), illuminating the bulb clearly.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesAs electric current flows through the tungsten filament, electrical energy is converted into thermal energy due to resistance. The filament temperature rises, and according to blackbody radiation, hotter objects emit brighter light with a shift from red to white as temperature increases. The gradual increase in power causes the observable color and brightness changes.VI. Experimental PrecautionsDo not exceed the rated voltage; avoid touching the hot bulb; ensure stable connections; keep camera focus fixed for clear comparison.

Minimum assumptions: a clear incandescent bulb with visible filament, controllable power increase, dim environment, fixed camera viewpoint.Phased storyline: (1) Dark filament at zero power; (2) gradual power increase causes heating; (3) filament glows dull red; (4) brightness and color shift to orange/yellow; (5) white-hot steady glow. Visibility constraints: filament must remain centered and in focus; lighting and camera position remain fixed to verify continuous progression.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Releasing a Hydrogen Balloon and an Air BalloonI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Releasing a Hydrogen Balloon and an Air Balloon2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the different motion behaviors of a hydrogen-filled balloon and an air-filled balloon after being released from the hand, and to practice correct preparation, holding, and release operations.II. Experimental EquipmentHydrogen-filled balloon (1, securely tied), air-filled balloon (1, securely tied), thin strings attached to each balloon (optional, for holding), open indoor space with still air, protective awareness (no open flames).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Select an indoor area with no noticeable airflow. Check that the hydrogen balloon and air balloon are intact, properly inflated, and securely tied. Ensure no ignition sources are present.2. Holding the Hydrogen Balloon: Hold the hydrogen-filled balloon gently by the string or neck with one hand, keeping the balloon still and positioned in front of the body.3. Releasing the Hydrogen Balloon: Open the fingers smoothly to release the balloon, keeping the hand stationary at the moment of release.4. Holding the Air Balloon: After the first release, hold the air-filled balloon in the same manner, at a similar height and position.5. Releasing the Air Balloon: Release the air-filled balloon using the same hand motion as before, then keep hands still for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before release: Both balloons remain stationary in the hand.2. At the moment of release: Each balloon separates from the hand and begins independent motion.3. After release: The motion path and behavior of each balloon can be observed and compared.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe experiment is based on the concept of gas density and buoyancy in air. Different gases inside balloons result in different interactions with surrounding air. When external support from the hand is removed, the motion behavior of the balloon is determined by the relationship between the gas density inside the balloon and the density of the surrounding air.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Dish Soap Added to an Oil–Water Mixture Forming a Stable EmulsionI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Formation of a Stable Emulsion by Adding Dish Soap to an Oil–Water MixtureSubject: Natural Science – ChemistryExperiment Objective: To observe and compare the behavior of an oil–water mixture with and without dish soap after shaking, and to understand the role of surfactants in forming stable emulsions.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical transparent jars with lids; clean water; cooking oil; liquid dish soap; measuring spoon or dropper; camera or smartphone fixed on a tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical empty jars side by side on a flat surface. Pour the same volume of water into each jar, then gently add an equal volume of oil so that a clear oil layer floats on top of the water in both jars.2. Soap Addition: Add a small, equal amount of dish soap to the right jar only. Do not add soap to the left jar, which serves as the control.3. Sealing: Tightly seal both jars with their lids to prevent leakage during shaking.4. Core Operation: Shake both jars vigorously at the same time for several seconds to ensure thorough mixing.5. Observation Setup: Place the jars back side by side, fix the camera focus and position, and record the changes over time using time-lapse photography.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Before shaking, both jars show clear separation, with oil floating above water.After Shaking: Immediately after shaking, both jars appear cloudy due to dispersed oil droplets.Standing Over Time: In the left jar without soap, the cloudiness gradually disappears and the oil separates back into a distinct top layer. In the right jar with dish soap, the mixture remains cloudy for a long time, forming a relatively stable emulsion.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesOil and water are immiscible due to differences in polarity and naturally separate into layers. Dish soap contains surfactant molecules with hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails. During shaking, these molecules surround oil droplets, reducing interfacial tension and preventing the droplets from merging. As a result, the oil remains dispersed in water, forming a stable emulsion. Without soap, no such stabilization occurs, so the oil droplets quickly coalesce and separate.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse identical jars and equal volumes to ensure fair comparison. Seal lids tightly before shaking. Avoid excessive soap, which may obscure observation. Keep the camera fixed to allow clear time-based comparison.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Surfactants enable the formation of stable oil–water emulsions by reducing interfacial tension. Minimum assumptions: oil is less dense than water, soap acts as a surfactant, and shaking provides mechanical dispersion.Phased Storyline: (1) Setup phase – two identical jars with clear oil-on-water layers placed side by side; visual symmetry is essential. (2) Intervention phase – dish soap is added only to the right jar, establishing a clear experimental variable. (3) Action phase – both jars are sealed and shaken vigorously, causing temporary mixing. (4) Outcome phase – during settling, the control jar separates into layers while the soap jar remains cloudy, demonstrating a stable emulsion. Camera focus and perspective must remain fixed to verify comparative changes over time.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Single Cloud of Smoke Collapsing Inward Under Uniform SuctionSubject: Natural Science - Astrophysics & AstronomyObjective: To visually demonstrate inward collapse of a diffuse medium under uniform external suction, analogous to gravitational contraction, using time-lapse imaging.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent sealed chamber with evenly distributed micro-perforated walls; controllable vacuum/suction system with uniform manifold; smoke generator (non-toxic); still-air preparation fans (off during run); high-resolution camera with tripod; fixed-focus lens; time-lapse controller; pressure gauge.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Clean and seal the transparent chamber. Ensure all fans are off to achieve still air. Mount the camera facing the chamber and lock focus, exposure, and framing.2. Smoke Suspension: Introduce a small amount of smoke to form a single diffuse cloud centered in the chamber. Wait until internal air motion ceases and the cloud is stationary.3. Baseline Recording: Start time-lapse recording for several frames with no suction to document the initial state.4. Uniform Suction Application: Activate the vacuum system to apply low, uniform suction evenly through the chamber walls. Maintain constant suction.5. Recording Collapse: Continue time-lapse recording as the smoke cloud contracts inward toward the center.6. Termination: Stop suction after clear inward collapse is observed. End recording and vent chamber safely.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: A diffuse, approximately spherical smoke cloud suspended in still air.During Suction: The smoke begins moving inward from all directions, maintaining approximate symmetry.Final State: The cloud becomes denser and smaller near the center, with reduced peripheral smoke density.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleUniform suction at the chamber boundaries creates a lower pressure near the walls, driving air flow inward. The smoke, acting as a tracer of the airflow, converges toward the center. This demonstrates a fluid-dynamic analogue of isotropic gravitational collapse, where a diffuse medium contracts inward under a uniform inward-directed force.VI. PrecautionsEnsure suction is uniform and weak to avoid turbulence; keep camera settings fixed; use non-toxic smoke; verify chamber sealing before operation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Enzyme-Based Glucose Test Strip Color ChangeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Enzyme-Based Glucose Test Strip Color Change2. Subject: Natural Science - Biochemistry & Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that enzyme-based glucose test strips change color in the presence of glucose and to compare results between a sugar solution and water control.II. Experimental MaterialsEnzyme-based glucose test strips (2 identical strips), sugar solution (glucose solution, clear), distilled water, two small transparent cups or beakers, tabletop, optional timer.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two transparent cups on a clean tabletop. Pour sugar solution into one cup and water into the other.2. Control Setup: Ensure both solutions are colorless and at room temperature. Remove two identical glucose test strips from the container.3. Core Operation: Dip the first test strip into the sugar solution for 1-2 seconds, fully wetting the reactive end, then remove it and hold it horizontally.4. Comparison Operation: Dip the second identical test strip into the water for the same duration, then remove it and hold it similarly.5. Observation: Place both strips side by side on the tabletop and observe color changes for several seconds.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both test strips are the same color before contact with liquids.2. Sugar Solution Result: The strip dipped into sugar solution gradually changes to a darker color according to the strip color scale.3. Water Control Result: The strip dipped into water shows no color change or remains very light.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleGlucose test strips contain specific enzymes such as glucose oxidase and peroxidase. When glucose is present, glucose oxidase catalyzes the oxidation of glucose, producing hydrogen peroxide. Peroxidase then catalyzes a reaction between hydrogen peroxide and a chromogenic substrate, causing a visible color change. In water without glucose, this enzymatic reaction does not occur, so no color change is observed.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Iodide-Catalyzed Decomposition of Hydrogen PeroxideI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Iodide-Catalyzed Decomposition of Hydrogen Peroxide2. Subject: Chemistry – Physical Chemistry (Chemical Kinetics)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the catalytic effect of iodide ions on the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide by visual comparison, and to understand the role of catalysts in uniform aqueous reactions.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTwo clear glass beakers (100–150 mL), hydrogen peroxide solution (approximately 3%, colorless), potassium iodide (solid or concentrated aqueous solution), glass stirring rods or gentle swirling by hand, lab bench, camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, dry clear beakers side by side on the lab bench. Put on safety goggles. Pour equal volumes of colorless hydrogen peroxide into each beaker.2. Control Setup: Label the left beaker as experimental and the right beaker as control. Do not add any substance to the right beaker.3. Core Operation: Add a small, equal amount of potassium iodide to the left beaker only.4. Mixing: Gently swirl both beakers in the same manner to ensure comparable conditions.5. Recording: Fix the camera focus and position, and record the reaction using time-lapse photography.6. Completion: After clear differences are observed, stop recording and allow the solutions to stand. Dispose of solutions according to laboratory waste guidelines and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers contain colorless, transparent hydrogen peroxide with no visible bubbles.2. Summary of Experimental PrincipleHydrogen peroxide decomposes into water and oxygen, but the reaction is slow under normal conditions. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Comparison of Refractive Indices of Water and OilI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Refractive Indices of Different Media (Water vs Oil)Subject: Natural Science – PhysicsObjective: To observe the refraction of light in different transparent media by comparing the apparent bending of the same wooden stick in water and edible oil, and to understand that different media have different refractive indices.II. MaterialsTwo identical transparent glasses; clear water; edible oil; one small straight wooden stick (e.g., chopstick or skewer).III. Experimental Procedure1. Place the two identical empty glasses side by side on a flat table.2. Pour clear water into the first glass until it is about two-thirds full.3. Pour edible oil into the second glass to the same height as the water.4. Take the same wooden stick and insert it vertically into the glass with water.5. Observe the stick from the side at the level of the liquid surface.6. Remove the stick and insert it vertically into the glass with oil.7. Observe again from the same side angle and compare the appearance of the stick.IV. Observation of Phenomena1. In air, the wooden stick appears straight.2. When inserted into water, the stick appears bent or displaced at the water surface.3. When inserted into oil, the stick also appears bent at the oil surface, and the bending is more obvious than in water.V. Experimental PrincipleLight changes speed and direction when it passes from one medium to another, a phenomenon called refraction. Water and oil have different refractive indices, and oil has a higher refractive index than water. Therefore, light rays bend more strongly when passing between air and oil than between air and water, making the wooden stick appear more bent in oil than in water.
