manual: Water Hardness Detection (Soap Bubble Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Water Hardness Detection Using the Soap Bubble Method2. Subject: Natural Science – Environmental Science3. Experiment Objective: To distinguish hard water from soft water by comparing the amount of foam produced after adding soap solution, and to understand the relationship between water hardness and soap lather formation.II. Experimental Equipment and Materials1. Test tubes: 2 clean, dry test tubes of the same size (labeled A and B)2. Test tube rack3. Dropper4. Soap solution (dilute, prepared in advance)5. Hard water sample6. Soft water sampleIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean test tubes on the test tube rack and label them A and B.2. Adding water samples: Pour an equal volume (about one-third of the test tube) of hard water into test tube A. Pour the same volume of soft water into test tube B.3. Adding soap solution: Use a dropper to add exactly 2 drops of soap solution into test tube A, then add exactly 2 drops of soap solution into test tube B.4. Shaking: Seal the mouths of both test tubes with your fingers or stoppers and shake them gently and equally for about 5–10 seconds.5. Observation: Place the test tubes back on the rack and observe the amount and persistence of bubbles or foam in each test tube.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Test tube A (hard water): Very few bubbles are formed, or the bubbles disappear quickly; the foam layer is thin or almost absent.2. Test tube B (soft water): A large number of bubbles are formed; the foam layer is thick and remains for a longer time.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleHard water contains higher concentrations of calcium and magnesium ions. These ions react with soap to form insoluble substances, reducing the amount of soap available to form bubbles. As a result, hard water produces little foam. Soft water contains few or no such ions, so soap can easily form stable bubbles. Therefore, the amount of foam produced after shaking with soap solution can be used to distinguish hard water from soft water.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both test tubes contain equal volumes of water for fair comparison.2. Add the same number of soap solution drops to each test tube.3. Shake both test tubes with similar force and duration.4. Use clean test tubes to avoid interference from residual substances.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Distinguishing hard water from soft water using the soap bubble method. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: hard water contains calcium/magnesium ions that inhibit soap lather, while soft water allows stable foam formation; equal soap quantity and shaking produce comparable conditions.Phased storyline: (1) Initial setup: two clearly labeled test tubes with equal volumes of water. (2) Intervention: exactly two drops of soap solution added to each tube. (3) Action: both tubes are shaken for a short, equal duration. (4) Outcome: foam forms—sparse and short-lived in hard water, abundant and persistent in soft water. Visibility constraints: foam height and persistence must be clearly visible after shaking, and the comparison between tubes should be shown side by side for direct verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Hydrogen Peroxide Decomposition With and Without a CatalystI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Decomposition of Hydrogen Peroxide With and Without a Catalyst2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To compare the rate of hydrogen peroxide decomposition with and without a solid catalyst by observing oxygen production and balloon inflation, and to understand the role of catalysts in chemical reactions.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical clear flasks, hydrogen peroxide solution (same concentration and volume for both flasks), two identical balloons, solid catalyst (e.g., manganese dioxide), spatula, tray or bench mat, safety goggles, fixed camera or phone for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear flasks side by side on a stable surface. Ensure they are clean and dry. Put on safety goggles.2. Reagent Addition: Pour equal volumes of hydrogen peroxide into each flask, keeping liquid levels the same.3. Balloon Setup: Stretch a balloon and securely fit it over the mouth of each flask without allowing air to escape.4. Camera Setup: Position the camera facing both flasks. Fix the focus and framing so both flasks and balloons remain fully visible. Start recording or time-lapse capture.5. Catalyst Addition (Core Operation): Using a spatula, carefully add a small amount of solid catalyst into the left flask only. Do not disturb the right flask.6. Observation Stage: Leave both flasks undisturbed and continue recording as the reaction proceeds.7. Completion: After observation, stop recording, remove balloons carefully, and dispose of chemicals according to safety rules.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both flasks contain clear, colorless hydrogen peroxide; balloons are flat.2. After Catalyst Addition: The left flask rapidly produces many bubbles; gas rises and inflates the balloon. Comparison Result: The balloon on the left flask inflates significantly faster and larger than the one on the right.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleHydrogen peroxide decomposes into water and oxygen gas. The solid catalyst lowers the activation energy of the reaction, greatly increasing the reaction rate without being consumed. Therefore, oxygen is produced much faster in the catalyzed flask, inflating the balloon.Core reaction equation: 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2↑VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use identical flasks, equal solution volumes, and identical balloons to ensure fair comparison.2. Add the catalyst to one flask only and avoid shaking either flask.3. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Capillary Phenomenon Experiment (Different Pipe Diameters)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Capillary Phenomenon Experiment (Different Pipe Diameters)2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics3. Experiment Objective: By inserting three glass capillary tubes of different diameters into red-colored water at the same time, observe and compare the rise height of water in each tube, and understand the relationship between capillary rise height and tube diameter.II. Experimental EquipmentGlass capillary tubes of three different inner diameters (one thin, one medium, one thick), beaker (1), red water (water mixed with red dye for easy observation), tube holder or rubber stopper (optional, for fixing tubes), paper towel.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Pour red water into the beaker until it reaches about half the beaker’s height. Place the beaker on a stable horizontal surface.2. Arrangement of Tubes: Select three clean and dry glass capillary tubes with clearly different inner diameters. Align the tubes vertically side by side, keeping their lower ends at the same horizontal level.3. Core Operation: Simultaneously insert the lower ends of the three capillary tubes into the red water, ensuring that all tube ends are submerged to the same depth and remain vertical.4. Observation: Keep the tubes still and observe the water level rising inside each tube.5. Completion: After the water levels stabilize, remove the tubes from the water, place them on a paper towel, and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before insertion, the water level inside all three capillary tubes is the same as the water level in the beaker.2. After Insertion: Red water rises inside all three tubes, but to different heights.3. Comparative Result: The thinnest capillary tube shows the highest water rise; the medium tube shows a moderate rise; the thickest tube shows the lowest rise.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe experiment demonstrates the capillary phenomenon. Due to surface tension and the interaction between water molecules and the glass wall (adhesion), water rises in narrow tubes. The height of capillary rise is inversely proportional to the inner diameter of the tube: the smaller the diameter, the greater the upward force from surface tension relative to gravity, resulting in a higher water column. Therefore, thinner capillary tubes produce higher water levels than thicker ones.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the capillary tubes are clean and dry before the experiment to avoid affecting water rise.2. Insert all tubes into the water simultaneously and to the same depth to ensure a fair comparison.3. Keep the tubes vertical and stable during observation to avoid measurement errors.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Capillary phenomenon in physics, focusing on the inverse relationship between capillary tube diameter and liquid rise height. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: water wets glass; surface tension and adhesion cause upward force; gravity limits the final height.Phased storyline: (1) Initial setup phase – three vertical glass capillary tubes of different diameters are aligned and placed above a beaker of red water; water levels are equal to the beaker. (2) Insertion phase – the three tubes are inserted simultaneously into the red water to the same depth. (3) Rising phase – red water climbs upward inside each tube. (4) Stabilization phase – water levels stop rising, showing a clear height difference: thinnest tube highest, thickest lowest. Visibility constraints: tube diameters, red water color, and final water level differences must be clearly visible in the same frame for comparison.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Zinc Metal Placed in Copper Sulfate SolutionSubject: Natural Science - ChemistryExperiment Objective: To observe the displacement reaction between zinc and copper sulfate through color change of the solution and copper deposition, and to demonstrate the process using a fixed camera for time-lapse observation.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Gently Pressing a Floating Ping-Pong Ball into Water and Releasing ItI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Gently Pressing a Floating Ping-Pong Ball into Water and Releasing It2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics3. Experiment Objective: To observe and verify that a ping-pong ball floats due to buoyancy, and that when pressed into water and released, it immediately floats back up and recovers its floating state.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent container (such as a clear glass bowl or beaker), clean water, one dry ping-pong ball, human hand (for pressing), camera or fixed recording device.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the transparent container on a stable surface and fill it with clean water to about two-thirds of its height. Ensure the water is still and clear.2. Initial State Setup: Gently place a dry ping-pong ball on the water surface and confirm that it floats steadily without external disturbance.3. Core Operation: Use one hand to gently press the ping-pong ball straight downward into the water. Keep the motion slow and controlled so the ball is submerged but not released yet.4. Release: Remove the hand smoothly and completely, allowing the ping-pong ball to move freely.5. Recording Requirement: Keep the camera fixed throughout the process, clearly showing the ball from pressing to release and its subsequent motion.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The ping-pong ball floats on the water surface, with part of the ball above the water.2. During Pressing: As the ball is pressed downward, it becomes more submerged, and resistance from the water can be observed.3. After Release: Once the hand is removed, the ping-pong ball immediately moves upward and quickly returns to the water surface, restoring its floating state.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates the principle of buoyancy. A ping-pong ball has a lower average density than water, so it experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the displaced water. When the ball is pressed into the water, the displaced water volume increases, increasing the buoyant force. Upon release, the buoyant force exceeds the ball’s weight, causing it to rise rapidly until it reaches a stable floating position where buoyant force and gravity are balanced.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Time-lapse Microscopy of an Animal Cell Undergoing Mitosis and CytokinesisI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Time-lapse Microscopy of an Animal Cell Undergoing Mitosis and Cytokinesis2. Subject: Natural Science – Cell & Developmental Biology3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the dynamic process of mitosis and cytokinesis in a single cultured mammalian cell using time-lapse microscopy, identify the key stages of mitosis, and relate observed morphological changes to underlying cellular mechanisms.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsInverted phase-contrast or fluorescence microscope with time-lapse imaging function, live-cell imaging chamber with temperature (37°C) and CO₂ (5%) control, cultured mammalian cells (e.g., HeLa or NIH/3T3 cells) grown on glass-bottom culture dishes, cell culture medium suitable for live imaging, optional fluorescent markers (e.g., DNA stain such as Hoechst or H2B-GFP cells), computer with image acquisition and analysis software.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Culture mammalian cells on a glass-bottom dish until they reach appropriate density (50–70% confluence). Replace growth medium with fresh, pre-warmed live-cell imaging medium. If fluorescent observation is required, ensure cells express or are stained with appropriate non-toxic markers.2. Microscope Setup: Turn on the microscope, camera, and environmental control system. Set temperature to 37°C and CO₂ to 5%. Select an objective lens (20× or 40×) suitable for observing single cells. Adjust focus and illumination to clearly visualize cell boundaries and nucleus.3. Field Selection: Identify a healthy single cell that is in interphase and well isolated from neighboring cells. Center this cell in the field of view and lock the stage position.4. Time-lapse Acquisition: Configure the time-lapse settings (e.g., one image every 2–5 minutes). Begin continuous image acquisition and allow imaging to proceed through mitosis into cytokinesis.5. Completion and Data Saving: Stop acquisition after two daughter cells are clearly separated. Save the image sequence or compiled video. Shut down the microscope following standard procedures.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Interphase: The cell appears flattened with an intact nuclear envelope; chromatin is diffuse.2. Prophase: Chromatin gradually condenses into visible chromosomes; the nucleus becomes more rounded.3. Metaphase: Condensed chromosomes align at the cell equatorial plane, forming the metaphase plate.4. Anaphase: Sister chromatids separate and move toward opposite poles of the cell.5. Telophase: Chromosomes decondense; two new nuclei form at opposite ends.6. Cytokinesis: A cleavage furrow forms at the cell center, deepens, and ultimately divides the cytoplasm into two independent daughter cells.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on the principle of live-cell time-lapse microscopy, which allows continuous observation of dynamic biological processes. Mitosis is the process by which duplicated chromosomes are equally segregated into two daughter nuclei, while cytokinesis completes cell division by physically separating the cytoplasm. Time-lapse imaging makes it possible to correlate changes in cell morphology (chromosome condensation, alignment, segregation, and cleavage furrow formation) with the sequential stages of the cell cycle, providing direct visual evidence of the mechanisms of cell division.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure sterile conditions to maintain cell viability, minimize light exposure to reduce phototoxicity, maintain stable environmental conditions, and avoid mechanical disturbances during imaging.

Phased storyline: (1) Interphase cell with intact nucleus; (2) chromosome condensation and cell rounding; (3) metaphase alignment at equator; (4) anaphase separation toward poles; (5) reformation of two nuclei; (6) cleavage furrow ingression and final separation into two daughter cells. Visibility constraints: stable microscopic field, consistent magnification, and clear contrast to verify chromosome and cell boundary changes.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Laser Pointer vs LED Flashlight on a Rough WallI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Laser Pointer vs LED Flashlight Producing Speckle and Interference on a Rough Wall2. Subject: Physics – Optics3. Experiment Objective: To compare the optical phenomena produced by coherent laser light and incoherent LED light when reflected from a rough surface, and to understand the roles of coherence and interference through visual observation and time-lapse recording.II. Experimental EquipmentRed laser pointer (continuous mode), white LED flashlight, rough wall or matte surface (e.g., painted concrete or plaster), camera or smartphone with manual focus and time-lapse function, tripod or stable mount for the camera, dark or dimly lit room, optional tape or stand to fix light positions.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Darken the room to reduce ambient light. Place the camera on a tripod facing the rough wall. Manually set and fix the camera focus on the wall surface and enable time-lapse or continuous recording.2. Arrangement of Light Sources: Hold or mount the red laser pointer and the white LED flashlight side by side, aiming both at nearby spots on the same rough wall. Ensure the wall and camera remain fixed throughout the experiment.3. Core Operation: Turn on both light sources. Gently wiggle the laser pointer for several seconds while keeping the flashlight relatively steady, then gently wiggle the flashlight as well. Maintain small, slow motions without changing the camera position.4. Recording: Allow the camera to record the changing light patterns on the wall during the wiggling motions.5. Completion: Turn off both light sources, stop recording, and restore normal room lighting.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The laser spot appears as a grainy, mottled pattern (speckle), while the LED flashlight produces a smooth, uniform bright patch.2. During Wiggling: When the laser pointer is gently wiggled, the speckle pattern rapidly changes and appears to shimmer or rearrange. When the LED flashlight is wiggled, the illuminated area moves smoothly without distinct speckle changes.3. Comparison: Over time-lapse playback, the laser illumination shows high-contrast, rapidly varying interference patterns, whereas the LED illumination remains relatively even and stable.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Laser Light Principle: Laser light is highly coherent, meaning the light waves have a fixed phase relationship. When reflected from a rough wall, many scattered waves interfere with each other, producing a speckle pattern. Motion changes the interference conditions, causing the speckle to change.2. LED Light Principle: LED light is incoherent with a broad spectrum and random phases. Scattered waves do not form stable interference patterns, so no clear speckle is observed.3. Core Conclusion: The presence or absence of visible speckle and interference directly demonstrates the role of coherence in optical interference phenomena.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Optical coherence and interference from rough-surface scattering. Minimum assumptions: a fixed camera and wall, one coherent red laser source, one incoherent white LED source, and a dim environment. Phased storyline: (1) Setup phase shows dim room, fixed camera, rough wall, and both light sources aimed side by side; (2) Action phase shows gentle wiggling of laser and LED; (3) Phenomenon phase reveals dynamic speckle for the laser and smooth illumination for the LED; (4) Comparison phase emphasizes causal contrast due to coherence differences. Visibility constraints: speckle graininess must be visible on the wall, colors must be distinguishable, and camera perspective must remain fixed to verify causal relationships.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Heat-Inactivated Yeast vs Live Yeast Fermentation in Sugar SolutionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Fermentation in Heat-Inactivated Yeast and Live Yeast2. Subject: Natural Science – Microbiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that live yeast can ferment sugar to produce gas, while heat-inactivated yeast cannot; to understand the role of living microorganisms in fermentation through direct visual comparison.II. Experimental EquipmentClear plastic or glass bottles (2, identical), granulated sugar, warm water (about 35–40°C), active dry yeast, heat-resistant container for boiling yeast, stove or hot plate, thermometer (optional), balloons (2, identical), measuring spoon, labels or marker, camera or phone with tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation of Sugar Solution: Add equal amounts of warm water to both clear bottles. Add the same amount of sugar to each bottle and swirl until fully dissolved.2. Preparation of Yeast:   (1) Live yeast: Place a measured amount of active dry yeast aside for direct use.   (2) Heat-inactivated yeast: Add the same amount of yeast to boiling water and boil for several minutes to kill the yeast. Allow it to cool to room temperature.3. Addition of Yeast: Pour the cooled, boiled yeast into the left bottle and the live yeast into the right bottle. Gently swirl both bottles to mix.4. Balloon Installation: Stretch identical balloons over the mouths of both bottles, ensuring an airtight seal.5. Observation Setup: Place both bottles side by side in a warm environment. Fix the camera focus and position, and start time-lapse recording.6. Observation Period: Leave the setup undisturbed while recording the changes over time.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both bottles contain clear sugar-water with yeast; balloons are flat and limp.2. Over Time: In the bottle with live yeast, bubbles form in the liquid and the balloon gradually inflates.3. Comparison Result: In the bottle with heat-inactivated yeast, few or no bubbles appear, and the balloon remains flat or shows minimal change.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesYeast is a living microorganism capable of fermentation. In the presence of sugar and suitable warmth, live yeast breaks down sugar to release energy, producing carbon dioxide gas as a byproduct. The gas accumulates and inflates the balloon. Heat-inactivated yeast is no longer alive, so it cannot carry out fermentation, and little or no gas is produced. This experiment demonstrates that fermentation depends on the metabolic activity of living yeast cells.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the boiled yeast is cooled before use; keep all quantities equal for fair comparison; do not seal bottles without balloons; maintain warmth but avoid excessive heat.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Visualization of the Standard Normal Distribution (μ=0, σ=1)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visualization of the Standard Normal Distribution N(0,1)2. Subject: Mathematics – Probability and Statistics3. Experiment Objective: To visually understand the shape, symmetry, mean, and standard deviation of the standard normal distribution by constructing its graph on a Cartesian coordinate system.II. Experimental Materials and ToolsWhite background (paper or digital canvas), Cartesian coordinate grid, plotting tool or software, color markers or digital colors (red, blue, green, yellow).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Set a white background and draw a Cartesian coordinate system. Mark the x-axis range from -3 to 3 and the y-axis range from 0 to 0.4.2. Axis Labeling: Clearly label the x-axis and y-axis with appropriate scales.3. Core Operation – Curve Drawing: Plot the standard normal distribution curve using the probability density function. Draw a smooth red bell-shaped curve that is highest at x=0 and decreases symmetrically toward x=±3.4. Mean Marking: Draw a blue dashed vertical line at x=0 to indicate the mean μ=0.5. Standard Deviation Marking: Draw green dashed vertical lines at x=1 and x=-1 to represent ±1σ.6. Annotation: Add yellow text near the curve reading N(0,1) or (μ=0, σ=1).IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The curve appears as a smooth bell shape.2. The graph is perfectly symmetrical about the y-axis.3. The highest point (peak) of the curve occurs at x=0.4. The dashed lines at ±1 divide the curve evenly around the mean.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe standard normal distribution is a continuous probability distribution with mean μ=0 and standard deviation σ=1. Its probability density function is symmetric about the mean, and the maximum probability density occurs at the mean. The parameters μ and σ determine the center and spread of the distribution, respectively. This visualization demonstrates how ±1σ represents one standard deviation from the mean and how symmetry reflects equal probabilities on both sides of μ.VI. NotesEnsure consistent scales and accurate alignment of dashed lines to correctly reflect statistical meaning.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Standard normal distribution N(0,1) and its graphical properties. Minimum assumptions: a 2D Cartesian plane, fixed axes ranges, and understanding that μ sets the center while σ controls spread. Phased storyline: (1) establish white background and coordinate system; (2) draw symmetric red bell curve peaking at x=0; (3) add blue dashed mean line at μ=0; (4) add green dashed ±1σ lines; (5) annotate N(0,1). Visibility constraints: axes, curve color, symmetry, and labeled reference lines must remain clearly visible throughout for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Reaction of Chlorine Water with Sodium BromideI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Reaction of Chlorine Water with Sodium Bromide2. Subject: Natural Science - Chemistry (Inorganic Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the displacement reaction between chlorine and bromide ions, verify the relative reactivity of halogens, and understand the principle of oxidation-reduction reactions through color change and liquid stratification.II. Experimental EquipmentTest tubes (2), test tube rack, dropper, sodium bromide solution (colorless), chlorine water (pale yellow-green), carbon tetrachloride (colorless, immiscible with water), safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean test tubes side by side on a test tube rack and wear safety goggles.2. Add Solutions: Using a dropper, add about 2–3 mL of sodium bromide solution into one test tube.3. Add Chlorine Water: Slowly add a small amount of chlorine water into the sodium bromide solution and gently shake.4. Add Carbon Tetrachloride: Add 1–2 mL of carbon tetrachloride to the test tube and allow it to stand until clear stratification forms.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Sodium bromide solution is colorless and transparent.2. After Adding Chlorine Water: The solution gradually turns yellow-brown due to the formation of bromine.3. After Adding Carbon Tetrachloride: The mixture separates into two layers; the lower carbon tetrachloride layer shows a clear orange-brown color, while the upper aqueous layer becomes lighter in color.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleChlorine is more reactive than bromine and can oxidize bromide ions to bromine in solution. The reaction is: Cl2 + 2NaBr = 2NaCl + Br2. The generated bromine preferentially dissolves in carbon tetrachloride, an organic solvent, forming an orange-brown lower layer. This demonstrates the displacement reaction and relative activity of halogens.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Perform the experiment in a well-ventilated area.2. Avoid direct contact with chlorine water and carbon tetrachloride.3. Dispose of waste liquids according to laboratory safety rules.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Halogen displacement reaction and solvent extraction of bromine. Minimum assumptions: chlorine water oxidizes bromide ions; bromine has higher solubility in carbon tetrachloride than in water; carbon tetrachloride forms a separate lower layer. Expected phased storyline: (1) Two test tubes positioned side by side with colorless sodium bromide solution visible; (2) chlorine water added causing yellow-brown coloration; (3) carbon tetrachloride added, followed by clear phase separation; (4) orange-brown color concentrates in the lower organic layer. Visibility constraints: transparent glassware, clear color contrast, stable camera angle showing vertical layering.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Tabletop Land–Sea Breeze DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Tabletop Land–Sea Breeze DemonstrationSubject: Natural Science – Atmospheric ScienceExperiment Objective: To simulate and observe land–sea breeze circulation by comparing the different heating rates of sand and water, and to understand how temperature differences cause air movement.II. Experimental EquipmentSand tray (representing land), water tray (representing sea), heat lamp, incense stick with holder, lighter or matches, flat tabletop.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the sand tray and water tray side by side on a flat tabletop, with their long sides adjacent.2. Setup: Position the heat lamp directly above the sand tray at a safe height. Place the incense upright at the boundary between the sand and water trays.3. Initial Observation: Light the incense and observe the smoke when the heat lamp is off. Record the general direction and speed of smoke movement.4. Heating Stage: Turn on the heat lamp to heat the sand tray. Continue observing the incense smoke for several seconds.5. Cooling Stage: Turn off the heat lamp and observe changes in the smoke movement.6. End: Extinguish the incense and turn off all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Lamp Off: Smoke rises slowly and mostly upward, with little horizontal movement.2. Lamp On: Smoke bends and flows horizontally from the water tray toward the sand tray, then rises above the heated sand.3. After Lamp Off: The horizontal movement weakens or may slowly reverse, indicating reduced or opposite airflow.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSand heats and cools faster than water. When heated by the lamp, the air above the sand becomes warmer, expands, and rises, forming a low-pressure area. Cooler, denser air above the water moves toward the sand to replace it, creating a land–sea breeze. When heating stops, the temperature difference decreases, weakening or reversing the airflow. This models natural land–sea breeze circulation driven by differential heating.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Land–sea breeze circulation caused by differential heating of land and water. Minimum assumptions: sand represents land, water represents sea, heat lamp represents sunlight, and incense smoke visualizes air movement. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) initial neutral state with weak vertical smoke rise; (2) lamp on causes sand to heat faster, air above sand rises, and smoke flows horizontally from water toward sand; (3) lamp off reduces temperature contrast, weakening or reversing airflow. Visibility requirements: fixed tabletop perspective, clear view of trays, lamp, and continuous smoke path to verify airflow direction and causal transitions.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Duchenne (Genuine) Smile vs Posed Smile ObservationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Duchenne (Genuine) Smile and Posed Smile2. Subject: Natural Science – Neuroscience3. Experiment Objective: To observe and distinguish facial muscle activation patterns in a genuine (Duchenne) smile versus a posed smile, focusing on eye crinkling and mouth movement under identical visual conditions.II. Experimental Materials1. One human participant.2. One photographer or camera operator.3. Camera or smartphone with fixed focus and exposure.4. Stable, uniform lighting source (unchanged throughout).5. Neutral background.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Seat the participant facing the camera. Adjust framing to include the full face, especially eyes and mouth. Fix lighting and camera position; do not change them during the experiment.2. Genuine Smile Induction: The participant listens to or hears a spontaneous joke or amusing stimulus. Capture the natural smile immediately as it occurs.3. Transition: Allow the participant’s face to return to a neutral expression while maintaining the same posture and framing.4. Posed Smile Induction: The photographer verbally cues the participant to ‘please smile’. Capture the resulting posed smile.5. Completion: Stop recording and save the images or video segments for comparison.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Genuine Smile: The corners of the mouth lift naturally, and the skin around the eyes shows visible crinkling or crow’s feet; the expression appears relaxed and symmetric.2. Posed Smile: The mouth corners lift deliberately, but the eye region shows little or no crinkling; the expression may appear more controlled or tense.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleA Duchenne (genuine) smile involves the coordinated activation of the zygomaticus major muscle (mouth corners) and the orbicularis oculi muscle (around the eyes), typically triggered by genuine positive emotion. A posed smile is usually under voluntary control and primarily activates mouth muscles without full engagement of the eye muscles. Observing eye crinkling and mouth movement under identical conditions allows differentiation between these two types of smiles.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Distinguishing Duchenne (genuine) smiles from posed smiles based on facial muscle activation, assuming basic human facial anatomy and emotional expression mechanisms.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Genuine emotional stimuli trigger involuntary activation of both eye and mouth muscles; posed smiles rely mainly on voluntary mouth movement.Expected Phenomena Storyline: Phase 1 – Neutral face under fixed lighting. Phase 2 – Spontaneous joke leads to immediate, natural smile with eye crinkling and smooth mouth lift. Phase 3 – Return to neutral. Phase 4 – Photographer cue produces a posed smile with clear mouth movement but reduced eye involvement. The camera remains static and frontal to ensure visibility of eyes and mouth for verification.
